title: Feedback that changes the next attempt
objective: Give specific, task-focused feedback before the next attempt, framed with high standards and belief in the person, so the work actually improves.
outcomes: Name one observable piece of work, the standard it is measured against, and the gap, without judging the person.
Open critical feedback by stating the high standard and your confidence that the person can meet it.
Time feedback so it arrives before the next attempt, and agree on a specific check of that attempt.
Adapt the channel, setting and pace to the person while keeping the same standard and the same level of detail for everyone.
Ask for feedback on your own feedback and use what you hear.

evidence.summary: Feedback helps on average, but not reliably. In the largest review of controlled studies, more than a third of feedback interventions lowered performance. Feedback worked best when it kept attention on the task and told people how to improve. It worked worst when it praised, discouraged or threatened the person's sense of self. Trust shapes whether accurate criticism is used: in field experiments with adolescents, one sentence naming high standards and belief in the student changed who revised their work. Workplace evidence shows givers soften or delay hard feedback, and some groups get kinder but less useful feedback. Limits: much of the strongest evidence comes from schools and labs, and there is little research on direct versus indirect delivery across cultures.

findings.claim: Feedback improved performance on average (d = 0.41), but over 38% of effects were negative, and positive versus negative sign did not explain which.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 607 effect sizes from 131 controlled studies, 12,652 participants; mostly lab and education tasks. 1996.

findings.claim: Feedback that included praise had almost no effect (d = 0.09 vs 0.34), discouraging feedback hurt (d = -0.14), and feedback high in threat to self-esteem barely helped (d = 0.08 vs 0.47).
findings.detail: Moderator analyses in the same meta-analysis after all exclusions; the authors conclude effectiveness drops as attention moves from the task to the self. 1996.

findings.claim: High-information feedback, which says what was right or wrong and how to improve, had a large effect (d = 0.99); simple reward or punishment had a small one (d = 0.24).
findings.detail: Random-effects meta-analysis of 435 studies and about 61,000 participants in education; overall d = 0.48 after removing outliers. 2020.

findings.claim: Among low-trust African American students, 0% revised an essay after critical comments with a neutral note, compared with 82% when the note named high standards and belief in the student.
findings.detail: Double-blind randomized field experiment, 44 seventh graders (22 African American, 22 White), White teachers; across all African American students, 71% vs 17% adjusted (raw 64% vs 27%). Two further experiments replicated the pattern. 2014.

findings.claim: Criticism paired with high standards and assurance of ability led Black students to respond as positively as White students; praise or high standards alone did not.
findings.detail: Two lab experiments with Black and White university students receiving critical essay feedback from a White reviewer. 1999.

findings.claim: People inflated their own earlier, gender-blind evaluations when giving feedback to a woman, and gave her more positive comments, while feedback to a man matched his scores.
findings.detail: Two experiments: 182 online participants and 66 university students. 2021 (online 2020).

findings.claim: Only 2.6% of people told a stranger about food or lipstick on their face, and across five experiments givers underestimated how much others wanted constructive feedback.
findings.detail: Pilot field study plus five experiments, N = 1,984; imagining the recipient's position closed the gap. 2022.

findings.claim: Audit and feedback improved health professionals' practice by a median 4.3 percentage points, with larger effects when a supervisor or colleague gave it, more than once, spoken and written, with targets and an action plan.
findings.detail: Cochrane systematic review of 140 randomized trials; 49 lower-risk studies for this estimate. 2012.

findings.claim: In child welfare, social service and mental health settings, supervisors' task assistance had the strongest link to good worker outcomes; effects were moderate (r about .30 to .40).
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 27 studies, 10,867 workers; correlational; worker outcomes, not client outcomes. 2009.
findings.source: Mor Barak, Travis, Pyun & Xie, 2009 (review by the Canadian Child Welfare Research Portal)

findings.claim: Supervisors delayed appraisals and feedback meetings longer for moderately low performers and inflated their ratings, more so when they had to deliver feedback in person.
findings.detail: Lab experiment, 64 business students with supervisory experience. 1988.

findings.claim: Frequent feedback was strongly linked to favorable reactions to appraisal (r = .45), and the link was stronger when performance standards were clear.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 35 studies, 39 samples, 10,672 responses; outcome is reactions, not measured performance. 2017 conference paper.

findings.claim: Employees who sought feedback about their own shortcomings had higher supervisor-rated job performance; those who sought only praise had lower ratings.
findings.detail: Field studies in two companies, 210 and 227 employees, three-month lag. 2017.

findings.claim: Improvement after 360-degree feedback was small (corrected d = 0.15 for direct-report ratings); managers who discussed their results with direct reports improved more.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 24 longitudinal studies; discussion finding from a five-year study of 252 managers reviewed in the paper. 2005.

findings.claim: In classroom research, praise had one of the smallest average effects (0.14), and the authors argue feedback about the self as a person is the least effective kind.
findings.detail: Review built on a synthesis of 12 meta-analyses, 196 studies and 6,972 effect sizes in schools. 2007.

findings.claim: Praising fifth graders for intelligence rather than effort reduced persistence and performance after failure, but a close replication with 624 children did not find this harm on most measures.
findings.detail: Six experiments with fifth graders (1998); three replication studies with Chinese children aged 9 to 13 (2019). Neither involved adults.

findings.claim: Employees whose managers were randomly assigned to feedforward training, and who received a feedforward interview, were rated by peers as performing significantly better four months later.
findings.detail: Randomized field experiment in one Canadian firm: 25 managers, 70 feedforward and 75 standard-appraisal employees (Budworth, Latham & Manroop, 2015), as summarized by CIPD. 2016.

findings.claim: 113 White teachers gave more praise and less criticism to the same weak essay when told the writer was a Black or Latino student than when told the writer was White.
findings.detail: Experiment with middle and high school teachers in two public school districts; for the Black-student condition, the bias appeared only when teachers lacked school social support. 2012.
findings.source: Harber et al., 2012 (Rutgers University news release)

findings.claim: In one law firm, women received more positive words in written evaluations but lower numeric ratings than men, and their words did not track their numbers.
findings.detail: Evaluations of more than 230 junior attorneys, about 35% women. 2012.

findings.claim: At one technology company, men's critical feedback was more often specific and developmental; managers softened criticism of women and then gave ratings that did not match their comments.
findings.detail: Analysis of written reviews and ratings at a Fortune 500 technology company, American Sociological Review; sample size not confirmed. 2020.
findings.source: Correll, Weisshaar, Wynn & Wehner, 2020 (Stanford GSB summary)

findings.claim: Ratings collected for administrative decisions were about one-third of a standard deviation more lenient than ratings collected for research or development.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 22 studies, total N = 57,775; larger in field settings with practicing managers. 1997.

findings.claim: Managers who sought negative feedback were rated as more effective by superiors, peers and direct reports; seeking positive feedback lowered those ratings.
findings.detail: Field study of 387 managers; the outcome was reputational effectiveness, not measured output (as described by Gong et al., 2017). 1991.

findings.claim: People are reluctant to pass on bad news, a pattern researchers named the mum effect.
findings.detail: Rosen & Tesser, Sociometry, 1970; lab experiment, summarized by The Decision Lab.

findings.claim: American newcomers reported more direct feedback inquiry than newcomers in Hong Kong, a difference the authors link to self-assertiveness and power distance.
findings.detail: Comparative survey study of newcomers; sample size not confirmed. Evidence on giving feedback across cultures is thin. 2004.

findings.claim: Predicted national differences in feedback preferences held for United States and Japanese respondents, but Chinese respondents consistently departed from the predictions.
findings.detail: Comparative survey study in three countries, Journal of International Business Studies; sample size not confirmed. 1997.

counterintuitive.headline: More than a third of feedback made the next attempt worse.
counterintuitive.text: Most supervisors assume feedback helps, and that the only risk is being too harsh. Kluger and DeNisi's 1996 meta-analysis of 607 effects found that over 38% were negative. Whether the message was positive or negative did not explain it. What mattered was where it sent attention. Feedback about the task and how to improve it helped. Feedback that praised, discouraged or threatened the person's sense of self helped little or hurt. Feedback that included praise had almost no effect. So a warm compliment can blunt a message as surely as a harsh one can.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.text: Feedback is information about a piece of work, given so the next attempt is better. That sounds simple, and it often fails. In the largest review of controlled studies, more than a third of feedback interventions lowered performance. The difference was not whether the message was positive or negative. It was where the message sent the person's attention. Feedback that kept attention on the task, and on how to improve it, helped. Feedback that turned attention to the person, through praise, discouragement or a threat to their sense of self, helped little or hurt.

sections.title: What that means for you
sections.text: Talk about the work, not the worker. "You're a strong writer" and "You need to be more professional" are both about the person. Neither tells someone what to change. Instead, point to one thing you saw, the standard it is measured against, and what happened as a result. Then say what the next attempt should do differently. Detailed, how-to-improve feedback had the largest effects in the research. Simple approval or disapproval had small ones.

sections.title: Say why you are giving it
sections.text: People act on criticism when they trust why it is given. In field experiments with seventh graders, a single sentence attached to teachers' comments changed who revised their essays. It read: "I'm giving you these comments because I have very high expectations and I know that you can reach them." The effect was largest for students who had the least reason to trust the school. No workplace trial has tested that note, but the reason behind it carries over. Name the standard and your confidence in the person.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: Before the next attempt, have a short conversation that covers four things. The standard, and that you believe the person can meet it. One specific example from the work. What the example caused. What to try next time, and when you will look at it together. Then follow through on that check. Feedback that arrives after the next attempt is already finished cannot change it.

sections.title: Why feedback backfires
sections.text:
Kluger and DeNisi reviewed 607 feedback effects from controlled studies. The average effect was positive and moderate. Yet over 38% of the effects were negative, far more than chance would produce. Their explanation is about attention. Feedback can point attention at the details of the task, at the task as a whole, or at the self. The closer it moves to the self, the less it helps. Feedback containing praise had almost no effect. Discouraging feedback lowered performance. Feedback rated high in threat to self-esteem barely helped. Feedback that showed the correct solution, or how performance was changing over time, helped more.

This explains a common surprise. A supervisor gives balanced, kind feedback and nothing changes. The kindness was about the person. The useful part was buried.

sections.title: What useful feedback contains
sections.text:
A 2020 meta-analysis of 435 education studies found that the content of feedback mattered most. Feedback that said what was right or wrong and how to improve had a large effect. Simple reward or punishment had a small one. Whether the feedback was spoken, written or digital did not matter.

In DHS work, useful feedback names the work, the standard and the consequence. Compare "Your guidance memo needs work" with this: "The service authorization section says counties 'should consider' the new limit. The policy makes it a requirement. Two county case managers read it as a choice." The second version gives the person something to change. It also keeps the conversation about the memo, not about them.

sections.title: Trust decides whether criticism is used
sections.text:
Accurate criticism is wasted if the person cannot tell why it is being given. Cohen, Steele and Ross gave Black and White university students critical feedback on an essay. With criticism alone, Black students rated the reviewer as more biased and were less motivated. When the criticism came with high standards and an assurance that the student could meet them, both groups responded well. Praise as a buffer did not do this, and neither did high standards alone.

Yeager and colleagues then ran three randomized experiments in real classrooms. In the first, teachers' comments on seventh graders' essays carried one of two notes. One said the comments were just feedback. The other named high standards and the teacher's confidence in the student. Among African American students, revision rates rose from 17% to 71% after statistical adjustment; the raw figures were 27% and 64%. Among African American students with low trust in school, 0% revised with the neutral note and 82% with the wise note. White students revised at high rates either way.

The lesson for supervisors is not a script. It is a reason. When someone may wonder whether criticism reflects your view of them, say plainly that you hold a high standard and believe they can meet it.

sections.title: Time it before the next attempt
sections.text:
Feedback can only change an attempt that has not happened yet. That sounds obvious, but supervisors delay. In a lab study, people acting as supervisors scheduled feedback later for moderately low performers than for high performers, and inflated their ratings. The pressure to deliver feedback in person made the delay longer.

The research does not support a rule that faster is always better. School studies suggest immediate correction helps with simple steps, while a short delay can help with hard, judgment-heavy work. What matters at work is the next attempt. If a revised policy draft is due Friday, feedback on Monday helps. Feedback in the annual review does not.

Frequency matters too, when standards are clear. A meta-analysis of appraisal studies found frequent feedback was strongly linked to employees seeing appraisal as fair and useful, especially when they knew the standards.

sections.title: Applying it in DHS work
sections.text:
Health care offers the closest large evidence base for professional adults. A Cochrane review of 140 trials found audit and feedback improved practice by a median 4.3 percentage points. Effects were larger when a supervisor or colleague gave the feedback, more than once, spoken and written, with a clear target and an action plan.

A meta-analysis of 27 human services studies covered child welfare, social service and mental health. Supervisors' task assistance had the strongest link to good worker outcomes. Feedback is one form of task assistance. It works best as part of helping someone do the work, not as a verdict on them.

For a call-line worker, that might mean listening to one call together and naming the moment the caller lost track of the next step. For a licensing reviewer, it might mean comparing one finding against the rule it cites. In each case, agree on the next attempt and look at it together.

sections.title: Kindness can be the bias
sections.text:
Supervisors worry about being too harsh with people who are different from them. The research points to a quieter problem: being too soft. Jampol and Zayas asked people to grade two weak essays privately, without knowing the writers' gender. When they then gave feedback directly, they inflated their own earlier scores for the woman and gave her more positive comments. The man's feedback matched his scores. In a related study, 113 White teachers graded the same weak essay. They gave more praise and less criticism when told the writer was a Black or Latino student. These are lab and school studies, not DHS workplaces.

Workplace records show a related pattern. In one law firm, women received more positive words in written evaluations, but lower numeric ratings, and their words did not track their numbers. A peer-reviewed study of one technology company found men's critical feedback was more often specific and developmental. Managers softened criticism of women and then gave ratings that did not match the comments.

Softened feedback feels kind. It withholds the information the person needs to grow and to be considered ready for the next assignment. The fix is one standard and one level of detail for everyone.

sections.title: Adapting across cultures without lowering the standard
sections.text:
People differ in how they prefer to receive feedback. Some expect it plainly and immediately. Others expect it privately, in writing, or with time to respond. Research on culture and feedback is thinner than popular books suggest. Most studies look at how people seek feedback, not how it is best given. One study found American newcomers asked for feedback directly more often than newcomers in Hong Kong. The authors linked this to differences in self-assertiveness and power distance. Another found that predicted national patterns held for some countries and not others.

That is a reason for caution. Do not sort people into national or ethnic feedback types. Ask the person what helps them use feedback. Adjust the channel, the setting and the pace. A written summary after a short conversation, or a day to respond, changes delivery without changing the message. What should not change is the standard, the specific example and the next step. Silence, a quick "okay" or a confident answer does not show that someone understood. Check understanding by looking at the next attempt together.

sections.title: Praise: what the evidence does and does not say
sections.text:
Praise is not forbidden. The evidence says praise of the person adds little to a task message and can dilute it. In Kluger and DeNisi's review, feedback containing praise had almost no effect on performance. Hattie and Timperley, reviewing classroom research, argued that praise about the self is the least effective form of feedback.

You may have heard that praising intelligence harms motivation while praising effort helps. That comes from Mueller and Dweck's 1998 studies of fifth graders. A later study of 624 children aged 9 to 13 closely replicated the design and did not find the harm on most measures. Neither study involved adults at work. So do not build your practice on the effort-versus-ability rule.

What holds up is simpler. Recognition works best when it is as specific as criticism. "The table in your briefing let the director compare three counties in one glance" tells someone what to repeat.

sections.title: Feedforward: looking at success to plan the next attempt
sections.text:
Kluger and Nir proposed the feedforward interview as an alternative to backward-looking review. The supervisor asks the employee to describe a time they did their best work, what made it possible, and how to recreate those conditions. One randomized field experiment tested it. In a Canadian business equipment firm, 25 managers were randomly assigned to a few hours of feedforward training or other training. Four months later, peers rated the performance of employees who had a feedforward interview significantly higher than that of employees who had a standard appraisal. Part of the effect ran through perceived fairness.

This is one study in one firm. It is promising, not proven. Feedforward also does not replace naming a gap when there is one. It is a useful opening when someone has been discouraged, and a useful way to plan the next attempt.

sections.title: Why supervisors avoid hard feedback
sections.text:
People are reluctant to deliver bad news. Researchers named this the mum effect in 1970. At work, it shows up as delay, softened ratings and vague comments. A meta-analysis covered 22 studies and 57,775 ratings. Ratings used for pay or promotion decisions were about a third of a standard deviation more lenient than ratings for development. The gap was largest with real managers rating real employees.

Givers also misjudge what recipients want. In five experiments, people consistently underestimated how much others wanted constructive feedback. The more important the feedback, the larger the error. A simple step closed the gap: imagining being in the other person's position. Ask yourself whether you would want to know. Usually you would.

sections.title: Ask for feedback on your own feedback
sections.text:
Leaders who ask for criticism tend to be seen as more effective. In a field study of 387 managers, seeking negative feedback raised superiors', peers' and direct reports' views of the manager's effectiveness. Seeking positive feedback lowered them. Note the limit: that study measured reputation, not output. A later study in two companies found employees who sought feedback about their shortcomings had higher supervisor-rated performance.

Feedback reports alone change little. A meta-analysis of 24 studies found small improvement after 360-degree feedback. Managers who discussed their results with their direct reports improved more. So after a hard conversation, ask: "What in how I gave that feedback helped, and what got in the way?" Then change something visible.

sections.title: Harder situations and limits of the research
sections.text:
Some situations need more than a feedback conversation. A concern may continue after clear feedback and support, or conduct may call for a formal response. Then consult the person or area responsible for human resources and labor relations. Follow the applicable bargaining agreement and DHS policy.

Keep the limits of the evidence in view. The strongest experiments on trust and critical feedback involved adolescents and university students, mostly comparing Black and White students with White evaluators. No workplace trial of the wise-feedback note was found. Evidence for other groups and for differences in disability, age or language is thin, so do not assume an effect for any group. Much of the feedback research comes from schools and labs. The human services evidence is correlational. Use the findings as strong guidance about mechanisms, not as guarantees.

simulation.setup: You are a Human Services Supervisor in the Disability Services Division. A Disability Services Program Consultant on your team, about eight months in the role, drafted guidance for county case managers on a change to service authorization limits. The person responsible for county partner communications flagged that one section reads as a suggestion when policy makes it a requirement. A revised draft is due Friday, and the guidance goes to counties the following week. The consultant's last supervisor described their work as fine. You want the next draft to be right, and you want the consultant to be able to write the next one without you.

steps.situation: It is Monday afternoon. You have read the draft and the note from the person responsible for county partner communications. Three paragraphs are clear and well organized. The authorization section says counties "should consider" the new limit.
steps.question: What do you do first?

choices.label: Send a quick message: "Good start overall. The authorization section needs some tightening before Friday."
choices.feedback: This is fast and friendly, and it leads with praise of the whole. It does not say what is wrong, why it matters or what tightening means. Praise and vague direction were among the weakest forms of feedback in the research. The consultant is likely to adjust wording without fixing the requirement.

choices.label: Book 20 minutes for Tuesday morning. Bring the policy language, the draft section and the communications note.
choices.feedback: This gets feedback in before the next attempt, with the evidence in hand. Comparing the draft to the policy keeps attention on the task. Health care trials found larger effects when a supervisor gave feedback with a clear target and a plan. You now have time to prepare how you will open.

choices.label: Rewrite the authorization section yourself tonight so the Friday deadline is safe.
choices.feedback: The draft will probably be right. The consultant will not learn why it was wrong, and the next guidance may repeat the problem. In human services, supervisors' task assistance is linked to good worker outcomes. Assistance that replaces the worker's attempt removes the learning.

steps.situation: Wednesday, the revised draft arrives. The consultant changed "should consider" to "are encouraged to apply." The section still reads as a choice. The person responsible for county partner communications flags it again.
steps.question: How do you respond now?

choices.label: Meet today. Say the standard is high because counties act on this, and you know the consultant can meet it. Then show the policy line next to the draft line.
choices.feedback: This recovers well. You name the standard and your confidence, then give high-information feedback: the exact gap and the source. The experiments on critical feedback found this pairing, not praise or standards alone, helped people use criticism. There is still time before Friday.

choices.label: Reply in writing: "Still not quite there. Please make it stronger."
choices.feedback: This is honest but still vague, and the repeat may feel like a judgment of the person. Two rounds without specifics can discourage someone. Discouraging feedback lowered performance in the largest review. The consultant now knows the section is wrong without knowing why.

choices.label: Fix the line yourself and tell the consultant it is handled.
choices.feedback: The deadline is safe and the tension ends. The consultant has now had two attempts with no usable information. When the next guidance comes, the same gap is likely. Supervisors often take over when time is short. The cost shows up in the next assignment.

steps.situation: Tuesday morning. The consultant arrives with a notebook and looks tense. You have the policy language and the draft side by side.
steps.question: How do you open the conversation?

choices.label: "First, you are a really strong writer, and I appreciate how hard you work. There is one small thing in the authorization section."
choices.feedback: This is meant to reduce tension. It puts attention on the person first and labels the gap as small when counties will act on it. Feedback containing praise had almost no effect in the largest review. The consultant may hear that the work is basically fine.

choices.label: "I am giving you detailed comments because this guidance has to be exact, and I know you can get it there. Here is the policy line and your line."
choices.feedback: This names the high standard and your confidence, then moves straight to the task. It removes the question of why you are being critical. In field experiments, one sentence like this changed who revised their work, most for those with the least reason to trust. The comparison gives high-information feedback.

choices.label: Walk through every issue you found in the draft, all nine, so nothing is missed.
choices.feedback: This is thorough and well intended. Nine items make the most important one hard to see, and complex tasks benefited least from feedback in the research. The consultant may fix commas and miss the requirement. Lead with the gap that matters most and handle smaller edits in writing.

steps.situation: Wednesday, the consultant sees the rewritten section in the shared draft. They stop by and ask, quietly, "Was something wrong with what I wrote?"
steps.question: What do you say?

choices.label: "No, it was fine. I just tightened it to save time."
choices.feedback: This protects the moment and withholds the truth. The section was not fine, and the consultant will not know what to do differently. Studies show givers soften feedback to protect feelings, and recipients lose information they need. The consultant also may not trust the next "fine."

choices.label: "Yes. I should have talked with you first. Let me show you the policy line next to yours, because the next guidance needs to be exact and I know you can do it."
choices.feedback: This is honest and repairs the shortcut. You own your part, name the standard and your confidence, and give the specific comparison. People underestimate how much others want constructive feedback. The question shows this consultant wants it. Owning the shortcut also models the kind of honesty you are asking for.

choices.label: "County partners need exact language. Read the policy and compare."
choices.feedback: This is accurate and points to the right source. It is also terse after a rewrite done without warning. It may read as a judgment of the person rather than the work. Without stating your confidence, the consultant has to guess why you are critical. In the trust experiments, that guess is where criticism gets discounted.

steps.situation: In the conversation, the consultant says little. They nod, say "Okay, I'll fix it," and add, "My last supervisor never raised this." You cannot tell whether the point landed.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Take the "okay" as agreement and end the meeting so it does not get awkward.
choices.feedback: Ending feels respectful. Silence and a quick "okay" are not evidence of understanding. The consultant also just told you earlier feedback was softer, so this may feel like a new and confusing standard. Without a check, you will learn on Friday whether it landed.

choices.label: Ask them to explain back, right now, exactly what they will change.
choices.feedback: Checking understanding is right. Pressing for an immediate explanation can feel like a test, especially to someone who prefers time to think. You may get a rehearsed answer rather than real understanding. The aim is a correct next attempt, not a perfect reply in the room.

choices.label: Say the standard is the same for everyone. Offer a written summary with the policy line, invite questions by tomorrow, and set a 15-minute look at the next draft Thursday.
choices.feedback: This adapts the channel and pace while keeping the standard and the detail. It also names that this is not personal. Health care trials found larger effects when feedback was spoken and written, with a target and a plan. The Thursday check shows understanding through the work itself.

steps.situation: Thursday. The authorization section now states the requirement clearly and cites the policy. One example in it still uses the old limit. The consultant asks, "Is it good now?"
steps.question: How do you close the loop?

choices.label: "Yes, it's great. I'll catch the example myself."
choices.feedback: This rewards real progress and avoids a third round. It also inflates the feedback. Research on gendered and racial patterns in feedback shows that kinder, less accurate feedback withholds what people need. The consultant will not know to check examples next time.

choices.label: Name the specific improvement, point to the one example, then ask: "What in how I gave you feedback this week helped, and what got in the way?"
choices.feedback: This gives specific recognition, names the remaining gap, and asks for feedback on your own feedback. Feedback on how performance is changing helped more in the large review. Managers who discussed feedback on themselves with staff improved more. You also show that criticism is part of good work.

choices.label: Note the improvement and the example in your performance notes for the annual review.
choices.feedback: Documentation has a place. Saving the point for the annual review means it arrives after the next attempt. Supervisors tend to delay feedback for weaker work, and ratings drift upward when they carry consequences. Tell the consultant now, while it can still change Friday's draft.

simulation.debrief: The strongest path did four things the research supports. It gave feedback before the next attempt, while it could still change the result. It kept attention on the task by putting the policy line next to the draft line, which is high-information feedback. It named a high standard and confidence in the consultant, the pairing that helped people use criticism in experiments on trust. And it adapted the channel and pace without lowering the standard. The tempting choices were kind or efficient: a warm message, a quiet rewrite, a quick "it's great." Each protected the moment and withheld information. Over 38% of feedback in the largest review made performance worse, often for reasons like these.

mistakes.mistake: Leading with praise of the person to soften criticism.
mistakes.why: It feels kind and protects the relationship. But it moves attention to the self, and feedback containing praise had almost no effect in the largest review.
mistakes.instead: Open with the standard and your confidence in the person, then go straight to the specific work. Make recognition specific to the work too.

mistakes.mistake: Giving some people softer or vaguer feedback than others.
mistakes.why: Supervisors want to avoid seeming harsh or biased. Studies show people inflate feedback to women and to students of color, which withholds what they need.
mistakes.instead: Use one standard and one level of detail for everyone. Adapt delivery, not content.

mistakes.mistake: Saving feedback for the annual review.
mistakes.why: Waiting feels safer, and supervisors delay most when work is weak. Feedback after the next attempt cannot change it.
mistakes.instead: Give feedback before the next attempt and agree on when you will look at it together.

mistakes.mistake: Giving a verdict instead of information.
mistakes.why: Words like "needs to be more professional" are quick to write. Simple approval or disapproval had small effects; detailed how-to-improve feedback had large ones.
mistakes.instead: Name the work, the standard, the consequence and the next step.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming the person does not want to hear it.
mistakes.why: Givers consistently underestimate how much others want constructive feedback, more so when it matters most.
mistakes.instead: Ask yourself whether you would want to know. Then say it, specifically and privately.

mistakes.mistake: Fixing the work yourself instead of giving feedback.
mistakes.why: Deadlines are real, and rewriting is faster. Task assistance helps workers, but replacing their attempt removes the learning.
mistakes.instead: Show the gap, let the person make the change, and check the result.

jobAid.title: Before-the-next-attempt feedback check
jobAid.use: Use it in the five minutes before any feedback conversation about a piece of work, and again at the follow-up check.
steps: What is the next attempt, and when is it? Plan to talk before then.
What one piece of work will you point to? Bring it or quote it.
What is the standard, and where is it written?
What did the gap cause, or what could it cause?
Open with the standard and your confidence that the person can meet it. Leave out praise of the person.
Ask what helps them use feedback: spoken, written or both, now or after time to think.
Agree on what the next attempt will do differently and when you will look at it together.
At the check, name what improved, name any remaining gap, and ask how your feedback could work better.

media.reason: Feedback has two sides. Hearing how the giver intended a message and how the receiver heard it shows the gap between kind intent and useful information in a way narration cannot.

title: Psychological safety in daily work
objective: Respond to concerns, errors and questions in ways that make the next concern more likely to reach you, while keeping standards high.
outcomes: Respond to a raised error by thanking the person, separating the fact from blame, and naming who will act and by when.
Close the loop by telling the person what changed because they spoke up.
Invite input from the people with the least status in the room before the most senior voices speak.
Ask for errors and doubts directly in routine meetings instead of waiting for them to surface.
Pair safety with clear standards so that candor does not turn into shared shortcuts.

evidence.summary: Psychological safety is a shared belief that a team is safe for interpersonal risk, such as admitting an error or questioning a plan. In a field study of 51 teams, safety predicted learning behavior, and learning behavior predicted performance. A meta-analysis of 136 samples links safety to engagement, satisfaction and commitment, and more moderately to performance. People with less status feel less safe, but inclusive leaders narrow that gap. Most of this evidence is cross-sectional, so cause and effect are not proven. Safety also has a limit: in one study of 126 teams, high safety made it easier for teams already inclined to cut corners to act unethically. Safety works best alongside clear standards.

findings.claim: Team psychological safety predicted team learning behavior, and learning behavior carried its link to observer-rated performance.
findings.detail: Multimethod field study of 51 teams in one manufacturing company; 427 members (86% response) and 135 outside observers; cross-sectional survey plus interviews; 1999.

findings.claim: Lower-status staff felt less safe, and leader inclusiveness narrowed the status gap; safety predicted engagement in improvement work (B = 0.62).
findings.detail: Survey of 1,440 health-care professionals in 23 neonatal intensive care units; cross-sectional; 2006.

findings.claim: Across 136 samples, safety was strongly associated with engagement, satisfaction and commitment, and moderately with task performance; leader and peer support and role clarity were positive correlates.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 136 independent samples, over 22,000 individuals and nearly 5,000 groups, mostly cross-sectional studies; Personnel Psychology 70(1), 2017. Sample figures checked against the abstract on the Old Dominion University repository record. Effect directions also summarized by the federal child welfare workforce center QIC-WD, 2020.

findings.claim: 34 of 40 employees (85%) had at least once felt unable to raise an important issue; fear of being seen negatively (30%) and of damaging relationships (27.5%) were common reasons.
findings.detail: Qualitative interviews with 40 full-time employees; 2003. Figures from a research index summary.

findings.claim: In teams with a utilitarian ethical leaning, high psychological safety made unethical team behavior more likely.
findings.detail: Study of 126 teams; 2011.

findings.claim: Among 227 public employees, psychological safety predicted more voice and lower intention to leave, with voice carrying the link.
findings.detail: Cross-sectional self-report survey of public employees in education, health care and public administration in Hanoi; 2025. Very high path coefficients suggest overlapping measures.

counterintuitive.headline: Safety can make it easier for a team to cut corners together.
counterintuitive.text: Most advice treats psychological safety as purely good. Pearsall and Ellis studied 126 teams and found something less comfortable. When team members already leaned toward judging actions only by their results, high psychological safety made unethical team behavior more likely, not less. Comfort with each other made it easier to agree on a shortcut. Edmondson's own definition already points to the fix. Safety is not permissiveness or constant agreement. It is confidence that you will not be punished for speaking up. In DHS work, that means making it safe to raise a doubt about a shortcut, and keeping the standard itself firm.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.text: Psychological safety is a shared belief on a team that it is safe to take interpersonal risks. Those risks are ordinary. Someone admits an error in a notice. Someone asks a question that might sound basic. Someone says a new procedure will not work for the cases they handle. Each of those moments costs the speaker something, and each one gives the team information it cannot get any other way. In a study of 51 teams, teams with more safety did more of this learning behavior. That learning behavior went with better performance, as judged by the people who received the teams' work.

sections.title: Why people stay quiet
sections.text: Silence is common, even among capable people. In one set of interviews, 34 of 40 employees said they had at least once felt unable to raise an issue they thought was important. The most common reasons were fear of being seen as a complainer and fear of damaging a working relationship. Many also said their own lack of rank held them back. Staff do not decide to speak based on what you say about your door being open. They decide based on what happened the last time someone spoke.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: The next time someone brings you an error or a concern, respond in three steps. First, thank them for the specific thing they raised. Second, separate the fact from blame: say what you will check, not who is at fault. Third, close the loop. Tell them later what changed because they spoke up. That last step answers the question staff are really asking. Is it worth it to tell you?

sections.title: Keep the standard
sections.text: Safety is not the same as being nice or lowering the bar. Edmondson describes it as confidence that the team will not embarrass, reject or punish someone for speaking up. You can hold a high standard and still make it safe to say the standard was missed.

sections.title: Why it matters in public work
sections.text: Public agencies depend on staff noticing problems early, because errors in notices, data or scripts reach the people served at scale. In a survey of 227 public employees in education, health care and public administration, psychological safety went with more speaking up and lower intention to leave. The study was cross-sectional, so it shows a pattern, not proof. It fits what larger studies find in other settings.

sections.title: What the evidence shows
sections.text: Edmondson's 1999 field study is the foundation. She surveyed 427 members of 51 teams in one company and asked outside managers who received each team's work to rate it. Teams with more psychological safety reported more learning behavior: seeking feedback, asking for help, talking about errors and experimenting. Learning behavior, in turn, carried the link between safety and performance. Safety did not improve performance by itself. It mattered because it let people do the uncomfortable things that improve work. A later meta-analysis combined 136 samples covering more than 22,000 people. It found that safety is strongly associated with engagement, job satisfaction and commitment, and more moderately associated with task performance and helping behavior. The federal child welfare workforce center that summarized it notes a key limit: most of these studies measured everything at one time, so they show association, not cause.

sections.title: The mechanism
sections.text: Speaking up has a cost that falls on the speaker now and a benefit that may arrive later for everyone. When people expect embarrassment or a damaged relationship, they discount the benefit and stay quiet. Safety changes that calculation. Leaders have outsized influence, because staff watch the leader's response more closely than anyone else's. In Edmondson's study, team leader coaching and support from the wider organization were both associated with safety, and safety in turn carried their link to learning. In practice, staff learn from small signals. Do you look up from your screen? Was the person who raised the last problem thanked or quietly sidelined? Did the issue go anywhere?

sections.title: Status shapes who feels safe
sections.text: Nembhard and Edmondson surveyed 1,440 health-care professionals in 23 neonatal intensive care units. Physicians felt safer than nurses, and nurses felt safer than respiratory therapists. Where leaders invited and appreciated input, that gap narrowed, and the lowest-status staff gained the most. Safety also predicted engagement in quality-improvement work. In DHS settings, status differences are everywhere. Think of a new eligibility worker and a senior policy specialist, or a contract staff member and a permanent supervisor. The person closest to the problem often holds the least status.

sections.title: Applying it in DHS work
sections.text: Think about where errors and doubts usually surface late in your area. It might be a notice that went to people with the wrong phone number. It might be a data definition that two units read differently. It might be a call-line script that does not match a recent policy change. In each case, someone usually noticed early. Three habits make it more likely that you hear about it in time. First, ask for problems directly and routinely. In a team huddle, ask what is not working this week, then wait through the silence. Second, ask the newest or least senior people first, before senior voices set the frame. Third, when someone raises a concern, separate checking the fact from assigning fault, name who will act and by when, and come back to tell them what happened.

sections.title: A public-sector check
sections.text: A 2025 survey of 227 public employees in education, health care and public administration found that psychological safety went with more speaking up and lower intention to leave. Speaking up carried that link. The study is cross-sectional and self-reported, and its measures overlapped heavily, so treat it as consistent with the broader evidence rather than proof. Evidence from US state human services agencies specifically is thin.

sections.title: What to watch for in yourself
sections.text: Silence is easy to misread from the top. If you rarely hear bad news, treat that as a question about the climate, not as proof that things are fine. Remember that 85% of the employees in one interview study had stayed quiet about something important at least once. A useful test: when was the last time someone told you that a decision of yours was wrong, and what did you do next?

sections.title: A short script for the moment
sections.text: When someone brings you a problem, a few plain sentences do most of the work. Try something like this. Thank you for telling me about the notice dates. Can you show me one example? I want to check the facts before anyone decides what went wrong. I will talk with the person responsible for the template today and let you know by Thursday what I found. Notice what the script does. It thanks the specific act, asks for evidence, separates the fact from blame, names an owner and sets a time. It does not promise that the concern is right, and it does not ask who made the error.

sections.title: What to watch in meetings
sections.text: Meetings show the climate quickly. Notice who speaks first and whose points get picked up. Notice whether anyone raises a problem in the room, or whether problems arrive later in private messages. Notice how senior staff respond when a newer person disagrees with them. In the NICU study, leader inclusiveness narrowed the gap between high- and low-status staff. Inclusiveness in that study meant words and actions that invite and appreciate others' contributions. In a meeting, that can be as simple as asking a quiet person directly and building on what they said.

sections.title: Safety is not comfort
sections.text: Edmondson draws a sharp line between psychological safety and group cohesiveness. Cohesive groups can become less willing to disagree, which is the opposite of what safety is for. She also says safety is not a careless permissiveness and not constant positive feeling. It is confidence that the team will not embarrass, reject or punish someone for speaking up. A team can be warm and unsafe, if warmth depends on never raising a hard point. A team can also be demanding and safe, if people know that admitting an error will lead to fixing it rather than to blame.

sections.title: The limit: shared shortcuts
sections.text: Pearsall and Ellis studied 126 teams. Teams that leaned toward judging actions only by their results were more likely to make unethical decisions. High psychological safety strengthened that pattern. When members trusted each other not to object, it became easier to agree on a shortcut together. This does not mean safety is harmful. It means safety amplifies whatever a team already values. In public programs, where shortcuts can affect eligibility, privacy or program integrity, safety needs a partner: clear standards that everyone knows are not up for quiet negotiation. The practical move is to make it safe to question a shortcut, not to make it comfortable to take one.

sections.title: Limits of the research
sections.text: Several cautions apply. Most studies are cross-sectional, so they cannot show that a leader's behavior caused safety to rise. The federal child welfare workforce summary calls the lack of experiments a significant research need. No meta-analysis has examined turnover directly. Edmondson's key study used one company and 51 teams. The silence interviews involved 40 people, mostly in private industries. The NICU study is from health care, which is close to human services but not the same. Evidence from state government is limited to a few surveys, including one non-US public-sector sample. The overall pattern is consistent across settings, but the size of any effect in your team is unknown.

sections.title: Differential effects
sections.text: The verified difference in who feels safe is professional status. In the NICU study, staff with lower professional status reported less safety, and inclusive leadership narrowed that gap. In the silence interviews, about a third of people named their own lack of experience, tenure or rank as a reason to stay quiet. Do not assume a particular racial, disability or other group feels less safe on your team. No verified finding in this review shows that. What you can do is notice who rarely speaks in meetings, who raises issues only in private, and whose concerns arrive late. Then make it easier for them to speak earlier.

sections.title: Harder situation: the concern is about you
sections.text: The most withheld topic in the silence interviews was concern about a colleague's or supervisor's competence. When the concern is about your own decision, your response teaches the whole team. Thank the person, ask what they saw, and check it. If they are right, say so in front of the people who saw the original decision. If they are wrong, explain your reasoning without signaling that they should not have raised it. Either way, the person should leave knowing it was worth speaking.

sections.title: Harder situation: the concern is wrong or repeated
sections.text: Not every concern is accurate. Responding well does not mean agreeing. It means checking the fact, sharing what you found, and explaining the decision. Sometimes a person raises the same point again after it has been checked. Say clearly what was checked, what was decided and why, and what new information would reopen it. That keeps the door open without turning one issue into a standing argument.

sections.title: Harder situation: safety across boundaries
sections.text: Many DHS problems cross units, counties, contractors or Tribal partners. You cannot create safety in another organization, but you can make your own response safe for people outside your team. A county partner or contract staff member may point out a problem in a DHS process. Route it to the person or area responsible, tell the person who raised it where it went, and follow up. For any matter involving a Tribal Nation, work through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations.

sections.title: Making it routine
sections.text: Safety grows from repeated, small responses more than from announcements. Build simple routines into existing work. Open a weekly huddle by asking what is not working. Ask the least senior person first. Track each concern raised, and report back on what happened to it. When you make an error, name it plainly. Each routine signals the same thing: speaking up here leads somewhere, and the person who speaks is not the problem.

sections.title: When safety meets deadline pressure
sections.text: Deadlines are where safety is tested most. A concern raised the day a batch is due feels like an obstacle, and the pressure to wave it through is real. Edmondson notes that learning behavior consumes time and that, for highly routine work, it can reduce efficiency in the short run. The answer is not to stop listening under pressure. It is to triage quickly. Check whether the concern affects people already served or about to be served. If it does, slow down enough to check. If it does not, say so, set a time to look at it after the deadline, and keep that promise.

sections.title: Knowing whether it is working
sections.text: You do not need surveys or counts to see change. Watch for signals in the work itself. Problems start reaching you earlier, before they reach the call line. Newer staff raise questions in meetings, not only in private. People bring you half-formed doubts, not only finished complaints. Staff correct each other without heat. If none of this is happening after a few months of steady effort, look again at what happens after someone speaks up. That is where the climate is set.

sections.title: Your own safety as a leader
sections.text: Supervisors also need to raise problems upward. If you do not feel safe telling your own manager about an error or a doubt, your team will likely sense it in how you handle their concerns. Model the behavior you want. Raise issues with the person or area responsible clearly and early, and tell your team when you have done so. That shows the same standard applies at every level.

simulation.setup: You are a Human Services Supervisor for an eligibility processing unit. Your unit sends renewal notices to people enrolled in a health care program. A new eligibility worker, three months in the role, stops by your desk late on a Tuesday. A senior team lead is sitting with you, reviewing a deadline. The new worker says something might be wrong with yesterday's batch of notices. What is at stake: people may have received unclear instructions about a renewal deadline, and your unit's response will shape whether this worker raises the next problem.

steps.situation: The new worker says that some notices in yesterday's batch list a response date that does not match the date in the system. They are not sure how many. The senior team lead says, without looking up, that the template was reviewed last month and the worker is probably reading the wrong field.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Thank the worker for raising it, ask them to show you one example now, and tell the team lead you want to look before deciding.
choices.feedback: The worker sees that a concern from the newest person gets checked, not dismissed by status. You learn quickly whether the problem is real. This matches the NICU finding that lower-status staff feel least safe and gain most when leaders invite their input. It costs you ten minutes and the team lead's mild irritation.

choices.label: Tell the worker you will look into it, and return to the deadline review with the team lead.
choices.feedback: This sounds reasonable and protects the deadline. But the worker heard the team lead dismiss them and saw you move on. Without a time or a next step, the message is that the concern is low priority. In the silence interviews, futility was one of the most common reasons people stopped raising issues.

choices.label: Agree with the team lead that the template was reviewed, and suggest the worker double-check which field they are reading.
choices.feedback: It is tempting because the team lead has more experience and the template was reviewed. But you have closed the question without checking a fact. The worker learns that status settles disputes in this unit. Edmondson's teams learned because people could raise errors without being embarrassed. This response does the opposite.

steps.situation: The example is real. About a fifth of the batch shows the wrong date. The team lead now says the fix is easy: correct the template quietly for the next batch and skip any follow-up to people who already received the notice, since most will respond on time anyway.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Fix the template, and also send the issue to the person or area responsible for notices so they can decide on corrections to people already affected. Tell the worker what you are doing.
choices.feedback: You keep the standard: people affected by an error get a decision about a correction, made by the person or area responsible. You also close the loop with the worker. This is the pairing the evidence supports, safety to raise the error plus a firm standard. Pearsall and Ellis found that safety without standards can make shared shortcuts easier.

choices.label: Fix the template and ask the team lead to estimate how many people might miss the deadline before deciding on follow-up.
choices.feedback: Gathering facts is useful, but it delays a decision that belongs to the person or area responsible for notices. It also leaves the shortcut on the table. The worker does not yet know what happened to their concern.

choices.label: Agree to fix the template quietly. Most people will respond on time, and a second notice could confuse them.
choices.feedback: The argument sounds practical, and it avoids extra work. But this is a shared shortcut that affects people's coverage. The team is comfortable agreeing with each other, which is the pattern Pearsall and Ellis found when safety is high and standards are loose. The worker who raised it also learns that problems are buried here.

steps.situation: Two days later, a call-line supervisor tells you that callers are confused about their renewal dates. It is the same issue the new worker raised. The worker has not mentioned it again. In your weekly huddle, they sit quietly at the back.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Go to the worker privately, say plainly that they were right and you should have checked sooner, and ask what else they noticed.
choices.feedback: Naming your own miss repairs the signal you sent. It also turns the worker back into a source of information. Leaders who admit errors show that admitting errors is safe. The cost is some discomfort, and you still need to act on the notices.

choices.label: Fix the problem with the call-line supervisor and the person or area responsible for notices, without going back to the worker.
choices.feedback: The problem gets fixed, which matters most for the people affected. But the worker never learns that their concern was correct. The lesson they keep is that speaking up went nowhere. That is the futility the silence interviews describe.

choices.label: Mention at the huddle that a notice issue came up and remind everyone that your door is always open.
choices.feedback: This feels inclusive, but the worker knows their concern was dismissed. A general invitation does not repair a specific experience. Staff judge safety by what happened last time, not by what a leader says about openness.

steps.situation: A month later, you want your unit to catch problems like this earlier. You have fifteen minutes at the start of each weekly huddle.
steps.question: What routine do you set up?

choices.label: Open each huddle by asking what is not working this week, ask the newest staff first, and report back on what happened to last week's items.
choices.feedback: This builds safety into routine work. Asking the least senior people first narrows the status gap the NICU study found. Reporting back closes the loop, which addresses futility. The evidence is mostly correlational, but these habits target the exact reasons people give for silence.

choices.label: Ask the team leads to collect concerns from their staff and bring them to you.
choices.feedback: This is efficient and respects the structure. But it routes concerns through people with more status, which is where they tend to be softened or filtered. Staff with the least rank, who most often stay quiet, still have no direct path.

choices.label: Set up an anonymous form for concerns so no one has to speak up in front of others.
choices.feedback: Anonymity can help people raise sensitive issues, and it is tempting because it seems to solve fear. But it does not build the shared belief that speaking up in the team is safe. You also cannot close the loop with a specific person. Use it as a supplement, not the main route.

simulation.debrief: The first moment decided most of what followed. When a new worker raised a concern in front of a senior team lead, checking the fact signaled that status does not settle questions here. That matches the NICU finding that lower-status staff feel least safe and gain most from inclusive leaders. When the concern was dismissed, the cost showed up later, as confused callers and a quiet worker. The second decision tested whether safety came with a standard. A quiet fix that skips people already affected is a shared shortcut, the pattern Pearsall and Ellis found can grow when safety is high. The last decision turned single responses into routine. Asking for problems directly, asking the newest people first, and reporting back address the reasons people give for silence: fear of being seen negatively, damaged relationships and futility.

mistakes.mistake: Treating an open-door statement as proof that staff feel safe.
mistakes.why: Leaders mean the invitation sincerely, so it feels like enough. Staff decide based on what happened last time, and 85% of employees in one interview study had stayed quiet about something important.
mistakes.instead: Judge safety by what reaches you and how early. Ask directly for problems, and watch who never raises one.

mistakes.mistake: Fixing the problem but never telling the person who raised it.
mistakes.why: Fixing feels like the real work, and following up feels like a courtesy. But futility is one of the most common reasons people stop speaking up.
mistakes.instead: Close the loop every time. Tell the person what you checked, what changed and who acted.

mistakes.mistake: Letting the most senior voice answer first.
mistakes.why: Senior staff often have the most context, so it seems efficient. But status predicts who feels safe, and early senior opinions frame what others are willing to say.
mistakes.instead: Ask the newest or least senior people first, then invite others to build on or challenge what they said.

mistakes.mistake: Equating safety with harmony or lowering standards.
mistakes.why: Safety is often described in warm terms, so leaders avoid firm expectations. Research shows cohesive groups can disagree less, and high safety can make shared shortcuts easier.
mistakes.instead: Keep standards explicit and firm. Make it safe to say a standard was missed or a shortcut is being considered.

mistakes.mistake: Responding to a concern by first asking who made the error.
mistakes.why: Accountability matters, and finding the source seems like the fastest way to fix things. But blame-first responses teach people that raising an error exposes them or a colleague.
mistakes.instead: Check the fact first, fix the impact, then look at the process that allowed the error. Address individual performance separately and privately if needed.

jobAid.title: When someone raises a concern
jobAid.use: Use it in the moment someone brings you an error, a doubt or a question about a decision, and again when you follow up.
steps: Stop what you are doing and look at the person. Thank them for the specific thing they raised.
Ask them to show you one example or say what they saw.
Separate the fact from blame. Say what you will check, not who is at fault.
Decide who acts. If it belongs to another unit, route it to the person or area responsible.
Hold the standard. If a shortcut is suggested, ask what it would mean for the people affected.
Give a time. Say when you will come back to them.
Close the loop. Tell them what changed because they spoke up, even if the answer is that no change was needed and why.

media.reason: Psychological safety lives in the gap between how a leader sees a response and how the person who spoke up experiences it. Two voices can show both sides of the same moment.

script.speaker: female
script.text: I think my unit is pretty open. I tell people all the time that they can bring me anything. But a renewal notice problem reached me through the call line last week, and someone on my team had noticed it days earlier.

script.speaker: male
script.text: That pattern is common. In one interview study, 34 of 40 employees said they had at least once felt unable to raise something important. The top reasons were fear of looking like a complainer and fear of damaging a relationship.

script.speaker: female
script.text: But I would never punish someone for raising a problem.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Most leaders would say that. The question staff ask is different. What happened the last time someone spoke? Were they thanked? Did the issue go anywhere? Did a senior colleague brush it off while the supervisor watched?

script.speaker: female
script.text: That last one stings. A team lead did dismiss a new worker's question a while back. I did not step in because I trusted the team lead's experience.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Status matters a lot here. A study of 23 neonatal intensive care units found that physicians felt safer speaking up than nurses, and nurses felt safer than respiratory therapists. Where leaders actively invited input, that gap narrowed. The lowest-status staff gained the most.

script.speaker: female
script.text: So the new worker watched me side with the senior voice, and drew a conclusion.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Probably. The good news is that repair is concrete. Go back, say they were right, and ask what else they have noticed. Then build small habits. Ask for problems in every huddle. Ask the newest people first. Report back on what happened to each issue.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Does safety mean I have to soften my standards? My unit handles eligibility. I cannot have people deciding rules are flexible.

script.speaker: male
script.text: No. In fact, a study of 126 teams found that high safety can make it easier for a team to agree on an unethical shortcut, when the team already leans that way. Safety amplifies what a team values. The fix is to make it safe to question a shortcut while keeping the standard itself firm.

script.speaker: female
script.text: So safety and standards work together. People can tell me the standard was missed without fearing blame, but the standard does not move.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Exactly. One caution: most of this research is correlational. It shows these habits go with learning and better work, not that they guarantee it. But they target the exact reasons people give for staying quiet.

prompts: Which recurring meeting will you open with a direct question about what is not working, and starting when?
Who on your team holds the least status and is closest to the work, and how will you invite their view first in the next two weeks?
Which concern raised in the past month has not been closed with the person who raised it, and when will you go back to them?
