title: Working through conflict
objective: Keep disagreements about the work focused on facts and reasoning, stop them from turning personal, and make sure the person who disagreed stays in the decision.
outcomes: Name whether a disagreement is about the work, the process or the relationship, and respond to each differently.
Move a heated discussion back to the content of what was said and the evidence behind it.
Explain the reasoning behind decisions about who does what, and assign work by expertise.
Notice when someone has been left out after disagreeing, and bring them back while their concern can still change the outcome.
Set conflict ground rules with a team before a hard decision, not during it.

evidence.summary: Researchers separate disagreement about the work (task conflict) from personal friction (relationship conflict) and disputes about who does what (process conflict). Relationship and process conflict are reliably linked to worse performance and lower trust. Task conflict is more mixed. A meta-analysis of 116 studies found no overall link between task conflict and performance, a negative link in teams below top management, and a more positive link when it stayed separate from personal friction. How a team handles conflict explained 13% more variance in outcomes than what the conflict was about. Evidence that dissenters get excluded is real but thin. No verified public-sector study was found.

findings.claim: Across 116 studies, task conflict had no overall relationship with group performance (rho = -.01), while relationship conflict (-.16) and process conflict (-.15) were negative.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 8,880 groups; task conflict figure based on 95 effect sizes and 7,201 participants; 2012.

findings.claim: In teams below top management, task conflict was negatively related to performance (rho = -.21); in top management teams it was slightly positive (.09).
findings.detail: Subgroup analysis in the same meta-analysis: 22 and 19 effect sizes; 2012.

findings.claim: All three conflict types were linked to lower trust (task -.45, relationship -.53, process -.59), but only relationship conflict was linked to lower cohesion (-.44 versus .00 for task conflict).
findings.detail: Same meta-analysis, proximal outcomes; 2012.

findings.claim: Task conflict was much more harmful when it traveled with relationship conflict (rho -.35) than when the two were weakly linked (-.10).
findings.detail: Earlier meta-analysis of team conflict; figures as reported in de Wit et al.; 2003.

findings.claim: How teams interact about differences explained an additional 13% of variance in performance and in team attitudes, beyond what the conflict was about.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 45 studies, 3,218 teams; 2013.

findings.claim: Where trust was high, disagreement about the work was less likely to turn into personal conflict, consistent with task debate being misread as a personal attack when trust is low.
findings.detail: Field survey of 70 top management teams; 2000.

findings.claim: Teams that sustained high performance focused on the content of what was said rather than its delivery, explained the reasoning behind work assignments, and assigned work by expertise.
findings.detail: Qualitative study of 57 autonomous teams over time; 2008.

findings.claim: Workplace ostracism was very strongly associated with deviance and strongly with lower performance and well-being; leadership characteristics were its strongest predictors.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of workplace ostracism; direction of some links uncertain; 2020.

findings.claim: Dissent against a majority's ideas stimulated ostracism, while disagreement about the group's process was associated with the dissenter taking a leadership role.
findings.detail: Small-group study; design and sample not reported in the summary; 2014.

findings.claim: An assigned devil's advocate did not prompt the same rethinking as a person who genuinely disagreed.
findings.detail: Researcher's description of her own group experiments in a 2018 interview; underlying study details not opened.

counterintuitive.headline: Debate about the work is not a reliable performance booster.
counterintuitive.text: Many leaders have heard that task conflict is healthy and relationship conflict is harmful. The 2012 meta-analysis by de Wit, Greer and Jehn, covering 116 studies, complicates that. Overall, task conflict had essentially no link to performance. In teams below top management, the link was negative. Task conflict helped mainly in specific conditions: decision-quality work, top management teams, and teams where disagreement stayed separate from personal friction. The lesson is not to avoid debate. It is that debate pays off only when it is handled well. How a team argues matters as much as what it argues about.

sections.title: Three kinds of conflict
sections.text: Not all conflict is the same. Researchers separate three kinds. Task conflict is disagreement about the work itself, such as how to read a policy or which data definition to use. Relationship conflict is personal friction: irritation, dislike, a sense of being disrespected. Process conflict is disagreement about how work gets done and who does what. Across 116 studies, relationship and process conflict were reliably linked to worse team performance. Task conflict, on its own, was not reliably good or bad.

sections.title: Why task conflict turns personal
sections.text: Disagreement about the work becomes harmful when it travels with personal friction. In one meta-analysis, task conflict was far more damaging when it came bundled with relationship conflict. A study of 70 leadership teams suggests why. When trust is low, people read a challenge to their idea as a challenge to them. The same sentence can land as useful pushback on one team and as an attack on another.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: When a disagreement starts to heat up, bring the conversation back to content. Restate each position in terms of the facts and reasoning behind it, not the tone it was said in. Then ask what evidence would settle the question. Teams that sustained high performance in one study did exactly this: they focused on what was said, not how it was delivered.

sections.title: Watch who drops out
sections.text: After a hard disagreement, notice who stops being invited, stops speaking, or gets left off the next email. Evidence suggests people who dissent from a majority's ideas can be pushed to the edge of a group. If that happens, bring them back while their concern can still change the decision.

sections.title: Process conflict is fixable
sections.text: Disputes about who does what are among the most damaging kinds, and also among the easiest to address. Across the meta-analysis, process conflict was linked to lower performance and the lowest trust of the three types. When people argue about workload or roles, settle the question directly. Assign work by expertise and explain the reasoning to everyone, so the decision does not look like favoritism.

sections.title: What the evidence shows
sections.text: De Wit, Greer and Jehn combined 116 studies of 8,880 groups. Relationship conflict was negatively related to performance (rho = -.16), and so was process conflict (-.15). Task conflict, across 95 effect sizes, showed no overall relationship (-.01). All three types were linked to lower trust, with correlations from -.45 to -.59. Only relationship conflict was linked to lower cohesion. That pattern matters. Disagreeing about the work does not by itself make people like each other less, but it does strain trust, which leaders then have to rebuild. An earlier meta-analysis by De Dreu and Weingart found task conflict negative overall, and the newer work narrowed that conclusion. The two agree on one point: task conflict is most harmful when it comes with personal friction.

sections.title: Front-line and middle teams
sections.text: One result deserves attention in government work. In teams below top management, task conflict was negatively related to performance (rho = -.21). In top management teams, it was slightly positive (.09). The authors did not test why. One reasonable reading is that front-line and middle teams often work under tight procedures and deadlines, where unresolved debate slows work without improving it. Do not overread this. It is a correlation across many kinds of teams. It is a reason to resolve task disagreements, not to suppress them.

sections.title: The mechanism: misreading
sections.text: Simons and Peterson studied 70 leadership teams. Where trust was high, disagreement about the work was less likely to spill into personal conflict. Their evidence fit one explanation best: people with low trust misread task disagreement as a personal attack. They found weaker support for a second path, in which harsh tactics turn a work debate personal. Both suggest specific things a leader can do. Build trust before hard debates. When disagreement starts, name it as a disagreement about the work. Discourage sarcasm, interruptions and comments about motives.

sections.title: How teams argue matters
sections.text: DeChurch and colleagues pooled 45 studies covering 3,218 teams. The way teams interacted about their differences explained an additional 13% of variance in both performance and team attitudes, beyond the amount and type of conflict. Behfar and colleagues followed 57 teams and found that the ones that stayed strong shared three habits. They focused on the content of what was said, not its delivery. They explained the reasoning behind decisions about dividing up work. They assigned work by expertise rather than by who volunteered or who was available.

sections.title: Applying it in DSD and DHS work
sections.text: Picture a policy team and a waiver operations team disagreeing about how to apply a new rule to service plans already in progress. The policy analyst reads the rule one way. The operations lead says that reading will stall hundreds of cases. Each starts to describe the other as rigid or careless. That is task conflict turning personal. As the leader, separate the strands. State the work question plainly: what does the rule require for plans already approved, and what is the operational impact of each reading? Ask each person for their evidence. Identify who has the authority to interpret the rule, and route the question to the person or area responsible if it is not you. Explain how you will decide and why. If the dispute is really about who does what, treat it as process conflict, and make the assignment by expertise with the reasoning stated.

sections.title: Managing your own reaction
sections.text: Leaders are often part of the conflict. When you feel your idea is under attack, the misreading Simons and Peterson describe can happen to you. Before you respond, restate the other person's point in your own words and ask whether you have it right. That slows the exchange, shows you are dealing with the content, and often reveals that the disagreement is smaller than it felt.

sections.title: A short script for the heated moment
sections.text: When a discussion turns sharp, a few sentences can redirect it. Try something like this. I want to pause here. I think the question is whether the rule applies to plans already approved. I have heard two readings. Can each of you give me the strongest evidence for yours? I will also check who has the authority to interpret this. Notice what the script does. It names the work question, treats both positions as readings rather than motives, asks for evidence and clarifies who decides. It does not tell anyone they are wrong, and it does not ask people to calm down.

sections.title: Who does what
sections.text: Process conflict often hides inside task conflict. Two people may seem to disagree about a rule when the real dispute is about who has to absorb the extra work. Behfar and colleagues found that lasting teams openly explained the reasoning behind decisions about accepting and dividing work. They assigned work by expertise rather than by volunteering, default or convenience. When you sense a dispute about workload, name it as its own question. Settle it with stated criteria, and apply the same criteria to everyone.

sections.title: When task conflict helps
sections.text: De Wit and colleagues found task conflict more positive under specific conditions. It was more positive when performance was measured as decision quality or financial results rather than overall performance. It was more positive in top management teams. And it was more positive when task and relationship conflict did not travel together. The common thread is work where better information changes the decision, and where people can disagree without feeling attacked. Policy interpretation, program design and data definitions often fit that description. Routine processing under a deadline often does not. Match the amount of open debate to the kind of decision.

sections.title: Devil's advocates are not enough
sections.text: Some teams try to get the benefits of disagreement by assigning someone to argue the other side. In an interview about her research, Charlan Nemeth describes experiments in which an assigned devil's advocate did not prompt the same rethinking as a person who genuinely disagreed. Real disagreement challenges people more than role-play. This makes genuine dissenters valuable and harder to manage. They are the people most likely to be sidelined.

sections.title: Exclusion after dissent
sections.text: The evidence here is thinner, and it is worth saying so. A small-group study summarized by Social Science Space found that people who dissented against the majority's ideas were ostracized. People who disagreed about the group's process were more likely to be seen as leaders. A meta-analysis of workplace ostracism found that being left out was strongly linked to lower performance and well-being, and very strongly linked to deviance. Leadership characteristics were its strongest predictors. That meta-analysis did not focus on dissent, and some outcomes may come before exclusion rather than after it. Together they suggest a risk worth watching, not a proven pattern.

sections.title: What exclusion looks like in practice
sections.text: Exclusion after dissent rarely looks dramatic. A program analyst stops inviting a call-line representative to briefings because the representative keeps questioning a planned change. Briefings run faster. The change goes out. Then the questions the representative raised arrive as calls from confused people. The analyst did not intend harm. The short-term gain was real. What was lost was the information the dissenter carried. If you notice this pattern, bring the person back into the decision while their concern can still change it, and say plainly that their view is needed.

sections.title: Limits of the research
sections.text: Most conflict studies are correlational and measure conflict through team members' own reports. Field studies trended more negative for task conflict than lab studies in the de Wit meta-analysis. The trust study looked at top management teams, not front-line staff. The team-habits study was qualitative. No verified study in this review examined conflict in public human services agencies specifically. The direction of the findings is consistent, but the size of any effect in your setting is unknown.

sections.title: Differential effects
sections.text: This review found no verified evidence that conflict affects particular racial, disability or other groups differently, so this course makes no such claims. What the research does show is that how a disagreement is read depends on trust. People who have less trust in a group, for any reason, may be more likely to read a challenge as personal. That is a reason to check how a disagreement landed with each person, not to assume.

sections.title: Harder situation: the conflict is between two strong performers
sections.text: When two capable people are in open conflict, leaders often avoid stepping in for fear of losing one of them. Meet with each person separately first. Ask what the work question is, what evidence they have, and what they need from the other person. Then bring them together with a narrow agenda: the work question, the evidence, who decides, and by when. Keep comments about motives off the table. If the relationship conflict persists after the work question is settled, address it as its own issue.

sections.title: Harder situation: the conflict crosses organizations
sections.text: Many DHS conflicts involve counties, providers, contractors or Tribal Nations. You cannot set ground rules for another organization, but you can set them for your side. Keep the focus on the work question and the evidence. Route interpretation questions to the person or area responsible. For any matter involving a Tribal Nation, work through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations, and do not speak for Tribal partners.

sections.title: Set ground rules before you need them
sections.text: Behfar and colleagues found that lasting teams anticipated conflict and agreed on approaches before disputes arose, and the approaches applied to everyone. Before a hard decision, agree with your team on a few rules. Disagree with ideas, not people. Bring evidence. Say who decides and how. Check that everyone affected has been heard before the decision is final. Rules set in a calm moment are easier to invoke in a heated one.

sections.title: When to stop debating
sections.text: More debate is not always better. Task conflict was negatively related to performance in teams below top management, and field studies trended more negative than lab studies. In practice, a debate has done its work when the key evidence is on the table and each side has been heard. At that point, the person responsible should decide and explain the reasoning. Say what would reopen the question, such as new data or an unexpected effect on the people served. Then move on. Endless debate is its own kind of process conflict.

sections.title: Repairing after it turned personal
sections.text: Sometimes a disagreement turns personal before you can redirect it. All three kinds of conflict were linked to lower trust, so expect some repair work even when the work question is settled. Meet with each person separately. Acknowledge what was said, including any comment about motives, and say plainly that it was not acceptable. Ask what each person needs to work together on the next issue. Then give them a small, concrete task to complete together, where success is likely. A shared success gives each person new evidence about the other, which talk alone cannot supply.

sections.title: Your own role
sections.text: Leaders are often one side of a conflict. If a staff member challenges your decision, the misreading Simons and Peterson describe can happen to you. You may hear a challenge to your judgment as a challenge to your authority. Apply the same tools to yourself. Restate the other person's point and check you have it right. Ask for their evidence. Separate the decision from your feelings about how it was raised. If you change your mind, say so openly, which shows the team that disagreeing with the leader is safe.

simulation.setup: You supervise a policy and operations team in the Disability Services Division. A rule change affects how service plans are reviewed. A policy specialist has drafted guidance. A lead worker from waiver operations, who handles the exceptions, says the guidance will stall plans already in progress. A call-line representative has raised the same concern twice. The guidance is due to counties in two weeks. What is at stake: accurate guidance for people receiving services, a working relationship between two strong staff, and whether dissent stays in the room.

steps.situation: In a team meeting, the lead worker says the draft will freeze hundreds of plans. The policy specialist replies that operations always wants exceptions and never reads the rule closely. The lead worker goes quiet. Others look at you.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Pause and restate the work question: what the rule requires for plans already approved, and what each reading would mean for those plans. Ask each person for their evidence.
choices.feedback: You move the exchange back to content before it hardens into personal conflict. That matches the habit Behfar and colleagues found in lasting teams. It also addresses the misreading Simons and Peterson describe, where task disagreement is heard as an attack. The tension does not vanish, but the question becomes workable.

choices.label: Say both points are valid and suggest the two of them work it out after the meeting.
choices.feedback: This avoids escalation in front of others, which feels kind. But the personal comment stands unanswered, and two people who are already reading each other as the problem are asked to resolve it alone. Task conflict is most harmful when it travels with relationship conflict, and this choice leaves them bundled.

choices.label: Support the policy specialist. The rule is clear, the deadline is close, and operations concerns can be handled through later questions.
choices.feedback: This is tempting because the policy specialist owns the drafting and the deadline is real. But you have settled a work question by role, and you have let a comment about motives stand. The lead worker, who sees the exceptions daily, now has reason to stop raising them.

steps.situation: Each person brings evidence. The lead worker shows that about 300 plans are mid-review. The policy specialist shows the rule language. It is unclear whether the rule applies to plans already approved. The policy specialist suggests the call-line representative not join the next working session because their repeated questions slow things down.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Route the interpretation question to the person or area responsible for the rule, and keep the call-line representative in the working session, explaining that their callers will face the result.
choices.feedback: You separate the question of who decides from the question of who contributes. Keeping the dissenter in protects the information they carry. Research suggests dissent against the majority view can lead to exclusion, and an assigned devil's advocate does not replace someone who genuinely disagrees.

choices.label: Route the interpretation question, and agree to brief the call-line representative afterward to keep the session small.
choices.feedback: Smaller sessions can be efficient, and you are not ignoring the representative. But briefing them afterward turns them from a contributor into an audience, and the concerns they raised will now arrive later, if at all. This is how exclusion after dissent usually looks: quiet and well-intended.

choices.label: Decide the interpretation yourself to keep the deadline, and agree to keep the session to the two leads.
choices.feedback: Speed is a real pressure. But you have made an interpretation that may belong to someone else, and removed the person most likely to spot problems. In teams below top management, unresolved task conflict was linked to worse performance. Resolving it by shrinking the group rather than settling the question is risky.

steps.situation: A week later, the two have not met. The lead worker emails you separately with a list of cases the guidance would stall. The policy specialist has finalized the draft. The call-line representative has stopped coming to team briefings.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Meet each person separately, then bring them together with a narrow agenda: the work question, the evidence, who decides, and by when. Invite the call-line representative back.
choices.feedback: You repair the process before the guidance goes out. Separate meetings lower the heat, and a narrow agenda keeps the joint meeting on content. Inviting the representative back restores the dissenting view while it can still change the guidance. It costs time you hoped not to spend.

choices.label: Forward the lead worker's list to the policy specialist and ask them to address it before the draft goes out.
choices.feedback: The concern now reaches the right person, which matters. But it reaches them as a list from someone they have already labeled as obstructive. Without trust or a shared conversation, the content is likely to be read as more of the same.

choices.label: Let the draft go out on time and plan to address problems through counties' questions.
choices.feedback: This keeps the deadline and avoids a hard meeting. But the problem has not gone away. It has moved to counties and to the people whose plans may stall. The relationship conflict remains, and the call-line representative's absence means fewer people are watching for problems.

steps.situation: The guidance question is settled for now. You know this team will face several more rule changes this year, and the same two people will lead them.
steps.question: What do you set up for the next one?

choices.label: Agree on ground rules with the whole team now: disagree with ideas, bring evidence, say who decides, and check that the people who handle exceptions have been heard before a decision is final.
choices.feedback: Lasting teams in Behfar's study anticipated conflict and used approaches that applied to everyone. Setting rules in a calm moment makes them easier to use under pressure. The rule about hearing from people who handle exceptions directly guards against exclusion after dissent.

choices.label: Ask the two leads to meet monthly to stay aligned.
choices.feedback: Regular contact can build trust, which Simons and Peterson found helps keep task conflict from turning personal. But it leaves out the rest of the team, including the people closest to the exceptions, and it does not set any shared rules for how to disagree.

choices.label: Separate the work so the two leads do not need to collaborate on future rule changes.
choices.feedback: This reduces friction and is tempting when a relationship is strained. But it removes the disagreement that improves decisions in policy work, where better information changes outcomes. It also signals that conflict is handled by avoidance.

simulation.debrief: The first decision set the course. Bringing the exchange back to the work question and the evidence kept task conflict from bundling with personal friction. In the meta-analyses, that bundling is when task conflict did the most harm. Leaving the two to work it out, or deciding by role, left a comment about motives standing and pushed the problem downstream. The second decision tested whether dissent stayed in the room. The call-line representative carried information that only showed up later as confused calls and stalled plans. Evidence on exclusion after dissent is thin, but it points in a clear direction. The last decision turned one repair into a team habit. How a team argues explained more variance in outcomes than what it argued about, so agreed rules are worth the time.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming all task conflict is healthy.
mistakes.why: Popular advice says debate about the work improves decisions. The meta-analytic evidence shows no overall link, and a negative link in teams below top management.
mistakes.instead: Encourage debate where better information changes the decision, and resolve task disagreements rather than letting them run.

mistakes.mistake: Responding to the tone instead of the content.
mistakes.why: Tone is what people feel first, so leaders react to it. But teams that sustained high performance focused on what was said, not how it was delivered.
mistakes.instead: Restate each position in terms of its facts and reasoning, and ask what evidence would settle it.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving a comment about motives unanswered.
mistakes.why: Stepping in feels like taking sides. But once a disagreement turns personal, task conflict becomes far more harmful.
mistakes.instead: Name it gently and redirect: the question is about the rule, not about anyone's intentions.

mistakes.mistake: Shrinking the group to get past a dissenter.
mistakes.why: It works in the short term, and meetings run faster. But dissent against the majority view can lead to exclusion, and the information the dissenter carries goes with them.
mistakes.instead: Keep the dissenter in the decision while their concern can still change it, and say why their view is needed.

mistakes.mistake: Assigning work by availability after a dispute about who does what.
mistakes.why: It feels neutral and fast. But lasting teams assigned work by expertise and explained the reasoning.
mistakes.instead: Assign by expertise, state the reasoning, and apply the same approach to everyone.

jobAid.title: Untangling a disagreement
jobAid.use: Use it when a disagreement in your team starts to heat up, or before a meeting you expect to be tense.
steps: Name the type: Is this about the work, about who does what, or about the relationship?
State the work question in one sentence that both sides would accept.
Ask each person for the facts and reasoning behind their position.
Redirect any comment about motives back to the work question.
Say who decides. If it is not you, route it to the person or area responsible.
Check who is missing. Has anyone who disagreed been left out of the next step?
Explain the decision and its reasoning to everyone affected, including those who disagreed.
If personal friction remains after the work question is settled, address it separately.

media.reason: Conflict is about two readings of the same moment. A dialogue between two roles shows how a work disagreement can be heard as personal, and how it can be brought back.

title: Earning and repairing trust
objective: Build trust through reliable, caring and principled action, and repair it after a failure with a response that fits what went wrong.
outcomes: Identify whether people see a failure as a lapse in competence or a lapse in integrity, and respond to each differently.
Make a specific promise about future behavior, and keep it visibly over the following weeks.
Tell the truth about a mistake early, without spin, minimizing or partial accounts.
Follow through on problems people raise, and tell them what happened.
Show care for the people affected by a decision, not only the reasons for it.

evidence.summary: Meta-analyses each pooling more than 100 samples or effects link trust in leaders to performance, citizenship and commitment, with direct supervisors an especially important source. People judge trustworthiness on ability, benevolence and integrity. Trust built on care predicted others' ratings of performance more strongly than trust built on reliability. Repair depends on what broke. In experiments, apology helped more after competence failures, while denial helped more after integrity accusations when the person was innocent. In a lab trust game, consistent good behavior restored trust, a promise sped recovery, a bare apology did little, and deception left damage that never fully healed. Most repair studies are lab experiments, so workplace evidence is thinner.

findings.claim: Trust in leadership related to key work outcomes across 106 effects, and direct leaders such as supervisors were an especially important referent.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of four decades of research; 2002.

findings.claim: A leader's ability, benevolence and integrity, plus a person's general tendency to trust, predicted risk taking and job performance, partly through trust.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 132 independent samples; results held for trust in leaders and coworkers; 2007.

findings.claim: Affective trust in a leader predicted performance and citizenship more strongly than cognitive trust; servant and ethical leadership added 31% and 30% explained variance in affective trust beyond transformational leadership.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 185 studies since 1988, using performance rated by others; 2021.
findings.source: Legood, van der Werff, Lee & Den Hartog, 2021

findings.claim: Apology repaired trust better than denial for competence violations; denial worked better for integrity violations when later evidence showed innocence, and apology worked best when evidence showed guilt.
findings.detail: Two experiments with participants judging a job candidate accused of a tax-filing error; 2004.

findings.claim: Consistent trustworthy actions restored trust after untrustworthy behavior, but trust harmed by deception never fully recovered, even after a promise, an apology and good behavior.
findings.detail: Laboratory repeated trust game with 262 participants and scripted partners; 2006.

findings.claim: A promise to change behavior sped trust recovery; an apology without a promise had no significant effect on early or long-term recovery.
findings.detail: Same experiment, 262 participants; 2006.

findings.claim: Among Federal Aviation Administration employees, trust in supervisors, coworkers and management was substantially related to job satisfaction and commitment, with trust in management strongest.
findings.detail: 2003 federal Employee Attitude Survey, structural equation modeling, cross-sectional; 2011.

counterintuitive.headline: An apology alone did not speed the return of trust.
counterintuitive.text: Most advice on repairing trust starts and ends with saying sorry. In a lab trust game with 262 participants, Schweitzer, Hershey and Bradlow tested apologies and promises separately. A bare apology, with regret and self-criticism but no commitment, had no significant effect on how quickly or how fully trust came back. A promise to change behavior did speed recovery. Consistent trustworthy actions did the most. The apology that worked in Kim and colleagues' experiments included a statement that it would not happen again. The lesson: say sorry, and then say exactly what will be different, and do it.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.text: Trust is a willingness to be vulnerable to someone because you expect them to act well. Staff trust a supervisor when they are willing to raise a problem, accept an uncertain assignment, or rely on a promise. Large reviews of the research link trust in leaders to better performance and commitment, and direct supervisors are an especially important source of trust. People judge whether to trust you on three things: whether you can do the job, whether you care about them, and whether you act on principle.

sections.title: Repair depends on what broke
sections.text: When trust breaks, first ask what people think went wrong. If they see a competence failure, such as a missed deadline or a wrong answer, an apology tends to work well. If they see an integrity failure, such as favoritism or a broken promise made knowingly, the response is harder. Experiments found that denial helped with integrity accusations only when the person was truly innocent. When the person was at fault, apology still worked better.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: After a trust failure, pair your apology with a specific promise about what will be different, then keep it where people can see. In one experiment, a bare apology did not help trust recover. A promise sped recovery. Consistent trustworthy actions did the most. Saying sorry opens the door. What you do next is what people trust.

sections.title: Never shade the truth
sections.text: In the same experiment, trust harmed by deception never fully recovered, even after a promise, an apology and a long run of good behavior. A partial account or a convenient explanation might ease today's conversation. It can cost trust you will not get back.

sections.title: Small acts build it
sections.text: Most trust is built in ordinary moments, not in repair. Do what you said you would do, when you said you would. Close the loop when someone raises a problem. Explain decisions, especially unwelcome ones. Show care for the people affected. Each act is small, but together they are the evidence people use to decide whether to rely on you.

sections.title: What the evidence shows
sections.text: Dirks and Ferrin combined four decades of studies, 106 effects in all, and found that trust in leadership relates to important work outcomes. They found that direct leaders such as supervisors are a particularly important referent. Colquitt, Scott and LePine pooled 132 samples. They found that perceptions of a leader's ability, benevolence and integrity predicted whether people took risks for the leader and how well they performed, partly through trust. Legood and colleagues analyzed 185 studies and used performance rated by others, not by the employees themselves, to reduce bias. Trust built on care and emotional connection predicted performance and helping behavior more strongly than trust built on judgments of reliability. Servant and ethical leadership styles explained substantially more of that care-based trust than transformational leadership did.

sections.title: Trust in public agencies
sections.text: Cho and Park studied employees of the Federal Aviation Administration using a federal workforce survey. Trust in supervisors, coworkers and management was substantially related to job satisfaction and commitment. Trust in management had the strongest link. The study was cross-sectional, so it cannot show which came first. For a supervisor at DHS, it is a reminder that staff trust is shaped by you and by the decisions above you that you carry out and explain.

sections.title: The mechanism: what people infer
sections.text: A trust failure raises a question in people's minds: what does this tell me about this person? Kim, Ferrin, Cooper and Dirks tested this in two experiments. Participants played managers judging a job candidate accused of a prior tax-filing error. When the error was framed as a competence problem, an apology repaired trust better than a denial. People accept that a capable person can make one mistake. When it was framed as an integrity problem, admitting it was more damaging, because people see one integrity failure as revealing character. Denial worked better there, but only when later evidence showed innocence. When evidence showed guilt, apology was the better response. The practical rule is simple: if you did it, own it, whatever kind of failure it is.

sections.title: Promises and actions
sections.text: Schweitzer, Hershey and Bradlow used a repeated trust game with 262 participants. Each participant's partner acted untrustworthily in the first two rounds and then trustworthily after that. Consistent good behavior restored trust. A promise to change sped the recovery. An apology alone, without a promise, did not change the speed or extent of recovery. When the early bad behavior came with deception, trust never fully recovered, and the promise lost much of its power.

sections.title: Applying it in DHS work
sections.text: Picture a licensing unit supervisor who told staff that a new specialized assignment would rotate fairly across shifts. Under deadline pressure, the supervisor gave it to a day-shift worker without posting it. The evening shift heard about it secondhand. Some staff see this as a competence lapse: the supervisor forgot. Others see an integrity lapse: the supervisor favors day shift. The response that fits the evidence is to say plainly what happened, take responsibility, and make a specific promise. For example, the next assignment will be posted to both shifts with a selection date, and the supervisor will explain the choice. Then keep that promise visibly. Do not explain away the decision with a partial account. If a reason was real, such as an expertise requirement, say it fully, including that you should have said it at the time.

sections.title: Everyday trust building
sections.text: Most trust is built in small acts. Follow through on what people raise and tell them what happened. Say when you will get back to someone, and do. Explain decisions, especially ones people will not like. Show care for the people affected, not only the logic of the decision. The research on care-based trust suggests that this last part matters more than many leaders expect.

sections.title: Diagnosing the failure
sections.text: Before you respond to a trust failure, find out how people see it. Ask a trusted staff member what people are saying, or ask the affected people directly. Listen for words like forgot, missed or did not know, which suggest a competence reading. Listen for words like unfair, favorite or never meant it, which suggest an integrity reading. Then check yourself honestly. Did you fall short? If so, the evidence points the same way for both readings: own it fully. The difference is in what follows. Competence repair needs a fix to the skill or process. Integrity repair needs visible, consistent fairness over time.

sections.title: What to say
sections.text: A repair conversation can be short. Try something like this. I told you the assignment would rotate across shifts, and I did not do that. I chose a day-shift reviewer because they had the training, and I should have said so at the time. I am sorry. For the next two assignments, I will post them to both shifts with a selection date and the criteria, and I will explain each choice. I will also make the training available to evening staff. Notice what it does. It names the broken promise, gives the full reason, apologizes, makes a specific promise and addresses the cause.

sections.title: Why the apology findings differ
sections.text: The apology evidence looks contradictory at first. Kim and colleagues found apology helpful after competence failures. Schweitzer and colleagues found a bare apology did nothing. The authors of the second study offer several explanations. Their apology had no promise, while the apology in Kim's study stated that the incident would not happen again. Their participants experienced a real loss in a game, while Kim's judged a hypothetical candidate. And their participants faced a repeated relationship, where future behavior matters most. Taken together, the evidence suggests that an apology works when it carries a commitment and is followed by action.

sections.title: Deception is different
sections.text: The strongest result in the trust game was about deception. Trust harmed by untrustworthy actions came back with consistent good behavior. Trust harmed by the same actions plus a false statement never fully recovered, even after a promise, an apology and a long run of good behavior. In workplace terms, a decision that hurt people can be repaired. A misleading account of that decision is much harder to repair. This matters most under pressure. That is when it is tempting to give a partial explanation, imply a decision came from above, or call something settled when it is not.

sections.title: Care-based trust
sections.text: Legood and colleagues found that trust grounded in care and emotional ties predicted others' ratings of performance and helping more strongly than trust grounded in reliability. Servant and ethical leadership explained 31% and 30% more of the variance in care-based trust than transformational leadership. For cognitive trust, the added variance was about 11%. This suggests that inspiring vision alone does not build the kind of trust that most affects behavior. Visible concern for people's interests and consistent ethical conduct do more.

sections.title: Limits of the research
sections.text: Most trust-repair evidence comes from lab games or scenario studies, often with students. Field experiments in workplaces are scarce. The trust-game partners were scripted, and stakes were small amounts of money. The meta-analyses are largely correlational, so they show that trust and good outcomes go together, not that building trust causes them. The public-sector study used one federal agency's survey at one time. Treat the repair findings as well-tested principles about how people reason, not as precise predictions for your team.

sections.title: Differential effects
sections.text: This review found no verified evidence that trust or trust repair works differently for particular racial, disability or other groups, so this course makes no such claims. One verified difference is in how a general tendency to trust others shapes trust, which Colquitt and colleagues found. People come to a new supervisor with different starting levels of trust, for many reasons. Expect that some people will need more consistent evidence before they rely on you, and do not read that as a judgment of you.

sections.title: Harder situation: you are blamed for a decision you did not make
sections.text: Supervisors often carry out decisions made above them. If staff lose trust because of such a decision, do not imply it was not yours if you agreed with it. Do not pretend you agreed if you did not. Say what was decided, by whom, and what you know about why. Say what you can and cannot change. Then promise something within your control, such as how you will apply the decision fairly, and keep it. Cho and Park's finding that trust in management mattered most is a reason to be accurate about where decisions come from.

sections.title: Harder situation: the accusation is wrong
sections.text: Sometimes staff believe you acted unfairly when you did not. Kim and colleagues found that denial helped with integrity accusations when the evidence later supported innocence. Denial only helps if it is true and can be shown. Explain the facts, show the evidence if you can, and acknowledge how the situation looked. If you are not certain you are blameless, do not deny. A denial later shown to be false combines an integrity failure with deception, the hardest kind of damage to repair.

sections.title: Harder situation: repeated failures
sections.text: One failure, repaired well, can leave trust intact. Repeated failures teach people that your promises do not hold. In the trust game, prior deception reduced the power of later promises. If you have broken promises before, make fewer and smaller promises, keep each one visibly, and let actions accumulate before asking for trust again.

sections.title: Following through
sections.text: A quiet form of trust failure is the concern that goes nowhere. An employee on an afternoon shift spots an error in call-back instructions and tells you. If they never hear what happened, they learn that raising problems is not worth it. Trace the issue to the person or area responsible and close the loop across shifts. Recognize both the person who spotted the issue and the person who fixed it.

sections.title: Care without favoritism
sections.text: Care-based trust predicted performance most strongly, but care can look like favoritism if it is uneven. A supervisor who checks in warmly with some staff and rarely with others builds trust with some and suspicion with the rest. Make care consistent. Check in with every team member on a regular rhythm, across shifts and work locations. Show concern for the effects of decisions on everyone affected, not only on the people you see most.

sections.title: How long repair takes
sections.text: In the trust game, trust came back through a consistent series of trustworthy actions, not a single gesture. Expect repair to take a run of kept commitments. Do not ask people whether they trust you again, which puts them on the spot. Keep acting, and watch what they do. Signs that trust is returning include people raising problems with you again, accepting assignments without extra checking, and planning around your commitments. If deception was involved, expect that some damage may not fully heal, and keep acting consistently anyway.

sections.title: Trust across boundaries
sections.text: Many DHS relationships cross organizations: counties, providers, contractors and Tribal Nations. Trust failures there can affect many people and take longer to repair. The same principles apply. Give a full, accurate account, own what is yours, and make specific commitments you control. Route decisions to the person or area responsible rather than promising outcomes you cannot deliver. For any matter involving a Tribal Nation, work through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations, and do not speak for Tribal partners.

simulation.setup: You supervise a licensing unit that reviews applications from day and evening shifts. Two months ago, you told your staff that a new specialized review assignment would rotate fairly across both shifts. Last week, under deadline pressure, you gave it to a day-shift reviewer without posting it. You chose that reviewer because they had already completed the relevant training. What is at stake: whether evening staff believe your word, and whether they keep raising problems with you.

steps.situation: An evening-shift lead reviewer asks to talk. They say evening staff heard about the assignment from a day-shift colleague. Some think you forgot your promise. Others think you favor day shift.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Say plainly that you broke the rotation you promised, explain the full reason, including the training requirement, and say you should have explained it at the time.
choices.feedback: You take responsibility and give a complete account. That addresses both readings: it owns a competence lapse and removes the basis for suspicion of favoritism. In Kim's experiments, owning a real fault worked better than denying it. The lead reviewer may still be frustrated, but has a true account to carry back.

choices.label: Explain that the training requirement made the choice necessary, so the rotation did not apply this time.
choices.feedback: The reason is real, which makes this tempting. But it frames the broken promise as no failure at all. Staff who already suspect favoritism hear a justification, not an acknowledgment. Integrity concerns are hard to clear with explanations alone, especially when the promise was not mentioned.

choices.label: Say the decision came from your manager because of the deadline.
choices.feedback: This would ease the conversation and shift blame upward. But it is not true. The trust game found that trust harmed by deception never fully recovered, even after later promises and good behavior. If the account comes apart, you add an integrity failure to the original lapse.

steps.situation: The lead reviewer appreciates the honesty but says evening staff want to know whether the rotation still means anything.
steps.question: What do you do next?

choices.label: Promise that the next two assignments will be posted to both shifts with a selection date and stated criteria, and that you will explain each choice. Offer the training to evening reviewers.
choices.feedback: A specific promise sped trust recovery in the trust game. Offering training addresses the reason behind the original choice, which shows care for evening staff's interests. Legood's meta-analysis found care-based trust predicted performance more strongly than reliability alone.

choices.label: Apologize again and say it will not happen again.
choices.feedback: The apology is sincere, and it includes a general commitment. But it is vague. Staff cannot tell what will be different, and you have not addressed the training gap that caused the choice. In the trust game, a bare apology did little; specific commitments and actions did more.

choices.label: Say you hope the honest explanation is enough and move on to other business.
choices.feedback: Honesty helped, but it only explains the past. Without a commitment, staff have no way to see whether the future will differ. Trust recovered with consistent trustworthy actions, and you have not named any.

steps.situation: A week later, two evening reviewers stop bringing you questions and go to a day-shift lead instead. One mentions to a colleague that the rotation was never real.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Meet with evening staff, say you broke the rotation and did not own it clearly, give the full reason, and make a specific, visible commitment for the next assignments.
choices.feedback: Late repair is harder but still possible. Owning the failure directly now, with a specific promise, gives people something new to evaluate. If your earlier account was misleading, correct it fully. Partial corrections tend to deepen suspicion.

choices.label: Post the next assignment to both shifts without discussing the past.
choices.feedback: The action is right, and consistent trustworthy actions were the strongest repair in the trust game. But without acknowledging the failure, staff may read it as a one-time gesture. Action does the most, and naming the failure helps people interpret the action.

choices.label: Ask the day-shift lead to tell evening staff the decision was fair.
choices.feedback: This uses a trusted colleague to vouch for you. But it asks someone else to repair your integrity, and it sidesteps the broken promise. Staff who suspect favoritism are likely to read it as more of the same.

steps.situation: Six weeks later, another specialized assignment comes up with a short deadline. The quickest choice is again a trained day-shift reviewer. One evening reviewer has now completed the training.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Post it to both shifts with a short selection window, apply the stated criteria, and explain the choice to everyone.
choices.feedback: This is where trust is earned or lost. Keeping a promise when it costs you something is the clearest evidence of integrity. Consistent trustworthy actions restored trust in the trust game, and this one is highly visible.

choices.label: Give it to the trained evening reviewer without posting, to balance the last decision.
choices.feedback: It feels fair and fast, and it helps evening staff. But it breaks the same promise in the other direction. Staff on both shifts learn that assignments depend on your judgment of balance, not on the process you committed to.

choices.label: Give it to the day-shift reviewer again because the deadline is real, and explain afterward.
choices.feedback: The deadline is real, which makes this tempting. But it repeats the original failure. The trust game found that prior failures reduce the power of later promises, so a second break will likely cost more than the first.

simulation.debrief: The first moment decided how hard the rest would be. Owning a real failure, with the full reason, gave staff a true account and matched Kim and colleagues' finding that apology works better than denial when the person is at fault. Justifying the decision as no failure left suspicion standing. Shifting blame upward, if untrue, risked the kind of damage the trust game found never fully heals. The second decision tested whether repair went beyond words. A specific promise sped recovery, and offering training showed care for evening staff, the kind of trust Legood's meta-analysis linked most strongly to performance. The last decision was the real test. Keeping a promise when it costs time is the evidence people use to decide whether your word means anything.

mistakes.mistake: Treating an apology as the whole repair.
mistakes.why: Apologizing feels like the hard part, and it is often what people say they want. But in the trust game, an apology without a promise had no significant effect on recovery.
mistakes.instead: Pair the apology with a specific commitment, and then keep it where people can see.

mistakes.mistake: Explaining a broken promise as if it were not broken.
mistakes.why: Leaders usually have real reasons, so the explanation feels honest. But people judging integrity hear justification, not acknowledgment.
mistakes.instead: Name the broken promise first, then give the full reason, including what you should have done differently.

mistakes.mistake: Giving a partial or convenient account under pressure.
mistakes.why: It eases a hard conversation and often goes unchallenged. But trust harmed by deception never fully recovered in the trust game, even after later good behavior.
mistakes.instead: Give the full, accurate account early. If you said something misleading, correct it completely.

mistakes.mistake: Denying an integrity accusation you cannot fully disprove.
mistakes.why: Denial protects your reputation in the moment. Experiments found denial helped only when later evidence showed innocence.
mistakes.instead: Deny only what is true and can be shown. If you share any fault, own it.

mistakes.mistake: Focusing only on reliability and ignoring care.
mistakes.why: Supervisors are trained to be competent and consistent, which builds one kind of trust. But care-based trust predicted performance and helping more strongly.
mistakes.instead: Show concern for the people affected by decisions, including what the decision costs them and what you can do about it.

mistakes.mistake: Letting raised problems disappear.
mistakes.why: Busy leaders fix the issue and move on. But staff who never hear back learn that raising problems does not matter.
mistakes.instead: Close the loop with the person who raised it, across shifts if needed.

jobAid.title: Repairing trust after a failure
jobAid.use: Use it when staff, partners or colleagues lose confidence in you after a decision, a mistake or a broken commitment.
steps: Ask what people think went wrong: a lapse in competence, or a lapse in integrity?
Check the facts. Did you actually fall short? If yes, own it. If no, can you show it?
Give the full, accurate account early. No partial explanations, no shifted blame.
Apologize for the specific failure and its effect on people.
Make a specific promise about what will be different, with a time and a way people can see it.
Address the cause, not only the symptom, such as a training gap or an unclear process.
Keep the promise when it costs you something. That is the moment people remember.
Close the loop with the people affected after the next decision.
