title: Empathy and emotional intelligence, without the hype
objective: Use specific, learnable emotional skills, especially asking instead of assuming, to support colleagues and the people they serve, while staying skeptical of inflated claims about emotional intelligence.
outcomes: Ask a colleague what a situation meant to them before offering solutions or interpretations.
Check your read of someone's emotion with a direct question instead of relying on imagination.
Separate support for a distressed colleague from the practical steps that protect the person they serve, and name who does each.
Respond to public correction by checking the fact first, without defensiveness.
Judge emotional intelligence claims by how they were measured and whether others, not just the person, rated the outcome.

evidence.summary: Emotional intelligence research is real but contested. Ability-based emotional skills predict performance most in jobs with heavy emotional demands. The link between emotional intelligence and leadership is weaker than often claimed: one meta-analysis found a corrected correlation of 0.13 across measures and 0.05 for ability tests, and leading researchers still debate it. Training raises test scores moderately across 58 studies, but effects on job behavior are largely unknown. Empathy research is more practical. Across 25 experiments, imagining someone's perspective did not improve accuracy, while asking did. People avoid empathy because it feels effortful. Compassion training increased helping in lab studies. Most of this is lab or self-report evidence.

findings.claim: Ability-based emotional intelligence predicted job performance positively in high emotional labor jobs, and the link varied by job type.
findings.detail: Integrative meta-analysis testing a cascade from emotion perception to understanding to regulation; 2010.

findings.claim: The corrected correlation between emotional intelligence and transformational leadership was 0.13 across measures and 0.05 for ability-based measures.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis, 2010; figures as stated by the authors in a 2022 published debate. The authors attribute stronger reported links to same-source ratings.
findings.source: Harms & Credé, 2010 (stated in Dasborough et al., 2022)

findings.claim: One of the meta-analysis authors wrote that the apparent link between emotional intelligence and leadership was largely driven by poorly designed studies using same-source ratings, and nearly disappeared in better designs.
findings.detail: Author's own summary of the 2010 meta-analysis, published on SAGE's Social Science Space; 2011.

findings.claim: Leading proponents and critics agree emotional intelligence must predict outcomes beyond personality and cognitive ability, but still disagree on whether it does.
findings.detail: Published structured debate among six researchers in The Leadership Quarterly; 2022.
findings.source: Dasborough, Ashkanasy, Humphrey, Harms, Credé & Wood, 2022

findings.claim: Emotional intelligence training raised scores moderately: d = 0.45 in treatment-control studies and 0.61 in pre-post studies.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 58 published and unpublished studies; published studies showed larger effects than dissertations; 2019.

findings.claim: Training appeared more effective with practice and feedback and without lecture, but its effects on actual behavior and job performance are largely unknown.
findings.detail: Federal child welfare workforce center summary of the 2019 meta-analysis; 2021.

findings.claim: Instructing people to take another's perspective did not improve accuracy about that person's thoughts or feelings, and slightly lowered it; getting the perspective through conversation improved accuracy.
findings.detail: 25 experiments, including reading emotions, detecting lies and predicting a spouse's preferences; 2018.

findings.claim: When free to choose, people avoided empathy because it felt effortful; raising their sense that they could empathize effectively removed the avoidance.
findings.detail: 11 studies, N = 1,204, plus an internal meta-analysis; 2019.

findings.claim: Short-term compassion training increased helping toward strangers compared with memory training.
findings.detail: Two experiments using a newly developed prosocial game; 2011.

findings.claim: After compassion training, people reported more positive feeling while watching others suffer, rather than only distress.
findings.detail: Training study with brain imaging compared with a memory-training group; 2013.

counterintuitive.headline: Imagining someone's point of view does not make you more accurate about it.
counterintuitive.text: Most people believe that putting yourself in someone else's shoes helps you understand them. Eyal, Steffel and Epley tested that belief in 25 experiments. Instructing people to take another person's perspective did not reliably improve their accuracy about that person's feelings, preferences or honesty. Overall, it slightly lowered accuracy, while sometimes raising confidence. What did work was getting the perspective: asking and listening. In one experiment, conversation improved accuracy where imagination did not. For a leader, the skill is not guessing better. It is asking sooner.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.text: Emotional intelligence is a popular idea with a disputed evidence base. Some parts hold up well. People who can perceive, understand and manage emotions tend to do better in jobs with heavy emotional demands, such as call lines and direct service. Other claims are inflated. One meta-analysis found that the link between emotional intelligence and leadership nearly disappears when it is measured with ability tests and rated by other people. Treat emotional intelligence as a set of specific skills, not a personality score that makes someone a good leader.

sections.title: The skill that matters most
sections.text: Across 25 experiments, imagining another person's perspective did not make people more accurate about what that person thought or felt. It slightly lowered accuracy, while sometimes raising confidence. Asking did work. When people got the other person's perspective through conversation, accuracy improved. Empathy at work is less about imagining and more about asking.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: When a colleague is upset, ask what the situation meant to them before you offer solutions or interpretations. A simple question works: what was hardest about that for you? Then listen. You may find the concern is not what you assumed. It might be the caller, an unclear instruction, or something they think they did wrong. Once you know, you can separate support for your colleague from the practical steps that protect the person they serve, and name who will take each step.

sections.title: Why this takes effort
sections.text: Empathy is work. In 11 studies, people avoided empathy when they could, because it felt effortful. The avoidance disappeared when people felt they could empathize effectively. Asking a good question is a concrete way to feel effective, which makes empathy easier to sustain.

sections.title: Two tracks, every time
sections.text: When a colleague is shaken after working with someone you serve, there are usually two needs at once. Your colleague needs support. The person served may need a fact checked or a follow-up call. Keep both in view. Acknowledge your colleague, and also name who will verify the fact and who will follow up, by when. Empathy and accuracy work together.

sections.title: What emotional intelligence is
sections.text: Emotional intelligence is measured in three different ways. Ability tests ask people to solve emotional problems and score answers as more or less correct. Self-report scales ask people to rate their own emotional skills. Broad self-report measures add many traits that overlap with established personality factors. A federal child welfare workforce summary notes that many researchers argue these broad measures do not actually measure emotional intelligence. Results depend heavily on which kind of measure a study used. Joseph and Newman's meta-analysis supported a cascade: perceiving emotion leads to understanding it, which leads to regulating it, which relates to performance. Ability-based emotional intelligence predicted performance positively in jobs with high emotional labor.

sections.title: The leadership dispute
sections.text: Harms and Credé meta-analyzed the link between emotional intelligence and transformational leadership. They report a corrected correlation of 0.13 across measures and 0.05 for ability-based measures. Harms has written that stronger links in earlier work were largely driven by poorly designed studies. In many, the same person rated both their own emotional intelligence and their leadership. In a 2022 published debate, leading proponents and critics agreed that emotional intelligence must predict outcomes beyond personality and cognitive ability. They still disagreed on whether the evidence shows it does. When you see a strong claim about emotional intelligence and leadership, ask two questions. How was it measured? And who rated the outcome?

sections.title: Can it be trained?
sections.text: Mattingly and Kraiger combined 58 studies of emotional intelligence training. Training raised scores moderately: d = 0.45 in studies with a control group and 0.61 in before-and-after studies. Published studies showed larger effects than unpublished dissertations, which suggests some inflation. The federal child welfare workforce summary adds that training seemed to work better with practice and feedback than with lecture. Effects on actual behavior and job performance are largely unknown. This course follows that pattern. It focuses on specific practices you can use and get feedback on.

sections.title: Empathy: ask, do not assume
sections.text: Eyal, Steffel and Epley ran 25 experiments. They asked people to predict others' emotions, detect lies, and predict a spouse's preferences. Telling people to imagine the other person's perspective did not improve accuracy. Getting the perspective through conversation did. The reason is simple. Imagination draws on what you already believe about a person. Asking brings in new information.

sections.title: Applying it in DHS work
sections.text: Picture a call-line worker who comes to a check-in upset after a hard call. A caller's services were reduced, and the caller was angry and frightened. You know the procedure and have three suggestions ready. Before offering any of them, ask what was hardest about the call. The worker might be worried about the caller's safety, unsure whether they gave the right information, or shaken by the caller's anger. Each needs a different response. Then separate two tracks. One is support for the worker: acknowledgment, a short break, help thinking through the call. The other is protection for the caller: who will verify the fact that is in question, and who will contact the caller, by when. Name both.

sections.title: Emotional skills under correction
sections.text: Emotional skills matter most when you are the one under pressure. If a colleague corrects you in a meeting, the useful response is to check the fact first, without defending yourself. Your response also teaches staff whether raising an error is safe. Notice, too, how easily you read emotion into small signals. A colleague tapping a pen might be impatient, concentrating or uncomfortable. The research on perspective suggests that if it matters, you should ask rather than guess.

sections.title: A sample check-in
sections.text: A short check-in after a hard call might sound like this. That sounded like a tough call. What was hardest about it for you? Then listen. If the worker says they are unsure about information they gave, respond to both tracks. Thank you for telling me. That would worry me too. I will check the number with you now. Do you want to call the caller back, or would you like someone else to? Can that happen before four? Notice that the script asks before advising, acknowledges the feeling in plain words, and ends with a named person and a time.

sections.title: Judging a training or assessment offer
sections.text: Emotional intelligence products are widely marketed. Before your area adopts one, ask a few questions. What kind of measure does it use: an ability test, or self-report? Have outcomes been rated by other people, or only by participants? Does the training include practice and feedback, which the federal child welfare workforce summary suggests matter more than lecture? Is there evidence of changes in behavior at work, or only in test scores? These questions do not rule a product out. They help you set realistic expectations.

sections.title: Why the hype persists
sections.text: Emotional intelligence claims spread partly because of how studies were designed. When the same person rates their own emotional intelligence and their own leadership or performance, the two will correlate for reasons that have little to do with skill. Harms and Credé's estimate of 0.05 for ability measures is close to zero. Proponents in the 2022 debate argue that newer meta-analyses using ratings from others show real incremental value. Critics reply that many studies are too small and that broad measures mix too many traits. You do not need to settle this debate. You need to be skeptical of any product, assessment or training that promises large leadership gains from an emotional intelligence score.

sections.title: Limits of the research
sections.text: Several limits apply across this course. The emotional intelligence meta-analyses rely largely on correlational studies. Training effects are measured mostly as changes in test scores, not changes in behavior at work. The empathy studies are laboratory experiments, often with students or online participants. The compassion training studies are small. No verified study here comes from public human services agencies, although the job-type finding about emotional labor is relevant to call lines and direct service. Treat the practical advice in this course as well-grounded in how people reason, and modest in what it promises.

sections.title: Empathy has costs
sections.text: Cameron and colleagues ran 11 studies with 1,204 participants. When people could choose, they tended to avoid situations that required empathy. They saw empathy as effortful, unpleasant and not very effective. When the researchers raised people's sense that they could empathize well, the avoidance disappeared. In human services, staff face others' distress constantly. If empathy feels like a demand with no payoff, people will protect themselves by pulling back. Leaders can help by making empathy feel effective: giving staff concrete things to ask and do, and showing them when their response helped.

sections.title: Compassion versus distress
sections.text: Klimecki and colleagues found that before training, watching others suffer produced negative feelings and activity in brain regions linked to sharing pain. After compassion training, people reported more positive feeling while watching suffering, with activity in regions linked to affiliation. Leiberg and colleagues found that short-term compassion training increased helping toward strangers in a lab game. These are small lab studies. They suggest a distinction worth knowing: sharing someone's distress can wear you down, while warm concern paired with a wish to help may be easier to sustain.

sections.title: Differential effects
sections.text: This review did not verify any differences in emotional intelligence or empathy by race, disability or other group, so this course makes no such claims. One verified difference is by job type: ability-based emotional skills mattered more for performance in high emotional labor jobs. Be careful, too, about reading emotion across cultural or communication differences. Expressions and signals vary. The perspective research gives the same answer here as elsewhere: ask rather than infer.

sections.title: Harder situation: the colleague does not want to talk
sections.text: Asking does not mean pressing. If a colleague says they are fine, accept it, and leave the door open with something specific, such as checking in at the end of the shift. Still handle the practical track: make sure the fact in question is verified and the caller is contacted. Support should never depend on someone's willingness to share feelings.

sections.title: Harder situation: empathy and accuracy conflict
sections.text: Sometimes the empathic response and the accurate response pull apart. A worker may want reassurance that they gave the right information when they did not. Empathy does not mean agreeing. Acknowledge how hard the call was, then be clear about what needs correcting and who will do it. The caller's interests and the worker's feelings both matter. Neither is served by hiding an error.

sections.title: Harder situation: someone uses emotional intelligence as a label
sections.text: Teams sometimes describe a colleague as having low emotional intelligence. It sounds like insight, but it is a label based on impressions, often of style. Given how disputed the measures are, do not use emotional intelligence scores or labels to judge people. Describe the specific behavior instead, such as interrupting callers or not checking a fact, and work on that.

sections.title: Practicing the skill
sections.text: Because training seems to work better with practice and feedback, pick one skill and practice it deliberately for a few weeks. For example, before offering advice in any check-in, ask one open question about what the situation meant to the other person. Afterward, notice whether the answer surprised you. Surprises are evidence that asking added information you would not have guessed.

sections.title: Empathy across difference
sections.text: The perspective research has a direct lesson for working across differences in culture, disability, age or experience. The more different someone's situation is from yours, the less your imagination has to work with, and the more likely you are to fill gaps with assumptions. Asking is even more important here. Ask open questions about what a situation means to the person, and accept answers that differ from what you expected. Do not assume that a person's background tells you how they feel.

sections.title: Protecting your own capacity
sections.text: Supervisors absorb their team's distress as well as their own. If empathy feels like a constant drain, the avoidance Cameron and colleagues found is likely to set in. You may start keeping check-ins short or steering away from hard topics. Two things from the research may help. First, feeling effective reduces avoidance, so focus on concrete steps you can take. Second, the compassion studies suggest that warm concern with a wish to help may be easier to sustain than sharing someone's distress. These are lab findings, and they do not replace rest, workload limits or professional support where needed.

sections.title: Using emotional skills in conflict
sections.text: Emotional skills are most useful when you are under pressure. In a tense meeting, it is easy to read emotion into small signals and to feel sure about it. The perspective research found that imagining can raise confidence without raising accuracy. Use the same habits. Ask rather than infer. If you think someone is frustrated, say what you noticed and ask whether you have it right. Check facts before responding to a challenge. Keep the conversation on the work question, not on motives.

simulation.setup: You supervise a disability services call line. An experienced call-line worker comes to a scheduled check-in visibly upset. A caller whose in-home services were recently reduced was angry and frightened, and said they did not know who to contact if a support worker did not show up. The worker gave a phone number from memory. What is at stake: the worker's well-being, the caller's access to the right help, and whether the worker brings the next hard call to you.

steps.situation: The worker sits down and says the call was rough. You already know the procedure for service reduction calls and have three suggestions ready.
steps.question: What do you do first?

choices.label: Ask what was hardest about the call for them, and listen before saying anything else.
choices.feedback: You get the perspective instead of guessing it. Across 25 experiments, asking improved accuracy about another person's thoughts and feelings, while imagining did not. You may learn the concern is not what you expected. It costs a few minutes before the practical steps.

choices.label: Say you can imagine how hard that must have been, then walk through the procedure for service reduction calls.
choices.feedback: This is warm and efficient, and the procedure matters. But you have guessed what was hard and moved to solutions. If the real concern is something else, your suggestions will miss it. Imagining a perspective felt helpful in the experiments but did not improve accuracy.

choices.label: Remind them that angry callers are part of the job and that they handled it as well as anyone could.
choices.feedback: Reassurance feels kind and protects the worker's confidence. But it closes the conversation before you know what happened. You also miss the chance to learn that the phone number given from memory may need checking.

steps.situation: The worker says the anger was hard, but what is really bothering them is the phone number. They are not sure it was right, and the caller may need it tonight if a support worker does not arrive.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Acknowledge their worry, then separate the tracks: you will verify the number now, and the worker or a colleague will call the caller back by a set time. Check whether the worker wants a short break first.
choices.feedback: You meet both needs. The worker gets support and a clear plan. The caller gets accurate information quickly, with a named person and time. Empathy here led directly to protecting the caller, because asking surfaced the real risk.

choices.label: Reassure them the number is probably right and suggest they check it tomorrow.
choices.feedback: This eases the worker's worry in the moment. But it puts comfort ahead of the caller's safety tonight. Empathy does not mean telling someone what they want to hear when a fact needs checking.

choices.label: Verify the number yourself and call the caller back, telling the worker you will handle it.
choices.feedback: The caller is protected, which matters most. But the worker loses a chance to close the loop and may feel the error was taken away from them. A short conversation about who calls back would serve both.

steps.situation: The worker nods and says thanks, but seems flat. As they stand to leave, they mention in passing that they gave the caller a number from memory and are not sure it was right.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Ask them to sit back down, say you are glad they mentioned it, and ask what worries them about it. Then verify the number and agree who will call the caller back and when.
choices.feedback: You recover the real issue. Thanking them makes it more likely they will raise the next one. Asking before acting gets you the full picture, and the caller still gets accurate information tonight.

choices.label: Tell them to check it when they get a chance.
choices.feedback: This trusts the worker, which is reasonable for an experienced person. But it leaves the timing and the caller's need unclear. The worker is already upset and may not prioritize it.

choices.label: Tell them not to worry, since numbers are usually right.
choices.feedback: It is tempting to end a hard check-in on a reassuring note. But a caller may need that number tonight. Reassurance without verification protects the conversation, not the caller.

steps.situation: At a team meeting the next week, you summarize the call as a lesson on handling angry callers. The same worker says, in front of everyone, that the real problem was that the reference sheet for service reduction calls has an outdated number.
steps.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Thank them, ask them to show the outdated entry, and say you will route it to the person or area responsible for the reference sheet and report back.
choices.feedback: You check the fact without defending your summary. That keeps it safe for the worker, and for everyone watching, to correct you. It also fixes the root cause. Emotional skill under pressure looks like curiosity, not composure for its own sake.

choices.label: Agree, and say both things matter: handling anger and keeping the sheet current.
choices.feedback: This is gracious and avoids friction. But without checking the entry and naming who will fix it, the correction may go nowhere. The team learns that corrections are welcomed but not acted on.

choices.label: Say you will discuss the reference sheet with them after the meeting, and continue with the lesson on angry callers.
choices.feedback: It keeps the meeting on track and avoids a public back-and-forth. But it signals that being corrected in public is unwelcome. Others with similar concerns may stay quiet. The worker's point was the more important one.

simulation.debrief: The first choice shaped everything after it. Asking what was hardest surfaced the real risk, a phone number a caller might need that night. That is the perspective-getting the experiments support. Imagining or reassuring felt kind but left the real concern hidden until the worker was leaving. Across the path, empathy and accuracy worked together. Acknowledging the worker's distress did not mean agreeing the number was fine. It meant naming who would verify it and who would call back. The last decision tested emotional skill under correction. Checking the fact and fixing the reference sheet treated the correction as information. None of this depends on an emotional intelligence score. It depends on specific habits: ask, separate support from protection, and check facts when challenged.

mistakes.mistake: Trusting your imagination about how someone feels.
mistakes.why: Putting yourself in someone's shoes feels like understanding, and most people believe it improves accuracy. In 25 experiments, it did not.
mistakes.instead: Ask what the situation meant to them, then listen. Treat surprises as useful information.

mistakes.mistake: Jumping to solutions before you know the concern.
mistakes.why: Supervisors know the procedures and want to help quickly. But the concern may not be the one you are solving.
mistakes.instead: Ask one open question first. Then offer help that fits what you heard.

mistakes.mistake: Letting empathy replace accuracy.
mistakes.why: Reassurance eases distress in the moment, so it feels like the empathic choice. But it can leave the person being served at risk.
mistakes.instead: Acknowledge the feeling, then name who will verify the fact and who will follow up with the person affected.

mistakes.mistake: Buying into large claims about emotional intelligence scores.
mistakes.why: The idea is appealing and widely marketed. But the leadership link nearly disappears with ability tests and independent ratings, and experts still dispute it.
mistakes.instead: Ask how a claim was measured and who rated the outcome. Focus on specific, practiced behaviors.

mistakes.mistake: Labeling colleagues as having low emotional intelligence.
mistakes.why: It sounds like insight. But it is usually an impression of style, and the measures are contested.
mistakes.instead: Describe the specific behavior and its effect, and work on that.

mistakes.mistake: Getting defensive when corrected in public.
mistakes.why: Being corrected in front of others feels like a loss of standing. But your response teaches the team whether correction is safe.
mistakes.instead: Thank the person, check the fact, and say who will act.

jobAid.title: Supporting a colleague after a hard interaction
jobAid.use: Use it in a check-in after a difficult call, meeting or case, or whenever a colleague seems shaken.
steps: Ask one open question before offering advice: What was hardest about that for you?
Listen for the real concern. Is it the person served, an instruction, something they think they did wrong, or the emotion itself?
Acknowledge what you heard in plain words.
Separate two tracks: support for your colleague, and protection for the person they serve.
Name who will verify any fact in question, and who will follow up with the person served, by when.
Offer something concrete for your colleague, such as a short break or help thinking through the next call.
Close the loop later. Tell them what happened with the follow-up.

media.reason: The gap between imagined and real understanding is easiest to see in a dialogue, where one voice assumes and the other explains what was actually going on.

prompts: In which recurring check-in will you ask one open question before giving advice, and starting when?

title: Onboarding through the first year
objective: Plan and lead a new employee's first year so they understand the role, gain confidence in the work and feel accepted by the team.
outcomes: Check a new employee's progress on three things: role clarity, confidence in the core tasks and social acceptance.
Set up the first day so the person meets you, has working equipment and access, and has a named peer guide.
Hold planned check-ins at set points in the first year instead of waiting for problems to surface.
Ask what strengths the new employee brings and give them an early chance to use one.
Spot and stop early undermining, including your own, such as public correction or withheld information.

evidence.summary: Onboarding works mainly by helping new employees adjust in three ways: knowing what the job requires, feeling able to do it and feeling accepted. A meta-analysis of 70 newcomer samples found these three carry the link between onboarding and later satisfaction, commitment, performance and staying. Support from experienced colleagues is among the strongest levers. Support also tends to fade within 90 days, and early support or undermining predicts later outcomes better than later change. A field experiment found that a first-day session on newcomers' own strengths cut turnover. Limits: most studies are correlational, few are in public human services, and effects on turnover and performance are modest rather than large.

findings.claim: Role clarity, self-efficacy and social acceptance carry the effects of onboarding on satisfaction, commitment, performance, intent to stay and turnover.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis and path model of 70 unique newcomer samples; the model was generally supported. 2007.
findings.source: Bauer, Bodner, Erdogan, Truxillo and Tucker, 2007

findings.claim: Supervisor and coworker support for new employees declines within the first 90 days, and early support predicts 90-day outcomes better than later change.
findings.detail: 14-wave longitudinal study of 264 newcomers. Supervisor undermining was uniquely linked to a higher chance of leaving. 2013.

findings.claim: Having a workstation ready on Day 1 related to adjustment, and meeting the manager on Day 1 related to early social acceptance.
findings.detail: Longitudinal study of 985 new hires followed from Day 1 to the end of the first year, using newcomer, manager and company data. Fortune 500 technology organization. 2020.
findings.source: Bauer, Erdogan, Caughlin, Ellis and Kurkoski, 2020

findings.claim: A one-hour first-day session on newcomers' own strengths lowered turnover: the control group's turnover was 47.2 percent higher than the strengths group's.
findings.detail: Field experiment, 605 agents (96 strengths condition, 101 organizational pride condition, 408 controls) at a business process outsourcing firm in India, about six months of follow-up, plus a lab replication. 2013.

findings.claim: Support from experienced employees and affirming newcomers' existing skills are the tactics most strongly tied to good outcomes; onboarding links moderately to attitudes and modestly to performance and turnover.
findings.detail: Child welfare workforce summary of two meta-analyses (Bauer et al. 2007; Saks, Uggerslev and Fassina 2007, about 30 studies). Notes that experimental tests are still needed. 2020.
findings.source: QIC-WD, summarizing Saks, Uggerslev and Fassina, 2007

findings.claim: Honest job previews reduce turnover only slightly, and mainly by signaling that the organization is honest.
findings.detail: Meta-analytic path analysis of 52 studies, about 17,000 participants. Post-hire and longer previews were slightly more effective. 2011.

findings.claim: A 2025 update of the newcomer meta-analysis again highlighted social acceptance as central to adjustment.
findings.detail: Review and meta-analysis: 256 studies identified, 183 analyzed; adjustment measured as role clarity, task mastery, social acceptance and fit. 2025.
findings.source: Bauer, Erdogan, Ellis, Truxillo, Brady and Bodner, 2025 (repository record)

counterintuitive.headline: Asking new staff about themselves beat teaching them pride in the organization.
counterintuitive.text: Many onboarding programs lead with the organization's mission, history and reputation. In a field experiment, Cable, Gino and Staats (2013) added a one-hour first-day session to standard training. One group reflected on their own strengths and how they might use them. Another heard about the company's achievements. Six months later, turnover in the standard-training group was 47.2 percent higher than in the strengths group. The pride group did better than standard training but worse than the strengths group. The study was in a company call center in India, so treat it as a strong signal, not a guarantee.

sections.title: What onboarding is for
sections.text: A new employee in DHS may already know Minnesota human services well. They still have to learn three things in your unit. First, what the job actually requires and who decides what. Second, whether they can do the core tasks well. Third, whether the team accepts them. Researchers call these role clarity, self-efficacy and social acceptance. A meta-analysis of 70 newcomer samples found these three carry most of the link between onboarding and later satisfaction, commitment, performance and staying. A welcome packet or an orientation session helps only to the extent that it moves one of these three.

sections.title: Why the first weeks count most
sections.text: Support for new employees tends to fade. In a study that checked in with 264 new hires 14 times, help from supervisors and coworkers dropped within the first 90 days. Early experiences mattered more than later improvement. Early undermining from a supervisor, such as public criticism or withheld information, was uniquely linked to people leaving. The busy weeks after a new person starts are exactly when attention slips. Plan for that before the first day.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: Before the first day, write a short first-year plan with three columns. List what the person needs to understand, what they need to be able to do and who they need to know. Then do four things. Meet the person yourself on the first day. Make sure equipment and system access work. Name a peer guide and give that peer real time to help. In the first week, ask the new employee what strengths they bring and how they would like to use them. Then find an early task that uses one. Put check-ins on the calendar at about two weeks, 30 days, 90 days, six months and one year. At each one, ask about the three areas rather than only asking how things are going.

sections.title: The three signs of adjustment
sections.text: Bauer and colleagues (2007) pooled 70 samples of new employees. They found that organizational onboarding practices and newcomers' own information seeking affect outcomes mainly through role clarity, self-efficacy and social acceptance. A 2025 update of that review, covering 183 studies in its analysis, again highlighted social acceptance. This gives you a practical test. At each check-in, ask yourself three questions. Can this person describe what good work looks like and who approves what? Do they feel able to handle the common cases, and the hard ones? Do they have people they can go to without hesitation? A no on any one of these is where to focus next.

sections.title: Who helps, and when
sections.text:
A child welfare workforce summary of two meta-analyses found the strongest onboarding tactics were support from experienced employees and affirming the skills newcomers already bring. It mattered less whether new staff went through a separate group program. That points to the peer guide. Choose a peer who explains the reasons behind routines, not just the steps. Give them protected time on their own workload. Keep your own role clear: you set priorities, expectations and feedback; the peer shows how the work is done day to day. Tell the new employee both roles so they know where to take a simple question and where to take a concern.

Timing matters too. In the 90-day study by Kammeyer-Mueller and colleagues, support fell over the first three months. Early levels of support and undermining predicted later outcomes better than changes did. Undermining includes things a busy supervisor might not notice. Examples are correcting someone in front of others, leaving them out of a key thread or making them feel foolish for asking. Supervisor undermining was the one behavior uniquely linked to higher odds of leaving.

sections.title: The first day and first month
sections.text:
A study of 985 new hires found that a ready workstation on Day 1 related to adjustment. Meeting one's manager on Day 1 related to early social acceptance. In DHS terms, that means requesting system access, a working laptop and badge access well before the start date. If an access request is still pending, plan real work the person can do without it, such as shadowing calls or reading current bulletins with the peer guide. Meet the person in the first hours, even briefly, if you work in different places or remotely.

In the first month, build learning around real tasks in a sensible order. Someone joining an eligibility or disability services team might start by observing how a colleague explains a common decision. Next they handle a routine case with the peer reviewing. Then they handle one alone and talk it through afterward. Point them to the current policy manuals and bulletins, and to the person or area responsible for each kind of exception.

sections.title: Start with their strengths
sections.text: Cable, Gino and Staats (2013) ran a field experiment with 605 new call-center agents. A one-hour first-day session asked one group to reflect on their best qualities and how to use them at work. Six months later, turnover in the standard-training group was 47.2 percent higher than in that group. In your first conversation, ask what work the person has done that they are proud of and what they would like to keep doing. Find an early, real assignment that uses that strength, such as plain-language writing, data work or experience with a county partner. This builds confidence and signals that the team values what they bring.

sections.title: Separate today's needs from later learning
sections.text: New employees in DHS often face a long list of required trainings in the first weeks, from data practices to security awareness. Required training matters, but it does little for confidence in the core tasks unless it connects to real work. Sort the first-year plan into three groups. The first group is what the person needs this week to act safely. Examples are data practices, how to route a sensitive call and who to ask before sending a decision. The second group is what they will learn through supported practice in the first three months, such as the common case types in your area. The third group is what can wait, such as rare exceptions and history. Tell the new employee which group each item is in. That alone reduces the anxiety of trying to learn everything at once, and it helps role clarity by showing what matters first.

sections.title: Check-ins that ask the right questions
sections.text: Set the check-in dates before the first day. At two weeks, ask what has been confusing and who they have gone to for help. At 30 days, ask which tasks feel solid and which still feel shaky. At 90 days, ask how connected they feel to the team and where they still feel like an outsider. At six months and one year, ask what they now understand about the role that they wish they had known earlier. Use the answer to fix the plan for the next new hire. Keep notes about the work, not about the person's personal life.

sections.title: How strong is this evidence?
sections.text: The onboarding research is large but mostly correlational. The QIC-WD summary of the two main meta-analyses describes links between onboarding and attitudes, such as satisfaction, commitment and intent to quit, as moderate. Links to performance and actual turnover are modest. That is honest and useful: good onboarding improves the odds, but it will not overcome a role that is badly designed or a team with deep conflict. Cable and colleagues ran one of very few field experiments, and it was in a company call center outside the United States with entry-level staff. Public human-services onboarding research with measured outcomes is scarce. Use the findings as solid guidance and watch what happens in your own unit.

sections.title: Experienced hires need onboarding too
sections.text: Supervisors often assume an experienced hire needs less support. The research reviewed here does not settle how much experience changes onboarding needs, so plan on a different kind of help, not none. Someone who has worked in a county human services agency or another state department brings deep knowledge. That knowledge can hide gaps. Their old agency may have handled an exception differently, used different systems or routed a decision to a different role. Ask experienced hires to tell you what they expect to be the same and what they expect to differ. Then check those assumptions against current DHS policy with them. Respect their expertise while being specific about local practice.

sections.title: Remote and hybrid starts
sections.text: The Day 1 study found that meeting the manager mattered for early acceptance. In hybrid work, a new person may go days without casual contact. Plan for the contact that would otherwise happen by chance. Schedule short daily touchpoints with you or the peer guide in the first two weeks. Invite the person to team calls where they can listen before they are expected to contribute. Introduce them by name and role in team channels and explain what they will be working on. If some staff work on site and some remotely, make sure the new person is not cut off from the informal channel where real answers get shared.

sections.title: Internal moves and promotions
sections.text: Onboarding is not only for new hires. When someone moves from a call line to a policy role, or a staff member becomes a supervisor, they face the same three questions. They need to know what the new role requires, whether they can do it and whether their new peers accept them. People who move inside DHS are often given less onboarding because they already know the systems. The research reviewed here studied organizational newcomers, so it does not directly test internal moves. Still, the three signs of adjustment are a sensible guide. A newly promoted supervisor may know every policy and still be unsure who approves overtime or how to handle a performance concern. Give internal movers a short first-year plan, a peer in a similar role and the same check-in schedule. Ask explicitly what is different in the new role, because old habits from the previous role can feel like competence when they no longer fit.

sections.title: When a newcomer is not adjusting
sections.text: Sometimes, at 90 days, a person still cannot describe what good work looks like or still seems isolated. Start by checking the system, not the person. Was the peer guide given time? Did access arrive late? Are instructions out of date or contradictory across teams? Are two leads giving different answers? Ask the new employee directly which of the three areas feels hardest. If the gap is role clarity, write down the decisions they own and the ones they should route elsewhere, including who to go to. If it is confidence, give a smaller set of case types and review them together until they feel solid. If it is acceptance, look honestly at how the team treats new people. Kammeyer-Mueller and colleagues found undermining from supervisors carried unique risk. Ask a trusted peer whether you have been short or dismissive under pressure.

sections.title: When you are new too
sections.text: Sometimes the supervisor is also recent to the unit. You may not know which instructions are current or who really owns an exception. Say so plainly, and make the search for answers part of onboarding. Ask the new employee and the peer guide to keep a shared list of questions that had no clear answer. Bring that list to your own manager or to the person or area responsible for each topic. This models information seeking, which the 2007 meta-analysis found works alongside organizational practices to build adjustment. It also gives you a faster route to your own role clarity.

sections.title: Fairness in who gets support
sections.text: Informal support tends to flow to people who resemble the existing team or who ask for help easily. Social acceptance is one of the three core signs of adjustment, so uneven informal support can produce uneven outcomes. The research reviewed here does not show different effects for specific racial, disability or other groups, so do not assume one. Instead, make the core supports structured and the same for everyone: the same first-day meeting, a named peer guide, the same check-in schedule and the same introductions. Ask each person what helps them learn and what gets in the way. Arrange disability accommodations and accessible materials before the first day when the person has asked for them, through the person or area responsible for accommodations.

sections.title: Honest previews and the hard parts of the job
sections.text: Some DHS jobs carry heavy emotional content, rigid timelines or difficult calls. A meta-analysis of 52 studies found honest previews of the job reduce turnover only slightly, and mainly because they show the organization is being honest. Post-hire previews were slightly more effective than pre-hire ones. So in the first weeks, name the hard parts plainly. Tell the person what tends to be difficult, how experienced staff handle it and where support is available. Do not oversell the job, and do not frighten people either. The goal is trust.

sections.title: Using the first year to improve the system
sections.text: Minnesota's executive branch lost about 9 percent of its workforce in FY 2023, and human services had particularly high turnover in recent years. Each departure brings another onboarding. Treat each first year as information. At the one-year check-in, ask what the person wishes they had been told in week one, which instructions were wrong or outdated and which colleague helped most. Thank that colleague and tell their supervisor if they report to someone else. Update the first-year plan template. Share stale or conflicting guidance with the person or area responsible for it. Over a few hires, the onboarding plan becomes a reliable map of how the work actually happens.

simulation.setup: You are a Human Services Supervisor on a Disability Services Division team that answers questions from county case managers and providers about waiver policy. A new Policy Specialist starts Monday. They spent six years at a county human services agency. Your team is short two people, a policy bulletin is due in three weeks, and the peer you planned to assign as a guide is covering the team inbox. What is at stake is whether this experienced hire settles in and stays, and whether the inbox and the bulletin hold together while they do.

steps.situation: It is Thursday before the start date. Laptop and system access requests are still pending. Your planned peer guide says they can help a bit but are buried in the inbox.
steps.question: How do you prepare for Monday?

choices.label: Escalate the access requests today, reassign part of the inbox so the peer guide has protected time, and block an hour on Monday morning to meet the new specialist yourself.
choices.feedback: This covers the three Day 1 basics linked to adjustment in a study of 985 new hires: working equipment, meeting the manager and a person to go to. Moving inbox work costs the team something this week, but support for new hires tends to fade fast, and early support predicts later outcomes better than later effort does.

choices.label: Since they have six years of county experience, send a welcome email with links to the policy manual and plan to meet once things calm down next week.
choices.feedback: It is tempting, because the person really is experienced. But meeting the manager on Day 1 related to early social acceptance, and experience can hide gaps in local practice. A link list does not tell them who decides what in your unit. Next week will not be calmer.

choices.label: Ask the peer guide to fit in an hour with the new specialist on Monday, and plan your own meeting for Wednesday.
choices.feedback: The peer contact helps, and an hour is better than nothing. But the peer has no protected time, so help is likely to be rushed, and you miss the Day 1 meeting linked to early acceptance. Also, pending access may leave the person with nothing real to do.

steps.situation: Monday goes well. Access arrives Tuesday. In your first conversation, the new specialist mentions they wrote plain-language guides for families at the county and liked that work most.
steps.question: What do you do with that?

choices.label: Ask them to draft the family-facing summary section of the upcoming bulletin, with the peer guide reviewing for current policy.
choices.feedback: This is the move from the strengths field experiment: an early, real task that uses what the person does well. It builds confidence and shows the team values what they bring. Pairing it with a peer review keeps the policy accurate, since county practice may differ from current DHS guidance. The task is also visible to the team, which helps acceptance.

choices.label: Note it for later. First they need to learn the waiver policy basics before taking on anything visible.
choices.feedback: Sequencing learning is sound, and caution about visible work is understandable with a bulletin due. But holding back a clear strength misses a cheap chance to build confidence and belonging. Affirming the skills newcomers already bring was among the strongest onboarding tactics in the meta-analytic evidence, and a reviewed draft carries little risk.

steps.situation: By Wednesday the new specialist has answered three inbox questions using their county agency's approach to a waiver exception. A county case manager has replied, confused, copying a lead worker. The lead worker corrects the answer in a reply-all.
steps.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Meet the specialist one to one that day, explain the current policy and who approves this exception, and ask the lead worker to bring corrections to you or the specialist directly next time.
choices.feedback: This fixes the role clarity gap and stops early undermining. A public correction, even an accurate one, is the kind of experience that predicted worse outcomes in the 90-day study. Talking to the lead worker addresses the team habit, not just the one email.

choices.label: Reply-all yourself to confirm the lead worker's correction so the county has one clear answer.
choices.feedback: Clear answers to counties matter, and the instinct to close the loop is sound. But a second public correction deepens the newcomer's sense of being an outsider. Supervisor undermining was uniquely linked to leaving in the 90-day study. You can give the county a clear answer without making the new person the example.

choices.label: Tell the specialist to hold off on the inbox until they finish the policy training modules.
choices.feedback: This prevents more errors in the short term, and it feels protective. But it removes the person from real work and does not explain what went wrong or who decides this exception. Confidence grows through supported practice on real tasks, not only through modules, and a sudden pullback can read as a judgment.

steps.situation: It is the 90-day mark. The specialist's work is now accurate. In your check-in they say they still feel like they are on the edge of the team and do not know who to ask about some county questions.
steps.question: What is your next step?

choices.label: Ask what would help them feel connected, introduce them to two colleagues who handle related county questions, and add them to the team's informal case-discussion channel.
choices.feedback: Accurate work shows role clarity and confidence are coming along. Social acceptance is the gap, and the 2025 update of the meta-analysis highlighted it. Specific introductions and access to where real answers get shared address it directly. Asking first respects how they prefer to connect.

choices.label: Reassure them that their work is strong and that feeling settled takes time.
choices.feedback: The reassurance is kind and partly true, since adjustment tends to rise over time. But the person has named a specific gap. Support fades after the early weeks unless someone plans for it, so waiting may let the gap harden.

simulation.debrief: The strongest path treated onboarding as three tasks: role clarity, confidence and acceptance. It front-loaded effort in the first days, because support fades within 90 days and early experiences predict later outcomes. Day 1 basics, a meeting with you and a peer with real time are small actions linked to better adjustment. Using the specialist's writing strength followed the field experiment in which a first-day focus on personal strengths reduced turnover. The public correction branch shows how ordinary team habits can become early undermining. At 90 days, good work did not mean full adjustment; acceptance still needed deliberate attention. These effects are moderate rather than dramatic, and most evidence is correlational, so watch what happens and adjust.

mistakes.mistake: Treating orientation as onboarding.
mistakes.why: Orientation is visible and easy to schedule, so it feels like the job is done. But the research shows onboarding works through role clarity, confidence and acceptance, which grow over months.
mistakes.instead: Plan the whole first year, with check-ins on the three areas at set points.

mistakes.mistake: Giving experienced hires less support.
mistakes.why: Respect for expertise is genuine. But past practice in a county agency or another department can differ from current DHS policy, and those gaps stay hidden until an error surfaces.
mistakes.instead: Ask what they expect to be the same and different, and check those assumptions together early.

mistakes.mistake: Assigning a peer guide with no time.
mistakes.why: Supervisors assume a good colleague will make it work. Support from experienced staff is one of the strongest tactics, but only if it actually happens, and support tends to fade within 90 days.
mistakes.instead: Move some of the peer's workload and tell both people what the guide role covers.

mistakes.mistake: Correcting a new person in front of others.
mistakes.why: Quick public corrections feel efficient and accurate. In a 90-day study, supervisor undermining was uniquely linked to leaving, and early negative experiences set a lasting tone.
mistakes.instead: Correct privately and promptly, and ask the team to bring concerns to you or the new person directly.

mistakes.mistake: Leading with the organization's history and pride.
mistakes.why: Mission matters, and leaders want new staff to share it. A field experiment found a session on newcomers' own strengths reduced turnover more than one on organizational pride.
mistakes.instead: Ask about their strengths early and give them a real task that uses one, then connect it to the mission.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming good work means the person has settled in.
mistakes.why: Performance is the easiest thing to see. Social acceptance is less visible and was highlighted in the 2025 meta-analysis as central to adjustment.
mistakes.instead: Ask directly who they can go to and where they still feel like an outsider.

jobAid.title: First-year onboarding plan
jobAid.use: Fill it in before a new employee starts and bring it to each check-in during their first year.
steps: Before Day 1: request equipment, system access and any accommodations the person has asked for; name a peer guide and move some of their work.
Day 1: meet the person yourself, explain your role and the peer guide's role, and ask what strengths they bring.
Week 1: give one real task that uses a strength, with a review step for current policy.
Weeks 2 to 6: sequence tasks from observing, to doing with review, to doing alone and debriefing.
At 2 weeks, 30 days, 90 days, 6 months and 1 year, ask: Do you know what good work looks like and who decides what? Which tasks feel solid and which feel shaky? Who can you go to without hesitation?
If any answer is weak, change the plan for that area, and check the system first: time, access and instructions.
At 1 year, ask what they wish they had known in week one, and update the plan and any outdated guidance with the person or area responsible.

media.reason: The core lesson is one framework applied across a timeline. A single calm narrator can walk the learner through the first year in order.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text:
Picture a new employee's first morning. They arrive knowing a lot about Minnesota human services. They do not yet know who approves an exception in your unit, whether they can handle a difficult call, or whether the team will welcome them. Those three questions are the core of onboarding. Researchers call them role clarity, self-efficacy and social acceptance. When Bauer and colleagues pooled 70 samples of new employees, these three explained most of how onboarding connects to later satisfaction, commitment, performance and staying.

So the test of any onboarding activity is simple. Does it help the person understand the role, feel able to do it, or feel accepted? If not, it may be ceremony.

Now think about timing. In one study, researchers checked in with 264 new hires 14 times across their first 90 days. Support from supervisors and coworkers dropped over that period. And the early weeks mattered most. Early support, or early undermining, predicted later outcomes better than any later change. Undermining is often small. It is a correction in front of others, a key email the new person was left off, or a sigh when they ask a basic question. Undermining by a supervisor was the one behavior uniquely linked to people leaving.

That means your effort should come early. Before the first day, make sure equipment and access will work. In a study of 985 new hires, a ready workstation on Day 1 was linked to better adjustment, and meeting the manager on Day 1 was linked to feeling accepted. Name a peer guide, and give that person real time by moving some of their work. Support from experienced colleagues is among the strongest tactics in the research.

Then ask about strengths. In a field experiment with 605 new call-center agents, a one-hour first-day session on each person's best qualities cut turnover. Six months later, the standard-training group's turnover was 47.2 percent higher. Ask what work the person is proud of, and find an early real task that uses it.

Finally, put check-ins on the calendar now: two weeks, 30 days, 90 days, six months and one year. At each, ask about the three questions. Good work at 90 days is encouraging, but it does not mean the person feels part of the team. Ask who they can go to without hesitation.

The evidence here is solid but modest. Most studies are correlational, and few come from public human services. Good onboarding improves the odds. It does not fix a poorly designed job. Watch what happens with each new hire, and improve the plan for the next one.

prompts: Who is the next person to join or change roles on your team, and which of the three areas, role clarity, confidence or acceptance, is likely to be hardest for them?
Which experienced colleague could serve as a peer guide, and what work could you move so they have real time, and when will you ask them?
Which check-in dates will you put on the calendar this week, and what one question will you ask at each?
