title: Why people stay
objective: Learn what keeps the people on your team in their jobs and act on the factors a supervisor can actually change.
outcomes: Explain why no single factor, including pay, explains most decisions to leave or stay.
Hold a stay conversation that surfaces what ties a person to the job and what is pulling them away.
Strengthen links, fit and what a person would give up by leaving, using changes within your authority.
Tell the difference between what you control, what you can raise with the person or area responsible, and what you cannot change.
Avoid treating one person's exit reasons, or talk of leaving, as the full story.

evidence.summary: The largest meta-analysis of why people leave, covering 316 articles, found many factors each matter a little. Job satisfaction, commitment, embeddedness and leadership each relate to leaving about as strongly as one another. Pay matters but less than many assume. Embeddedness, meaning a person's links to others, fit with the work and what they would give up by leaving, predicts staying even after satisfaction is accounted for. In human services, attitudes, stress, burnout and support predict intent to leave more than demographics do. Limits: nearly all of this is correlational, many studies measure intent rather than actual leaving, and ways to raise embeddedness are suggested but untested.

findings.claim: Job satisfaction (rho = -.28), organizational commitment (-.29), embeddedness (-.26) and leadership (-.24) each relate to leaving about equally; pay relates less strongly (-.17).
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 316 articles; satisfaction k = 174, N = 107,625; pay k = 55, N = 177,634; leadership k = 42. 2018 (online 2017).

findings.claim: Intent to leave is the strongest single predictor of leaving (rho = .56), but intent is not the same as leaving, and some people quit with no other job lined up.
findings.detail: Same meta-analysis; withdrawal cognitions k = 211, N = 73,405; job alternatives rho = .23, k = 79. 2018.

findings.claim: Embeddedness on and off the job predicts lower intent to leave and lower actual turnover, even after controlling for satisfaction, commitment and alternatives.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 65 independent samples, N = 42,907. 2012.
findings.source: Jiang, Liu, McKay, Lee and Mitchell, 2012

findings.claim: In U.S. public child welfare, commitment and job satisfaction most strongly predicted intent to leave; demographics had small or negligible effects; stress and burnout had medium to high effects; fairness perceptions were relatively high.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 22 studies and 36 predictors. 2014.

findings.claim: Across child welfare, social work and other human services, burnout, dissatisfaction, available alternatives, low commitment, stress and lack of support predicted leaving or intent to leave.
findings.detail: Review and meta-analysis of 25 studies. 2001.

findings.claim: Strategies to increase embeddedness, such as building connections and better fit, are suggested but untested.
findings.detail: Child welfare workforce evidence summary; embeddedness described as moderately predictive of turnover. 2020.

findings.claim: About 9 percent of Minnesota executive branch employees left state service in FY 2023; about two-thirds of them resigned and the rest retired. Human services had particularly high turnover in recent years.
findings.detail: State workforce report, FY 2023 data. 2024.

counterintuitive.headline: Liking the job is only part of why people stay.
counterintuitive.text: Many supervisors assume people stay because they are satisfied and leave because they are not. Jiang and colleagues (2012) pooled 65 samples covering 42,907 people. Embeddedness, meaning links to colleagues, fit with the work and what a person would give up by leaving, predicted both intent to leave and actual leaving. It did so even after accounting for satisfaction, commitment and job alternatives. In other words, two equally satisfied employees can differ in how likely they are to stay. The one with more ties and more to lose is more likely to stay. This shifts attention to connections and fit, which supervisors can often influence.

sections.title: No single reason
sections.text: When a good employee leaves, it is natural to look for the reason. Usually there is not one. The largest meta-analysis of why people leave pooled 316 articles. Job satisfaction, commitment, embeddedness and the quality of leadership each related to leaving at about the same modest strength. Pay mattered too, but less than any of those. Intent to leave was the strongest predictor, yet it is not the same as leaving. Some people who talk about leaving stay, and some people quit with no other job lined up. So a retention plan built on one reason, such as a pay request, usually misses most of what keeps people.

sections.title: What ties people to the work
sections.text: Researchers use the term embeddedness for the web that holds someone in a job. It has three parts. Links are the relationships a person has with colleagues, partners and the people they serve. Fit is how well the work matches their skills, values and goals. Sacrifice is what they would give up by leaving, such as a schedule that works, projects they care about or trusted colleagues. Across 65 samples, embeddedness predicted staying even after satisfaction and commitment were taken into account.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: Have a stay conversation with each person on your team, not only with people you fear might leave. Ask three questions. What keeps you in this work? What would make it harder to picture yourself here in a year? What is one thing that could change to make the job work better for you? Listen for links, fit and what matters most to them. Then act on one thing you control within a stated time, and tell the person what you did. If the issue sits outside your authority, say so, and raise it with the person or area responsible. Do not promise what you cannot deliver.

sections.title: What the big meta-analysis shows
sections.text:
Rubenstein, Eberly, Lee and Mitchell (2018) updated decades of turnover research using 316 articles. Their corrected correlations give a sense of scale. Job satisfaction was -.28 with leaving, based on 174 samples and more than 107,000 people. Organizational commitment was -.29. Embeddedness was -.26. Leadership was -.24. Pay was -.17, based on 55 samples and more than 177,000 people. Stress or exhaustion was +.21, and the availability of other jobs was +.23. These are all modest. No single factor decides whether people stay. Each one shifts the odds a little.

Two practical points follow. First, pay is real, but it is not usually the whole story, and it is often outside a supervisor's control in state service anyway. Second, several factors with similar weight, such as satisfaction, leadership and embeddedness, are ones a supervisor shapes every day.

sections.title: Intent is a signal, not a verdict
sections.text: Intent to leave was the strongest predictor in the meta-analysis, at .56. The authors still warned against treating intent as the same as leaving. Some people who mention leaving are venting after a hard week. Some people leave suddenly, without another job, after an event that changes how they see the work. When someone tells you they are thinking of leaving, treat it as useful information and ask what is behind it. When someone says nothing, do not assume they are settled.

sections.title: Embeddedness: links, fit and sacrifice
sections.text:
Jiang and colleagues (2012) pooled 65 samples covering 42,907 people. Embeddedness predicted lower intent to leave and lower actual turnover after controlling for satisfaction, commitment and job alternatives. A child welfare workforce summary describes it as moderately predictive of turnover. In DHS work, links might include a strong relationship with a county partner, a peer who reviews hard cases together, or a project team. Fit might mean an analyst gets to use data skills rather than only manual checks. It might mean a call-line worker who values direct service still gets direct service. Sacrifice might include a schedule that fits caregiving, a stretch project or flexibility they value.

The summary is honest about a limit. Strategies to raise embeddedness, such as building connections and better fit, are suggested but not tested. Use them as reasoned practice, not as proven programs.

sections.title: What the human services evidence adds
sections.text: Two meta-analyses focus on human services. Mor Barak, Nissly and Levin (2001) reviewed 25 studies of child welfare, social work and other human service employees. Burnout, job dissatisfaction, available alternatives, low commitment, stress and lack of social support predicted leaving or intent to leave. Kim and Kao (2014) pooled 22 studies of U.S. public child welfare workers. Commitment and job satisfaction had the strongest links to intent to leave. Stress and burnout had medium to high effects. Fairness perceptions were relatively strong. Demographic factors such as age, race and gender had small or negligible effects. Both reviews point to working conditions and relationships, which leaders can influence, rather than to who the employee is.

sections.title: Running a stay conversation
sections.text: A stay conversation is a planned one-to-one about what keeps a person in the job. Hold it at a calm time, not during a performance concern or right after a crisis. Explain the purpose: you want to understand what works and what could work better. Ask open questions about links, fit and what matters most. What part of your work do you look forward to? Who do you rely on here? What would you miss if you left? What would make the next year harder? Listen more than you talk. Then choose one change within your authority. Examples include adjusting an assignment, connecting the person with a mentor or protecting time for a project they value. Give a date and follow up. Leave out personal details the person has not offered, and keep any notes about the work itself.

sections.title: Minnesota context
sections.text: In FY 2023, about 9 percent of Minnesota executive branch employees left state service. About two-thirds of those resigned and the rest retired. Minnesota Management and Budget noted that human services has had particularly high turnover in recent years, making it hard to rebuild staffing. Each departure means lost knowledge and more work for the people who stay, which can add to their stress. Retention work protects both the person and the team.

sections.title: Why correlations this small still matter
sections.text: A correlation of -.26 can sound weak. It means the factor explains only a small share of who leaves. But turnover has many causes, and each modest factor adds up. Small shifts across a team can change how many people leave in a year. The same small sizes are a caution. Do not expect a single program, such as a recognition event or a wellness week, to transform retention. Expect several steady practices to make a difference together.

sections.title: Limits of the research
sections.text: Almost all of this evidence is correlational. People who are more embedded may stay for reasons the studies did not measure. Kim and Kao measured intent to leave, not actual leaving. Randomized tests of retention practices, including stay conversations, are scarce, and the child welfare workforce summary describes embeddedness strategies as untested. The leadership correlation in the big meta-analysis averages many different measures of leadership, so it does not tell you which leader behaviors matter most. Treat the findings as a map of where to look, not as a promise that a given action will keep a given person.

sections.title: Pay, promotion and the limits of a supervisor's authority
sections.text: In state service, pay is set by classification and bargaining agreements. Supervisors usually cannot change it. Pay did predict leaving in the meta-analysis, at -.17, and the authors noted the effect is consistent. So do not dismiss it. When someone raises pay, be honest. Explain what you can and cannot change. If there is a legitimate classification question, raise it with the person or area responsible for classification. Then look at what you can change. Development, fit and recognition of skills often matter to the same person who raises pay.

sections.title: When the person wants growth you cannot offer
sections.text: Sometimes the best fit for a person's goals is another role, perhaps in another division or agency. Supporting that move can feel like losing. But fit is part of embeddedness, and a person stuck in a role with no growth may leave state service entirely. Helping someone find a next step inside DHS or state government keeps their knowledge in public service and shows others on the team that growth is possible. Talk with the person about stretch assignments, mentoring and visible project work that build toward their goal while they are still with you.

sections.title: Links in hybrid and remote work
sections.text: Many DHS teams now work in hybrid arrangements. Links, one of the three parts of embeddedness, can thin out when people rarely work alongside each other. The research reviewed here does not test hybrid work directly, so treat this as reasoned practice. Notice who has regular contact with colleagues and who works mostly alone. Build links into the work itself rather than adding social events people must attend on their own time. Pair people for case reviews. Rotate who presents at team meetings. Give newer staff a role on a cross-team project or a contact with a county partner. These ties are part of the job, so they also strengthen fit. Ask people how they prefer to connect, since some value quiet focus and some value frequent contact.

sections.title: When one person's ties create risk for others
sections.text: Embeddedness has a shadow side. A team where a few people are deeply linked can feel closed to newer staff, who may then be less embedded and more likely to leave. Watch who has links and who does not. Spread project roles, peer review and partner contacts so newer staff build ties too. Also watch for the person who stays only because leaving would cost too much, such as a schedule they cannot get elsewhere. Their satisfaction and fit may be low. Staying is not always thriving. That person may be quietly burning out, and stress and burnout predicted leaving in both human services meta-analyses.

sections.title: Recognition that fits the person
sections.text: Recognition is part of reward, and lack of support appeared as a predictor of leaving in the human services meta-analysis. But recognition works only when it lands as genuine. Some people value public thanks at a team meeting. Others find that uncomfortable and prefer a specific note or a word with their manager's manager. Ask. Make recognition specific: name the case, the partner or the problem the person solved and what difference it made. Recognition that names a skill also strengthens fit, because it tells the person their abilities are seen and used. Avoid treating recognition as a substitute for fixing an unworkable load. Thanks for carrying too much can sound like a request to keep doing it.

sections.title: Exit conversations and what they cannot tell you
sections.text: Exit interviews give one person's account at a moment when they have little reason to be fully candid. They may name pay or a new opportunity because those are easy to say. Use exit information, but weigh it with what you hear in stay conversations while people are still here. Patterns across several people tell you more than any single exit. Look for repeated mentions of workload, fairness, support or lack of growth, since those appeared as predictors in the human services research.

sections.title: Fairness across the team
sections.text: Kim and Kao found that perceptions of fairness and policy had relatively strong links to intent to leave. Stay conversations can create unfairness if only some people get them or if changes flow to the people who ask loudest. Hold stay conversations with everyone. Keep a simple, consistent process. When you change an assignment for one person, consider who else might want the same chance. The evidence reviewed here shows small or negligible demographic effects on intent to leave in child welfare. So do not assume that any group is more or less likely to leave. Ask each person.

sections.title: Harder situations
sections.text: Sometimes the reason a person is thinking of leaving is you, or a peer they work with closely. Leadership relates to leaving about as strongly as satisfaction does, so take this seriously. If someone hints at a problem with your style, ask for one specific example and thank them. If the problem is with a peer, address the behavior without exposing who raised it. If the problem is with workload across the whole unit, document the pattern and raise it with your own manager with a clear choice about what could move. Some departures cannot be prevented, such as retirement, a move or a family need. In those cases, focus on a good handoff and on the people who remain.

simulation.setup: You supervise a team of eligibility specialists in a DHS unit that processes Medical Assistance applications. Over six months, two experienced specialists have left. In each exit conversation they mentioned pay and better offers. Your manager has asked for a retention plan within a month. One of your strongest remaining specialists, who trains new staff and handles complex cases, has seemed quieter lately. What is at stake is whether you keep the people who hold the team together and whether your plan targets what you can actually change.

steps.situation: You are starting the retention plan. You have the two exit summaries and an hour blocked this week.
steps.question: Where do you begin?

choices.label: Schedule stay conversations with everyone on the team over the next three weeks, starting with people whose roles carry the most knowledge.
choices.feedback: This goes to the source while there is still time to act. Exit reasons such as pay are real but partial, and the big meta-analysis shows many factors each matter a little. Talking with everyone, not only those you worry about, also protects fairness, which predicted intent to leave in child welfare research.

choices.label: Draft a request to your manager for higher pay classifications, since both people named pay.
choices.feedback: It takes the exit reasons seriously, and pay does predict leaving. But pay was a weaker predictor than satisfaction, leadership or embeddedness, and classification is usually outside your control. Two exit summaries are also a thin base for a plan.

choices.label: Send a short anonymous survey asking what would make people stay.
choices.feedback: A survey can surface patterns and feels efficient. But it misses the follow-up questions that reveal links, fit and what matters to each person, and anonymous answers are hard to act on individually. It works better alongside conversations than instead of them.

steps.situation: In your stay conversation, the strong specialist says they like the work but feel stretched. They train every new hire on top of complex cases, and the peer they used to review hard cases with has left. They say a county agency has been recruiting them.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Thank them, ask which part of the load matters most to them, and within two weeks share new-hire training with a second specialist and set up a weekly hard-case review with a peer.
choices.feedback: This acts on what you heard: stress, a lost link and a sense of being stretched. It restores a link and reduces a demand while keeping the training role they may value. Stress and lack of support predicted leaving in human services meta-analyses. A specific date builds trust.

choices.label: Tell them how valued they are and ask them to let you know before they accept any offer.
choices.feedback: Recognition matters, and asking for notice is understandable. But it does not change the stretch or the lost peer link they named. It can also feel like you are managing the risk to you rather than the problem for them.

steps.situation: Your manager replies that pay classifications are set at the enterprise level and will not change this year. Meanwhile, the strong specialist sends you a calendar request titled 'quick question about a reference'.
steps.question: How do you respond to the specialist?

choices.label: Meet with them soon, ask openly what is prompting the reference and what would make the job work better, and listen before discussing anything else.
choices.feedback: Intent to leave is the strongest predictor, but it is not a verdict. This conversation is late, yet it can still surface what you control, such as load, links and fit. Listening first shows respect and gives you real information.

choices.label: Agree to give a strong reference and wish them well, since pay is the issue and you cannot fix it.
choices.feedback: Supporting someone's career is good practice, and a strong reference is a fair thing to give. But you are assuming pay is the whole story based on other people's exits. Embeddedness, workload and support may matter just as much to this person, and you have not asked. The chance to act may still be open.

steps.situation: Six weeks later, the specialist has stayed. Training is shared and the case review is running. Another specialist mentions they heard about the changes and would like a chance to train new staff too.
steps.question: What is your next step?

choices.label: Welcome the interest, set up a fair way for anyone interested to take part in training, and add what you have learned to the retention plan for your manager.
choices.feedback: This spreads links and development across the team and keeps the process fair, which matters because fairness perceptions predicted intent to leave. It also turns one success into a plan based on what people told you rather than on assumptions.

choices.label: Explain that training is covered for now and you will keep them in mind.
choices.feedback: Keeping the new arrangement stable is reasonable. But a clear request for development is a chance to build fit and links for a second person. Saying no without a path can quietly lower their sense that growth is possible here.

steps.situation: The specialist accepts the county position. On their last day, they mention that losing their review partner and carrying all the training mattered more than pay.
steps.question: What do you do with this?

choices.label: Thank them, then start stay conversations with the rest of the team and look first at load and peer support.
choices.feedback: This learns from the loss and acts while others are still here. The reasons the specialist gave match the human services research, which points to stress and support more than pay alone. Thanking them keeps the relationship open and a good handoff protects the team. It is the right move, just later than it could have been.

choices.label: Note it as one person's view and keep the plan focused on pay advocacy.
choices.feedback: One account is limited, that is true, and caution about overreacting is reasonable. But three departures now point beyond pay, and stress and lack of support are well-established predictors in human services. Holding to pay alone keeps you working on what you control least, while the people who remain carry the extra load.

simulation.debrief: The strongest path treated exit reasons as partial and asked current staff what keeps them in the work. That reflects the meta-analysis of 316 articles: many factors each matter a little, and pay matters less than satisfaction, leadership or embeddedness. The specialist named stress, a lost link and an uneven load. Acting on those within your authority, with a date, matches the human services evidence on stress and support and the embeddedness research on links and fit. Opening training to others kept the process fair. The weaker path waited for signs of leaving and anchored on pay, which is real but largely outside a supervisor's control. These findings are correlational, so they shift odds rather than guarantee outcomes.

mistakes.mistake: Taking exit reasons as the full story.
mistakes.why: Exit answers are concrete and easy to act on. But they give one person's account at a moment when they have little reason to be fully candid, and pay is an easy reason to name.
mistakes.instead: Weigh exit information with stay conversations and look for patterns across several people.

mistakes.mistake: Focusing retention on pay alone.
mistakes.why: Pay is visible and does predict leaving. But in the largest meta-analysis it was a weaker predictor than satisfaction, commitment, embeddedness or leadership, and supervisors rarely control it.
mistakes.instead: Be honest about pay limits and act on the factors you do influence.

mistakes.mistake: Only talking with people you think might leave.
mistakes.why: It feels efficient to focus on visible risk. But some people leave without warning, and selective attention can feel unfair to others, and fairness predicted intent to leave.
mistakes.instead: Hold stay conversations with everyone on a regular cycle.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming a quiet employee is a settled one.
mistakes.why: No complaints can look like satisfaction. Intent to leave is not always spoken, and some people quit with no job lined up.
mistakes.instead: Ask directly what keeps them and what would make the next year harder.

mistakes.mistake: Promising changes you cannot deliver.
mistakes.why: Wanting to keep a valued person creates pressure to say yes. Broken promises damage trust and leadership quality, which relates to leaving about as strongly as satisfaction.
mistakes.instead: Say what you control, what you will raise with the person or area responsible, and when you will follow up.

jobAid.title: Stay conversation guide
jobAid.use: Use it for a planned one-to-one with each person on your team, at a calm time, about once or twice a year.
steps: Explain the purpose: to understand what works for them and what could work better.
Ask: What part of your work do you look forward to?
Ask: Who do you rely on here, and who relies on you?
Ask: What would make it harder to picture yourself here in a year?
Listen for links, fit and what they would give up by leaving; ask one follow-up question before responding.
Name one change within your authority and a date; name anything you will raise with the person or area responsible.
Follow up on the date and tell them what happened, including what could not change and why.

media.reason: Retention decisions often hinge on a supervisor's assumptions. A dialogue lets a supervisor state the common assumptions and a more experienced manager test them against the evidence.

prompts: Which person on your team holds knowledge or links the team relies on, and when will you hold a stay conversation with them?
What is one link, fit or load change within your authority that you could make for someone this month?
Which issue that you heard about is outside your authority, who is the person or area responsible for it, and by when will you raise it?

theme: Teams and the work they carry

photo.alt: Two colleagues face each other across a small table, with a notebook open for the conversation.

title: Preventing burnout
objective: Recognize early signs of burnout and secondary traumatic stress on your team and change the work conditions behind them.
outcomes: Describe burnout as exhaustion, cynicism and reduced effectiveness caused by unmanaged chronic work stress, not a personal weakness.
Use the six areas of work life to find which conditions are driving strain on your team.
Choose a change to demands or resources before reaching for individual wellness programs.
Tell burnout apart from secondary traumatic stress and respond to each appropriately.
Check that relief for one person does not simply move the load to someone else.

evidence.summary: The World Health Organization describes burnout as a work phenomenon caused by chronic workplace stress that has not been managed. It is not a medical condition. Burnout grows from mismatches between people and their work in six areas: workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values. Meta-analyses show job demands raise burnout and job resources lower it. In controlled trials with physicians, changes to the organization of work reduced burnout more than programs aimed at individuals. A survey of 46,336 workers found people in individual wellbeing programs were no better off. Human services staff also face secondary traumatic stress from exposure to others' trauma. Limits: few strong trials exist, most are in health care, and evidence on preventing secondary traumatic stress is weak.

findings.claim: Burnout is a syndrome from chronic workplace stress that has not been managed, with three dimensions: exhaustion, mental distance or cynicism, and reduced professional efficacy. It is not classified as a medical condition.
findings.detail: ICD-11 definition, World Health Organization, 2019.

findings.claim: Burnout is more likely when people and their jobs are mismatched in six areas: workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values. Most interventions target individuals even though causes are largely situational.
findings.detail: Narrative review of four decades of research, World Psychiatry, 2016. Notes randomized trials are rare.

findings.claim: Job demands are positively associated with burnout and job resources negatively; demands seen as hindrances lower engagement while demands seen as challenges raise it.
findings.detail: Meta-analytic structural modeling test of the job demands-resources model, 2010.

findings.claim: Organization-directed interventions reduced burnout more (SMD -0.45) than physician-directed ones (SMD -0.19); overall effect SMD -0.31.
findings.detail: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 18 studies, 1,104 physicians, mostly randomized trials. Organization-directed changes were mainly workload or schedule changes, and were rare. 2017.

findings.claim: Workers who took part in resilience training, mindfulness or wellbeing apps appeared no better off on wellbeing measures than those who did not.
findings.detail: Cross-sectional survey of 46,336 workers in 233 UK organizations. Cannot establish cause. 2024.

findings.claim: Emotional exhaustion relates more strongly to job demands and resources than the other burnout dimensions do.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis largely of human service workers, 1996.

findings.claim: More than half of 992 child welfare workers and supervisors reported secondary traumatic stress symptoms in the prior week; support at work is protective, but intervention evidence is weak.
findings.detail: Child welfare workforce evidence brief summarizing meta-analyses (for example Cieslak et al. 2014, 41 papers) and a multi-site survey. 2023.

findings.claim: Social workers in direct practice are commonly exposed to secondary trauma, and many report at least some symptoms.
findings.detail: Mailed survey of 282 master's-level social workers, 2007.

counterintuitive.headline: Wellness programs for individuals showed little benefit.
counterintuitive.text: When burnout rises, organizations often offer resilience training, mindfulness sessions or wellbeing apps. Fleming (2024) surveyed 46,336 workers in 233 UK organizations. People who took part in these programs appeared no better off on several wellbeing measures than people who did not. The study is cross-sectional, so it cannot prove the programs fail. But it fits a meta-analysis of controlled trials with physicians by Panagioti and colleagues (2017). Changes to how work was organized, mostly workload and schedules, reduced burnout more than programs aimed at individuals. Supports for individuals can still help some people. They are not a substitute for changing the work.

sections.title: What burnout is
sections.text: The World Health Organization describes burnout as the result of chronic workplace stress that has not been managed. It has three parts. The first is exhaustion. The second is mental distance from the job, often felt as cynicism. The third is a sense of reduced effectiveness. Burnout is a work phenomenon, not a medical diagnosis or a character flaw. That matters for leaders, because it points to the work, not the person, as the main place to act. It also means burnout is not a sign that someone cares too little. Often it shows up in the people who care the most and carry the most.

sections.title: Where it comes from
sections.text: Researchers Maslach and Leiter describe six areas where people and their work can be mismatched: workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values. The bigger the mismatch, the more likely burnout becomes. Meta-analyses using the job demands and resources model reach a similar conclusion. Demands such as heavy caseloads and conflicting instructions raise burnout. Resources such as support, autonomy and clear roles lower it. In human services there is a second strain to watch. Secondary traumatic stress comes from hearing about or helping with other people's trauma. It is related to burnout but not the same.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: Look for the demand you can change before you suggest a wellness program. In controlled trials with physicians, changes to workload and schedules reduced burnout more than programs aimed at individuals. A large survey found people in individual wellbeing programs were no better off. Ask your team which recurring demand costs the most energy and what it pushes aside. Pick one you can change, such as a duplicate report, an unclear handoff or uncovered after-hours work. Change it, then check in two weeks that the relief did not simply land on someone else's desk.

sections.title: Recognizing the signs
sections.text: Burnout often shows first as exhaustion. A person starts the day already tired, ordinary tasks feel hard to begin or they stay late to catch up. Cynicism can follow. A caring worker starts speaking about callers or partners with distance or irritation. Then comes a sense that nothing they do makes a difference. Maslach and Leiter note that cynicism alone may be closer to the core of burnout than exhaustion alone. These signs have many possible causes, including events outside work. You do not need to diagnose anyone. Your job is to notice a pattern, ask about the work, and look at the conditions around it.

sections.title: The six areas in DHS work
sections.text: Use the six areas as a checklist for your team. Workload: are people regularly working past scheduled hours or skipping breaks? Control: can they decide how and when to do parts of their work? Reward: is the hidden work, such as coaching new staff or fixing routing errors, recognized? Community: do people have colleagues to talk through hard cases with? Fairness: do assignments and flexibility feel evenly shared? Values: are people asked to do things that conflict with why they chose human services, such as rushing calls with people in crisis? A mismatch in any one area can drive strain, and mismatches tend to compound.

sections.title: Demands and resources
sections.text: Crawford, LePine and Rich (2010) tested the job demands and resources model with meta-analytic modeling. Demands were linked to higher burnout and resources to lower burnout. They also found a useful distinction. Demands people see as hindrances, such as red tape, role conflict or unclear priorities, lowered engagement. Demands people see as challenges, such as a complex case they are equipped to handle, raised engagement. An earlier meta-analysis by Lee and Ashforth (1996), largely of human service workers, found demands and resources related most strongly to emotional exhaustion. In practice, removing a hindrance often does more than adding a perk. Clarify which of two conflicting instructions applies. Remove a duplicate approval. Give people the authority to resolve routine issues themselves.

sections.title: Why changing the work comes first
sections.text: Panagioti and colleagues (2017) pooled 18 controlled studies with 1,104 physicians. Interventions overall produced a small reduction in burnout. Changes directed at the organization, mostly reduced workload or changed schedules, had a larger effect than those aimed at individual physicians. Fleming (2024) surveyed 46,336 workers and found people in resilience, mindfulness or wellbeing app programs appeared no better off. Neither study proves individual support is useless. Both point the same way: change the work first. Then offer individual supports, such as the Employee Assistance Program, as an addition, not a replacement. Individual supports also matter for people facing strain from outside work, which no change to the job will fix.

sections.title: Secondary traumatic stress
sections.text: Many DHS and DSD roles involve hearing about abuse, crisis, loss or danger. Secondary traumatic stress mirrors trauma symptoms: intrusive thoughts, avoidance and feeling on edge. It comes from exposure to others' trauma rather than from workload or red tape. A child welfare workforce brief reports that more than half of 992 child welfare workers and supervisors had such symptoms in the prior week. A survey of 282 social workers found secondary exposure was common in direct practice. Predictors include the share of trauma-exposed cases a person carries and their own trauma history. Support from colleagues and supervisors is protective. If someone's work includes heavy trauma exposure, consider how that exposure is spread across the team, not just the total caseload.

sections.title: Check where the relief lands
sections.text: A common mistake is solving strain for one person by moving it to another. Give the overflow calls to the most reliable worker and you may protect one person while burning out the next. After any change, ask who picked up the work that moved. Check again in two weeks. Look at hours, breaks and who is covering after-hours or urgent follow-ups.

sections.title: Talking with someone who seems strained
sections.text: Choose a calm moment and a quiet one-to-one setting. Describe what you have noticed in work terms, such as late nights or skipped breaks, without guessing at causes. Ask an open question: What is taking the most energy right now? Listen for demands you can change. Ask what would help, and offer one or two concrete options, such as moving a deadline or sharing the escalated calls. Mention the Employee Assistance Program as one support among others, not as the answer. Agree on a time to check in again. The person decides what personal details to share, and you do not need any to act on the work.

sections.title: How strong is the evidence?
sections.text: The link between work conditions and burnout is well established across many studies. Evidence about what reduces burnout is much thinner. Maslach and Leiter note that randomized trials are rare and most studies lack follow-up. The best pooled trial evidence comes from physicians, not human services staff, and the organization-directed studies in that review were few. Fleming's survey is cross-sectional, so people who chose to join wellness programs may already have been more stressed. Read the evidence as a strong direction, not as a precise prescription. Changing the work is the better first bet, and you should watch what happens and adjust.

sections.title: Burnout is not a diagnosis, and you are not a clinician
sections.text: The World Health Organization does not classify burnout as a medical condition. Maslach and Leiter also caution against reducing burnout to exhaustion alone, which can lead to misreading what is going on. As a leader, avoid labeling anyone as burned out. Describe what you see in work terms: missed breaks, late nights, shorter replies to partners. Ask about the work. If someone describes symptoms that sound like depression, anxiety or trauma, point them to the Employee Assistance Program or their own health care provider. Respect their choice about what to share. Do not ask for or keep notes about health details.

sections.title: When the demand is not yours to change
sections.text: Some of the heaviest demands in DHS come from outside a unit: statutory timelines, federal reporting, system outages or a policy change with a hard start date. You may not be able to remove them. You can still change resources around them. Clarify which work can pause during a peak. Protect breaks during long call surges. Arrange coverage so people can step away after a hard call. Make the demand visible to your own manager with a clear picture of what it displaces. Explain to the team what you have raised and what you have not been able to change. Honesty about limits supports fairness, one of the six areas.

sections.title: Hindrances you can remove
sections.text: The distinction between challenge and hindrance demands is useful in planning. A complex disability waiver question can be energizing for a worker who has the knowledge and authority to answer it. The same question becomes a hindrance when the worker cannot find current guidance, needs three approvals or gets different answers from two leads. Ask your team which demands feel like obstacles rather than stretches. Answers might include duplicate data entry, unclear ownership of exceptions, outdated scripts and approvals that add delay but no value. Removing one of these may do more for exhaustion than any added perk, because it reduces a demand without asking anyone to try harder.

sections.title: Burnout and secondary traumatic stress together
sections.text: The child welfare brief reports that measures of burnout and secondary traumatic stress overlap substantially. In one meta-analysis of 41 papers, they shared about a third of their variance when measured with separate tools. A person may have both. The responses differ, though. Burnout responds to changes in demands and resources. Secondary traumatic stress calls for attention to how trauma exposure is spread, structured time to talk through hard cases, and access to trauma-informed support. The brief is candid that no definitive studies exist on preventing secondary traumatic stress from everyday exposure in child welfare and similar workforces. Critical incident debriefing has mixed evidence, and individual debriefing has been linked to harm in some reviews. Do not require people to retell a traumatic event in a group. Offer, and let them choose.

sections.title: Recovery, rest and the pace of human services
sections.text: Human services work often carries a sense that another person is always waiting. That makes it easier to encourage a colleague to step away than to step away yourself. Leaders set the norm. If you send messages late at night, people will feel they should answer. If you skip breaks during a surge, others will too. Model the behavior you want. Build recovery into the schedule rather than leaving it to individual willpower. Rotate the hardest assignments, such as crisis lines or complaints, so no one carries them all the time. Give people a short buffer after a difficult call before the next one.

sections.title: Fairness and who carries the hidden load
sections.text: Some work never shows up on a count of completed cases. It includes answering colleagues' questions, coaching new staff, fixing routing errors and smoothing relationships with partners. This hidden load tends to fall on the most experienced or most willing people. Fairness is one of the six areas, and reward is another. Make the hidden work visible by asking people to describe an ordinary week, including the parts that never appear on calendars. Then share it out, recognize it, or reduce it. The research reviewed here does not show differences in burnout by race, disability or other group, so do not assume one. Look at the actual distribution of work on your own team.

sections.title: When a person is already burned out
sections.text: If someone is already exhausted and detached, small fixes may not be enough. Talk with them about what would help in the short term, such as reduced exposure to the hardest work, leave, or a temporary change in duties. Work with the person or area responsible for human resources and accommodations when needed. Keep the conversation about the work and what support they want. Afterward, look at what conditions led there and whether others face the same ones. One person's burnout is often an early signal of a team-wide mismatch.

sections.title: Checking your own strain
sections.text: Supervisors carry their own demands, plus the weight of their team's strain. The same six areas apply to you. If your workload has no ceiling, or you lack anyone to talk through hard decisions with, raise it with your own manager. Leaders who are exhausted tend to have less patience and less capacity to notice others. Taking your own strain seriously is part of the job, not a distraction from it.

simulation.setup: You supervise a call-line team in the Disability Services Division that answers questions from people receiving services, families and providers. Over two months, call volume has risen after a policy change. Several staff are skipping breaks. One experienced worker, who also coaches new staff and handles escalated calls from families in crisis, has started arriving early and leaving late, and their replies in team chat have become short. You have a modest budget for a team wellness activity. What is at stake is the team's health and the quality of calls for people who depend on them.

steps.situation: Your manager suggests using the budget for a resilience workshop next month. You have not yet talked with the team about what is driving the strain.
steps.question: What do you do first?

choices.label: Hold off on the workshop. At the next team meeting, ask which recurring demand costs the most energy and what it pushes aside, and ask people to describe an ordinary day including hidden work.
choices.feedback: This starts with the conditions behind the strain. In controlled trials with physicians, organization-directed changes reduced burnout more than individual programs, and a large survey found individual wellbeing programs showed no benefit. Asking about hidden work also surfaces fairness and reward issues, two of the six areas.

choices.label: Book the workshop. It is a visible sign that you care, and people can use the skills during busy weeks.
choices.feedback: It is a kind and visible gesture, which is why it is tempting. But the evidence suggests individual programs do less than changing the work, and a workshop during a call surge may add another demand. People may read it as asking them to cope better with a load that has not changed.

choices.label: Do both: book the workshop and also ask the team about workload at the next meeting.
choices.feedback: Asking about workload is the right instinct. Pairing it with a workshop is not harmful in itself. But the workshop may set the frame that the solution is personal coping, and it uses time and budget that could support a work change. Start with the work, then decide what individual support fits.

steps.situation: The team names three things: repeated calls about the same policy question with no clear written answer, escalated crisis calls all going to the experienced worker, and new staff interrupting them constantly for help.
steps.question: What change do you make?

choices.label: Ask the person or area responsible for the policy for a clear written answer and script, rotate escalated crisis calls among three trained staff, and set two daily coaching times instead of constant interruptions.
choices.feedback: Each change targets a named demand or adds a resource. The script removes a hindrance demand. Rotating crisis calls spreads trauma exposure, a predictor of secondary traumatic stress. Set coaching times protect the experienced worker's focus while keeping support for new staff. It addresses workload, control and fairness together.

choices.label: Give the experienced worker two afternoons a week off the phones to catch up, and route their escalated calls to the next most experienced person.
choices.feedback: Relief for the most strained person is a good impulse. But this moves the crisis calls onto one other worker, who now carries the exposure. It also leaves the repeated policy question and the constant interruptions untouched, so the underlying demands continue.

steps.situation: The workshop happens. Feedback is polite. Two weeks later, the experienced worker emails you after a hard crisis call. They need to step away for the afternoon, and they are not sure how much longer they can keep this up.
steps.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Tell them to take the afternoon, arrange coverage, and set a time tomorrow to talk about what has been happening and what would help, starting with their share of crisis calls and coaching.
choices.feedback: This meets the immediate need and opens a real conversation about the work. Crisis exposure and hidden coaching load are exactly the demands the six areas and the secondary traumatic stress evidence point to. Asking what would help respects their choices about what to share.

choices.label: Approve the afternoon and remind them about the Employee Assistance Program and the workshop strategies.
choices.feedback: Approving time off and naming the Employee Assistance Program are both appropriate. But leaning on the workshop strategies frames this as a personal coping problem. Their crisis call share and coaching load are unchanged, so the strain will likely return tomorrow.

steps.situation: Two weeks after your changes, breaks are being taken more often. But a newer worker mentions they now handle more escalated calls than before and have started dreading their phone shifts.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Thank them for telling you, review how escalated calls are now distributed, adjust the rotation, and set up a short weekly space for staff who take crisis calls to talk through hard cases if they want to.
choices.feedback: This checks where the relief landed and corrects it. Spreading trauma exposure and offering peer support both match the secondary traumatic stress evidence, where support at work is protective. Making the peer space a choice avoids requiring anyone to retell distressing calls.

choices.label: Reassure them that it gets easier with experience and pair them with the experienced worker for tips.
choices.feedback: Pairing for support has value, and experience can build confidence. But the newer worker is describing more exposure, not a skill gap. This also puts coaching back on the experienced worker you just relieved, recreating the original strain in a new form.

simulation.debrief: The strongest path started with the work, not with personal coping. That follows the evidence: organization-directed changes reduced burnout more than individual programs in physician trials, and a large survey found individual wellbeing programs showed no benefit. The team's three named demands mapped onto the six areas of work life: workload, control and fairness. Rotating crisis calls spread trauma exposure, a known predictor of secondary traumatic stress. The final step showed why relief must be checked. Moving demands can shift burnout from one person to another. The evidence on preventing secondary traumatic stress is weak, so offering peer support as a choice and watching how people respond is the honest approach.

mistakes.mistake: Reaching first for a wellness program.
mistakes.why: Workshops and apps are visible, quick and feel caring. But evidence from physician trials and a survey of 46,336 workers suggests they do less than changing the work.
mistakes.instead: Find and change one recurring demand first, then add individual supports.

mistakes.mistake: Labeling someone as burned out.
mistakes.why: The label feels like an honest description. But burnout is not a medical diagnosis, and labels can shift attention from the work to the person.
mistakes.instead: Describe what you see in work terms and ask about the work.

mistakes.mistake: Giving relief to one person by moving their load to another.
mistakes.why: It solves the visible problem quickly. But the demand still exists and lands on someone else, often the next most capable person.
mistakes.instead: After any change, check who picked up the work and adjust.

mistakes.mistake: Treating secondary traumatic stress as ordinary burnout.
mistakes.why: They overlap, so they are easy to confuse. But secondary traumatic stress comes from trauma exposure, and reducing paperwork will not address it.
mistakes.instead: Look at how trauma exposure is spread and offer support people can choose.

mistakes.mistake: Requiring group debriefs after every hard call.
mistakes.why: It seems supportive. But evidence for critical incident debriefing is mixed, and individual debriefing has been linked to harm in some reviews.
mistakes.instead: Offer a place to talk and let people decide whether to use it.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring your own strain.
mistakes.why: Leaders often put the team first. But the same six areas apply to you, and an exhausted leader has less capacity to notice others.
mistakes.instead: Raise your own workload with your manager and model breaks and reasonable hours.

jobAid.title: Burnout prevention check
jobAid.use: Use it at a team meeting or in one-to-ones when strain is rising, or every few months as a routine check.
steps: Ask: Which recurring demand costs you the most energy, and what does it push aside?
Ask people to describe an ordinary week, including work that never appears on calendars.
Check the six areas: workload, control, reward, community, fairness, values. Which one shows the biggest mismatch?
Choose one demand to remove or reduce, or one resource to add, that is within your authority.
If the work involves trauma exposure, look at how it is spread and offer peer support people can choose.
Raise demands outside your authority with the person or area responsible, and tell the team what you raised.
After two weeks, ask who picked up any work that moved, and adjust.

media.reason: Burnout is easy to misread as a personal problem. A calm narrator can walk through what it is, where it comes from and what to change, in a steady order.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text:
Think of someone on your team who used to light up when they solved a hard case. Lately they arrive early, leave late and answer questions in a few clipped words. It is tempting to think they need to take better care of themselves. The research points somewhere else.

The World Health Organization describes burnout as the result of chronic workplace stress that has not been managed. It has three parts: exhaustion, mental distance from the job, and a sense of not making a difference. It is a work phenomenon, not a medical condition. That tells you where to look first. At the work.

Researchers Christina Maslach and Michael Leiter describe six areas where people and their work can be mismatched. Workload. Control. Reward. Community. Fairness. Values. When the mismatch grows in any of these, burnout becomes more likely. Meta-analyses tell a similar story. Job demands such as conflicting instructions or constant interruptions raise burnout. Job resources such as support and clear authority lower it.

So what helps? In a review of 18 controlled studies with physicians, changes to how work was organized, mostly reducing workload or changing schedules, reduced burnout more than programs aimed at individuals. And a survey of more than 46,000 workers in the United Kingdom found that people who joined resilience training, mindfulness sessions or wellbeing apps appeared no better off than those who did not. That survey cannot prove cause. But together these findings point one way. Change the work first. Then offer individual support as an addition.

In human services there is a second strain. Secondary traumatic stress comes from hearing about or helping with other people's trauma. It can look like intrusive thoughts, avoidance or feeling on edge. In one survey of 992 child welfare workers and supervisors, more than half reported such symptoms in the past week. It is related to burnout, but cutting paperwork will not touch it. What helps is attention to how trauma exposure is spread across the team, and support from colleagues and supervisors. The evidence on specific prevention programs is weak. So offer support, and let people choose how to use it.

One last check. When you relieve one person, ask who picked up the work. Strain that moves has not been solved. Two weeks after any change, look again at hours, breaks and who is carrying the hardest calls. Prevention is not one fix. It is a habit of looking at the work.

prompts: Which recurring demand on your team seems to cost the most energy, and when will you ask the team about it?
Which one change within your authority could reduce that demand, and who might the work shift to if you are not careful?
If your team handles trauma exposure, how is it spread now, and what is one adjustment you could make by the end of the month?
