theme: Teams and the work they carry

photo.alt: Two people work quietly at opposite ends of a table, one with a laptop and one with a book.

title: Managing workload
objective: Plan workload realistically, set priorities by consequence rather than urgency, protect focused time, and bring a clear trade-off to the person who sets priorities.
outcomes: Estimate how long work will take using past experience and the task's parts, not only the plan in your head.
Compare competing requests by who is affected and what waiting costs, not by which arrived first or feels most urgent.
Set up protected focus time and agreed interruption norms with your team.
Present an overloaded period to a manager as a specific choice with its effects on service and a date for a decision.
Check that a workload fix does not quietly move the load to someone else.

evidence.summary: People reliably underestimate how long their own work will take. Linking a new estimate to how long similar work took before removes much of that bias, and breaking a task into parts helps too. When choosing what to do next, people tend to pick urgent tasks over more important ones, especially when they feel busy. Interruptions carry hidden costs: people work faster to compensate, but report more stress, and even very short interruptions raise errors in step-by-step tasks. A meta-analysis of 336 studies links heavy workload to strain and intent to leave. A field study found scheduled quiet time helped a team, then faded. Limits: much of this comes from lab studies, and workload evidence from human services is thin.

findings.claim: Students predicted they would finish their theses in 33.9 days; they took 55.5, and only 29.7 percent finished by their own best-guess date.
findings.detail: Five studies; Study 1 had 33 analyzed participants. Even worst-case estimates (48.6 days) were too short. Linking past experiences to the current task eliminated the bias in Study 4; observers did not show the bias. 1994.

findings.claim: Interrupted work was finished faster with no loss in quality, but people reported significantly more stress, frustration, time pressure and effort after about 20 minutes.
findings.detail: Lab experiment, 48 participants answering email in an HR role, interrupted every two minutes. 2008.

findings.claim: Interruptions averaging 2.8 seconds doubled the rate of sequence errors in a step-by-step task; 4.4 seconds tripled it.
findings.detail: Lab experiment, about 300 participants on a sequential computer procedure. 2014.

findings.claim: Scheduled quiet time three mornings a week raised the share of engineers rating their productivity above average from 41 to 65 percent, but the gains faded when the underlying crisis pattern did not change.
findings.detail: Nine-month field study of one software team (12 engineers plus leads), self-rated productivity. 1999.

findings.claim: In five experiments, people chose tasks that only seemed urgent over tasks with objectively better payoffs, even when other reasons for choosing urgent work were ruled out.
findings.detail: Five experiments, Journal of Consumer Research, 2018 (abstract opened). Secondary summaries add that the effect is stronger in people who see themselves as busy and weaker when payoffs are made visible at the moment of choice.

findings.claim: Heavier workload relates to lower well-being (correlations mostly in the -.20s and -.30s) and higher intent to leave (.16), and to more role conflict (.44).
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 336 studies. Supervisor support related to lower workload (-.20). 2015.

findings.claim: No meta-analysis exists of child welfare caseload or workload studies, caseload counts miss case demands, and workload-reduction strategies are little studied.
findings.detail: Child welfare workforce evidence summary, 2021.

findings.claim: Breaking a multi-part task into its components raises time estimates and reduces the planning fallacy, though it helps less for tasks with few parts.
findings.detail: Experiments, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 2004.

counterintuitive.headline: Interrupted people work faster, and pay for it in stress.
counterintuitive.text: Most people assume interruptions slow work down. Mark, Gudith and Klocke (2008) gave 48 people an email task in a simulated workplace. Some were interrupted every two minutes. Surprisingly, interrupted participants finished faster, with no difference in errors. They wrote shorter replies and sped up to make up for lost time. The cost showed up elsewhere. After only about 20 minutes, they reported significantly more stress, frustration, time pressure and effort. Output can look fine while the price is paid by the person. That is one reason heavy interruption can go unnoticed by leaders who only watch output.

sections.title: Plans are usually too optimistic
sections.text: When people estimate their own work, they imagine the plan going smoothly. In a classic study, students predicted their theses would take 33.9 days. They took 55.5. Fewer than a third finished by their own best guess, and even their worst-case estimates were too short. The fix was simple. When people were asked to connect how long similar work took in the past to the new task, the bias disappeared. Breaking a task into its parts also helps.

sections.title: Urgent is not the same as important
sections.text: Experiments show people choose urgent tasks over more important ones, even when the important one clearly pays off more. The effect is strongest when people feel busy. Interruptions add another hidden cost. People who are interrupted often work faster to keep up, but they report more stress. Very short interruptions can also double errors in step-by-step work, like checking an eligibility determination. Because output can look fine, the cost of constant interruption is easy for a leader to miss. Agreeing on blocks of focus time, with a clear route for real emergencies, is one way to reduce it.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: Look at the next four to six weeks for yourself or for one person on your team. List each major commitment, including hidden work such as preparing materials, arranging accessible formats, coaching and follow-up. Estimate hours by looking at how long similar work took last time, not how long it should take. Compare the total with the hours actually available after leave and routine work. If it does not fit, bring a specific choice to the person who sets priorities. Name what could move, what that would affect, and when you need an answer. A specific choice is easier for a leader to make than a general request for help.

sections.title: Why estimates fall short
sections.text:
Buehler, Griffin and Ross (1994) ran five studies on what they called the planning fallacy. Think-aloud data showed people focused mostly on future plans and rarely on past experience. When reminded of past delays, they tended to explain them away as one-time events. Observers did not show the same bias. They used the person's track record and tended to overestimate. In Study 4, the bias disappeared only when people linked specific past experiences to the current task. Simply recalling the past was not enough.

In DHS work, this means asking a concrete question. How long did the last bulletin, the last legislative report or the last partner meeting actually take, from first draft to final approval? Include waiting for reviews, accessibility checks and revisions. Kruger and Evans (2004) found that breaking a task into its parts also raised estimates and reduced bias. A partner listening session is not one item. It includes scheduling, interpreters or captioning, materials, the session, follow-up notes, verification and reporting back.

sections.title: A simple workload picture
sections.text: Choose a period long enough to see collisions coming, such as three two-week blocks. Give each major responsibility a row: routine service, project work, preparation, follow-up, coaching, development and planned time away. Estimate hours from past experience. If hours are hard to estimate, mark each as small, medium or large and label it so others can read it. Then compare the total with available hours. Suppose an analyst has 64 hours in the next block after leave, and routine requests typically take 32. That leaves 32 hours for everything else. If preparing a partner workshop took 24 hours last time and a data request is due the same week, the collision is visible weeks ahead.

sections.title: Prioritizing by consequence
sections.text: Zhu, Yang and Hsee (2018) found people tend to choose the task with the nearer deadline even when another task is clearly more valuable. The effect was strongest when people felt busy and weaker when the payoffs were made visible at the moment of choice. So make consequences visible. For each competing request, ask four questions. Who is affected and how? What does waiting cost each of them? What is the earliest step someone else is waiting on? Where did the deadline come from? A wrong phone number on a public page may harm people every hour it stays up. A presentation due Friday may be needed in accessible form by Wednesday. A request marked urgent may have a flexible date once you ask.

sections.title: Making the trade-off visible
sections.text: A workload picture becomes useful when it changes a decision. Share it with your supervisor before the collision, not after. Keep it simple enough to read in a minute: the rows, the estimated hours and the gap. Point to the one or two items that cause the overflow. Then describe what each realistic option would mean for the people affected. If the inbox slows, which partners wait longer, and for what? If a training moves, what do county staff lose in the meantime? Leaders can weigh these effects only if someone names them. This is not complaining about workload. It is giving the person who sets priorities the information they need to set them.

sections.title: Interruptions and focus
sections.text: Mark and colleagues (2008) found interrupted people finished faster, with no loss of quality, but reported more stress, frustration and effort within about 20 minutes. Altmann and colleagues (2014) found interruptions of only 2.8 seconds doubled errors in a step-by-step task. Much DHS work is step by step: eligibility checks, data validation, licensing reviews and payment processing. Perlow (1999) tested scheduled quiet time with a software team. With quiet time three mornings a week, the share rating their productivity above average rose to 65 percent, compared with 41 percent in a phase without it. Work with your team to agree on focus blocks, a way to flag true emergencies, and set times for questions.

sections.title: Why it matters for people
sections.text: Bowling and colleagues (2015) pooled 336 studies. Heavier workload went with lower well-being, more role conflict and higher intent to leave. Supervisor support went with lower perceived workload. Workload is not only a scheduling issue. It is one of the main conditions behind strain and turnover.

sections.title: Applying it as a supervisor
sections.text: If you supervise others, use the same method with them. Ask each person to bring a short workload picture to one-to-ones during busy periods. Look across the team for collisions that individuals cannot see, such as two people both preparing for the same partner meeting. When someone brings you a trade-off, make the call promptly and tell everyone affected. A decision delayed is often a decision made by default, usually by the most conscientious person working late.

sections.title: Limits of the evidence
sections.text: Most of the research on planning and interruptions comes from lab studies, often with students. The effects are consistent and plausible for desk work, but they were not tested in DHS. Perlow's quiet-time study is one team with self-rated productivity. The urgency research is a set of experiments, not field trials. The workload meta-analysis is correlational. A child welfare workforce summary notes that no meta-analysis of caseload or workload studies exists in that field, and that workload-reduction strategies are little studied. Use these findings as reasons to try a practice and watch the results, not as proof that a given method will work on your team.

sections.title: Asking leadership for a workable plan
sections.text: When work does not fit, the person who sets priorities needs to make a choice. A useful question to bring is: When another urgent request comes in, which commitment should move? Bring the workload picture. Show the pattern over several weeks, not just one bad day. One unusually busy day may call for short-term help. The same collision every reporting cycle calls for a decision about ownership, staffing or scope. Offer two or three realistic options and describe the effect of each on service. For example, the partner briefing could move a week. The data request could go to another analyst. Or routine response times could slip from two days to four for a month. Name a date by which you need an answer, and who else needs to hear the decision. Describe the work without disclosing personal information about people served.

sections.title: Estimating work you have never done
sections.text: The planning fallacy fix depends on past experience, but some work is new. A first legislative report or a new type of partner engagement has no track record. In that case, use other people's experience. Ask a colleague who has done similar work how long it took them, including reviews and revisions. Observers in Buehler's studies used track records and did not show the optimistic bias, so a colleague's estimate of your task may be more realistic than your own. Break the new task into parts and estimate each one. Then add explicit time for review, accessibility checks and the waiting that approvals involve. Revisit the estimate at the first checkpoint and adjust the plan early, while there is still room to move other work.

sections.title: When several managers assign work
sections.text: In matrixed teams, different managers may each approve work without seeing the combined effect. Each request is reasonable alone. Together they exceed available hours. Bowling and colleagues found role conflict was one of the strongest correlates of workload, at .44. Make the combined picture visible to everyone who assigns work. Ask them to agree on an order, or to name one person who decides when requests collide. Without that, the person doing the work ends up making priority decisions that belong to leaders.

sections.title: Protecting focus without cutting people off
sections.text: Perlow's study also shows the limits of quiet time. Gains faded after the researcher left, because the underlying pattern of crises and last-minute requests had not changed. Engineers later said quiet time alone did not work. One lasting change was that managers checked on people less often. So treat focus time as part of a larger change. Reduce the causes of constant interruption, such as unclear guidance or approvals that require repeated status checks. Keep a reliable route for real emergencies. In call-line and front-line roles, focus time may mean protected blocks off the phones for case work rather than silence. Rotate those blocks fairly, so the same people do not always cover.

sections.title: Interruptions you create
sections.text: Leaders are a major source of interruptions. A quick question in chat, a status check or a last-minute change in priority each seems small. Perlow found one lasting effect of quiet time: managers checked on engineers less often. They learned to define a task and give people time to do it. Before you interrupt, ask whether the question can wait for a set check-in time. Batch your questions. When you change a priority, say what drops as a result. These habits cost little and protect the focus your team needs for careful work.

sections.title: Hidden work and fairness
sections.text: Some of the heaviest work never appears in counts of completed tasks. It includes answering colleagues' questions, coaching new staff, fixing routing errors, arranging accommodations and smoothing partner relationships. When you build a workload picture, ask people to include this work. It often falls on the most experienced or most willing people. If one person's plan always overflows, look at whether they are carrying the team's informal load. Then share it, recognize it, or reduce it. Check after any change that the work did not simply move to someone else.

sections.title: Urgency culture
sections.text: If everything is marked urgent, nothing is. The urgency research suggests that a sense of busyness strengthens the pull toward urgent tasks. A team that feels constantly behind may keep choosing quick, urgent items while important work, such as fixing a recurring error or improving a template, keeps slipping. Set aside regular time for important but not urgent work, and protect it like an appointment. When you assign work, give a real date and explain what it is based on. Ask requesters the same. Many deadlines turn out to be flexible once someone asks where they came from.

sections.title: When the answer is no
sections.text: Sometimes leaders cannot move anything. A legislative deadline is fixed, staffing cannot change and every item is required. In that case, the workload picture still helps. It lets you agree in advance which quality standards can flex, such as a shorter format, fewer review rounds or a later follow-up. It also documents the pattern for future planning and staffing requests. Tell the team honestly what was raised and what could not change. Then look for anything you can remove, even small things, and plan recovery time after the peak.

sections.title: Your own workload
sections.text: Supervisors are subject to the same planning fallacy. Apply the same method to your own calendar. Count meetings, reviews, one-to-ones, hiring and the time it takes to respond to escalations. If you are always the bottleneck for approvals, consider which decisions could be delegated with clear limits. Model the practices you want: realistic dates, focus time and honest trade-offs.

simulation.setup: You are a Policy Analyst in a DHS policy unit that supports county and Tribal partners through the person or area responsible for each partnership. In the next two weeks you have a legislative report section due, a county training presentation, the routine inbox, and two days of planned leave. This morning a director's staff member asks for a new data summary by Friday. Your supervisor approved the training and the report; a different manager approved the data request. What is at stake is the quality of each deliverable and your own capacity.

steps.situation: You need to decide how to respond to the new data request.
steps.question: What do you do first?

choices.label: Build a quick workload picture for the two weeks using how long similar work took last time, and ask the requester where the Friday date comes from.
choices.feedback: This counters the planning fallacy by using past experience, which removed the bias in Buehler's studies. Asking about the date tests whether the urgency is real. Many deadlines turn out to be flexible once someone asks, and you need the facts before you can propose a trade-off.

choices.label: Say yes and plan to work late a couple of evenings. It is a director's request.
choices.feedback: Responding to leadership quickly is a reasonable instinct. But you have not checked whether the work fits, and the planning fallacy means it probably takes longer than you think. Working late hides the conflict from the people who should decide it, and heavy workload predicts strain and intent to leave.

choices.label: Reply that you are fully booked and cannot take it on.
choices.feedback: Protecting your capacity matters, and you may be right. But a flat no without the picture or options leaves the requester stuck and pushes the conflict back without information. It also skips the person who sets your priorities, who may decide differently.

steps.situation: Your picture shows about 70 hours of work against 52 available. The requester says the director wants the summary for a meeting next Thursday, so Friday was a buffer. The training and report dates are fixed.
steps.question: How do you handle the gap?

choices.label: Bring your supervisor the picture and two options: deliver the data summary Wednesday by slowing inbox response times for the week, or ask the other manager whether another analyst can take it. Ask for a decision by tomorrow and copy the other manager on the outcome.
choices.feedback: This puts the priority decision with the people who own it. The options name the effect on service, and the date keeps it moving. Including the other manager addresses the role conflict that comes from two people assigning work, a strong correlate of workload in the meta-analysis.

choices.label: Since the real date is Thursday, quietly fit the summary in by trimming time on the training presentation.
choices.feedback: Finding the real date was useful, and it does reduce the crunch. But trimming the training without telling anyone makes a priority decision that belongs to your supervisor. The county partners may get a weaker session, and no one who assigned the work sees the trade-off.

steps.situation: It is Wednesday. The data summary has taken twice as long as you planned, the training draft is behind, and you keep getting pulled into inbox questions while doing careful number checks. You notice an error in a table you built.
steps.question: What now?

choices.label: Tell your supervisor today what is behind and what is at risk, propose moving one item, and block two hours of focus time with your inbox covered to finish the checks.
choices.feedback: This surfaces the problem while there is still time to choose. Focus time matters for step-by-step checking, since even very short interruptions doubled sequence errors in a lab study. Raising it now is better than finding out on Friday that the training is not ready.

choices.label: Push through. Fix the error, stay late, and try to finish everything by Friday.
choices.feedback: Persistence is admirable and sometimes needed. But interrupted, rushed work brings more stress, and interruptions raise errors in exactly this kind of checking. Without telling anyone, the people who set priorities cannot help, and the same collision will repeat next cycle.

steps.situation: The two weeks are over. Looking back, this kind of collision happens almost every reporting cycle because two managers assign work separately.
steps.question: What do you do next?

choices.label: Bring a short summary of the last three cycles to your supervisor and propose that both managers agree on one order of priority, or one person who decides when requests collide.
choices.feedback: A repeated pattern calls for a decision about ownership, not more personal effort. Showing several cycles makes the pattern visible, and a single decision point reduces role conflict. It also follows the lesson from the quiet-time study: fixes fade if the underlying pattern does not change.

choices.label: Keep a better personal plan next time and start each cycle earlier.
choices.feedback: Earlier planning helps, and personal habits matter. But the cause is structural: two managers each approving work without seeing the total. Personal planning alone cannot fix that. You will keep making priority decisions that belong to leaders, and the extra effort will hide the pattern from the people who could change it.

simulation.debrief: The strongest path began with a realistic picture based on past experience, which counters the planning fallacy documented by Buehler and colleagues. Asking where a deadline came from tested urgency, which the mere urgency research shows can pull people away from more important work. Bringing a specific choice to the person who sets priorities kept the decision where it belongs and made the effect on service visible. Focus time for careful checking reflected interruption research showing errors rise with even brief interruptions. Finally, a collision that repeats every cycle calls for a change in how work is assigned. Most of this evidence comes from labs and one field study, so try these practices and watch the results.

mistakes.mistake: Estimating from the plan rather than from the past.
mistakes.why: Imagining how the work will go feels like careful planning. But people focus on future plans and explain away past delays, so even worst-case estimates run short.
mistakes.instead: Ask how long similar work actually took last time, including reviews and waiting.

mistakes.mistake: Doing what arrived first or feels most urgent.
mistakes.why: Urgency pulls attention, especially when people feel busy. Experiments show people pick urgent tasks over more valuable ones.
mistakes.instead: Compare who is affected and what waiting costs, and ask where each deadline came from.

mistakes.mistake: Absorbing overload by working late.
mistakes.why: It feels responsible and avoids conflict. But it hides the problem from the people who should decide, and heavy workload is linked to strain and intent to leave.
mistakes.instead: Bring a specific trade-off and a decision date to the person who sets priorities.

mistakes.mistake: Judging interruptions by output alone.
mistakes.why: Interrupted people often keep output steady by speeding up, so nothing looks wrong. The cost appears as stress and, in step-by-step work, errors.
mistakes.instead: Agree on focus blocks, an emergency route and set times for questions.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a recurring collision as a planning failure.
mistakes.why: It is natural to blame your own planning. But when several managers assign work separately, the cause is structural.
mistakes.instead: Show the pattern across cycles and ask leaders to agree on one order or one decision point.

jobAid.title: Workload and trade-off planner
jobAid.use: Use it at the start of each two- to six-week period, or whenever a new request lands on a full plan.
steps: List every major commitment for the period, including preparation, accessibility work, coaching and follow-up.
Estimate each from how long similar work took last time; break large items into their parts.
Subtract leave and routine work to get the hours actually available, and compare with the total.
For competing requests, ask: Who is affected? What does waiting cost? Where did the date come from?
Block focus time for step-by-step checking, with a route for true emergencies.
If it does not fit, bring two or three options with their effects on service and a date for a decision.
After the period, note what collided and whether it repeats; raise repeats as a question of ownership.

media.reason: Workload problems are usually resolved in a conversation between the person doing the work and the person who sets priorities. Hearing both sides shows how a specific trade-off changes that conversation.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Do you have ten minutes? I need help with the next two weeks. A new data request came in this morning for Friday, and I do not think everything fits.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Can you squeeze it in? It is for the director's meeting.

script.speaker: male
script.text: That was my first instinct too. So I checked how long similar work took last time instead of guessing. The last data summary took about 14 hours with reviews. The training presentation took 20. With the report section, the inbox and my two days of leave, it comes to about 70 hours of work. I have 52.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Seventy against fifty-two. I would have guessed it was tight, not that far over.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Most people underestimate. In one study, students thought their theses would take about 34 days. They took about 55. Looking at the last similar task is what fixes it.

script.speaker: female
script.text: All right. Is Friday the real deadline?

script.speaker: male
script.text: I asked. The meeting is next Thursday, so Friday was a buffer. That helps, but it still does not fit. I have two options. I can deliver the summary Wednesday if inbox response times slow from two days to four this week. Or the data team's manager could assign it to another analyst.

script.speaker: female
script.text: That is clear. I would rather not slow the inbox. Counties are waiting on answers about the policy change. Let me ask the data team's manager about another analyst.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Thank you. Could I hear by tomorrow? If it stays with me, I need to start Thursday.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Tomorrow morning. And I am noticing this is the third reporting cycle with a collision like this.

script.speaker: male
script.text: It is. Two managers approve work separately, so nobody sees the total until it lands on one person.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Then the fix is not you planning harder. I will ask both managers to agree on one order of priority, or one person who decides when requests collide. Bring this picture to that conversation. It makes the choice visible.

prompts: Which period in the next six weeks looks most crowded for you or one person you supervise, and when will you build a workload picture for it?
Which recent task can you use as a realistic guide for how long the next similar task will take?
Who sets priorities when requests collide on your team, and what one specific choice could you bring to them, by what date?

title: Delegating real authority
objective: Hand a colleague a real decision, with the knowledge, limits and support to make it, and then let the decision stand.
outcomes: Name the specific decisions a colleague will own, the ones that need a conversation first, and the ones that stay with you.
Check a colleague's current workload and take something off it before adding new authority.
Give the knowledge, access and skill a decision needs, not only the task.
Set one early checkpoint and agree on what support looks like, so autonomy is not read as absence.
Respond to a decision you would have made differently without taking it back.

evidence.summary: Across 105 samples, leaders who share real authority tend to see better performance, more helpful behavior and more creativity, mostly because staff trust them and feel more capable. The benefit is not automatic. One study found two paths: empowerment can raise confidence and performance, and the same behaviors can raise strain that cuts into those gains. Teams given authority often start slower and then learn faster. Federal workforce studies point to the practices that matter most: knowledge, skill and discretion over how work is done. A 2019 review calls the overall record mixed, and much of it relies on surveys taken at one point in time. The honest reading is that delegation helps when it is real, resourced and clearly agreed.

findings.claim: Empowering leadership was positively related to performance, citizenship behavior and creativity, working mainly through trust in the leader and a sense of empowerment.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 105 samples, individual and team levels, published 2018. Knowledge sharing showed no significant indirect effect at the team level.

findings.claim: Empowering leadership has an enabling path that raises self-efficacy and performance, and a burdening path in which some behaviors raise job tension that weakens the performance gain.
findings.detail: Empirical study in The Leadership Quarterly, 2016. Results broadly supported both paths. Sample details are not on the public record.

findings.claim: Teams led by an empowering leader performed worse early (mean 3.52 versus 7.33 for directive-led teams) but improved faster over time through learning and coordination.
findings.detail: Lab experiment, 60 five-person teams (300 senior undergraduates), 10-round simulation, 2013. Leadership by time interaction 0.34, p < .05.

findings.claim: Both directive and empowering leadership raised task proficiency, but only empowering leadership raised proactive behavior.
findings.detail: Field experiment in work units in the United Arab Emirates, customer-rated outcomes, 2013. Empowering leadership had stronger effects in units less satisfied with their leader.

findings.claim: When autonomy did not match what a follower expected, too much or too little, the follower tended to see the leader as hands-off, and rated the leader as less effective.
findings.detail: Two-stage field study of 150 leader-follower dyads, polynomial regression, 2018.

findings.claim: In federal agencies, giving employees job knowledge, skills and discretion to change work processes had a substantively significant link to perceived performance; goal information and performance rewards had little.
findings.detail: Survey study of US federal employees, published 2011. Public sector. Outcome is perceived, not objective, performance.

findings.claim: Empowerment as an overall approach increased encouragement to innovate among federal employees, but single practices had divergent effects and some may discourage innovation.
findings.detail: Survey study of US federal employees, 2013. Public sector.

findings.claim: A review of the empirical literature found incongruent and mixed results and called for rethinking how effective empowering leadership is.
findings.detail: Literature review, The Leadership Quarterly, 2019. Points to nonlinear effects, reverse causation and opposing mechanisms.

counterintuitive.headline: Handing over authority can feel like being left alone.
counterintuitive.text: Most supervisors assume more autonomy is always welcome. A field study of 150 leader-follower pairs by Wong and Giessner (2018) found otherwise. When the amount of autonomy did not match what a person expected, followers tended to see the leader as hands-off, and they rated that leader as less effective. This happened when leaders gave less than expected and when they gave more. The same act can read as trust or as absence. The difference is whether the two of you agreed, out loud, on what the person owns and what support stays in place.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.text: Delegating a task is not the same as delegating authority. A task is something to do. Authority is the right to decide how it gets done and to have that decision stand. Research across 105 samples links real authority-sharing with better performance, more helpful behavior and more creativity. The gains come mostly through two things: staff trust you more, and they feel more able to act. Those gains disappear when the authority is not real, when the person lacks what the decision needs, or when the new work lands on top of a full load.

sections.title: Why it can go wrong
sections.text: The same empowering behavior has two faces. It can raise someone's confidence and performance. It can also raise strain, and that strain eats into the gain. Autonomy can also be misread. In one field study, people who got more or less autonomy than they expected tended to see their leader as hands-off. Clear agreement is what turns autonomy into trust.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: Before you hand over the next piece of work, write three short lists with the person. First, the decisions they own outright. Second, the decisions that need a quick conversation with you first. Third, the decisions that stay with you or with the person or area responsible above you. Then ask one question: what can come off your plate so this fits? Agree on one early checkpoint, not a series of approvals. When the person makes a call you would have made differently, let it stand unless it creates real risk to people served, to law or to policy.

sections.title: What this looks like at DHS
sections.text: A Human Services Supervisor asks a senior worker to lead a fix to a confusing provider notice. The worker owns the wording and the test with three readers. The supervisor keeps the release date because it ties to a policy change. Legal review stays with the person or area responsible for it. The worker drops two weekly reports for a month. That is delegation with authority, limits and room to do it well.

sections.title: What the evidence shows
sections.text:
The largest summary of empowering leadership pooled 105 samples (Lee, Willis and Tian, 2018). Leaders who shared authority saw better task performance, more citizenship behavior and more creativity, for individuals and for teams. At the individual level, the effect traveled through two routes. People trusted the leader more, and they felt more empowered: their work had meaning, they felt capable, and they had a say. At the team level, the effect ran through a shared sense of team empowerment.

A field experiment in the United Arab Emirates compared directive and empowering leadership in real work units (Martin, Liao and Campbell, 2013). Both styles improved task proficiency as rated by customers. Only empowering leadership raised proactive behavior, meaning people spotting problems and acting before being told. For public service work, that matters. Many of the most valuable actions, such as catching a pattern in denied claims, are ones no procedure lists.

sections.title: The mechanism: enabling and burdening
sections.text:
Cheong and colleagues (2016) showed that empowering leadership works through two paths at once. In the enabling path, authority raises self-efficacy, and self-efficacy raises performance. In the burdening path, some empowering behaviors raise job-induced tension. More decisions mean more responsibility, more ambiguity and more to carry. That tension weakens the performance gain.

This explains a familiar pattern. A supervisor gives a capable worker a big decision as a sign of trust. The worker is pleased, and also already full. Three weeks later the work is late, the worker is stressed, and the supervisor concludes the person was not ready. The real problem was load, not readiness.

sections.title: Expect a slow start
sections.text: In a ten-round team simulation, empowered teams performed worse early than directive-led teams. Their average was 3.52, versus 7.33 (Lorinkova, Pearsall and Sims, 2013). The empowered teams then improved faster. Their gains came from learning, coordination and building shared mental models. The early dip was part of how they learned. A supervisor who takes the work back during the dip cuts off the learning that would have paid off later.

sections.title: What to hand over in public service work
sections.text:
Studies of US federal employees offer the clearest public-sector guidance (Fernandez and Moldogaziev, 2011). Two practices had a substantive link to perceived performance: giving people the job knowledge and skills they need, and giving them discretion to change work processes. Sharing goal information and tying rewards to performance had little bearing. A later study found that empowerment as a whole encouraged innovation, but single practices pulled in different directions (Fernandez and Moldogaziev, 2013). Delegation works as a package, not as one gesture.

In DHS terms, a worker asked to redesign a call-line script needs three things. They need access to the call data and the policy it must reflect. They need time with a policy lead who can answer questions. And they need permission to change the script itself, not just to suggest changes.

sections.title: How to apply it
sections.text:
Start with the decision, not the task. Ask yourself what the person will decide that you used to decide. If the answer is nothing, you are assigning work, which is fine, but do not call it delegation.

Sort decisions into three groups with the person. Own: they decide and tell you after. Consult: they propose and you talk before it moves. Keep: it stays with you or with the person or area responsible, such as legal review, a contract change, a policy interpretation or anything involving a county or Tribal partner. Tribal matters always go through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations.

Check load before adding authority. Ask what can stop, slow or move. This is the most direct way to protect the enabling path.

Give the knowledge, access and skill. Name who they can call and make the introduction yourself.

Agree on support. Say how often you will check in and what will prompt a call. This keeps autonomy from reading as absence.

Let the decision stand. Disagree in conversation if you need to. Reverse it only for real risk to people served, to law or to policy.

sections.title: A quick DHS example
sections.text: A licensing supervisor hands a senior licensor the redesign of the pre-inspection checklist. The licensor owns the checklist's order and wording. Changes to what a provider must show stay with policy. The supervisor moves two inspections to a colleague for a month and introduces the licensor to the policy lead. They agree to meet once, at the first draft. The licensor reorders the list by how inspections actually flow. It is not how the supervisor would have done it, and it stands.

sections.title: How strong is the evidence?
sections.text:
The evidence for empowering leadership is real but uneven. The 105-sample meta-analysis is large, but most of the studies inside it are surveys taken at one point in time, often with the same person rating the leader and the outcome. That design cannot show cause. A 2019 review found results that were incongruent and mixed. It urged researchers to look for nonlinear effects and reverse causation (Cheong, Yammarino, Dionne, Spain and Tsai, 2019). Reverse causation is plausible here. Leaders may hand authority to people who already perform well, which would make empowerment look more powerful than it is.

The stronger designs point the same way but have their own limits. The Lorinkova team study is a controlled experiment, but with students in a simulation. The Martin field experiment ran in real work units, but in one country, and the public record does not give its sample size. The federal studies use large public-sector surveys, but the outcome is perceived performance, not measured results. Taken together, the evidence supports a careful claim: real, resourced delegation tends to help, and it can strain people when it is not.

sections.title: Too much of a good thing
sections.text:
The burdening path suggests that more authority is not always better. Cheong and colleagues (2016) found that some empowering behaviors raised job tension, which weakened the gain in performance. The 2019 review lists nonlinear effects as one of the main open questions. In practice, this means you should not judge delegation by how much you hand over. Judge it by fit: the size of the decision, the person's current load and the support around it.

Watch for signs of the burdening path. The person starts sending you every small question. Deadlines slip on work that used to be routine. They stop raising problems early. These are signals to talk about load and support, not to take the work back.

sections.title: When autonomy reads as absence
sections.text:
The study of 150 leader-follower pairs by Wong and Giessner (2018) shows that people judge autonomy against what they expected. When the leader gave more or less than expected, followers tended to see the leader as hands-off. That perception was linked to lower ratings of the leader's effectiveness.

This matters most in hybrid and remote work, where a quiet supervisor can look absent. It also matters when a person comes from a team where the supervisor approved every step. For that person, sudden freedom may feel like being dropped. The fix is not to give less autonomy. It is to talk about it. Ask how they like to work on something new. Agree on the first checkpoint. Say what you will and will not be watching.

sections.title: Differences between people and settings
sections.text:
Martin and colleagues (2013) found that empowering leadership had stronger effects in units that were less satisfied with their leader. One reading is that sharing authority can rebuild a strained relationship. That is a single study, so treat it as a possibility, not a rule.

The evidence does not show that delegation works differently for any racial, disability or other group. No verified study in this review tested that, so this course makes no such claim. What the evidence does support is checking access. Who gets the visible, decision-rich assignments on your team? If the answer is always the same two people, the benefits of authority will flow only to them. Rotate real decisions, and ask people directly what they want to own.

sections.title: Harder situations
sections.text:
Someone you trust makes a poor call. Ask first whether it is poor or only different. If it creates real risk to people served, to law or to policy, step in, explain why, and give the decision back as soon as the risk is handled. If it is only different, let it stand and talk about what each of you would weigh. Lorinkova and colleagues warn that leaders who appear to share authority but are not willing to give it up may be seen as insincere. One reversal of a decision that was truly theirs can undo months of trust.

The person does not want the authority. Some people are full, unsure or wary because a past supervisor punished mistakes. Start with a smaller decision and a clear safety net. Ask what would make it workable.

Your own leader wants every decision run past them. Be honest about what you can hand over. Delegating a decision you do not hold is a promise you cannot keep. Name the limit to your team, and work upward to widen it.

The work crosses areas. A change to an eligibility notice may touch policy, legal, communications and a county partner. Delegate the parts you own. Make the introductions for the rest, and be clear that county and Tribal partners are reached through the person or area responsible for those relationships.

sections.title: What delegation cannot fix
sections.text:
Delegation is not a cure for a broken process or too few staff. If a unit is short-staffed, handing out more authority spreads the shortage across more people. The burdening path will win. In that case, the honest move is to narrow the work, not to share it.

Delegation also cannot replace direction when the work is new to everyone. The Lorinkova study shows that directive teams do better early. If a deadline is days away and no one has done the work before, it may be right to lead closely this time. Then plan a later round where the person owns the decision. Be open about the choice. Say that this round is directive because of the deadline, and that the next one will be theirs.

Finally, delegation cannot work if information is held back. The federal studies found that knowledge and skill were among the practices most linked to performance. A person given a decision but not the data behind it has been handed risk, not authority.

sections.title: A short test before you delegate
sections.text: Ask five questions. What will this person decide that I used to decide? What comes off their plate? What knowledge, access or skill do they need, and who will provide it? When is the first checkpoint, and what would prompt a call before then? What would I need to see before I reversed a decision, and have I said that out loud? If you cannot answer the first question, you are assigning a task. If you cannot answer the second, you may be starting down the burdening path.

simulation.setup: You are a Human Services Supervisor in a disability services unit. A new state requirement changes how waiver providers must report staffing. Providers are calling with questions, and your team needs a plain-language guide within six weeks. A senior program consultant on your team knows the providers well and has asked for more responsibility. They also carry a full caseload of provider reviews. Your manager has said the guide must match policy and go through legal review. What is at stake is the guide's quality, the consultant's growth and your team's trust in what you mean by ownership.

steps.situation: You meet the consultant to hand off the guide. They are pleased and clearly want it. You know their review queue is already long.
steps.question: How do you set up the handoff?

choices.label: Ask them to lead the guide and tell them you trust them to figure out the approach.
choices.feedback: The consultant leaves energized, but nothing came off their plate and no decision rights were named. This is the setup for the burdening path Cheong and colleagues describe: real trust, added strain. It also leaves the consultant guessing about what they own, which Wong and Giessner link to seeing a leader as hands-off.

choices.label: Sort the decisions together, move four provider reviews to a colleague for six weeks, and set one checkpoint at the first draft.
choices.feedback: You named what they own, what needs a conversation and what stays with others, including legal review. You also protected the enabling path by reducing load. Federal workforce studies suggest that discretion plus the knowledge to use it is what links to performance. One checkpoint signals support without approval at every step.

choices.label: Have them draft the guide, and plan to review each section before it moves forward.
choices.feedback: This feels careful, and it protects quality. It is task assignment, though, not delegation. Section-by-section approval keeps every real decision with you. Lorinkova and colleagues found that directive structure helps early but limits the learning that makes a team stronger later. The consultant asked for responsibility and got supervision.

steps.situation: Three weeks in, the consultant sends you many small questions a day and two provider reviews are late. They say they are fine.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Take the guide back so they can catch up on reviews.
choices.feedback: It solves the backlog, and it teaches the consultant that authority here is temporary. The real problem is load and unclear decision rights, not ability. Taking the work back during the early dip cuts off the learning Lorinkova and colleagues found that empowered teams build. Trust is harder to rebuild than a schedule.

choices.label: Meet, name the strain you are seeing, and reset: move reviews off their plate and agree on which decisions are theirs to make without asking.
choices.feedback: You treated the questions and late reviews as signals of the burdening path, not as proof the person was not ready. Clarifying what they own cuts the stream of questions, and reducing load gives the enabling path room to work. This is a late fix, but a real one.

choices.label: Answer the questions quickly and say nothing about the late reviews.
choices.feedback: Fast answers feel supportive. They also keep you as the decision-maker and leave the strain unspoken. The consultant may conclude that asking is what you want. The load problem grows quietly, and the late reviews affect providers who are waiting.

steps.situation: At the first checkpoint, the draft is good. The consultant has organized it by provider questions rather than by the rule sections, which is how you would have done it.
steps.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Ask them to reorganize it by rule section so it lines up with the policy text.
choices.feedback: Your reason is sensible, and this was a decision you said they owned. Reversing it now tells the consultant the list of what they own was not real. Lorinkova and colleagues warn that leaders who appear to share authority without giving it up may be seen as insincere. If alignment matters, ask the policy lead to check it instead.

choices.label: Say what you would have done, ask what they weighed, and let their structure stand.
choices.feedback: You shared your view without taking the decision back. Asking what they weighed often surfaces knowledge you lack. Here, the consultant knows which questions providers actually ask. This protects the trust that Lee and colleagues found carries much of empowerment's effect, and the guide is likely more usable for it.

choices.label: Approve it without comment and move to the next item.
choices.feedback: The decision stands, which is good. But a silent approval wastes a chance to build judgment, and the consultant may read it as indifference. Wong and Giessner found that autonomy without visible engagement can look like absence. A short conversation about the choice would cost little and teach a lot.

steps.situation: Legal review flags one section as inconsistent with the rule. The deadline is ten days away. Your manager asks whether you should just rewrite the section yourself.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Rewrite the section yourself tonight so the deadline is safe.
choices.feedback: It is fast and it protects the deadline. It also takes back a decision at the moment the consultant could learn the most. The legal finding is a real constraint, but it is a constraint for the owner to work within, not a reason to remove the owner. Your manager will also learn that delegation on your team does not hold under pressure.

choices.label: Give the legal finding to the consultant, set up a short call with the legal reviewer, and tell your manager who owns the fix and when it will be ready.
choices.feedback: You treated legal review as a limit the owner works within, which is how you set it up. Connecting the consultant directly to the reviewer gives them the knowledge they need, which federal workforce studies link to performance. Telling your manager who owns the fix shows that delegation on your team is real and accountable.

choices.label: Ask the consultant to fix it, and review their rewrite before it goes back to legal.
choices.feedback: The consultant keeps the work, and you add a safety step. That is reasonable for a legal issue with a short deadline. Be clear that your review is a check for the legal point only, and that the rest stays theirs. Without that, the extra review can quietly become approval of everything.

simulation.debrief: The path through this situation turned on three choices. First, whether you named the decisions and reduced load at the start. Cheong and colleagues found that the same empowering behavior can raise confidence and raise strain, and load is what tips it. Second, whether you let a decision stand when it differed from yours. Trust in the leader carries much of empowerment's effect, and reversing a decision that was truly theirs spends that trust quickly. Third, whether you kept the owner in place under pressure. Legal review, policy and partner relationships are real limits. Good delegation treats them as limits the owner works within. The federal studies add one more lesson: discretion works when it comes with knowledge and access, so make the introductions yourself.

mistakes.mistake: Delegating a task and calling it authority.
mistakes.why: Supervisors often feel they have delegated when they hand off work. Without a named decision right, the person carries the effort while you keep every real choice. The benefits Lee and colleagues found run through people feeling empowered, which requires a real say.
mistakes.instead: Name the specific decisions the person will make and have stand. If there are none, call it an assignment.

mistakes.mistake: Adding authority on top of a full load.
mistakes.why: Giving a big decision to a strong performer feels like recognition. But Cheong and colleagues found that some empowering behaviors raise job tension, which weakens the performance gain. Strong performers are often the most loaded.
mistakes.instead: Ask what can stop, slow or move before you hand anything over, and move it.

mistakes.mistake: Going quiet to show trust.
mistakes.why: Stepping back feels respectful, and many supervisors were told not to micromanage. Wong and Giessner found that autonomy that does not match expectations tends to be read as a hands-off leader, rated less effective.
mistakes.instead: Agree out loud on one early checkpoint, how to reach you, and what would prompt a call.

mistakes.mistake: Taking the work back during the early dip.
mistakes.why: When a delegated project starts slowly, rescuing it feels responsible. Lorinkova and colleagues found that empowered teams start behind and then learn faster. Taking work back cuts off that learning.
mistakes.instead: Expect a slower start. Address load and support, and keep the owner in place.

mistakes.mistake: Reversing a decision because you would have done it differently.
mistakes.why: Your way may be good, and correcting feels like quality control. But a reversed decision tells the person the authority was never theirs. Lorinkova and colleagues warn that leaders who fake empowerment may be seen as insincere.
mistakes.instead: Share your view, ask what they weighed, and reverse only for real risk to people served, to law or to policy.

mistakes.mistake: Handing over a decision without the knowledge to make it.
mistakes.why: Supervisors assume capable people will find what they need. Federal workforce studies found that job knowledge, skills and discretion over process are what link to performance, while goal statements alone have little bearing.
mistakes.instead: Provide the data, the policy context and the right contacts, and make the introductions yourself.

jobAid.title: Real authority handoff: one page
jobAid.use: Use it in the conversation where you hand a colleague a piece of work you want them to own.
steps: Name the result and why it matters to the people DHS serves.
List with them the decisions they own, the ones to talk through first, and the ones that stay with you or the person or area responsible.
Ask what can stop, slow or move so this fits their week, and move it.
Name the data, policy and contacts they need, and make the introductions.
Agree on one early checkpoint and what would prompt a call before then.
Say what you would need to see before you reversed a decision.
When they make a call you would not have made, ask what they weighed and let it stand.

media.reason: Delegation fails in the gap between what a supervisor means and what the colleague hears. Two voices let the learner hear both sides of a handoff and how a few questions close that gap.

script.speaker: female
script.text: I want you to lead the provider staffing guide. You know these providers better than anyone on the team.

script.speaker: male
script.text: I would like that. Can I ask what leading means here? On my last team, leading meant writing a draft and then waiting for edits on every page.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Fair question. Let's sort it out now. You decide the structure, the wording and who tests it with you. Legal review stays with the person or area responsible for it. The release date stays with me, because it ties to the rule change.

script.speaker: male
script.text: And if I want to add a section on common mistakes providers make?

script.speaker: female
script.text: That is yours. Talk to me first only if a choice changes what providers are required to do. Then it needs a policy check.

script.speaker: male
script.text: That helps. Honestly, my review queue is already long. I was going to fit this in at night.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Please don't. Research on empowering leadership finds that the same trust that raises confidence can also raise strain, and strain eats the gain. Which four reviews can move to someone else for six weeks?

script.speaker: male
script.text: The two day-service reviews and the two renewals that are not due until spring.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Done. I will move them today. What else do you need to make good decisions on this?

script.speaker: male
script.text: Time with the policy lead who wrote the rule summary, and the call-line notes on provider questions.

script.speaker: female
script.text: I will introduce you to the policy lead this week and ask the call-line supervisor to share the notes. Let's check in once, when you have a first draft. Call me sooner if something touches requirements.

script.speaker: male
script.text: One more thing. If you would have done the structure differently, will you change it?

script.speaker: female
script.text: I will tell you what I would have done and ask what you weighed. I will only reverse something that puts people served, the law or policy at risk. Otherwise, it stands.

prompts: What is one decision you currently make that a colleague could own, and who is that colleague?
What will come off that person's plate so the new authority fits, and when will you have that conversation?
By what date will you hold the handoff conversation, and when is the one checkpoint you will set?
