theme: Teams and the work they carry

photo.alt: A colleague stands beside the meeting table to speak while seated participants listen.

title: Real participation inside the team
objective: Involve your team in decisions in a way that clears the threshold where participation starts to pay off: share the information first, ask for what only each person knows, and show how input changed the result.
outcomes: Share the facts, limits and data behind a decision before asking for input.
State plainly whether the team is deciding, advising or being informed.
Use a structured round that draws out what each person uniquely knows, not only what the group already shares.
Respond to a raised problem in a way that makes the next one more likely.
Close the loop by telling the team what their input changed and what it did not.

evidence.summary: Asking for input now and then does not seem to help. In two samples, participative leadership was unrelated to performance until it passed a moderate level. Above that point, more participation went with better performance, especially when leaders shared a lot of information. A meta-analysis of 72 studies found that teams perform better when they share information, and much better when they share what only some members know. Structure helps. Voice research adds that people speak up when they believe it will make a difference, and stay quiet when it feels unsafe. Effects on voice are modest, much of the team evidence comes from lab tasks, and no verified public-sector study with numbers was found for this course.

findings.claim: Participative leadership was unrelated to performance below a moderate level; above that threshold, more participation went with better performance, and the effect was stronger when leaders shared more information.
findings.detail: Two field samples: employees in offices and call centers, and factory workers, the second with objective performance. Published 2015. Sample sizes are not on the public record.

findings.claim: Information sharing predicted team performance (corrected correlation .42), and sharing unique information predicted it more strongly than general openness (.50 versus .32).
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 72 studies, 4,795 groups, 17,279 people, 2009. Many studies used lab decision tasks; the link with objective measures was smaller (.21).

findings.claim: Structured discussion was associated with more information sharing (.41) and strengthened the link between unique information and performance (.46 versus .34 when structure was low).
findings.detail: Same meta-analysis, moderator analyses. Openness, by contrast, was more strongly related to cohesion than to performance. Member heterogeneity, how information was distributed and informational interdependence were linked to less sharing.

findings.claim: Managerial openness was the leader behavior most consistently linked to employees speaking up, working through psychological safety; leadership explained an added 6% and 2% of voice in two studies.
findings.detail: 3,149 restaurant crew members (survey) and 223 shift managers (over time), published 2007. Private sector.
findings.source: Detert & Burris, 2007 (Psych Safety Field Guide summary)

findings.claim: Suggesting improvements and raising problems are different behaviors: they have different predictors, including psychological safety and leader openness, and suggestion-type voice is linked to higher rated performance while problem-raising shows the opposite pattern.
findings.detail: Meta-analyses of voice and its promotive and prohibitive forms, 2017. Number of studies not on the public record.

findings.claim: Voice responds most to whether people believe it will have an impact, while silence responds most to psychological safety; formal channels drew helpful ideas but made people more selective about raising anything that might disturb group harmony.
findings.detail: Review of 158 papers from 2014 to 2021, summarizing a meta-analysis and six-month panel study by Sherf, Parke and Isaakyan.

findings.claim: Among proactive employees, speaking up was negatively associated with later career progression.
findings.detail: 180 full-time employees and their supervisors, two-year lag, structural equation model, 2001.

counterintuitive.headline: A little participation seems to do no good at all.
counterintuitive.text: Many supervisors assume that some input is better than none. Lam, Huang and Chan (2015) found a threshold instead. Below a moderate level, participative leadership was unrelated to performance. Only above it did more participation go with better results. The curve was steeper when leaders shared more information. In practice, an occasional 'any thoughts?' at the end of a meeting, or a survey after the decision is made, may not reach the point where participation starts to matter. Doing it fully, on fewer decisions, is likely to help more than doing it lightly on many.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.text: Participation is not asking for opinions. It is giving people the information and the timing to shape a decision before it is made. Research on participative leadership found a threshold. Below a moderate level, participation was unrelated to performance. Above it, more participation went with better results, especially when the leader shared a lot of information. Light participation, such as a quick poll after the plan is set, may never reach that threshold.

sections.title: Why information comes first
sections.text: Teams get better results when members share what only some of them know. A meta-analysis of 72 studies found that sharing unique information was more strongly linked to team performance than general openness. Yet groups tend to spend their time on what everyone already knows. Structure helps draw out the rest. People also speak up more when they believe it will make a difference.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: For your next team decision, do three things. First, send the facts, the limits and the data at least a day ahead. Say what is fixed, such as a statute, a federal rule or a budget line, and what is open. Second, say plainly whether the team is deciding, advising you or being told. Third, run a short round in which each person names one thing they see that others might not. Start with the people closest to the work and with those who usually speak last. Afterward, tell the team what their input changed, and what it did not change and why.

sections.title: What this looks like at DHS
sections.text: A call-line supervisor needs to change how callback requests are sorted. Before the team meeting, they share the call data, the staffing limits and the one rule that cannot change. They tell the team it is advising, and that the supervisor will decide by Friday. In the meeting, each worker names one pattern they hear on calls. Two workers who handle Spanish-language calls point out a delay no report shows. The new sort fixes it. On Friday, the supervisor tells the team which ideas shaped the plan.

sections.title: The threshold
sections.text:
Lam, Huang and Chan (2015) studied participative leadership in two very different settings. One sample was employees in offices and call centers. The other was factory workers, with objective measures of performance. In both, the pattern was J-shaped. Below a moderate level, participative leadership had no link to performance. Above that level, more participation went with better performance.

The second part of the finding matters as much. The curve was steeper when leaders shared a lot of information and flatter when they shared little. Asking for input without sharing what you know gives people little to work with. They are guessing at limits you could have named.

sections.title: The information people hold
sections.text:
Mesmer-Magnus and DeChurch (2009) pooled 72 studies covering nearly 4,800 groups. Information sharing was linked to team performance, with a corrected correlation of .42. The type of sharing mattered. Sharing unique information, the facts only some members hold, was more strongly linked to performance (.50) than general openness (.32). Openness was more strongly tied to cohesion. So a friendly, open meeting builds good feeling, but it does not by itself surface what the team needs.

Structure made a difference. Structured discussions were linked to more sharing (.41), and they strengthened the payoff from unique information. Many of these studies used lab tasks, and the link with objective outcomes was smaller (.21). The direction is still clear.

sections.title: Why people speak up or stay quiet
sections.text:
A study of more than 3,000 restaurant workers looked at what leaders do that gets people to speak up (Detert and Burris, 2007, as summarized by the Psych Safety Field Guide). Managerial openness was the most consistent link. It worked through psychological safety. The effect was modest. Leadership explained an added 6% of voice in one study and 2% in a second.

A later review adds a useful split (Morrison, 2023, summarizing Sherf, Parke and Isaakyan). Voice responds most to whether people believe speaking up will have an impact. Silence responds most to whether it feels safe. These are separate levers. Making a meeting feel safe may reduce silence, but people still need to see their input change something before they offer more.

sections.title: Suggestions and problems are different
sections.text: Chamberlin, Newton and LePine (2017) found that suggesting improvements and raising problems have different predictors. Psychological safety and leader openness are among the differences. Suggestion-type voice was linked to higher rated performance, while problem-raising showed the opposite pattern. That pattern is a warning. The people who flag risks may be rated lower for doing it, even when the warning is right.

sections.title: How to apply it at DHS
sections.text:
Pick fewer decisions and involve people fully. Choose the ones where front-line knowledge matters, such as a notice, a workflow, a schedule or a training plan.

Share first. Send the data, the limits and your current thinking before the meeting. Name what is fixed by statute, federal rule, budget or a decision above you.

Name the role. Say whether the team decides, advises or is being informed. Do not invite advice on something already settled.

Use structure. Ask each person for one thing they know from their own work that others might not. Go around in a set order, starting with those who usually speak last. In hybrid meetings, take written input from people who are remote or on the phones.

Protect problem-raising. When someone flags a risk, thank them for the specific point and act on it or explain why not.

Close the loop. Tell the team what their input changed. When the answer is no, say why.

sections.title: A worked DHS example
sections.text: A program integrity team must change how it selects provider claims for review. The supervisor shares the selection data, the federal requirement that sets the minimum sample and the budget for reviewers. The team is told it is advising and that the decision comes in two weeks. Each reviewer names one pattern they see in their claims. A newer reviewer points out that one billing code is often miscoded by small providers, not misused. That changes how the team flags it. In the follow-up note, the supervisor credits the newer reviewer by name and explains why one other suggestion was not used: it would have dropped below the federal minimum.

sections.title: How strong is the evidence?
sections.text:
The threshold finding comes from two field samples in one well-regarded paper. The public record does not give the sample sizes, and one paper is not a settled law. The finding has not been tested in a state agency. It does offer a useful explanation for a common experience. If most participation a team sees is light, people will reasonably conclude that it does not matter, even if full participation would help.

The information-sharing meta-analysis is large and was read in full for this course. Its limits are clear. Many of the studies were lab tasks where facts were split among members on purpose. The link with objective measures was .21, about half the overall figure. Real teams in public service rarely have such neat puzzles. Still, the core lesson holds up across task types: what only some people know is where the value lies.

Voice research is mostly from private-sector settings such as restaurant chains. The effects of leadership on voice are real but modest. No verified study with numbers on participation in a state agency was found for this course. Apply these findings with judgment, not as precise predictions.

sections.title: Status and who gets heard
sections.text:
The 2023 review notes that supervisors give more credit for voice to higher-status employees, even when lower-status employees speak up more often. Status on a DHS team can come from job class, years of service, a lead role or simply being the one who speaks first. The result is that the same idea is weighed differently depending on who said it.

The evidence reviewed here does not show that this pattern differs by race, disability or any other group, so this course does not claim that. It does support a practical habit. Notice who you credit. Name the person whose point shaped the plan. Go around in a set order, and start with people who hold the least formal status.

sections.title: The risk of raising problems
sections.text:
Two findings point the same way. Chamberlin and colleagues found that problem-raising voice was associated with lower rated performance. Seibert, Kraimer and Crant (2001) found that, among proactive employees, speaking up was negatively associated with career progression over two years. Neither study shows why. One plausible reading is that leaders, often without meaning to, treat the bearer of bad news as the problem.

In program integrity, licensing or eligibility work, problem-raising is often the most valuable input a team can give. A worker who says a new process will create errors may be saving the agency from a correction later. If performance reviews quietly punish that person, the team learns to stay quiet. Protecting problem-raising is a leader's job, and it has to show up in how you rate and assign work.

sections.title: When participation is the wrong tool
sections.text:
Not every decision should be shared. Some are fixed by statute, federal requirements, a court order or a decision above you. Inviting input on those is token participation. It spends trust, and the threshold research suggests it may not help performance anyway.

Some decisions are urgent. A system outage on the call line needs a fast call. In that case, decide, explain why, and invite input on what to do next time.

Some decisions involve partners outside the team. A change that affects counties should go through the person or area responsible for county relationships. A change that affects Tribal Nations goes through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations. The team can advise on the internal parts. It should not be asked to speak for partners.

sections.title: Harder situations
sections.text:
The team says nothing. Silence often means people doubt their input will matter or do not feel safe. Morrison's review suggests these are separate problems. Ask which it is, privately and in groups. Then show impact on a small decision first.

One person dominates. Structure is the fix, not a private talk. Use written input before discussion and a set speaking order.

Input conflicts. Say what you will weigh and decide. Explain the choice. Restate each side's strongest point before you announce it, so people can see they were understood.

You disagree with the team's advice. You can still decide otherwise. Say so openly, explain why, and name what you took from their input. Pretending to follow advice you are not following is worse than declining it.

Remote and shift staff miss the meeting. Hybrid work makes the unique-information problem worse. The people on the phones or in the field often hold the facts no report shows. Collect written input before the meeting and send a summary after.

sections.title: Unique knowledge and differences on the team
sections.text:
The meta-analysis found that member heterogeneity, meaning differences in background and role, was linked to less information sharing. That may seem backward. Teams are often built to be varied so they hold more knowledge. The finding suggests that variety alone does not bring the knowledge out. People with different roles or backgrounds may assume others will not value what they know, or may not know what others lack.

This is a structure problem, not a people problem. On a DHS team, the person who handles interpreter-assisted calls, the person who works with providers and the person newest to the unit each see something different. The leader's job is to ask for those differences directly. A useful question is: what do you see in your part of the work that the rest of the team probably does not?

The same meta-analysis found that how information was spread across members mattered. When most facts were already shared, groups talked about what they had in common. Ask for the unshared part on purpose.

sections.title: What to watch for over time
sections.text: Participation is a pattern, not an event. Watch three signals over a few months. Does input arrive earlier, before you ask? Do problems reach you while they are still small? Do people who rarely spoke now offer points in the round? If the answers are yes, the team likely believes its input has impact. If not, look first at whether you closed the loop on the last few decisions.

sections.title: A short test before you invite input
sections.text: Ask four questions. Is this decision still open? Have I shared the data and the limits? Will I say whether the team decides, advises or is being told? How will people learn what their input changed? If any answer is no, fix it first or skip the invitation.

simulation.setup: You supervise an eligibility support team that answers questions from county workers about a program rule. A federal change takes effect in two months, and your team must update its internal guide and call scripts. Your manager has said the rule text is fixed, but how your team explains and applies it is up to you. Your team includes long-time staff, new hires and two people who handle most of the hardest calls. What is at stake is the quality of the guide and whether your team believes its input matters.

steps.situation: You are planning the first team meeting about the change. Time is short, and you already have a rough draft of the new guide.
steps.question: How do you set up the meeting?

choices.label: Share your draft at the meeting and ask the team for any thoughts.
choices.feedback: It is efficient and it feels inclusive. But with no time to read and no data, most people will react to your draft rather than add what they know. This is the light participation that Lam and colleagues found fell below the threshold. The people with the hardest calls may say little in the room.

choices.label: Send the rule summary, call data and your draft two days ahead, say the team is advising and you will decide by a set date, and ask each person to bring one call pattern others may not see.
choices.feedback: You shared information first, named the team's role and asked for unique knowledge. That combination is what the research links to better results: high information sharing above the threshold, and structure that draws out what only some members know. The set date also shows the decision is still open.

choices.label: Ask two senior staff to review the draft before the meeting, then present the improved version to the full team.
choices.feedback: The senior staff will likely improve the draft, and this is a reasonable shortcut. It also concentrates input in people who already have status. The newer staff and the people on the hardest calls may hold the facts no one else has. Mesmer-Magnus and DeChurch found that unique information is where most of the value lies.

steps.situation: In the meeting, the discussion stays on wording. Two long-time staff do most of the talking. One of the workers who handles the hardest calls stays quiet.
steps.question: What do you do now?

choices.label: Wrap up and thank everyone for their input.
choices.feedback: The meeting ends on time, and the guide reflects mostly what the group already knew. The quiet worker learns that this format does not invite what they know. Research on voice suggests people speak up when they believe it will make a difference. Nothing here showed that.

choices.label: Switch to a short round: each person names one situation the draft does not cover, starting with those who have not spoken.
choices.feedback: You added structure mid-meeting. Structure was linked to more information sharing in the meta-analysis, and starting with quieter people reduces the weight of status. It is a late fix, so some people may still hold back. Following up in writing would help.

choices.label: Ask the quiet worker directly, in front of the group, what they think.
choices.feedback: Your intent is to include them. Being singled out can feel exposing, especially for someone who may already doubt the format. It may work, but a round that asks everyone the same question is safer and draws out more. A private follow-up is another good option.

steps.situation: In the round, a worker who handles the hardest calls says the new rule will create a gap for people with irregular income. They say the draft will lead county workers to give wrong answers. A senior staff member disagrees sharply.
steps.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Note the concern and move on so the meeting stays on track.
choices.feedback: Staying on schedule feels respectful of time. But the worker just raised a problem, and the review literature links problem-raising to lower ratings for the person who does it. Moving on signals that risks are unwelcome. You also lose the most valuable input the meeting produced.

choices.label: Thank them for the specific point, ask both people to walk through one real example, and say you will check the policy question with the person or area responsible.
choices.feedback: You treated the problem as a contribution, not a disruption. Walking through an example turns disagreement into shared information. Routing the policy question to the person or area responsible keeps the team inside its role. This builds the sense of impact that voice research says keeps people speaking up.

choices.label: Side with the senior staff member, who has more experience with the rule.
choices.feedback: Experience matters, and the senior person may be right. But crediting voice by status is exactly the pattern the 2023 review describes. The worker on the hardest calls may see cases the senior person does not. Check the facts before you weigh the people.

steps.situation: You have made your decision on the guide. Some of the team's advice shaped it. Some you did not take, including one idea several people liked.
steps.question: How do you close the loop?

choices.label: Send out the final guide without comment.
choices.feedback: The work is done, but the team cannot see what its input changed. Voice research suggests impact is what drives future speaking up. Without it, the next request for input will draw less. Silence about the idea you declined can read as if it was never heard.

choices.label: Send the guide with a short note on what changed because of the team's input, who raised each point, and why you did not take the idea several people liked.
choices.feedback: You showed impact and credited people by name for specific points, including those with less status. You also explained the no, which shows the idea was heard and weighed. This keeps participation above the threshold over time, not just for one meeting.

choices.label: Thank the team at the next meeting for a great discussion.
choices.feedback: Thanks are good, and the team will appreciate them. But general thanks do not show impact. Voice research suggests impact is what keeps people speaking up. Name what changed and who raised it, including the idea you declined. Without that, people cannot tell whether their input mattered or was just welcomed.

simulation.debrief: This situation tested three moves the research supports. First, share information before asking for input. Lam and colleagues found that participation only paid off above a threshold, and more so when leaders shared a lot of information. Second, use structure to draw out what only some people know. The meta-analysis of 72 studies found unique information was most strongly linked to performance, and structure helped surface it. Third, protect problem-raising and show impact. Voice responds to whether people believe it matters, and problem-raising can be quietly penalized. A team that sees its input change real decisions will keep offering it. A team that gets polite thanks and no change will learn to stay quiet.

mistakes.mistake: Asking for input after the decision is made.
mistakes.why: Leaders want buy-in and believe any input is good. The threshold research suggests light or late participation is unrelated to performance, and it spends trust.
mistakes.instead: Invite input only while the decision is open. If it is settled, inform people and explain why.

mistakes.mistake: Asking for opinions without sharing the facts.
mistakes.why: Leaders assume the team already knows the context. Lam and colleagues found participation pays off more when leaders share a lot of information.
mistakes.instead: Send the data, limits and your current thinking ahead of time.

mistakes.mistake: Running an open discussion and calling it participation.
mistakes.why: Open, friendly meetings feel inclusive. The meta-analysis found openness tied more to cohesion, while unique information drove performance.
mistakes.instead: Use a structured round that asks each person for what they see that others may not.

mistakes.mistake: Weighing ideas by who said them.
mistakes.why: Status is a fast shortcut, and experience often is a good guide. Research reviewed in 2023 found supervisors credit voice more from higher-status staff.
mistakes.instead: Check the facts of a point before weighing the person. Credit ideas by name.

mistakes.mistake: Treating the person who raises problems as negative.
mistakes.why: Bad news is uncomfortable, and problem-raisers can seem resistant. Studies link problem-raising voice to lower ratings and slower career progress.
mistakes.instead: Thank the person for the specific point and act on it or explain why not. Watch for it in your ratings.

mistakes.mistake: Not closing the loop.
mistakes.why: Leaders move on once the decision is made. Voice responds to perceived impact, so unseen impact means less input next time.
mistakes.instead: Tell the team what changed, who raised it and why some ideas were not used.

jobAid.title: Participation that pays off: one page
jobAid.use: Use it when planning any team decision where front-line knowledge could change the result.
steps: Is the decision still open? If not, inform the team instead of asking.
Name what is fixed by statute, federal rule, budget or a decision above you, and what is open.
Send the data and your current thinking at least a day ahead.
Say whether the team decides, advises or is being informed, and when the decision will be made.
Run a round: each person names one thing they see that others might not, quietest first.
Collect written input from remote and shift staff before the meeting.
Route county or Tribal questions to the person or area responsible for those relationships.
Tell the team what changed, who raised it and why some ideas were not used.

media.reason: The core lesson is a mechanism, the threshold and the role of unique information, best taught step by step through one connected story.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: A call-line supervisor at DHS needs to change how callback requests are sorted. The usual approach is familiar. Bring a draft to the team meeting. Ask for thoughts. Thank everyone. Move on. It feels inclusive. The research suggests it may do almost nothing.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: In 2015, researchers studied participative leadership in two settings: workers in offices and call centers, and factory workers whose output was measured directly. They expected that more participation would mean better performance. Instead they found a threshold. Below a moderate level, participation was not linked to performance at all. Only above it did more participation go with better results. And the effect was strongest when leaders shared a lot of information.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Think about what that means. An occasional 'any thoughts?' may never reach the level where participation starts to matter. Asking without sharing the data leaves people guessing about limits the leader already knows.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: A second body of research explains why. A meta-analysis of 72 studies, covering nearly 4,800 groups, looked at how teams share information. Sharing was linked to better performance. But the type of sharing mattered. Sharing what only some members knew was more strongly linked to performance than simply being open. Openness built cohesion. Unique information built results. And left alone, groups tend to talk about what everyone already knows.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: So the supervisor changes the plan. Two days before the meeting, they send the call data, the staffing limits and the one rule that cannot change. They say the team is advising, and the decision will be made Friday. They ask each person to bring one pattern they hear on calls that others may not.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: In the meeting, they go around in a set order, starting with those who usually speak last. Structure matters here. In the same meta-analysis, structured discussion was linked to more sharing and a bigger payoff from unique information.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Two workers who take most of the Spanish-language calls describe a delay that no report shows. Another worker raises a problem: the new sort could push urgent callbacks behind routine ones. A senior colleague disagrees.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: This is the moment that decides whether people keep speaking up. Research on voice finds that raising problems is often rated lower than offering suggestions, even when the warning is right. So the supervisor thanks the worker for the specific point, and asks both people to walk through a real call. The risk turns out to be real. The plan changes.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: On Friday, the supervisor sends the final plan with a short note. It names what changed, who raised each point, and why one popular idea was not used. A review of voice research found that people speak up when they believe it will have an impact. The note is the evidence of impact.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The lesson is simple to say and harder to do. Involve people on fewer decisions, and do it fully. Share first. Ask for what only they know. Protect the people who raise problems. And show what changed.

prompts: Which upcoming decision is still open and would benefit most from what your front-line staff know?
What data and limits will you share ahead of time, and who on your team usually speaks last?
By what date will you send the materials, and when will you tell the team what their input changed?

title: Developing people on purpose
objective: Grow each person on your team through stretch assignments, regular coaching and planned cross-training, so the team can cover its critical work and people move toward the roles they want.
outcomes: Choose a stretch assignment at the right level of challenge and pair it with a feedback plan.
Coach in short, regular conversations that ask before they tell, including with the people you are least drawn to coach.
Map which critical tasks only one person on your team can do, and plan cross-training to close the gaps.
Run a short debrief after key work so experience turns into learning.
Build a development plan with each person that names one assignment, one skill and one support.

evidence.summary: People mostly grow through work that stretches them, but more challenge is not always better. In a study of 60 managers, skill growth showed diminishing returns as challenge rose, and access to feedback offset that. Whether supervisors coach depends a lot on belief: managers who think ability is fixed coach less, and that belief can be shifted. A two-wave study found coaching and engagement feed each other, and nurses in a military health system seldom saw coaching from first-line supervisors. Structured debriefs improve performance by about 25%. Cross-training builds shared understanding and coordination, though that evidence is from lab simulations. Research on supervisors as coaches in human services is thin.

findings.claim: Leadership skill development rose with developmental challenge but with diminishing returns, and access to feedback offset those diminishing returns at high challenge.
findings.detail: 225 on-the-job experiences across 60 managers, published 2009.

findings.claim: Managers who believed ability is fixed coached less, as rated by their employees; a short intervention that shifted the belief increased their willingness to coach a poor performer and the quality of their suggestions.
findings.detail: Two field studies plus an experimental intervention, Personnel Psychology, 2006.

findings.claim: Managerial coaching predicted later role clarity and commitment, and employee attitudes predicted later coaching, so the effect runs both ways.
findings.detail: Two-wave study of 313 full-time US employees, 2024.

findings.claim: Managerial coaching was related to lower role ambiguity, but nurses seldom perceived coaching from their first-line supervisors.
findings.detail: 382 nurses in the US Military Health System, 2024. Public sector, health services.

findings.claim: Workplace coaching had a positive overall effect on outcomes (delta = 0.36), with internal coaches showing stronger effects than external ones.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 17 studies, 2016. Coaching was by coach practitioners, not supervisors.

findings.claim: Leadership training improved learning (delta = .73) and transfer to the job (delta = .82); practice, feedback and spaced sessions were among the features linked to better results.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 335 independent samples, 2017.

findings.claim: Cross-training improved teams' shared understanding of each other's roles, and better coordination carried that into team performance.
findings.detail: Two experiments with 45 and 49 teams in a computer simulation, 2002. The depth of cross-training needed was inconsistent across the two experiments.

findings.claim: A federally funded child welfare workforce center describes the supervisor-as-coach model as under-researched.
findings.detail: Umbrella summary of coaching research by the Quality Improvement Center for Workforce Development, 2021. Human services.

findings.claim: Debriefs improved performance over control groups by about 25% (d = .67), with similar effects for teams and individuals and in real and simulated settings.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 46 samples, 2,136 people, 2013.

findings.claim: A review of the evidence behind the claim that 70 percent or more of workplace learning is informal found that evidence weak and concluded the rule should be set aside.
findings.detail: Critical literature review of five research traditions, Human Resource Development Review 17(2), 153-178, 2018. The review faults inconsistent concepts and flawed research methods. It does not test a different ratio.

counterintuitive.headline: The biggest stretch is not the best one.
counterintuitive.text: It is tempting to think the hardest assignment builds the most skill. DeRue and Wellman (2009) tracked 225 work experiences across 60 managers. Skill growth rose with challenge, but each added step of challenge added less. At very high challenge, the extra difficulty stopped paying off much. The one thing that changed the picture was feedback. People with access to feedback kept learning even from the hardest assignments. So the question is not only how big the stretch is. It is also who will tell the person how it is going, and how often.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.text: People grow most through work that stretches them, coached by someone who pays attention. Development is not a form filled out once a year. It is a series of chosen assignments, short coaching conversations and planned chances to learn each other's work. Done on purpose, it also protects the team. When only one person knows how to run a key report or handle a complex case type, the team is one absence away from a backlog.

sections.title: What the research says
sections.text: In a study of 60 managers, skill growth rose with challenge but leveled off at high challenge. Access to feedback kept people learning even then. Supervisors who believe ability is fixed tend to coach less, and that belief can be changed. Structured debriefs after key work improve performance by about 25%. Cross-training helps team members understand each other's roles, which improves coordination.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: Pick one person and one piece of real work this month. Make it a stretch: new to them, visible and with real stakes, but not so far beyond them that stress takes over. Before it starts, agree on how they will get feedback and from whom. When it ends, hold a fifteen-minute debrief. Ask what went well, what did not and what they would do differently. Then do the same for someone you are less drawn to coach. Research shows supervisors tend to coach the people they already believe in.

sections.title: What this looks like at DHS
sections.text: A supervisor in a disability services unit notices that only one consultant can run the quarterly waiver capacity report. A newer consultant wants to build data skills. The supervisor asks the newer consultant to run the next report with the experienced one available for questions. They agree on two check-ins. Afterward, they debrief together. By the next quarter, two people can run the report, and the newer consultant has a skill they asked for.

sections.title: Stretch assignments, and how big
sections.text:
DeRue and Wellman (2009) followed 60 managers through 225 on-the-job experiences. They asked how much each experience challenged the person and how much leadership skill they built. More challenge meant more growth, but with diminishing returns. At high levels of challenge, each extra bit of difficulty added less learning. Access to feedback changed this. People who could get feedback kept learning even from the hardest experiences.

The practical lesson has two parts. First, aim for a stretch, not a leap. A good assignment is new to the person and has real stakes, but they can see a path to doing it. Second, build feedback into the assignment from the start. Name who will give it and when.

sections.title: Coaching is a belief before it is a skill
sections.text:
Heslin, VandeWalle and Latham (2006) found that managers who believe ability is fixed coach less, as their employees see it. When a short workshop moved managers toward believing that people can grow, they became more willing to coach a poor performer, and their suggestions improved.

A two-wave study of 313 employees found that coaching predicted later role clarity and commitment (Stone, Nimon and Ellinger, 2024). It also found that engaged employees drew more coaching over time. Together, these findings warn of a quiet pattern. Coaching flows to people who are already doing well, and away from people a supervisor has privately written off.

In public service, coaching may be scarcer than supervisors think. Among 382 nurses in the US Military Health System, coaching was linked to lower role ambiguity, but nurses seldom saw coaching from their first-line supervisors (Ferro, Swiger and Yoder, 2024).

sections.title: What coaching looks like
sections.text:
Coaching means helping someone learn on the job through questions, feedback and support, rather than solving the problem for them. It is short and regular. A useful pattern is ask, then tell. Ask what they are trying to do and what they have tried. Ask what they think the next step is. Then add what you see. End with one thing they will try.

Coaching by professional coaches has a clear positive effect overall (Jones, Woods and Guillaume, 2016, 17 studies), and internal coaches did better than external ones. That research was not about supervisors, so treat it as a sign that coaching works, not a measure of how well supervisors do it.

sections.title: Debriefs turn experience into learning
sections.text: A meta-analysis of 46 samples found that debriefs improved performance by about 25% over groups that did not debrief (Tannenbaum and Cerasoli, 2013). The effect held for teams and individuals and in real work settings. A debrief is a short, structured look back. What was intended? What happened? Why? What will change next time? It is the cheapest development tool a supervisor has.

sections.title: Cross-training and bench strength
sections.text:
Marks and colleagues (2002) found that cross-training helped teams build a shared picture of how each role works. That shared picture improved coordination, and coordination improved team performance. These were lab simulations, and the amount of cross-training needed varied. The direction still applies.

Start by listing your team's critical tasks. Mark who can do each one. Any task with only one name is a risk to the people DHS serves. Plan cross-training for those first, pairing the person who knows the work with someone who wants to learn it.

sections.title: A development plan that gets used
sections.text: Keep the plan to one page and three lines. One assignment that stretches the person. One skill they want to build, in their words. One support you will give: feedback, an introduction or time. Revisit it in regular one-on-ones, not once a year.

sections.title: Fitting this into DHS work
sections.text: Development competes with deadlines, caseloads and call volume. Three habits make it fit. First, use work that already has to happen. A legislative report, a provider training or a new procedure can be someone's stretch assignment. Second, put coaching into existing one-on-ones. Ten minutes of ask, then tell, is enough. Third, debrief at the end of work that matters, such as a monitoring cycle or a system change, while memory is fresh. None of these needs a separate program. Each needs a supervisor who decides, ahead of time, who will learn from the work.

sections.title: How strong is the evidence?
sections.text:
The evidence here comes in different strengths. The debrief meta-analysis is solid: 46 samples, more than 2,000 people, and similar effects across settings. The leadership training meta-analysis is very large, with 335 samples, and it supports practice, feedback and spaced sessions as features that help.

The assignment research is narrower. DeRue and Wellman studied 60 managers. Their finding fits common sense, but one study cannot set an exact point where challenge becomes too much. Coaching research has its own gaps. The strongest meta-analysis is of professional coaches, not supervisors. A child welfare workforce summary calls the supervisor-as-coach model under-researched (QIC-WD summary of coaching research). Cross-training evidence comes from lab simulations.

You will also hear that 70% of learning happens on the job, 20% through others and 10% in formal training. That ratio is popular, but no study reviewed for this course supports it. A 2018 review by Clardy found the evidence behind the 70 percent claim weak and concluded the rule should be set aside. Use the studies above, not the ratio, to plan.

sections.title: Who gets developed
sections.text:
The coaching research points to a fairness problem. Managers who think ability is fixed coach less, and engaged staff draw more coaching over time. Stretch assignments can follow the same path. Supervisors give visible work to people they already trust, and those people grow faster.

The studies reviewed here do not show that this pattern affects any racial, disability or other group differently, so this course makes no such claim. What the research does support is checking your own pattern. List your team. Next to each name, write the last stretch assignment and the last real coaching conversation. Look for the gaps. Ask the people with the fewest entries what they want to learn, and start there.

Access also depends on the job. Staff on call lines, in the field or on fixed shifts may have less room for stretch work. Build it into their schedule rather than expecting it on top.

sections.title: When stretch becomes strain
sections.text:
The diminishing returns DeRue and Wellman found are a warning. A person given a very large assignment with little feedback may learn less, not more, and carry more stress. Signs to watch include long hours, reluctance to ask questions and a drop in quality on routine work. When you see them, add feedback and support before you cut the assignment. Feedback is what offset the diminishing returns in the study.

Also check workload. A stretch assignment on top of a full caseload is not development. It is overload. Take something off before you add.

sections.title: Coaching people you have doubts about
sections.text:
The Heslin research is the most useful here. Supervisors who privately believe a person cannot improve coach that person less. The belief then confirms itself. The same research found the belief could be shifted.

Start by naming the doubt to yourself. Then look for one recent example of the person improving at anything. Coach on one specific, small behavior. Ask first, then tell. Follow up within a week. If performance does not improve after real coaching and clear feedback, that is a separate conversation. Make sure it comes after coaching, not instead of it.

sections.title: Cross-training without losing quality
sections.text:
Cross-training takes time from the person who knows the work. In a busy unit, it can feel impossible. Start with the single most fragile task. Pair rather than shadow: the learner does the work while the expert watches and coaches, not the other way around. Debrief afterward. Cross-training also has a side benefit the Marks research points to. When people understand each other's roles, handoffs improve, even if they never cover for each other.

Some tasks need formal authority, such as signing for a licensing decision or approving a contract. Cross-training builds knowledge, but it does not grant authority. Be clear about the difference, and route questions about who may sign to the person or area responsible.

sections.title: Development and the roles people want
sections.text: A development plan should start with the person's goals, not the team's gaps. Some people want to move up. Some want to go deeper in their current work. Some want to move to another area of DHS. Ask, and listen. Then look for overlap between what they want and what the team needs. Where there is none, be honest. Help them find development elsewhere, through a project with another unit or a training through the state's enterprise learning system. Developing someone who later leaves for another DHS role is still a win for the people DHS serves.

sections.title: Using formal training well
sections.text:
Formal training still has a place. The leadership training meta-analysis found strong average gains in learning and transfer to the job across 335 samples. Several design features were linked to better results: a needs analysis first, practice, feedback, sessions spread over time and face-to-face delivery. Training that ends in a single day with no practice afterward misses most of those features.

When a staff member attends a course, treat it as the start of a stretch, not the end. Before the course, ask what they hope to apply. After it, find one piece of real work where they can use it within two weeks. Then give feedback on how it went. That turns a class into the practice and feedback the research links to transfer.

sections.title: When the plan meets a hard limit
sections.text: Sometimes development runs into limits you cannot change. A job class may cap what work a person can be assigned. A union agreement may shape how assignments are offered. A hiring freeze may mean there is no role to grow into. Be honest about these limits rather than offering growth you cannot deliver. Route questions about job classes and assignment rules to the person or area responsible for human resources. Within the limits, there is usually still room for a new skill, a project or deeper expertise.

sections.title: A short test for your team
sections.text: Ask five questions. Does each person have a current stretch assignment with a named source of feedback? When did I last have a real coaching conversation with each person? Which critical tasks have only one name? When did my team last debrief a piece of work? Whose development have I been putting off, and why?

simulation.setup: You supervise a contracts and grants team that manages agreements with community providers. A senior grants specialist who handles the most complex agreements will be on extended leave in three months. Two team members could learn parts of that work: an experienced specialist who seems disengaged, and a newer specialist who is eager but has less background. Your team must also finish an annual monitoring cycle. What is at stake is continuity for providers, the growth of both specialists and the senior specialist's ability to leave without worry.

steps.situation: You need to decide how to prepare for the senior specialist's leave.
steps.question: What do you do first?

choices.label: Ask the eager newer specialist to shadow the senior specialist for the next three months.
choices.feedback: The newer specialist will be grateful, and shadowing is easy to arrange. But watching is not the same as doing, and you have quietly skipped the experienced specialist. The coaching research finds supervisors tend to invest in people who already seem engaged. That pattern can leave a capable person behind.

choices.label: List the senior specialist's critical tasks with them, then talk with both specialists about which parts each wants to learn.
choices.feedback: You started with the work and the people, not with an assumption. Mapping critical tasks shows where the single points of failure are. Asking both specialists avoids writing off the one who seems disengaged. Heslin and colleagues found that supervisors coach less when they believe people cannot change. Asking is a check on that belief.

choices.label: Ask the senior specialist to write a detailed procedures manual before leaving.
choices.feedback: A manual is useful, and it feels thorough. But complex agreements involve judgment that a manual does not capture. Cross-training research found that teams build shared understanding by working in each other's roles. A manual alone may leave the team with documents and no one who has done the work.

steps.situation: Six weeks in, the newer specialist is struggling with the most complex agreement and working late. The experienced specialist has said nothing.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Reassure the newer specialist that it is a stretch and they will get there.
choices.feedback: Encouragement helps, but it does not change the conditions. DeRue and Wellman found that learning levels off at high challenge unless feedback is available. Late nights are a sign the stretch has become strain. Reassurance without feedback leaves the person carrying more than the assignment can teach.

choices.label: Set a weekly review where the newer specialist walks through their work with the senior specialist, and move one routine task off their plate.
choices.feedback: You added the thing the research says matters most at high challenge: regular feedback. You also cut load so the stretch fits. This is a late correction, and the experienced specialist is still out of the picture. Consider asking them about the parts they could own.

choices.label: Take back the most complex agreement and assign it to yourself during the leave.
choices.feedback: This protects the providers in that agreement, which matters. It also ends the learning for the newer specialist and adds to your own load. A smaller piece of the complex work, with feedback, could keep both the learning and the quality.

steps.situation: The experienced specialist surprises you. They want to learn the complex agreements but say they stopped asking for new work after past requests went nowhere. The newer specialist wants to learn monitoring.
steps.question: How do you set up the cross-training?

choices.label: Have each specialist do the work while the senior specialist coaches, with a short debrief after each major task.
choices.feedback: Pairing with the learner in the driver's seat builds the shared understanding cross-training research describes. Debriefs after each task add the learning gain the debrief meta-analysis found, about 25% on average. You also acted on what the experienced specialist told you, which begins to repair the pattern they described.

choices.label: Send both specialists to a formal grants management course first.
choices.feedback: Formal training can help, especially with practice and feedback built in, as the leadership training meta-analysis found. But three months is short, and a course alone will not teach these specific agreements. Pair the course with doing the actual work.

choices.label: Give the experienced specialist all the complex work at once, since they have the background.
choices.feedback: Their background makes this tempting. But taking on all of it at once, in three months, risks the diminishing returns DeRue and Wellman found at high challenge. It also leaves no room for feedback. Stage the work and build in review.

steps.situation: The leave starts next week. Both specialists have done real parts of the work. You have a final one-on-one with each before the senior specialist leaves.
steps.question: What do you focus on?

choices.label: Confirm coverage and say you are available if they need anything.
choices.feedback: Coverage matters, and availability is kind. But an open offer to call is vague. Without a set time for feedback, the learning may stop just when the work gets real. Name a weekly check-in and what each person owns, so feedback stays in place during the leave.

choices.label: Debrief what each learned, set a weekly check-in during the leave, and update each person's development plan with the skill they built and what comes next.
choices.feedback: You closed the loop on the experience, kept feedback in place during the hardest period and tied the work to each person's goals. This turns a coverage plan into development. It also signals that the experienced specialist's request was heard and acted on.

choices.label: Focus on the risks and tell them to escalate anything unusual to you.
choices.feedback: Naming risks is responsible, and the leave is a real risk for providers. But a focus only on escalation tells people to bring problems to you rather than solve them. It can undo the confidence they built over three months. Pair risk talk with what they now own and when you will meet.

simulation.debrief: This situation tested three lessons from the research. First, check who you develop. Supervisors tend to coach people they already believe in, and the experienced specialist's story is a common one. Asking both people what they wanted surfaced a capable learner who had stopped asking. Second, match challenge with feedback. DeRue and Wellman found learning levels off at high challenge unless feedback is available. Weekly review and lighter loads keep a stretch from becoming strain. Third, learn by doing and then look back. Cross-training builds shared understanding when the learner does the work, and debriefs improve performance by about a quarter on average. A leave became a chance to build bench strength and grow two people.

mistakes.mistake: Giving the biggest stretch to show confidence.
mistakes.why: A big assignment feels like a vote of trust. DeRue and Wellman found learning levels off at high challenge unless feedback is in place.
mistakes.instead: Choose a stretch the person can see a path through, and name who gives feedback and when.

mistakes.mistake: Coaching only the people who are already thriving.
mistakes.why: Engaged people are easier and more rewarding to coach. Research finds coaching flows toward engaged staff, and supervisors who think ability is fixed coach less.
mistakes.instead: List each person and the last time you coached them. Start with the longest gap.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a development plan as a yearly form.
mistakes.why: Plans are often tied to review cycles, so they feel finished once filed. Learning happens in the work, not on the form.
mistakes.instead: Keep a three-line plan and revisit it in regular one-on-ones.

mistakes.mistake: Relying on shadowing or manuals for cross-training.
mistakes.why: Watching and writing feel efficient. Cross-training research found shared understanding grows from working in each other's roles.
mistakes.instead: Pair with the learner doing the work and the expert coaching, then debrief.

mistakes.mistake: Skipping the debrief because the work went fine.
mistakes.why: When things go well, looking back feels unnecessary. The debrief meta-analysis found about a 25% performance gain from debriefs across settings.
mistakes.instead: Hold a fifteen-minute debrief after any key piece of work, success or not.

mistakes.mistake: Adding development on top of a full load.
mistakes.why: Supervisors want to offer growth and assume people will make room. A stretch on a full plate turns into strain.
mistakes.instead: Take something off before you add the stretch, especially for staff on fixed shifts.

jobAid.title: Developing people on purpose: one page
jobAid.use: Use it once a quarter for your whole team, and before any one-on-one where you talk about growth.
steps: List your team's critical tasks and mark every task with only one name.
For each person, note their last stretch assignment and last real coaching conversation.
Ask each person what skill they want to build and what role they want next.
Choose one stretch assignment per person that is new, real and reachable, and remove something to make room.
Name who gives feedback on each assignment and how often.
Pair for cross-training with the learner doing the work, starting with the most fragile task.
Debrief key work in fifteen minutes: intent, what happened, why, next time.
Keep a three-line plan per person: one assignment, one skill, one support.

media.reason: Development depends on what the supervisor believes and what the staff member wants. Two voices let the learner hear how a coaching conversation surfaces what a supervisor assumed wrong.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Thanks for making time. The senior grants specialist starts leave in three months. I want to talk about what you might take on.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Honestly, I assumed you would give it to the newer specialist. They are always the first to volunteer.

script.speaker: male
script.text: I will be honest too. I did assume you were not interested. You have not asked for new work in a while.

script.speaker: female
script.text: I stopped asking. I asked twice for the complex agreements a few years ago, under a different supervisor, and nothing came of it.

script.speaker: male
script.text: That helps me understand. Research on coaching finds supervisors tend to invest in people they already see as engaged. I may have been doing that. What would you want to learn?
