title: Owning your development
objective: Take the lead on your own growth by choosing varied work, seeking feedback, reviewing your own experience and asking for development that connects to a real path.
outcomes: Name one skill you want to build and one piece of real work that would stretch it.
Ask for specific feedback from at least two people who see your work differently.
Debrief your own work, including what went well, in a few minutes after key tasks.
Explain the value of your work to a supervisor in terms of the people DHS serves and the problems you solve.
Ask for development support that is tied to a role, assignment or path you can name.

evidence.summary: People who take initiative on their careers, try new approaches and learn how their organization works tend to do better over time, though the links to pay and promotion are modest. The links to career satisfaction are stronger. Practice matters, but a large meta-analysis found deliberate practice explained less than 1% of performance differences in professions, and a replication of the famous violin study found a smaller effect than the original. Learning from experience works best with review: debriefs raise performance about 25%, and reviewing successes as well as failures helps more than reviewing failures alone. Support for development predicted more leaving when people saw no career opportunity. Most of this research is private-sector, and none is from Minnesota state government.

findings.claim: Proactive employees did three things linked to later career progress and satisfaction: they innovated, learned how the organization works and took career initiative; speaking up was negatively linked to career progress.
findings.detail: 180 full-time employees and their supervisors, two-year lag, structural equation model, 2001.

findings.claim: Proactive personality was modestly linked to salary (corrected correlation .14) and promotion (.11), and more strongly to career satisfaction and other subjective success (.31).
findings.detail: Meta-analytic values from Fuller and Marler (2009) as reported in a 2022 meta-analysis; salary k = 10, n = 3,031; subjective success k = 32, n = 9,592.

findings.claim: Feedback seeking declined with tenure and age, rose with a learning orientation and good relationships, and had only a small link with performance.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 30 years of feedback-seeking research, 2015. Number of studies not on the public record.

findings.claim: Support for development predicted better performance only when people saw career opportunity, and predicted more people choosing to leave when they did not.
findings.detail: 264 exempt-level employees and their supervisors, 2011.

findings.claim: In the original 2014 analysis, deliberate practice explained 26% of performance differences in games, 21% in music, 18% in sports, 4% in education and less than 1% in professions.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis, Psychological Science 25(8), 2014. The authors published a corrigendum in Psychological Science 29(7), 2018. Its corrected figures could not be opened for this review, so these percentages are from the 2014 abstract.

findings.claim: A replication of the classic violin study found practice alone explained 26% of performance differences, compared with 48% in the original comparison, and the best violinists had not practiced significantly more than the good ones.
findings.detail: 39 violinists in three groups of 13, double-blind procedure, 2019.

findings.claim: Soldiers who reviewed both their successes and failures after each day improved significantly more than those who reviewed only failures.
findings.detail: Quasi-field experiment with 98 soldiers in two companies doing successive navigation exercises, 2005. Military, public sector.

findings.claim: Debriefs improved performance by about 25% (d = .67), with similar effects for individuals and teams.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 46 samples, 2,136 people, 2013.

findings.claim: Skill growth rose with the challenge of an experience but leveled off at high challenge, unless feedback was available.
findings.detail: 225 on-the-job experiences across 60 managers, 2009.

counterintuitive.headline: Development without a path can push people out.
counterintuitive.text: Most people assume that more support for development always builds loyalty. Kraimer and colleagues (2011) studied 264 professional employees and their supervisors. Support for development predicted better performance only when people saw real career opportunity inside the organization. When they did not, that same support predicted more people choosing to leave. Training without a path can feel like preparation for a job somewhere else. For you, the lesson is practical. When you ask for development, connect it to a role, an assignment or a kind of work you can see ahead. If no path exists, it helps to know that before you invest.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.text: Your development is yours to lead. A supervisor can open doors, but the person who decides what to learn, asks for feedback and reflects on experience is you. Research on proactive careers finds that people who try new approaches, learn how their organization works and take career initiative tend to report more career satisfaction over time. The links to pay and promotion are real but modest.

sections.title: What helps and what does not
sections.text: Practice matters, but less than many people believe. A large meta-analysis found deliberate practice explained less than 1% of performance differences in professions. What seems to matter more in professional work is varied, challenging experience with feedback and review. Debriefs raise performance by about 25% on average. Reviewing what went well, not only what went wrong, helps more. One more finding is worth knowing. When people received development support but saw no career path, they were more likely to leave.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: This week, choose one skill you want to build. Then find one real piece of work that would stretch it. Ask your supervisor for it, and say why it matters to the people your work serves. Ask two people who see your work differently for one specific piece of feedback. After the work, take five minutes to think it through. What did you intend, what happened, what worked and what would you change?

sections.title: What this looks like at DHS
sections.text: A senior eligibility worker is at the top of their job class. They want to grow without leaving the work they love. They ask to lead the team's training for new hires on one complex rule. They ask a policy lead and a new hire for feedback. After each session, they take a few minutes to review what landed and what did not. Six months later, they can name a skill they built and point to the evidence.

sections.title: What proactive people actually do
sections.text:
Seibert, Kraimer and Crant (2001) followed 180 employees for two years. They asked what proactive people do that leads to career success. Three behaviors stood out. Proactive people innovated: they tried new ways of doing their work. They built political knowledge: they learned how decisions get made and who influences them. And they took career initiative: they planned, sought out development and made their goals known. All three were linked to later salary growth, promotions and career satisfaction.

One behavior was not helpful for careers in this study. Speaking up was negatively linked to career progress. That does not mean you should stay quiet about real problems. It does mean that how you raise issues, and with whom, matters.

sections.title: Expect modest gains in pay, larger gains in satisfaction
sections.text: Meta-analytic values reported in a 2022 review show that proactive personality is modestly linked to salary and promotion, with corrected correlations of .14 and .11. The link to career satisfaction and other subjective success is stronger, at .31 (as reported by Zhang and colleagues, 2022). In state service, where pay and promotion follow job classes and openings, satisfaction may be the more realistic goal for many people. It is not a lesser one.

sections.title: Practice is not the whole story
sections.text:
You may have heard that expertise comes mostly from long hours of the right kind of practice. Macnamara, Hambrick and Oswald (2014) tested the broader claim. In their original analysis, deliberate practice explained a fair share of performance differences in games, music and sports. In education it explained 4%, and in professions less than 1%. A careful replication of the original violin study found that practice alone explained 26% of differences, not the 48% the original comparison suggested (Macnamara and Maitra, 2019).

Practice still helps. But in professional work, much of what separates strong performers seems to come from other things. Varied experience, feedback and reflection are among the factors the research in this course supports.

sections.title: Learn from your own experience
sections.text:
A meta-analysis of 46 samples found that debriefs improved performance by about 25%, and the effect held for individuals, not just teams (Tannenbaum and Cerasoli, 2013). You can debrief yourself. After an important piece of work, ask four questions. What did I intend? What happened? Why? What will I do next time?

Include what went well. In a study of 98 soldiers, those who reviewed both successes and failures improved more than those who reviewed only failures (Ellis and Davidi, 2005). Most people learn from mistakes by habit. They rarely ask why something worked, so they cannot repeat it on purpose.

sections.title: Ask for feedback, especially as you gain tenure
sections.text: A meta-analysis of feedback seeking found that people ask for feedback less as their tenure and age grow (Anseel and colleagues, 2015). The link between asking and performance was small, so asking is not magic. But DeRue and Wellman (2009) found that feedback is what keeps people learning from hard experiences. Ask specific questions. Instead of asking how you are doing, ask what one thing would make your next provider notice clearer.

sections.title: Ask for support that connects to a path
sections.text: Kraimer and colleagues (2011) found that support for development predicted better performance only when people saw career opportunity. Without it, support predicted more leaving. When you ask for training or an assignment, connect it to a role, a kind of work or a direction you can name. Explain the value in terms of the people your work serves and the problems you solve.

sections.title: Putting it together in a normal month
sections.text: Owning your development does not need a separate program. In a normal month, it can look like this. In the first week, pick one skill and tell your supervisor which work would stretch it. During the month, ask one peer and one person you support for a specific piece of feedback. After each important task, take five minutes to review it, including what went well. At the end of the month, look back across those reviews. Is there a pattern in what works? Is the stretch still the right size, or has it become strain? Adjust, and pick the next step. Small, repeated cycles of work, feedback and review are what the research in this course supports.

sections.title: How strong is the evidence?
sections.text:
The proactive-career evidence includes a two-year study of 180 employees and meta-analytic values reported in a 2022 review. Most of it is from private-sector settings in the United States. No study of Minnesota state employees was found. The pay and promotion links are small. In a system where advancement depends on job classes and postings, initiative may matter less for promotion than in the private sector. The research did not test that, so treat it as a question.

The deliberate-practice findings are well documented, but they are also debated. The authors published a correction to the 2014 meta-analysis in 2018. The corrected figures could not be checked for this course, so the domain percentages above come from the original 2014 abstract. Treat them as approximate. What both the meta-analysis and the replication support is a narrower claim: practice does not explain most of the difference between people, especially in professions.

The debrief research is strong and consistent. The study of successes and failures is one quasi-experiment with soldiers. It is a careful design, but one study.

sections.title: At the top of a job class
sections.text:
Many DHS staff reach the top of their job class and face a choice. They can move toward supervision, move to a different kind of work, or go deeper in the work they do now. None of these is the right answer for everyone.

The research in this course offers three guides. First, satisfaction is a more reliable outcome of proactive behavior than pay or promotion, so define success in terms you can reach. Second, varied and challenging experience with feedback builds skill. You can find it inside your current role by leading a project, training others or taking on a complex case type. Third, if you want a new role, ask about the path directly. Development without a visible path was linked to more leaving. Knowing early lets you choose.

sections.title: Explaining the value of your work
sections.text:
Asking for development is easier when your supervisor can see the value of what you already do. Explain your work in terms of outcomes, not tasks. Instead of 'I process renewals,' say 'I catch the income documentation gaps that would otherwise lead to wrongful closures.' Use examples, not adjectives.

Political knowledge, one of the three behaviors linked to career success, includes knowing who decides what and what they care about. A program manager may care about error rates. A director may care about how a change affects counties. Learn what each person needs to see, and frame your work for them. This is not spin. It is translation.

sections.title: When speaking up seems to cost you
sections.text:
The 2001 study found that speaking up was negatively linked to career progress. The study does not show why. It may be that problem-raising is sometimes heard as complaint, or that it creates friction with people who influence careers.

This is not a reason to stay silent about risks to people served. In program integrity, licensing or eligibility, raising a problem early can prevent real harm. It is a reason to raise problems with care. Bring the issue with evidence and a possible fix. Raise it first with the person or area responsible. Frame it around shared goals. If the issue involves a Tribal Nation, route it through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations.

sections.title: Feedback that actually helps
sections.text:
The feedback-seeking meta-analysis found only a small link between asking for feedback and performance. One reason may be that general requests get general answers. Specific requests get usable ones.

Ask people who see your work from different angles: a peer, someone you serve or support, and someone more senior. Ask about one thing at a time. Then try something different and ask again. That sequence of action, feedback and adjustment is what DeRue and Wellman found keeps learning going when work is hard.

If feedback is hard to hear, wait a day before responding. Look for the part that is true, even if the delivery was poor. Then thank the person and tell them what you will try. Closing the loop this way makes the next request easier, and you will need feedback again the next time the work gets hard.

sections.title: When your supervisor is not supporting you
sections.text:
Some supervisors are stretched thin, uninterested in development or unsure how to help. You can still lead your own growth. Look for stretch work you can propose. Find a mentor elsewhere in DHS. Join a cross-unit project. Use the state's enterprise learning resources, and pair any course with a real piece of work where you can apply it soon after.

If the barrier is a policy or job class rule, ask the person or area responsible for human resources what is possible. If the barrier is the relationship, it may help to name it directly and calmly: say what you want to learn and ask what would make it possible.

sections.title: Growing as an individual contributor
sections.text:
Not everyone wants to supervise, and the research does not suggest they should. The behaviors linked to career satisfaction, such as innovating, learning how decisions are made and taking career initiative, are open to anyone. Think of the deep experts on your own team. One may be the person everyone calls about a complex waiver rule. Another may be the analyst who knows where the data goes wrong.

If this is your path, define growth as depth and reach. Depth means handling harder cases or questions. Reach means more people benefit from what you know, through training others, writing guidance or advising on policy. Both are real growth. Both can be named in a development conversation, and both can be stretched with feedback and review.

sections.title: A short test for yourself
sections.text: Ask five questions. What skill am I building right now, and what work is stretching it? Who gave me specific feedback this month? When did I last review a piece of my own work, including what went well? Can I explain the value of my work in one sentence about the people it serves? Is the development I want connected to a path I can see?

simulation.setup: You are a senior program specialist in a disability services policy area. You are at the top of your job class and have done strong work for years. You want to keep growing, but you are not sure whether you want to supervise. Your supervisor is supportive but busy. A new state initiative to simplify provider enrollment is starting, and a lead role on one workstream is open. What is at stake is your growth, your satisfaction in the work and whether the time you invest connects to where you want to go.

steps.situation: You hear about the open workstream lead role. You are interested but unsure you have the right background.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Wait to see if your supervisor suggests you for it.
choices.feedback: Waiting feels modest and avoids seeming pushy. But career initiative, making your goals known and seeking development, was one of the behaviors linked to later career progress in the two-year study by Seibert and colleagues. Busy supervisors often do not know who wants what. The role may go to someone who asked.

choices.label: Ask your supervisor for the role, explaining what you would bring and what skill you want to build through it.
choices.feedback: You took career initiative and framed the request around value and growth. Seibert and colleagues found initiative was linked to later progress and satisfaction. Naming the skill you want to build also sets up the feedback conversation. This is a stretch with a clear purpose.

choices.label: Take a course on project leadership first, then ask for a role next time.
choices.feedback: Preparing is sensible, and a course can help. But the research in this course points to real, challenging work with feedback as the engine of skill growth. A course with no assignment to apply it to misses that. The workstream is the stretch. Consider asking for it now and taking the course alongside.

steps.situation: Someone else is named workstream lead. Your supervisor asks if you would help with the provider outreach piece.
steps.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Agree, and treat it as part of your regular work.
choices.feedback: Saying yes is good. Treating it as routine wastes a chance. The research suggests experience builds skill most when it is chosen for a purpose and reviewed. Without a goal or feedback, you may finish the work and not notice what you learned. Naming one skill and one source of feedback costs little.

choices.label: Agree, name one skill you want to build through it, and ask who could give you feedback along the way.
choices.feedback: You turned a smaller assignment into a deliberate stretch. DeRue and Wellman found feedback keeps people learning from challenging work. Naming the skill also tells your supervisor what you want, which helps next time a lead role opens. This recovers much of what waiting cost you.

choices.label: Decline, since it is not the lead role you wanted.
choices.feedback: The disappointment is understandable. But outreach work builds knowledge of how decisions are made and who influences them. That political knowledge was one of the three behaviors linked to career success. Declining also signals less interest than you have, which may matter when the next lead role opens.

steps.situation: You are named workstream lead. Two months in, a provider meeting goes well, and a draft procedure gets sharp criticism from a county partner relayed through the person or area responsible for county relationships.
steps.question: How do you learn from these two events?

choices.label: Focus on the criticism and revise the draft carefully.
choices.feedback: Fixing the draft is right. But reviewing only failures misses half the lesson. Ellis and Davidi found soldiers who reviewed both successes and failures improved more than those who reviewed failures only. Ask why the provider meeting worked, too, so you can repeat it on purpose.

choices.label: Take ten minutes to debrief both: what you intended, what happened, why and what you will do next time.
choices.feedback: You reviewed both the success and the failure, the pattern Ellis and Davidi found led to more improvement. Debriefs improved performance about 25% across 46 samples. A short, honest look back is the cheapest development tool you have, and you used it on your own work.

choices.label: Ask your supervisor what they think went wrong with the draft.
choices.feedback: Asking for feedback is a good habit, and it fades with tenure for many people, according to the feedback-seeking meta-analysis. A general question about what went wrong may get a general answer, though. Ask about one specific choice, and do your own review first.

steps.situation: Your supervisor offers to fund a leadership certificate. You are still unsure whether you want to supervise, and there are no supervisor openings in your area soon.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Accept, since development is always worth it.
choices.feedback: The offer is generous, and learning has value. But Kraimer and colleagues found development support predicted more leaving when people saw no career path. If you take the certificate with no role in sight, you may find yourself looking elsewhere. Talk about the path before you start.

choices.label: Thank your supervisor, and ask to talk about what paths exist: supervision, a senior specialist role or deeper policy work, and which the certificate would serve.
choices.feedback: You connected the support to a path before investing in it. That is the condition under which Kraimer and colleagues found development support predicted better performance. You also kept your options open. You may still take the certificate, but now with a reason you can name.

choices.label: Decline, since you are not sure you want to supervise.
choices.feedback: Honesty about your goals is good. Declining outright may close a door you have not explored, though. A conversation about paths would let you find out whether the certificate could serve other goals, such as leading projects without supervising. It also tells your supervisor what you do want.

simulation.debrief: This situation followed three habits the research supports. First, take career initiative. Seibert and colleagues found that people who made their goals known, sought development and learned how decisions get made had better career outcomes over two years. Waiting to be noticed costs opportunities. Second, review your own experience, including what went well. Debriefs improve performance about a quarter on average, and reviewing successes as well as failures led to more improvement in the Ellis and Davidi study. Third, connect development to a path. Support without a visible career opportunity predicted more leaving. Asking about the path first lets you invest your time where it leads somewhere you want to go.

mistakes.mistake: Waiting to be noticed.
mistakes.why: Many people were taught that good work speaks for itself. Seibert and colleagues found career initiative was linked to later progress and satisfaction. Busy supervisors often do not know who wants what.
mistakes.instead: Tell your supervisor the skill you want to build and the work that would build it.

mistakes.mistake: Counting hours of practice instead of variety and feedback.
mistakes.why: The idea that expertise comes from practice hours is widely repeated. A meta-analysis found deliberate practice explained less than 1% of differences in professions.
mistakes.instead: Seek varied, challenging work, and pair each stretch with a source of feedback.

mistakes.mistake: Reviewing only what went wrong.
mistakes.why: Failures grab attention, so people review them by habit. Ellis and Davidi found reviewing successes as well as failures led to more improvement.
mistakes.instead: After key work, ask why the good parts worked so you can repeat them on purpose.

mistakes.mistake: Asking less for feedback as you gain experience.
mistakes.why: Experienced people may feel they should already know, and asking can feel exposing. Research finds feedback seeking declines with tenure.
mistakes.instead: Ask specific questions of people who see your work from different angles.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting development with no path in mind.
mistakes.why: Training feels like an unmixed good. Kraimer and colleagues found support for development predicted more leaving when people saw no career opportunity.
mistakes.instead: Connect each request to a role, assignment or kind of work you can name.

mistakes.mistake: Describing your work as tasks instead of outcomes.
mistakes.why: Tasks are concrete and easy to list. Supervisors and leaders respond to what the work prevents or achieves for people served.
mistakes.instead: Explain your work in one sentence about the problem it solves and who it helps.

jobAid.title: Owning your development: one page
jobAid.use: Use it once a month on your own, and before any conversation with your supervisor about growth.
steps: Name one skill you are building now, in your own words.
Name the real work that is stretching it, or the work you will ask for.
Ask two people who see your work differently for one specific piece of feedback.
After key work, debrief in five minutes: intent, what happened, why, next time, including what went well.
Explain the value of your work in one sentence about the people it serves.
Before accepting training or an assignment, ask which path it serves.
Route policy or job class questions to the person or area responsible.

media.reason: This course speaks to the learner about their own choices. A single calm narrator can walk through the evidence and the habits as a personal reflection.

prompts: What one skill do you want to build in the next three months, and what real work would stretch it?
Which two people see your work from different angles, and what specific question will you ask each?

title: Opening opportunity fairly
objective: Hand out stretch assignments, visible roles and advocacy using criteria set in advance, so that opportunity reaches everyone who can grow into it.
outcomes: Write down what a stretch assignment requires before you think about who should get it.
List who has had the last several visible assignments and who has carried the low-visibility tasks.
Rotate or assign non-promotable tasks instead of waiting for someone to say yes.
Act as a sponsor: name a specific person for a specific opportunity in a room where the decision is made.
Explain an assignment decision to your team in terms of the criteria you set.

evidence.summary: Mentoring helps careers, but the measured effects are small. Advancement depends more on who gets challenging, visible work and who speaks up for a person when decisions are made. Studies show that challenging assignments are not shared evenly, even when interest is equal. Women are asked more often to take on tasks that do not lead to promotion. Evaluators also bend the criteria to fit the person they already favor, and believing a process is fair can make bias worse. Two things help: setting criteria before looking at candidates, and making decisions accountable and visible. Limits: most studies are experiments or private firms, most concern gender, and no verified public-sector study of sponsorship was found.

findings.claim: Workplace mentoring is linked to better outcomes, but every effect was small, from about r = .03 to .19.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 112 studies and reports, 116 independent samples across youth, academic and workplace mentoring. Mostly correlational. 2008.

findings.claim: Mentoring is tied to career benefits, but effects on objective outcomes such as pay are small.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of studies comparing mentored and non-mentored people and the type of mentoring received. Journal of Applied Psychology, 2004.

findings.claim: Mentors in senior positions were linked to more promotions; men still received more promotions and larger raises per promotion than women after controls.
findings.detail: Survey of 4,143 high-potential MBA graduates, 2008 data, cross-sectional with career histories. Introduces sponsorship: a senior person who advocates when decisions are made. 2010.

findings.claim: Men and women managers had a similar number of developmental experiences, but men's were more challenging (4.71 vs 4.23 on a 7-point scale). In experiments, men and women were equally interested in challenging work.
findings.detail: Five studies: surveys of U.S. energy-industry managers and UK health care managers, plus three experiments. Benevolent sexism predicted fewer challenging assignments given to women. 2012.
findings.source: King, Botsford, Hebl, Kazama, Dawson & Perkins, 2012

findings.claim: Women are asked more often to do low-promotability tasks and accept more often. In lab groups, women were about 50% more likely to volunteer; in same-sex groups the gap disappeared.
findings.detail: Lab experiments with university undergraduates and field data from a request to 3,271 faculty. American Economic Review, 2017. Lab percentages from the Harvard Kennedy School Gender Action Portal summary.

findings.claim: Evaluators redefined job criteria to fit the applicant from the favored gender. Committing to criteria before seeing the applicant eliminated the bias.
findings.detail: Three experiments. In one (73 undergraduates), participants who rated themselves as most objective showed the bias; those low in self-rated objectivity did not. The commitment study had 117 adult community volunteers rating police chief applicants. 2005.

findings.claim: When a company was described as meritocratic, managers gave an equally performing man a larger bonus than a woman: $418.75 vs $372.37 out of $1,000.
findings.detail: Three experiments, 445 participants with managerial experience. The pattern reversed when the company was not described as meritocratic. 2010.

findings.claim: Adding accountability and transparency to pay decisions shrank gaps for women, ethnic minorities and non-U.S.-born employees with the same performance scores.
findings.detail: Longitudinal field study of nearly 9,000 employees in one large private company, before and after the procedures. 2015.

counterintuitive.headline: Believing your process is fair can make it less fair.
counterintuitive.text: In three experiments with 445 people who had managerial experience, Castilla and Benard (2010) described one company as strongly valuing merit. In that condition, evaluators gave a man a larger bonus than a woman with the same performance record, $418.75 against $372.37. When the company was not described that way, the gap reversed. The authors suggest that a merit label gives evaluators moral cover, so they check themselves less. The protection is not the label. It is criteria set in advance, plus decisions that others can see and question.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.text: Careers grow through work that stretches people and puts them in front of decision makers. That might be leading a county workgroup, presenting to a division director, or drafting a policy that others will read. As a supervisor, you control much of that flow. You decide who leads, who presents and who takes the meeting notes. You also decide whose name you mention when a manager asks who is ready for more.

sections.title: What the research says
sections.text: Mentoring helps, but the measured effects on careers are small. What moves careers more is challenging work and someone senior who advocates for you. That advocacy is called sponsorship. Studies show that challenging assignments are not shared evenly, even when people are equally interested. Women are asked more often to take tasks that do not lead to promotion, and they say yes more often. People also bend the criteria to fit the person they already favor, usually without noticing.

sections.title: The trap
sections.text: Most supervisors believe they choose on merit. That belief can make bias more likely, because it lowers the guard. In one set of experiments, simply describing a company as merit-based widened a bonus gap between a man and a woman with the same record.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: Before your next stretch assignment, write down what the work requires. Do it before you think about names. Then look at who has had the last several visible roles and who has carried the quiet tasks. Choose against the criteria you wrote. Tell the team what the criteria were. For recurring tasks that nobody wants, such as notes, scheduling or the backup phone line, set a rotation instead of asking for a volunteer. Finally, when you get a chance to speak for someone in a room where decisions are made, name a specific person for a specific opportunity. Small habits like these change who gets seen, and they cost very little time.

sections.title: Mentoring and sponsorship are different tools
sections.text: A mentor gives advice, perspective and support. A sponsor uses position and credibility to open a door. Both matter, but they do different things. A large meta-analysis of mentoring found that it is linked to better attitudes and career outcomes. Every effect was small, though, roughly r = .03 to .19 for workplace mentoring. An earlier meta-analysis found the same pattern for pay and promotion. A Catalyst survey of 4,143 high-potential graduates found that mentors in senior positions were linked to more promotions. Even so, men received more promotions than women after accounting for experience, starting level and industry. The authors concluded that advice alone is not enough. People also need someone who speaks for them when promotions and visible assignments are decided.

sections.title: Who gets the stretch work
sections.text: In a survey of energy-industry managers, men and women reported about the same number of developmental experiences. Men rated theirs as more challenging, 4.71 against 4.23 on a seven-point scale. A survey of health care managers found a similar pattern. Then the researchers ran experiments. Men and women were equally interested in challenging assignments. But men who believed women should be protected gave women fewer of them. The intent can be kind, as in sparing someone a hard project. The effect is fewer chances to grow.

sections.title: Who gets the quiet work
sections.text: Every unit has tasks that must be done but do not lead anywhere. Examples are meeting notes, room booking, the holiday schedule and covering the shared inbox. In economics experiments, women were about 50 percent more likely to volunteer for such a task in mixed groups. Both men and women were more likely to ask a woman. In groups of all one gender, the gap disappeared. The researchers concluded that the gap comes from expectations about who will say yes, not from preference. A request to more than 3,000 faculty members showed the same pattern outside the lab.

sections.title: How criteria bend
sections.text: In one experiment, people chose a police chief from two candidates. One was more streetwise and the other more formally educated. Evaluators decided that whichever strength the male candidate had was the one that mattered most. The people most sure of their own objectivity showed the most bias. When evaluators committed to the criteria before learning who the applicant was, the bias disappeared. A field study of nearly 9,000 employees found something similar for pay. After the company made reward decisions accountable and visible, gaps for women, ethnic minorities and employees born outside the United States shrank.

sections.title: What sponsorship looks like day to day
sections.text: Sponsorship sounds like something senior executives do. In practice, supervisors do it often without naming it. It happens when your manager asks who could brief the division director, who should join a cross-division team, or who is ready for an acting role. Your answer in that moment is sponsorship. The Catalyst survey found that mentors in senior positions were linked to more promotions. The authors argue the difference is advocacy: a sponsor uses their standing to put a person forward when the decision is made. For a supervisor, this means three habits. Keep a short, current list of what each person has done well and what they want to grow into. When a chance comes up, name a person and give the evidence. Then follow up, so the person learns what was said and what comes next. Spread this across your team. If you only ever put forward the same one or two people, you are sponsoring, but not fairly.

sections.title: Applying it in DHS work
sections.text: Think about the opportunities you control. In a disability services unit, that might be leading a waiver policy workgroup, presenting a data summary to leadership, or representing the unit with county partners. Before you assign one, write two or three requirements. For example: knows the waiver rules, can explain them to county staff, and can manage a timeline. Add one growth requirement, such as someone who has not yet led with partners. Check the last few assignments of this kind. If the same two people keep getting them, the criteria may be fine but the habit is not. Explain your choice to the team using the criteria. For quiet tasks, post a rotation. When a manager asks who is ready for more, name a person, a reason and an opportunity. Do this for more than the people who remind you of yourself.

sections.title: What the evidence can and cannot tell you
sections.text: The evidence for this course is real but uneven. The mentoring meta-analyses are large, but most of the studies behind them are correlational. People who get mentors may already differ from those who do not. The sponsorship evidence comes mainly from a survey of MBA graduates in private firms, not from experiments that assigned sponsors at random. The strongest causal evidence comes from experiments on criteria and on the merit label. Those used hypothetical decisions by students, managers in training and community volunteers. The pay transparency study is a real company with real money, but it is one company. No verified study of how stretch work or sponsorship is shared in state government was found. So treat the practices here as well-supported reasoning, not guaranteed results.

sections.title: Most findings concern gender
sections.text: Most of the verified studies compare women and men. The pay study also found gaps for ethnic minorities and for employees born outside the United States, and those gaps shrank under accountability. It is reasonable to expect that unchecked criteria and habits can disadvantage other groups too. That is an inference, though, not a finding. The research here does not show effects for disability status, age or other groups. Do not assume who is being overlooked in your unit. Look at your own pattern of assignments and ask.

sections.title: Protection can look like kindness
sections.text: The stretch-work experiments point to a harder problem than open bias. People who withheld challenging work often meant well. They wanted to spare someone stress, travel or a difficult partner. You may do the same for someone who is a caregiver, is new to the country, has a disability, or had a hard year. Sometimes that is right, and the person asked for it. Often, though, the person was never asked. The fix is simple. Offer the opportunity, describe what it involves honestly, and let the person decide. If accommodations or schedule changes would help, talk them through with the person or area responsible.

sections.title: When the same person really is the best fit
sections.text: Sometimes one person clearly meets the criteria best, and the deadline is real. Fairness does not mean rotating every high-stakes task regardless of readiness. It means three things. First, the criteria were set before you thought about names. Second, you looked at who has had recent chances. Third, you are building readiness in others so the choice is wider next time. A practical move is to pair a ready person with a developing one, with a clear role for each. Pairing only helps if the developing person does visible work, such as presenting one section or leading one meeting. Taking notes for the expert is not development.

sections.title: Sponsorship without favoritism
sections.text: Sponsorship can slide into favoritism, which is the very thing this course aims to prevent. The difference is in the method. A sponsor ties the advocacy to evidence, such as specific work, specific results and a specific next step. A sponsor also spreads advocacy across people and checks the pattern over time. Try this test. Over the last year, whose names have you put forward, and for what? If the list is short and familiar, widen it. Being a sponsor also costs something. You put your credibility behind someone. That is why it matters, and why people often save it for those they already know well.

sections.title: When someone points out a pattern
sections.text: At some point a staff member may tell you that opportunities seem to go to the same few people. The natural reaction is to defend your choices, and each one may have been reasonable. In one experiment, the evaluators most confident in their own objectivity were the ones who showed bias. Thank the person. Ask what they have noticed. Then look at the record of who led, presented and represented the unit, and who did the quiet tasks. Share what you find and what you will change. Do not ask the person who raised it to fix it. Do not treat raising it as a complaint about them or about the people who were chosen.

sections.title: Quiet tasks need a rule, not a request
sections.text: The volunteering research has a practical lesson that is easy to miss. In mixed groups, women volunteered for unrewarded tasks more often and were asked more often. In same-gender groups, the gap disappeared. That pattern suggests the cause is shared expectations, not personal preference. So asking for volunteers, even politely, tends to send these tasks to the same people. A rule removes the expectation. Rotate recurring tasks on a posted schedule. Include yourself, because that shows the task is part of everyone's job. For one-time tasks, assign them with the same care you use for visible work, and note who did the last few. Keep an eye on informal work as well, such as onboarding new staff, planning team events or covering for absent colleagues. These tasks matter to the unit. They should be recognized in performance conversations and shared across the team.

sections.title: Explaining decisions in a public agency
sections.text: DHS work is public, and many staff work under union contracts and state hiring rules. Formal promotions and appointments follow those rules, and questions about them go to the person or area responsible for human resources. This course is about the informal opportunities that sit around those rules. Those include who leads a project, who presents, who joins a cross-division group and whom you mention to your manager. These are where habits matter most, because no formal process checks them. Stating your criteria out loud also helps. It gives people a fair target to aim for next time, and it lets them question a choice on its merits.

sections.title: A short review you can repeat
sections.text: Fair access is not a one-time fix. Habits drift back. Twice a year, take fifteen minutes to list the visible opportunities in your unit and who received them. Do the same for the quiet tasks. Compare the two lists with what people have told you they want to develop. Look for anyone who has had neither kind of opportunity, because people who are overlooked often go unseen in both lists. Then pick one change for the next six months. This review needs no personal data beyond work assignments you already know. Keep it about the pattern of opportunity, not about anyone's background.

simulation.setup: You are a Human Services Supervisor in a Disability Services Division unit of eight staff. A division manager asks you to name someone to lead a three-month workgroup with county case management partners on a waiver policy change. The lead will present results to division leadership. It is the most visible assignment your unit will have this year. You also need someone to take notes and manage logistics for the same group. Two of your staff have led the last three projects of this kind. Both are capable, and both are already busy.

steps.situation: The manager wants a name by Thursday. You already have one in mind: a Program Consultant who led the last workgroup well and who partners trust.
steps.question: What do you do first?

choices.label: Name the Program Consultant. The partners know them, the timeline is tight and the last group went well.
choices.feedback: This is fast and defensible, and the consultant may be the best fit. But you chose the person before you defined the work. That is the moment the experiments show criteria quietly bend toward the favored candidate. It also continues a pattern in which the same people get the visible work while others never build the record.

choices.label: Before thinking about names, write down three requirements for the lead and one growth requirement. Then check who led the last several projects.
choices.feedback: This matches the strongest evidence in the course. Committing to criteria before weighing candidates removed bias in experiments. Checking the history shows you the pattern your memory smooths over. It takes about twenty minutes. You may still choose the consultant, but now you will know why.

choices.label: Send the team an email asking who would like to lead the workgroup.
choices.feedback: This feels open, and it can surface interest you did not know about. But open calls tend to draw people who already feel invited. The research on volunteering shows that expectations shape who steps forward and who gets asked. Without stated criteria, you still have to choose among the replies, and the bias can return.

steps.situation: The consultant accepts but mentions being stretched thin. A Human Services Specialist who joined two years ago stops by. She says she has been hoping to work with county partners and asks how people get picked for these groups.
steps.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Tell her the truth: you picked quickly. Then explain what the role required and ask what experience she would bring.
choices.feedback: Owning the quick choice builds trust, and naming the requirements gives her a fair target. Asking about her experience may show she meets more of them than you assumed. The stretch-work studies found interest was equal; what differed was being offered the work.

choices.label: Tell her the consultant had the most partner experience, and you will keep her in mind for next time.
choices.feedback: This is honest and kind, but 'next time' has no criteria and no date, so it rarely comes. Experience is a reasonable requirement, but it also locks in whoever got the early chances. Without a concrete path, the same people stay most experienced.

choices.label: Offer her the note-taking and logistics role so she can learn how the group works.
choices.feedback: This is tempting and well meant. But note-taking is the kind of low-promotability task that studies show is offered to women more often. It gives exposure without visible work. Unless it comes with a real speaking or leading part, it can confirm the pattern it seems to fix.

steps.situation: Your criteria: knows the waiver rules, can explain them clearly to county staff, can manage a timeline, and has not yet led with partners. Two people meet the first three well. The Human Services Specialist and a Program Consultant on another team each meet three of four, including the growth requirement.
steps.question: How do you decide?

choices.label: Choose the Human Services Specialist as lead and pair her with the experienced consultant as a partner adviser for the first month.
choices.feedback: This uses your criteria, includes the growth requirement, and manages the real risk of a tight timeline. The adviser role is defined and time-limited, so the specialist does the visible work herself. This is how pairing builds readiness rather than putting someone in a supporting role. It also gives the specialist a real record of partner work, which is what tends to open the next opportunity.

choices.label: Choose the experienced consultant again. The growth requirement can wait for a lower-stakes project.
choices.feedback: This is a defensible risk call. But there is rarely a lower-stakes version of a visible assignment. If growth always waits, the pattern holds. The criteria help only if the growth requirement carries real weight. If you keep this choice, be specific with the team about when the growth requirement will carry weight and for which assignment.

choices.label: Ask the two experienced staff to co-lead so nobody feels passed over.
choices.feedback: This avoids a hard choice, but it drops the growth requirement you wrote. It also adds work for the two busiest people. Splitting leadership between the usual leads protects comfort, not fairness. Ask instead which single person best meets all four requirements, and what support that person needs.

steps.situation: Three people reply: the two who led the last projects, and a Human Services Specialist who writes that she 'would be glad to take notes if that helps.' Nobody else answers.
steps.question: What do you do with the replies?

choices.label: Write criteria now, apply them to the whole team, and talk with the specialist about whether she would want to lead.
choices.feedback: This recovers well. Writing criteria now still limits bending, because you have not chosen yet. Talking with the specialist matters. Her offer to take notes may reflect what she expects to be asked, which the volunteering studies identify as the driver of the gap. Before you decide, tell the whole team what the criteria are, so others who did not reply can see whether they fit.

choices.label: Pick one of the two experienced volunteers. They asked, and the others did not.
choices.feedback: It seems fair to reward initiative. But the studies show that who steps forward and who gets asked reflect expectations about who will say yes, not only interest. Choosing from replies alone turns an old pattern into a fresh choice. Initiative is worth rewarding, but it should be one requirement among several, not the whole decision.

choices.label: Accept the specialist's offer to take notes and choose a lead from the other two.
choices.feedback: Everyone gets what they asked for, and it feels respectful. But you have now assigned the quiet task to the person who offered it, just as the research predicts. Ask whether she would also want visible work in the group. If she does want more, consider giving her one visible task, such as presenting a section to partners.

steps.situation: A month later, a Program Consultant tells you privately that the same people seem to get the visible work in your unit. She says others have noticed too. She is not complaining about anyone by name.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Thank her, look at a year of assignments and quiet tasks, share what you find with the team, and set a rotation for recurring tasks.
choices.feedback: This treats her observation as information. The record shows the pattern better than memory does, and sharing it makes your decisions open to question, which the pay study tied to smaller gaps. A rotation removes the 'who will say yes' dynamic from quiet tasks.

choices.label: Explain why each recent choice made sense, so she understands there was no unfairness.
choices.feedback: Each choice may well have made sense. But defending choices one at a time hides the pattern. In one experiment, evaluators most confident in their objectivity were the ones who showed bias. Your explanation may convince her that raising concerns does not change anything.

choices.label: Ask her to suggest names for the next few assignments.
choices.feedback: This shows openness, but it hands her a job that belongs to you. It can also put her in an awkward spot with peers. Ask for her observations, then do the review and the changes yourself. Her role is to tell you what she sees. Yours is to look at the full record and decide what to change.

simulation.debrief: The choices that worked best did three things the evidence supports. They defined the work before naming a person, because people bend criteria to fit a favored candidate, and committing in advance stopped that in experiments. They looked at the record of who got visible and quiet work, because stretch work and low-promotability tasks are not shared evenly even when interest is equal. They also made decisions visible and open to question, which shrank pay gaps in a large field study. The tempting choices were not unkind. Picking a proven performer, calling for volunteers or offering note-taking as a first step all feel reasonable. Without stated criteria, though, each one tends to repeat the existing pattern.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing the person first and the reasons second.
mistakes.why: Under time pressure, a proven performer comes to mind first. Experiments show people then define the job around that person's strengths without noticing.
mistakes.instead: Write the requirements, including one growth requirement, before you think about names.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming your process is fair because you value fairness.
mistakes.why: Believing a process rests on merit lowers self-checking. In experiments, a merit label alone widened a bonus gap.
mistakes.instead: Check the record of who got which opportunities, and explain choices against stated criteria.

mistakes.mistake: Asking for volunteers for tasks nobody wants.
mistakes.why: It feels democratic. But people expect certain colleagues to say yes, and those colleagues often do. Over time they collect work that does not lead anywhere.
mistakes.instead: Rotate recurring quiet tasks, or assign them by a stated rule.

mistakes.mistake: Protecting someone from a hard assignment without asking them.
mistakes.why: It comes from care. Studies found that well-meant protective beliefs were linked to fewer challenging assignments, even though interest was equal.
mistakes.instead: Offer the work, describe it honestly and let the person decide. Discuss any needed adjustments with the person or area responsible.

mistakes.mistake: Treating mentoring as enough.
mistakes.why: Mentoring is valuable and easy to offer. Its measured career effects are small, and advice does not open doors on its own.
mistakes.instead: Add sponsorship: name a specific person for a specific opportunity where the decision is made, and spread that advocacy widely.

jobAid.title: Before you hand out an opportunity
jobAid.use: Use this when you assign a stretch project, a lead role, a presentation, a partner-facing role or a recurring task.
steps: What does this work require? Write two or three requirements before naming anyone.
What growth requirement will you add, such as someone who has not yet done this?
Who had the last three to five opportunities like this one?
Who has been carrying the quiet tasks, such as notes, scheduling and inbox coverage?
Did you offer the work directly, or wait for people to step forward?
If you pair people, does the developing person do visible work?
How will you explain the choice to the team using the criteria?
Whose name will you put forward the next time a manager asks who is ready for more?

media.reason: Opportunity looks different from the supervisor's chair than from the staff member's. A two-voice exchange shows both views and lets the learner hear how a fair process sounds in practice.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Thanks for coming in. I want to ask you about the county workgroup. You mentioned last month that you had been hoping for partner work. What made you bring it up?

script.speaker: female
script.text: Honestly, I had watched the same two people lead three groups in a row. I did not think anyone was being unfair. I just could not see how anyone else got in.

script.speaker: male
script.text: That is fair. I looked back at the year after you said that. You were right about the pattern. Each choice felt reasonable at the time, but together they told a different story.

script.speaker: female
script.text: What changed this time? You did not just ask for volunteers.

script.speaker: male
script.text: I wrote the requirements before I thought about names. Know the waiver rules, explain them clearly to county staff, manage a timeline. Then I added one more: someone who has not led with partners yet. Research shows people bend the criteria to fit whoever they already have in mind. Writing them first is the simplest guard.

script.speaker: female
script.text: I noticed you asked me directly. If you had sent an email, I probably would have offered to take notes.

script.speaker: male
script.text: That is exactly what the studies on quiet tasks found. People are asked based on who they expect will say yes. So notes now rotate for everyone, including me.

script.speaker: female
script.text: I was nervous about the timeline. Pairing me with the consultant for the first month helped. But I am glad she advised and did not run the meetings.

script.speaker: male
script.text: That was deliberate. If she had run the meetings, you would have learned by watching and nobody would have seen your work. The point was for you to build a record.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Can I ask what happens with the leadership presentation?

script.speaker: male
script.text: You present it. And when the division manager asks me who is ready for more, I plan to say your name and point to this work. A mentor gives advice. A sponsor speaks for you where the decision is made. I want to do both, and for more people than the two I used to think of first.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Then I will make sure the presentation gives you something specific to point to.

prompts: Which opportunity will you hand out next, and what two or three requirements will you write before you think about names? By when?
Which recurring quiet task will you move to a rotation, and how will you explain the change to your team?
Whose name will you put forward for a specific opportunity in the next month, to whom, and with what evidence?
