title: Leading people through change
objective: Lead your team through a change by treating objections as information, involving people in how the change works, and being clear about what is settled and what is still open.
outcomes: Separate what is decided, what is still open, and when the open questions will be answered, and say so plainly to staff and partners.
Turn one objection into a test case and walk a real case through the new process with the people who raised it.
Give staff a real say in how a change is carried out, with the information they need to contribute.
Connect the change to what it means for the people DHS serves, without overselling it.
Check what frontline staff actually know about a change instead of assuming the message landed.

evidence.summary: How people react to change depends heavily on how it is handled: the process, whether it seems to help or harm, and the context before it began. Resistance is not only a trait of change recipients; leaders help create it, and objections can improve a change. Support comes most from wanting the change or feeling it is right, not from feeling forced. In one study of public youth care professionals, participation and confidence in handling the change were linked to commitment, while simply receiving information was not. Direct supervisors matter, not only executives. Limits: most studies are surveys at one point in time, and the public-sector evidence is mostly descriptive.

findings.claim: Reactions to change are shaped by who the recipients are, the context before the change, the change process, perceived benefit or harm, and the content of the change.
findings.detail: Review of 79 quantitative studies published from 1948 to 2007. 2011.

findings.claim: Change agents help create resistance through what they do and fail to do, and resistance can be a resource that improves a change.
findings.detail: Conceptual review article, Academy of Management Review. No new sample. 2008.

findings.claim: Commitment to the specific change predicted support better than general commitment to the organization; wanting or feeling obliged to support it predicted more support than feeling there was no choice.
findings.detail: Three studies: scale development with 224 university students, then validation with hospital nurses. Journal of Applied Psychology, 2002.

findings.claim: Among youth care professionals in a public reform, participation and confidence in handling the change were linked to commitment to it; receiving information was not. Seeing the change as meaningful for clients also mattered.
findings.detail: Cross-sectional survey, five Dutch youth care organizations, 577 responses (47.7%), 221 frontline professionals analyzed. Change-process factors raised explained variance from about 1% to 21%. 2017.

findings.claim: Direct supervisors' transformational leadership contributes to implementing change in public organizations, not only executives' leadership.
findings.detail: Survey study in a public-sector organization; sample details not in the abstract. Public Management Review, 2016.

findings.claim: Participation relates to performance only above a moderate threshold, and more strongly when leaders share a lot of information.
findings.detail: Two field studies (office and call-center employees; factory workers). Academy of Management Journal, 2015. Reused from the leadership styles research.

findings.claim: During a two-year downsizing, staff without management roles and middle managers scored lower than senior managers on every aspect of information received.
findings.detail: Health care organization that went from 660 to 350 staff; self-report comparison of groups. 2004.

findings.claim: In English local government, changes in top management improved performance when prior performance was poor and worsened it when prior performance was good.
findings.detail: Panel analysis of English local authorities. Public Administration Review, 2011.

findings.claim: Research on change in public organizations gives limited detail on how change processes and outcomes unfold.
findings.detail: Review of 133 articles published 2000 to 2010. Public Administration, 2014.
findings.source: Kuipers, Higgs, Kickert, Tummers, Grandia & van der Voet, 2014

counterintuitive.headline: More information did not build commitment; involvement did.
counterintuitive.text: Leaders often respond to unease about a change by sending more updates. In a survey of 221 frontline youth care professionals during a public reform, van der Voet, Steijn and Kuipers (2017) found that receiving information about the change was not linked to commitment to it. Participation in how the change was carried out, and confidence in handling it, were. So was seeing the change as meaningful for clients. Information still matters; people cannot take part without it. But a well-informed team that has no say may still not be on board.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.text: Change in DHS arrives from many directions. It may be a new law, a federal rule, a new system, a reorganization or a new leader with different priorities. Your team will feel it before the details are settled. How they react depends less on their personalities than on how the change is handled. That part is largely in your hands.

sections.title: What the research says
sections.text: A review of 79 studies found that reactions depend on the change process, on whether the change seems to help or harm, and on the context before it started. Resistance is not only a flaw in the people resisting. Leaders help create it, and objections often contain information that makes the change better. People support a change most when they believe in it or feel it is right, not when they feel forced. In a study of public youth care professionals, taking part in how the change was carried out was linked to commitment. Simply receiving more information was not. Supervisors matter here, not only executives.

sections.title: The trap
sections.text: When people push back, it is natural to explain the change again, louder and in more detail. That treats the objection as a misunderstanding. Often it is a real concern about a real case.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: Take the next objection you hear and turn it into a test. Ask the person for a real case where they think the new process will break. Walk that case through the new steps with them. Either the process holds, and they have seen it hold, or it breaks, and you have found a gap before a person waiting for services finds it. Then tell your team three things: what is decided, what is still open, and when the open questions will be answered. Saying what you do not yet know is not weakness. It keeps rumors from filling the gap, and it gives people a date to hold you to.

sections.title: What drives reactions to change
sections.text: Oreg, Vakola and Armenakis reviewed 79 quantitative studies of how people respond to organizational change. Reactions have three parts: how people feel, what they think and what they intend to do. Those reactions grow from several sources. Some come before the change, such as people's experience and the trust already in place. Others come from the change itself: how it is carried out, whether it seems to help or harm people, and what it actually changes. The practical point is that you cannot control people's personalities. You can shape the process, explain the benefit honestly and protect trust.

sections.title: Resistance as information
sections.text: Ford, Ford and D'Amelio argue that the usual story about resistance is one-sided. It casts change leaders as rational and resisters as the problem. In practice, leaders help create resistance through what they do and fail to do. How a change is explained, and how objections are received, are part of that. Resistance can also be useful. A worker who says the new intake step will fail for people who use interpreters may be right. Treating that comment as a test case turns friction into quality control.

sections.title: Three kinds of commitment
sections.text: Herscovitch and Meyer separated three reasons people support a change. Some want to, because they believe in it. Some feel they ought to, out of obligation. Some feel they have to, because the cost of not going along is too high. Wanting to and feeling it is right were linked to more support than feeling forced. Commitment to the specific change mattered more than general loyalty to the organization. A team that likes the agency can still resist a particular change, and a team that is unhappy can still back a change it believes in.

sections.title: Involvement over information
sections.text: In a survey of frontline youth care professionals during a national reform, participation and confidence in handling the change were linked to commitment. Receiving information was not. Seeing the change as meaningful for clients and society also mattered. Another line of research on participation adds a warning. A little involvement does little; only meaningful participation, with real information shared, is linked to better performance. So asking 'any thoughts?' at the end of a meeting does not count. Real involvement means people help decide how the change will work in their part of the process.

sections.title: You matter, not only executives
sections.text: A public-sector study found that direct supervisors' leadership contributes to how change is implemented, not only the leadership of executives. You translate a division decision into Tuesday's caseload. You also likely know less than you think about what your staff have heard. In a health care downsizing, frontline staff and middle managers scored lower than senior managers on every aspect of information received. Ask your team what they have heard, and listen to what they say.

sections.title: What real involvement looks like
sections.text: Involvement is not a survey after the decision. It is a working session where people shape how the change runs in their part of the process. Start by sharing what is fixed and why, along with the data or rules behind it. Research on participative leadership found that participation is linked to better performance only above a moderate level, and more strongly when leaders share a lot of information. Then hand the team real questions. In what order should the new steps happen in this unit? How should exceptions be flagged? What should the job aid say? Which cases should be tested first? Give people enough time to answer well, and use what they say. When you cannot use an idea, explain why. That explanation is part of the involvement. It shows the input was weighed, not collected and set aside. Over time, these sessions also build confidence in handling the change, which the youth care study linked to commitment.

sections.title: Applying it in DHS work
sections.text: Suppose a waiver policy change alters how your unit reviews service plans. Start by sorting what you know. What is decided? What is still open? When will the open questions be answered, and by whom? Say this to your team and to county partners in the same words. Next, pick two or three real cases, including one that someone predicts will break. Walk them through the new steps together. Decide with the team how the unit will handle the gaps you find, and send the issues you cannot solve to the person or area responsible. Connect the change to the people it serves, but do not oversell it. People trust a leader who admits a cost.

sections.title: How strong is this evidence?
sections.text: The research on change is wide but not deep. The 79-study review is large, but most of the studies behind it are surveys taken at one point in time. These show what goes together, not what causes what. The youth care study is relevant to DHS because it involves public human-services workers in a real reform. It is still one survey in one country. The authors note that self-reports collected at once can inflate relationships. The review of 133 articles on public-sector change concluded that the field offers limited detail on how change unfolds. So the guidance here is consistent with the evidence. It is not proven to work in every setting.

sections.title: When a concern keeps coming back
sections.text: Sometimes the same objection returns week after week. It is tempting to resend the same answer. If a concern keeps returning, either the answer does not fit the case people are thinking about, or the concern is real. Ask for the specific case behind it. Walk it through the process with the people raising it. If the process truly works, they now have seen it work. If it does not, you have found a gap. Either way, the concern stops being a debate about attitude and becomes a question with an answer. When the answer belongs to someone else, take it to the person or area responsible and tell staff when they will hear back.

sections.title: Your own resistance
sections.text: Supervisors resist change too. You may doubt a change you are asked to lead, and your doubt may be valid. The same tools apply to you. Name the specific case where you think it will fail and test it. If the test shows a real gap, raise it with evidence through the right channel. If the change still goes forward, be honest with your team. Say what you raised, what was decided and how the unit will make it work. Avoid acting out enthusiasm you do not feel. Also avoid quietly undermining the decision, which leaves your team stuck between two messages.

sections.title: Leadership transitions
sections.text: A new commissioner, director or manager often brings new priorities. Staff and partners will ask what is changing before anyone knows. The most useful thing you can do is separate what is confirmed from what is still open, and say both plainly. Avoid passing on rumors as plans. Also avoid promising that nothing will change. Evidence from English local government suggests that a change at the top tends to help when an organization was struggling and to hurt when it was doing well. That finding comes from one country and from top teams, not supervisors. Still, it supports a careful point. What is working is worth protecting during a transition, and what was struggling may benefit from a fresh look.

sections.title: Different people, different reasons
sections.text: People resist or support the same change for different reasons. Some want it because they think it will help the people served. Some go along because they feel they ought to. Others go along only because refusing would cost them. The research on commitment suggests the first two groups give more support than the third. That has a practical meaning. Pressure can produce compliance, but it tends to produce the weakest kind of support. Reasons produce more. Talk with people one on one about what the change means for their work. A long-tenured worker may worry about losing skills that took years to build. A newer worker may worry about learning two systems at once. Neither worry is a character flaw. Each points to something you can address: training, a mentor, a clear timeline or a test of the case they fear most. Avoid assuming that the people who object are the ones who care least. Often they care most about getting it right.

sections.title: Information still matters
sections.text: The youth care finding does not mean information is useless. People cannot take part in shaping a change they do not understand. The participation research suggests that involvement works best when leaders share a lot of information. The lesson is to use information to make involvement possible, not to replace it. A long update email with no chance to respond does little. A short message followed by a working session on real cases does more.

sections.title: When participation is limited
sections.text: Some changes come with little room to adjust, such as a federal requirement with a fixed date. You can still involve people in how the change works in your unit. That might include the order of steps, how to handle exceptions, or what a job aid should say. Be honest about the limits. Saying you want input on something already decided damages trust. It is better to say: the requirement and the date are fixed, and how the unit carries it out is open.

sections.title: Meaning, not slogans
sections.text: Seeing a change as meaningful for clients was linked to commitment among youth care workers. Many DHS staff chose this work because of the people it serves. Connect the change to them in concrete terms. For example: under the new review, a person waiting for a service plan change should hear back sooner. Be careful. If the change has costs for staff or for the people served, name them. Overselling a change spends trust you will need later. Also take care not to describe any group of people served as a burden or a problem. Talk about what the change does, not about who is difficult.

sections.title: Changes with no clear owner
sections.text: Some changes cross units or divisions, and exceptions fall between them. Before you expand a shared process, trace who accepts exceptions, who decides them and who tells the person waiting. If nobody owns a step, the change will fail at that step. Raise it with the person or area responsible before rollout, not after the first complaint. County and Tribal partners may be affected too. Coordinate with counties through the person or area responsible for county relations. Route Tribal matters through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations rather than acting alone.

sections.title: After launch
sections.text: The work does not end on the start date. Early weeks are when gaps show up in real cases. Set a short check-in two weeks after launch and again at six weeks. Ask what is working, what is not and what has been raised. Keep a simple list of issues, who owns each one and when an answer is due. Share that list with the team, so people can see their concerns moving. When a fix comes from a staff suggestion, say so. When an issue is closed, say how. These small loops keep the participation that built commitment from fading once the launch is over.

simulation.setup: You are a Human Services Supervisor in a Disability Services Division unit that reviews service plan changes for people on a home and community-based services waiver. A new review process starts in six weeks. It moves some decisions from your unit to county case managers and adds a new documentation step. A new division director started last month, and staff have heard she may change priorities. Two senior Program Consultants have said in team meetings that the new process will not work. County partners have started calling with questions.

steps.situation: At the weekly team meeting, a senior Program Consultant says again that the new process will break for people whose plans change often. Several staff nod. You have heard this objection three times.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Ask for one real case where they expect it to break, and set a time this week to walk it through the new steps together.
choices.feedback: This turns a recurring objection into a test. Resistance often carries real information, and this group knows the cases best. If the process holds, they see it hold. If it breaks, you have found a gap before a person waiting for services does. It also gives them real participation, which was linked to commitment among public human-services workers.

choices.label: Walk through the policy rationale again, with the slides from the division briefing.
choices.feedback: This is clear and respectful, and some staff may not have seen the slides. But this is the fourth time the objection has come up. Repeating the answer treats it as a misunderstanding. In a study of youth care professionals, receiving information was not linked to commitment, while participation was.

choices.label: Say the decision is made, and that the team's job now is to make it work.
choices.feedback: This is honest about the decision, and clarity has value. But it shuts down information you may need, and it pushes staff toward going along because they feel they have no choice. That kind of commitment predicted weaker support than believing in the change. The objection will likely go underground. The consultants may also stop bringing you the cases you most need to see.

steps.situation: You and the two consultants walk through a real, anonymized case. The new process mostly works. But when a plan changes twice in one month, the new documentation step has no clear owner. Nobody knows whether the county or your unit records the second change.
steps.question: What do you do with the gap?

choices.label: Write up the case and the gap, send it to the person or area responsible for the new process, and tell the team when you expect an answer.
choices.feedback: This routes the gap to someone who can fix it and closes the loop with the team. The consultants see their concern taken seriously and acted on. It also models second-order problem solving: fixing the cause, not just working around it.

choices.label: Tell the team your unit will record every second change until further notice, so nothing is missed.
choices.feedback: This protects the people being served in the short term, and it is a reasonable stopgap. But if you do not raise the gap, the workaround hides it. It also adds work to your unit without anyone deciding that. Use it if needed, but send the gap to the person or area responsible at the same time.

choices.label: Note the gap, but hold it until the process is live so you can see how often it happens.
choices.feedback: Wanting data is sensible. But you already have a real case showing the gap, and launch is six weeks away. Waiting means the first failures will happen to real people. The consultants may also conclude that raising concerns changes nothing.

steps.situation: After the meeting, the objection stops coming up in meetings. A week later, a Human Services Specialist tells you staff are saying privately that the new process was designed by people who never worked a case.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Go back to the consultants, say you moved past their concern too quickly, and ask for a real case to test together.
choices.feedback: This repairs the misstep. Leaders help create resistance through what they do, and they can reduce it the same way. Owning the quick answer and offering a real test shows the objection mattered. It also brings their case knowledge back into the work. It may feel awkward to reopen a point you closed, but leaders who help create resistance can also help undo it.

choices.label: Send a longer email explaining how the process was designed and who was consulted.
choices.feedback: This adds information, which has some value. But the complaint is about not being heard, and an email does not hear anyone. Information alone was not linked to commitment in the youth care study. Pair the email with a working session where staff test a real case together.

choices.label: Remind staff that complaints should be raised in meetings, not in private.
choices.feedback: Wanting issues raised openly is reasonable. But staff already raised this one openly, three times, and the answer closed it off. A reminder like this teaches people that raising concerns is risky. Ask instead what concern is behind the comment, and test it with a real case.

steps.situation: A county case management supervisor calls. They have heard the new director may delay or change the process. They ask whether they should start training their staff.
steps.question: What do you tell them?

choices.label: Say what is confirmed (the start date and the steps), what is still open, and when you expect to know more. Suggest they start training on the confirmed steps.
choices.feedback: This separates what is settled from what is open, which is the most useful thing during a transition. It avoids passing on rumor and avoids false promises. It also gives the county a practical next step and keeps your message the same as the one your team hears.

choices.label: Tell them you have heard the same rumor and suggest they wait a few weeks before training.
choices.feedback: This is candid and friendly. But it turns a rumor into guidance. If the date holds, county staff start late, and people waiting for plan changes feel it. Share only what is confirmed, and say what is not. The rumor would also now carry your name with a partner who relies on you.

choices.label: Tell them nothing will change and they should go ahead as planned.
choices.feedback: This gives clarity and keeps training on track. But you do not know that nothing will change. If priorities shift, your credibility with this partner suffers. Better to say what is confirmed and when you will know more. Saying what is confirmed and what is open protects trust either way.

simulation.debrief: The strongest path treated objections as information and gave staff a real part in testing the change. That fits the evidence that leaders help create resistance and that objections can improve a change. It also fits the finding that participation and confidence, not more information, were linked to commitment among public human-services workers. When a gap appeared, the strong move sent it to the person or area responsible instead of hiding it with a workaround. With the county partner, the strong move separated what was confirmed from what was still open. The tempting moves were reasonable on their face: explaining again, insisting on the decision, waiting for data, or reassuring a partner. Each one either closed off useful information or traded short-term comfort for later trust.

mistakes.mistake: Answering a recurring objection with the same explanation.
mistakes.why: If you believe the change is sound, objections look like misunderstandings. Repeating the rationale feels patient.
mistakes.instead: Ask for the real case behind the objection and test it together.

mistakes.mistake: Sending more updates to build buy-in.
mistakes.why: Information feels like respect, and it is easy to send. In the youth care study, information was not linked to commitment, while participation was.
mistakes.instead: Use information to make real involvement possible, then let people help shape how the change works in your unit.

mistakes.mistake: Asking for input on something already decided.
mistakes.why: Leaders want people to feel included. But fake participation is noticed and damages trust.
mistakes.instead: Say plainly what is fixed and what is open, and ask for input only on what is open.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming your team knows what you know.
mistakes.why: You sat in the briefings. In one downsizing, frontline staff and middle managers scored lower than senior managers on every aspect of information received.
mistakes.instead: Ask staff what they have heard and correct gaps directly.

mistakes.mistake: Passing on rumors or promising stability during a transition.
mistakes.why: Partners and staff want certainty, and it feels kind to give it.
mistakes.instead: Separate confirmed facts from open questions and give a date for the next update.

mistakes.mistake: Patching a gap in the new process quietly.
mistakes.why: Workarounds protect the people waiting today and avoid friction.
mistakes.instead: Use the workaround if needed, but send the gap to the person or area responsible so it gets fixed.

jobAid.title: Leading a change in your unit
jobAid.use: Use this when a new policy, process, system or leader changes how your team works.
steps: Write three lists: decided, still open, and when and by whom the open questions will be answered.
Say those three lists to staff and partners in the same words.
Ask staff what they have heard, and correct anything that is wrong.
Choose two or three real cases, including one someone expects to break, and walk them through the new steps together.
Send gaps with no clear owner to the person or area responsible, and tell staff when to expect an answer.
Decide with the team how the change will work in your unit, within the fixed parts.
Describe what the change means for the people served, including any costs.
Check back in two weeks: what is working, what is not, and what has been raised.

media.reason: Change looks different to the supervisor leading it than to the experienced worker who expects it to fail. Two voices show how an objection becomes a test, and why that matters to both.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Thanks for walking that case with me. I want to be honest. When you raised the concern the third time, my first instinct was to explain the policy again.

script.speaker: male
script.text: I could tell. And I understand it. But I was not confused about the policy. I was thinking about one person whose plan changes almost every month.

script.speaker: female
script.text: That is what I missed. You were describing a real case, and I was treating it as an attitude problem.

script.speaker: male
script.text: When we walked it through, most of the new process held up better than I expected. I will say that to the team.

script.speaker: female
script.text: That will carry more weight from you than from me. And the second change in one month really had no owner. I have sent that to the person responsible for the process. I expect an answer by the end of next week.

script.speaker: male
script.text: What helps me is knowing when. Before, I kept hearing that things would be worked out, with no date.

script.speaker: female
script.text: That fits what research on change in public agencies has found. In one study of youth care workers, getting more information was not linked to commitment. Taking part in how the change worked was. So was feeling able to handle it.

script.speaker: male
script.text: That matches how I feel. I do not need more emails. I need to know my concerns go somewhere.

script.speaker: female
script.text: There is also a lot of talk about the new director changing things. I am telling staff and counties the same thing. The start date and the steps are confirmed. The training schedule is still open, and I will update everyone on Friday.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Honestly, saying what you do not know makes me trust the rest more.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Can I ask you to help with one more thing? Would you bring two more tough cases to next week's meeting? I would rather find the gaps now than have a person waiting for services find them in March.

script.speaker: male
script.text: I can do that. I will bring the hardest ones I have.

Which objection will you turn into a test case, with whom, and when will you walk it through?

title: Diagnosing problems before fixing them
objective: Find the likely cause of a recurring problem by stating the result you want, testing more than one explanation against real cases, and fixing the system rather than the nearest person.
outcomes: State a problem as a gap between what should happen and what is happening, without naming a person to blame.
List at least two explanations and at least two options before choosing a fix.
Pull a small set of real cases and trace where each one first went off track.
Help the person waiting today while the cause is still being investigated.
Choose a fix that changes the process, and check whether the problem actually stops.

evidence.summary: Decisions fail often, and a common cause is jumping to a solution and considering only one option. In a study of 356 organizational decisions, about a quarter in public agencies, managers developed more than one option in fewer than one in five decisions. When they did, success rose from 56% to 70%. Frontline workers usually work around problems without telling anyone who could fix the cause, which keeps the problem alive. Managers also tend to blame workers rather than the system, and the feedback they get can seem to confirm the mistake. Formal root cause reviews help less than hoped when they look for one cause and settle for weak fixes. Limits: the evidence is mostly case studies and observation, not experiments.

findings.claim: Managers developed more than one option in fewer than 20% of decisions. When they did, success rates rose from 56% to 70%.
findings.detail: Case database of 356 decisions by senior managers in medium to large U.S. and Canadian organizations; about a quarter in public agencies. Not a random sample. 1999.

findings.claim: When managers framed a decision as finding and fixing a problem, only 44% of the solutions were fully used, no better than adopting a ready-made idea. Stating the result wanted worked better.
findings.detail: Same 356-decision database; problem framing was used in more than 26% of cases. The author links the weak results to blame and hasty problem definitions. 1999.

findings.claim: For 93% of problems, frontline nurses did what it took to keep working and did not tell anyone who could fix the cause. About 33 minutes per shift were lost to coping with removable failures.
findings.detail: Qualitative observation: 239 hours with 26 nurses at nine hospitals, plus interviews with 12 nurses. 2003.

findings.claim: Managers tend to blame workers rather than the system for poor performance, and the feedback they receive can appear to confirm the wrong explanation.
findings.detail: Inductive field study of one firm's process-improvement effort, followed by a dynamic model. Administrative Science Quarterly, 2002.

findings.claim: The popular idea that people explain their own behavior by the situation and others' by character is weak overall (average d about 0 to 0.1). It held mainly for negative events.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 173 studies. Psychological Bulletin, 2006.

findings.claim: Root cause reviews tend to seek a single cause, are skewed by hindsight, and settle for weak fixes such as reminders and training. Action plans are estimated to be carried out only 45% to 70% of the time.
findings.detail: Expert analysis of root cause analysis in health care, with cited evidence. BMJ Quality & Safety, 2017.

counterintuitive.headline: Hunting for the problem can work no better than skipping diagnosis.
counterintuitive.text: It seems obvious that defining the problem should come first. In Nutt's 1999 study of 356 decisions, managers who started by naming a problem and searching for its cause had only 44% of their solutions fully used. That was no better than managers who adopted a ready-made idea. Nutt's explanation is that problems prompt blame, so people defend themselves instead of looking for answers. Hasty definitions also mislead. Managers who first stated the result they wanted, and then looked at several options, did better. Diagnosis works when it is framed as a gap to close, not a culprit to find.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.text: When something goes wrong in your unit, the pressure is to fix it fast. Callers are waiting, a partner is upset, or a manager wants an answer. The fastest fix is usually the first one that comes to mind. That might be more staff, a reminder email, retraining one person, or a new form. Sometimes that fix is right. Often it treats a symptom, and the problem comes back. It can also land on the wrong person, when the real cause was a letter, a screen or a handoff.

sections.title: What the research says
sections.text: In a study of 356 decisions in organizations, about a quarter of them public agencies, managers considered more than one option in fewer than one in five decisions. When they did, success rose from 56% to 70%. Frontline workers usually work around problems quietly. In one hospital study, nurses did this for 93% of problems and rarely told anyone who could fix the cause. Managers also tend to blame people rather than the process, and the results they see can seem to confirm it.

sections.title: The trap
sections.text: Defining 'the problem' can backfire too. When the question is 'what went wrong and who did it,' people defend themselves. In the same decision study, problem-hunting worked no better than skipping diagnosis. Asking what result you want, and what stands in the way, works better.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: State the gap without a culprit: what should happen, what is happening, and for whom. Then pull five real cases and trace where each one first went off track. Write down at least two explanations and two possible fixes before you choose. Meanwhile, help the person who is waiting today. Fixing the cause and helping the person in front of you are separate jobs, and both matter. Last, choose a fix that changes the process, not one that asks people to try harder, and set a date to check that the problem actually stopped.

sections.title: Why decisions fail
sections.text: Paul Nutt studied 356 decisions made by senior managers in the United States and Canada. About a quarter were in public agencies, including state Medicaid, transportation and natural resources agencies. Failure was traced to three habits: imposing a solution early, limiting the search for alternatives, and using power to push the plan through. Tactics prone to failure were used in two of every three decisions. Managers developed more than one option in fewer than 20 percent of decisions. When they did, success rates rose from 56 to 70 percent. The study is a large case collection, not a random sample, so treat the numbers as a strong signal rather than a precise rate.

sections.title: Diagnose the gap, not the culprit
sections.text: Nutt found something surprising about diagnosis. When managers began by defining a problem and searching for its cause, only 44 percent of their solutions were fully used. That was no better than simply adopting an existing idea. He explains that problem-hunting prompts blame, so people protect themselves rather than look for answers. Hasty problem definitions also point at symptoms. What worked better was stating the result wanted first. For example: people who call about a service authorization should get a correct answer on the first call. That frames the work as closing a gap, which invites everyone to help.

sections.title: Workarounds hide causes
sections.text: Anita Tucker and Amy Edmondson spent 239 hours observing 26 nurses in nine hospitals. Most failures they saw were problems such as missing information, missing supplies or waiting for a resource. For 93 percent of these problems, nurses did what it took to keep caring for the patient and then moved on. They rarely told the person or area responsible. About 33 minutes per shift went to coping with failures that could have been removed. The workarounds were skilled and caring. They also kept the problem invisible to anyone who could fix it. Your staff do the same, and it is a sign of commitment. It is also why you may not know a problem exists until it is large.

sections.title: Blaming the nearest person
sections.text: Nelson Repenning and John Sterman studied a firm's attempt to improve its processes. Managers tended to blame workers for poor performance rather than the system. They then tightened control, and the short-term results seemed to prove them right. Over time, distrust grew and real improvement stalled. In DHS work, this can look like retraining one staff member when the real cause is unclear guidance, a confusing letter or a system screen that invites errors.

sections.title: Hold more than one explanation
sections.text: Once one explanation feels right, people stop looking. That is how a single plausible story becomes the plan. A simple discipline helps. Write at least two explanations that could fit the facts, and for each, note what you would expect to see if it were true. If the letter is the cause, callers should be asking about the letter. If county guidance differs from state guidance, the confusion should cluster in certain counties. Then look at the cases. Often both explanations are partly right. This step also widens the options. Nutt found that managers who developed more than one option succeeded more often. Options come more easily when you hold more than one explanation, because each explanation suggests its own fixes. Ask staff who handle the work to help write the explanations. They see patterns you cannot, and involving them makes it easier for them to report what they see next time.

sections.title: Applying it in DHS work
sections.text: Suppose callers keep phoning a disability services line about the same authorization letter. Before asking for more staff, pull ten recent calls. What did callers actually ask? Where did the confusion start: the letter, the county, the web page or the call script? Trace each case back to where it first went off track. Write down at least two explanations, such as 'the letter is unclear' and 'county guidance differs from state guidance.' Then list at least two options for each. Test the leading explanation against a few more cases. Meanwhile, give call-line staff a short, accurate answer for today's callers. When the cause sits with another area, send the cases to the person or area responsible. Finally, decide how you will know the fix worked. Pick one simple measure, such as calls about the letter per week, and a date to check it. If the number does not move, return to the cases with your team.

sections.title: How strong is the evidence?
sections.text: None of the core studies is a randomized experiment. Nutt's study is a large set of real decisions, but the cases were gathered through contacts and may lean toward successes, as he notes. Tucker and Edmondson observed nurses directly, which is strong for describing what happens and weaker for estimating how often it happens elsewhere. Repenning and Sterman built their model from one firm. The root cause analysis paper is an expert critique, not a trial. Together they point the same way: decisions improve when people consider more options and look past the nearest person. The specific percentages should not be treated as targets.

sections.title: Be careful with bias stories
sections.text: Many training courses teach that people blame others' character and excuse their own behavior. A meta-analysis of 173 studies found this pattern is weak overall, with average effects near zero. It did show up for negative events, which is exactly when supervisors diagnose problems. The practical point is narrower than the popular version. When something goes wrong, it is easy to see a person and miss the system around them. You do not need a theory of bias to correct for that. You need a habit of asking what about the process made the error likely.

sections.title: One cause is rarely the whole story
sections.text: Health care has used root cause analysis for years. A review of that experience found three recurring weaknesses. First, the name suggests that one cause can be found, when most failures come from several factors working together. Second, investigations are shaped by hindsight, which makes the error look obvious after the fact. Third, teams often choose weak fixes such as reminders, posters and retraining. In one example, a protocol, training session and poster were followed by the same error a year later. Action plans were estimated to be carried out only 45 to 70 percent of the time. So when you trace a problem, expect more than one contributing cause. Favor fixes that change the process, such as clearer letters, better screens or a defined handoff, over fixes that ask people to try harder.

sections.title: Deciding when the cause is uncertain
sections.text: Often you cannot be sure of the cause before you must act. A person is waiting for a service decision today, and the investigation will take weeks. Separate the two jobs. For today, give staff an interim answer that is accurate and safe, and say that it is interim. For the cause, set a short investigation with a date to decide. Trace where the guidance first diverged, perhaps a policy manual update that did not reach the call script. Keep a written note of your current best explanation and what evidence would change your mind. This helps you avoid two errors: waiting so long that people are harmed, and committing so early that you fix the wrong thing.

sections.title: Hindsight makes causes look obvious
sections.text: After something goes wrong, the path to the error looks clear. The review of root cause analysis names hindsight bias as a recurring weakness in investigations. Knowing the outcome makes the warning signs look louder than they were at the time. This matters most when a person was harmed or a complaint reached leadership. The pressure to find someone who should have known is strong. To counter it, reconstruct what the staff member knew and saw at each step, using the case record and the guidance in place at the time. Ask what made the action seem reasonable then. If several capable people would have done the same thing, the cause is in the system. Fixing it protects the next person, both the worker and the person served.

sections.title: When a concern keeps coming back
sections.text: A recurring complaint is useful evidence. If the same question returns after you have answered it, the answer may not fit the cases people are dealing with. Ask for a real example and walk through it with the person raising it. Often the walk-through shows where the official process and the real work part ways. When it does, fix the process. When it shows the process works, the person has now seen that for themselves.

sections.title: Asking for resources
sections.text: Supervisors often diagnose a problem as a staffing shortage. Sometimes it is. But extra staff can absorb a broken process without fixing it, and the workarounds grow. Before asking for resources, compare what callers or clients actually asked with what the process assumes they need. If many calls come from one unclear letter, a better letter may cost less than a new position. If the cases show real demand beyond capacity, your request is stronger because you can show the evidence.

sections.title: Making it safe to surface problems
sections.text: Tucker and Edmondson found that nurses rarely reported problems to someone who could fix the cause. That was not because they did not care. The authors point to time pressure and to simple rules of thumb: fix what blocks the task, then move on. If you want problems surfaced, make reporting quick, respond visibly and never treat a report as a mark against the person who made it. When a fix comes from a staff report, say so. Over time, your unit will tell you about problems while they are still small.

sections.title: Cross-unit and partner problems
sections.text: Many DHS problems cross boundaries: state and county, two divisions, or a contractor and a program area. In these cases, the cause may sit outside your authority. Your job is to bring clear evidence to the person or area responsible: the cases, where each went off track and what you believe would help. For county issues, work through the person or area responsible for county relations. Matters involving Tribal Nations go through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations, not around them.

sections.title: Check that it worked
sections.text: Diagnosis is a hypothesis until the problem stops. The root cause review found that action plans are carried out only part of the time, and that weak fixes are common. So decide in advance what you will measure and when. For a confusing letter, that might be calls about the letter per week, compared with the weeks before the change. For an outdated script, it might be a spot check of ten calls. If the problem does not drop, your explanation was incomplete. Go back to the cases. That is not a failure of leadership. It is the method working.

simulation.setup: You supervise a Disability Services Division call line staffed by six Human Services Specialists. For three weeks, calls about a new service authorization letter have doubled. Wait times are up, and two specialists have given callers conflicting answers. Your manager asks whether you need temporary staff. A county case manager has emailed to complain that callers are being told different things. You need a plan by Friday. The answer you give will shape how your staff, your manager and the county see the problem.

steps.situation: Your manager wants a quick answer. You can request two temporary staff, retrain the two specialists who gave conflicting answers, or take a few days to look into it.
steps.question: What do you do first?

choices.label: Request two temporary staff now. Wait times are the urgent problem.
choices.feedback: This addresses wait times, and the request may be justified. But it imposes a solution before you know why calls doubled. Decisions made this way failed more often in Nutt's study of 356 decisions. If the letter is causing the calls, extra staff will absorb the problem without ending it. Ask for staff if the cases show real demand, and bring the evidence.

choices.label: Retrain the two specialists who gave conflicting answers.
choices.feedback: This responds to a visible error, and accuracy matters. But it assumes the cause is the people. Managers tend to blame workers rather than the system, and quick improvements can seem to confirm it. If the guidance itself is unclear, others will give conflicting answers next week.

choices.label: Give staff a short interim answer for today, and spend two days pulling ten recent calls to see what callers asked and where answers diverged.
choices.feedback: This separates helping callers today from finding the cause. Tracing real cases is quick and shows where the confusion begins. It also keeps options open. In Nutt's study, decisions that considered more than one option succeeded more often. Accuracy matters, so check the guidance first.

steps.situation: A week later, wait times have eased a little, but call volume is still double. A specialist mentions that most callers are reading the same paragraph of the letter aloud and asking what it means.
steps.question: What do you do with this?

choices.label: Thank the specialist, pull ten calls to confirm the pattern, and look at where the letter's wording came from.
choices.feedback: This treats the specialist's observation as evidence and tests it against real cases. Frontline staff often know the cause but solve problems quietly without reporting them. Thanking them makes it more likely they will tell you next time. It also shows the team that reporting a pattern leads somewhere.

choices.label: Add a script line explaining that paragraph so calls go faster.
choices.feedback: This helps callers right away and is a reasonable stopgap. But it is a workaround: it absorbs the problem without fixing the letter. In the hospital study, workarounds like this kept problems invisible to anyone who could fix them. Use the script line for now, and send the letter problem to the person or area responsible.

choices.label: Note it, but wait for the temporary staff to settle in before changing anything else.
choices.feedback: Stability has value. But you now have a likely cause and are choosing not to test it. The extra staff are absorbing a problem that may be fixable at its source. A short check of ten calls would take little time and could save weeks of extra volume.

steps.situation: In seven of ten calls, callers asked about the same paragraph in the letter. In three, specialists used an older call script that conflicts with the current policy manual. The county complaint matches the older script.
steps.question: What is your next step?

choices.label: Write down both explanations, the unclear letter and the outdated script, and list at least two options for each before choosing.
choices.feedback: You have evidence for two contributing causes, not one. Keeping both in view avoids the single-cause trap that weakens many root cause reviews. Listing options for each makes it more likely you will choose a fix that changes the process. Ask the specialists who handle these calls to help you weigh the options.

choices.label: Conclude the letter is the root cause and focus only on it.
choices.feedback: The letter explains most calls, so this is tempting. But the outdated script explains the conflicting answers and the county complaint. Most failures have more than one cause. Fixing only one leaves part of the problem in place. Then address each cause.

choices.label: Tell the two specialists to stop using the old script.
choices.feedback: This fixes one visible error. But it treats the old script as a personal mistake. If the old script is still on the shared drive, others will find it too. Fix where the script lives, not only who used it.

steps.situation: The letter belongs to another unit, and the call scripts are managed by a team outside your area. Your manager asks for your recommendation.
steps.question: What do you recommend?

choices.label: Bring the cases to the person or area responsible for the letter and the scripts, propose specific changes, keep the interim answer in place, and set a date to check call volume.
choices.feedback: This sends evidence to the people who can fix the causes. It favors process changes over reminders, keeps callers served in the meantime, and includes a check to see whether the fix worked. Weak follow-through is one of the main reasons root cause reviews fail.

choices.label: Ask for temporary staff until the other units fix the letter and scripts.
choices.feedback: This may be needed if the fix will take months. But without the evidence and a proposed change, the request treats the symptom. If you ask, attach the cases and a date to review. Pair any temporary request with the letter and script changes, so the extra help has an end date.

choices.label: Send a reminder to all specialists to read the policy manual before answering letter questions.
choices.feedback: Reminders are among the weakest fixes in the root cause research. They ask people to try harder while the confusing letter and outdated script stay in place. The calls will continue. A reminder is better than nothing for today, but it should not be the plan.

simulation.debrief: The strongest path did three things the research supports. It separated helping today's callers from finding the cause, so nobody waited for the investigation. It traced real cases and kept more than one explanation and option in view. That matters because decisions with multiple options succeeded more often, and most failures have more than one cause. It also brought evidence to the person or area responsible and chose process fixes over reminders. The tempting moves, such as adding staff, retraining the visible offenders or adding a script line, each helped a little. Each also treated a symptom or a person, while the letter and the outdated script kept generating calls.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing the first fix that comes to mind.
mistakes.why: Under pressure, action feels responsible. In Nutt's study, managers considered more than one option in fewer than one in five decisions.
mistakes.instead: Write down at least two explanations and two options before deciding.

mistakes.mistake: Starting with 'what went wrong and who did it.'
mistakes.why: It feels like rigorous diagnosis. But problem-hunting prompts blame, and people defend themselves instead of helping.
mistakes.instead: State the result you want and the gap, without naming a person.

mistakes.mistake: Retraining or reminding the person nearest the error.
mistakes.why: The person is visible and the system is not. Managers tend to blame workers, and short-term improvement seems to prove it.
mistakes.instead: Ask what about the process made the error likely, and fix that.

mistakes.mistake: Looking for the single root cause.
mistakes.why: One cause makes a clean story and a clear fix. Most failures come from several factors working together.
mistakes.instead: Expect more than one contributing cause, and address each.

mistakes.mistake: Letting workarounds stand.
mistakes.why: Workarounds keep people served and show commitment. They also hide the problem from anyone who could fix it.
mistakes.instead: Keep the workaround if needed, but report the cause to the person or area responsible.

mistakes.mistake: Waiting for certainty before acting.
mistakes.why: Acting on a wrong cause feels worse than acting late.
mistakes.instead: Give an accurate interim answer today, and set a date to decide on the cause.

jobAid.title: Before you fix it
jobAid.use: Use this when a problem keeps coming back, when you are asked for a quick fix, or before you request resources.
steps: What should happen, what is happening, and for whom? Write it without naming a person.
What will you do for the people waiting today while you investigate?
Pull five to ten real cases. Where did each first go off track?
Write at least two explanations that fit the cases.
List at least two options for each explanation.
Does your fix change the process, or does it ask people to try harder?
Who is responsible for each cause, and what evidence will you bring them?
When will you check whether the problem actually stopped?

media.reason: Diagnosis is a sequence of habits, and a single calm voice can walk through one realistic case step by step without the distraction of competing views.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Picture a disability services call line on a Monday morning. Calls about a new authorization letter have doubled. Wait times are up. Two staff members have given callers different answers, and a county partner has noticed. Your manager asks a simple question. Do you need more people?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Most supervisors would say yes, and some would be right. But consider what research on decisions has found. Paul Nutt studied 356 real decisions in organizations across the United States and Canada. About a quarter were made in public agencies. Managers considered more than one option in fewer than one in five of those decisions. When they did, success rose from 56 percent to 70 percent. The most common way to fail was to settle on a solution early and stop looking.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: There is a second trap, and it is less obvious. You might think the answer is careful problem-finding: what went wrong, and who did it. Nutt found that this approach worked no better than skipping diagnosis altogether. Problems invite blame. When people feel blamed, they defend themselves instead of helping you find the answer. So start somewhere else. Name the result you want. Callers should get a correct answer on the first call. Now the question is how to close a gap, and everyone can help.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Next, look at real cases. Pull ten recent calls. What did people actually ask? In this example, seven callers read the same paragraph of the letter aloud. Three calls were answered from an older script that no longer matches policy. That is two causes, not one, and both matter.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Notice something else. Your staff had probably known about that paragraph for weeks. In a study of hospital nurses, researchers watched them work around problems ninety-three percent of the time. The nurses kept patients cared for and moved on. They rarely told anyone who could fix the cause. That is not carelessness. It is commitment. But it keeps problems invisible. When a staff member tells you about a pattern, thank them, and act on it.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Be careful, too, about the person nearest the error. Retraining the two specialists who gave conflicting answers feels decisive. Studies of improvement efforts show that managers tend to blame workers rather than the system. A quick dip in errors can make that seem true. Meanwhile, the old script is still on the shared drive.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Finally, choose fixes that change the process. A clearer letter. A single current script. A review of health care investigations found that teams often settle for reminders and posters, and the same error returns. So bring your cases to the person or area responsible for the letter and the script. Keep an interim answer in place for today's callers. And set a date to check whether the calls actually drop. That last step is how you know the diagnosis was right.

prompts: Which recurring problem in your unit will you restate as a gap between what should happen and what is happening? By when?
Which five to ten real cases will you trace, and who on your team will you ask to trace them with you?
Who is the person or area responsible for the likely cause, and when will you bring them your evidence?
