title: From vision to plan
objective: Turn a broad priority into a short plan with a specific team goal, the right kind of goal for the task, if-then steps, progress checks, and a clear line on what must not be traded away.
outcomes: Restate a vision or priority as one specific, challenging team goal that people can track.
Decide whether the work calls for a performance goal or a learning goal, and explain why.
Write if-then plans that name when, where and how the first steps will happen.
Name what the goal must not cost, such as accuracy, access or fair treatment, and check for it.
Use the priority to choose between two good options and explain the choice to your team.

evidence.summary: Specific, challenging goals beat telling people to do their best, with effect sizes of about .42 to .80 across meta-analyses. Group goals raise group performance, but individual goals that reward personal output can harm work that depends on teamwork. On new, complex tasks, goal effects shrink, and a learning goal can work better than a performance target. Plans that name a date and time raised follow-through modestly in a large field experiment. In public and private organizations, formal strategic planning is linked to better performance. Goals also have side effects: narrow focus, shortcuts and unethical behavior. Limits: much goal research uses lab tasks, and the planning evidence is correlational.

findings.claim: Specific, difficult goals led to higher performance than 'do your best' goals, with effect sizes from .42 to .80 across meta-analyses.
findings.detail: Summary of 35 years of goal-setting research, including multiple meta-analyses. American Psychologist, 2002.

findings.claim: Goal effects are smaller on complex tasks (d = .41 vs .77 for specific-difficult vs do-your-best). On new, complex tasks, a specific learning goal can work better than a performance goal.
findings.detail: Same review, citing Wood, Mento and Locke 1987 and later learning-goal studies. 2002.

findings.claim: Group goals improved group performance (d = 0.56 overall; d = 0.80 for specific, difficult group goals). In interdependent groups, individual goals focused on personal output hurt group performance (d = -1.75), while goals focused on contribution to the group helped.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 49 effects. The individual-goal results rest on only 6 and 4 studies. Few recent field studies. 2011.

findings.claim: Prompting people to write down the date and time they planned to act raised flu vaccination by 4.2 percentage points over a 33.1% baseline. Writing only a date had no significant effect.
findings.detail: Randomized field experiment with 3,272 employees of one large U.S. utility, 2009 flu season. 2011.

findings.claim: Strategic planning has a positive, moderate effect on organizational performance, strongest when planning is formal and performance is measured as effectiveness. The effect holds in public and private sectors.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 87 correlations from 31 empirical studies. Public Administration Review, 2019.

findings.claim: Goals can narrow focus away from non-goal areas, raise unethical behavior, distort risk-taking and harm culture. In one case, a $147-per-hour sales goal for auto repair staff was followed by overcharging.
findings.detail: Critical review essay drawing on research and cases. Academy of Management Perspectives, 2009.

counterintuitive.headline: On new, complex work, a hard target can slow people down.
counterintuitive.text: Goal research usually says specific, challenging goals beat vague ones. Locke and Latham's 2002 review adds an important exception. When a task is new and complex, a specific performance target can make people anxious. They scramble for strategies in an unsystematic way and fail to learn what works. On complex tasks, goal effects in meta-analyses were about half the size seen on simple tasks. The review's remedy is a specific learning goal, such as finding and testing a set number of approaches. Performance targets come later, once people know how to do the work.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.text: Visions and priorities arrive in broad language. Examples are 'people get the right services sooner' or 'partners can count on clear answers.' These statements matter, but nobody can act on them directly. Your job is to turn one into a plan your team can use on Monday morning. That means a goal people can track, first steps that will actually happen, and a clear line on what must not be traded away. It also means knowing what you will say no to, because a priority that excludes nothing guides nothing.

sections.title: What the research says
sections.text: Specific, challenging goals beat telling people to do their best. Group goals raise group performance. But individual targets that reward personal output can hurt work that depends on teamwork. On new, complex work, a learning goal often works better than a hard number. Plans that name exactly when people will act raised follow-through in a large field experiment. Formal planning is linked to better results in public agencies as well as private firms. Goals also have side effects: people focus on what is measured and may cut corners on what is not.

sections.title: The trap
sections.text: A vision with no goal changes little. A goal with no limits can change the wrong things. A number like 'close 20 percent more reviews' may be met by rushing hard cases. A plan with no first step, owner or date tends to stay a plan.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: Write one specific team goal that serves the priority. Decide whether the team already knows how to reach it. If not, start with a learning goal, such as testing three ways to shorten a step. Write one if-then plan for the first step, naming when, where and who. Then write one sentence on what the goal must not cost, such as accuracy, access for people who use interpreters, or fair treatment of hard cases. Check that line every time you check progress.

sections.title: Why specific goals work
sections.text: Edwin Locke and Gary Latham summarized 35 years of goal research. Specific, difficult goals led to higher performance than urging people to do their best, with effect sizes from about .42 to .80 across meta-analyses. Goals work by directing attention, raising effort, building persistence and prompting people to find strategies. 'Do your best' fails because it has no external reference point, so almost any result can count as success. Goals also need feedback. People must be able to see progress toward the goal to adjust what they are doing.

sections.title: Team goals for team work
sections.text: Most DHS work depends on handoffs: intake to eligibility, eligibility to services, state to county. A meta-analysis of group goals found that group goals improved group performance, with an overall effect of d = 0.56. Specific, difficult group goals did better still. The same review found that in interdependent groups, individual goals focused on maximizing personal output hurt the group. Individual goals focused on each person's contribution to the group helped. These two results rest on only a handful of studies, so hold them loosely. Still, the direction is clear: when work flows between people, set the goal at the level of the flow.

sections.title: Learning goals for new work
sections.text: Goal effects shrink on complex tasks. In the meta-analyses Locke and Latham cite, the advantage of specific goals over do-your-best was about .41 for the most complex tasks and .77 for the simplest. When a task is new and complex, a performance target can make people anxious and unsystematic. A learning goal helps more. Examples are testing three ways to shorten the documentation step, or finding the two most common reasons a case stalls. Set the performance target once you know what works.

sections.title: From intention to action
sections.text: Good intentions often fail at the first step. In a field experiment with 3,272 employees, a mailing that asked people to write down the date and time they would get a flu shot raised vaccination by 4.2 percentage points. Writing only the date did not have a significant effect. The gain was modest, but it came from one line on a form. In team planning, write if-then steps in the same way. For example: 'On Tuesday after the team meeting, the two program consultants will pull ten stalled cases and list where each one stopped.'

sections.title: Feedback keeps a goal alive
sections.text: Locke and Latham are clear that goals need feedback. People must see progress toward the goal to adjust effort or strategy. A goal checked once a quarter is easy to forget. A simple, frequent view of progress keeps it in mind. For a review team, that might be the median days from complete plan to decision, shown every two weeks, alongside the guardrails. Keep the display simple and about the team, not about ranking individuals. Use the review to ask what the numbers mean. Which cases are slow, and why? Which test is working? What should change next? When progress stalls, the same view tells you early, before the deadline. Then you can change strategy, add a learning goal, or reset the target with a clear reason.

sections.title: Planning in public agencies
sections.text: A meta-analysis of 31 studies found that strategic planning has a positive, moderate effect on organizational performance. The effect was strongest when planning was formal and when performance was measured as effectiveness, meaning whether the work achieved its purpose. It held in both public and private sectors. These studies are correlational, so they show that planning and performance go together rather than proving one causes the other. The lesson for a supervisor is practical. A short written plan with a clear purpose, named owners and dates is worth the hour it takes.

sections.title: Applying it in DHS work
sections.text: Suppose your division's priority is that people get waiver services started sooner. Your unit reviews service plans. A vague goal would be to process plans faster. A better team goal: cut the median days from complete plan to decision from 21 to 14 by June. If nobody knows yet why plans take 21 days, start with a learning goal: within three weeks, find the three most common delays and test one fix for each. Write the first if-then step with a day, a place and named roles. Add a guardrail: accuracy and appeal rates must not get worse, and complex cases must not be pushed to the back of the line. Review progress and guardrails together every two weeks.

sections.title: How strong is the evidence?
sections.text: Goal-setting theory is among the best-supported ideas in workplace psychology, with decades of meta-analyses. Much of that work, though, uses lab tasks or simple, countable work. Field evidence on group goals is thinner; the group-goal meta-analysis notes a lack of recent field studies in organizations. The implementation-intention field experiment is strong in design but covers one employer and one behavior, and the effect was modest. The public planning meta-analysis pools correlational studies. Together, the evidence supports the practices in this course. It does not promise a specific gain in your unit. Evidence on vision statements themselves was not verified for this course. The guidance here treats a vision as useful when it becomes goals, choices and dated steps.

sections.title: When goals backfire
sections.text: Lisa Ordonez and colleagues argue that goal setting has been oversold and its harms underreported. Goals can narrow attention so that unmeasured work suffers. They can push people toward risky or unethical shortcuts, especially near a deadline. They can also damage cooperation when people compete for targets. One example they cite: an auto repair chain set a sales goal of $147 an hour, and staff began overcharging and doing unneeded repairs. Their paper is an argument built from research and cases, not a new study. Its warning fits public work well, where the people served cannot easily go elsewhere. A goal for speed with no guardrail for accuracy or access can quietly shift harm onto the people with the most complex needs.

sections.title: Write the guardrails before the goal
sections.text: A practical protection is to write what must not get worse before you set the target. In disability services, guardrails might include decision accuracy, timely notices, appeal rates, language access, and attention to people whose situations are complex. Review guardrails at the same meetings as progress, using the same level of detail. If a guardrail moves the wrong way, pause and adjust the approach even if the target is on track. Ask staff directly whether the goal is pushing them to cut corners. They may see it before the numbers do.

sections.title: Choosing between two good options
sections.text: A vision is most useful when it helps you say no. Suppose you can either build a training on the new review process or redesign the most-used letter. Both are worthwhile, and you cannot do both this quarter. Return to the priority: people get services started sooner. Which option is more likely to shorten the time from plan to decision? If the evidence from your cases points to letters causing rework, the letter comes first. Explain the choice to your team in those terms, and name the evidence that would change your mind. Saying no to a good option is easier when everyone can see the reason.

sections.title: Who sets the goal
sections.text: People often assume goals work only when staff set them. The group-goal meta-analysis found that participation in setting the goal did not change the effect. Locke and Latham report that assigned goals can work about as well as participative ones when the reason is explained. Commitment matters more than authorship. That does not make staff input unimportant. Staff often know which steps cause delay and which targets would distort the work. Use their knowledge to set a realistic goal and good guardrails, and explain why the goal matters.

sections.title: Setting the right level of difficulty
sections.text: The research shows that harder goals lead to more effort and performance, up to a point. Locke and Latham note that performance levels off or drops when the limits of ability are reached or when commitment to a very hard goal fades. A target nobody believes is reachable may be ignored. To set the level, look at recent performance and at what the cases suggest is possible. Then choose a goal that requires a real change in how the work is done, not just more effort. Explain the reasoning. If the team reaches the goal early, raise it. If the cases show it was unrealistic, reset it openly. Quietly dropping a goal teaches people that goals are not serious.

sections.title: Individual targets in shared work
sections.text: Many units track individual productivity. In work that depends on handoffs, the group-goal meta-analysis suggests individual targets focused on personal output can hurt the group. This rests on only six studies, so it is a caution, not a rule. If you track individual work, frame it as each person's contribution to the shared goal. Watch for signs that people are holding easy cases or passing hard ones along. Union agreements and human resources rules may also govern how individual performance is measured, so check with the person or area responsible.

sections.title: Keeping the plan alive
sections.text: Plans fade when the first step has no date, owner or place. The flu-shot experiment shows that naming exactly when you will act adds follow-through, even if the gain is modest. Build if-then steps into the plan and review them briefly at a set time. Keep the written plan short, about one page: the priority, the team goal, the type of goal, the first three if-then steps, the guardrails and the review date. A short plan is more likely to be used. When the plan changes, update the page and say why.

sections.title: Partners and shared goals
sections.text: Some goals depend on counties, providers or other divisions. Your team cannot promise a result it does not control. Set the goal for your part of the process, and share what you are measuring with partners through the person or area responsible for that relationship. If a goal involves Tribal Nations, work through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations rather than setting targets for them.

sections.title: Sharing the plan
sections.text: A plan only works if people can find it and use it. Share the one-page plan with the team in a meeting, not only by email, and ask what is unclear. Post it where the team works. When the director or a partner asks how the priority is going, use the same page. Over time, the page becomes the record of what the team tried, what worked and what changed. That record is useful for the next priority, because it shows how the team learns. It also helps a new supervisor or staff member understand why the work is organized the way it is.

simulation.setup: You are a Human Services Manager in the Disability Services Division. The division director has named a priority for the year: people should get waiver services started sooner after their service plan is complete. Your two teams review service plans. Right now the median time from complete plan to decision is 21 days. You have a team meeting on Monday and need a plan your supervisors and staff can use.

steps.situation: Your supervisors want a clear target. One suggests 'every reviewer closes 15 plans a week.' Another suggests simply asking staff to do their best to speed things up.
steps.question: What goal do you set?

choices.label: A shared team goal: cut the median from 21 to 14 days by June, with accuracy and appeal rates as guardrails.
choices.feedback: This is specific and challenging, set at the level of the shared work, and paired with limits on what must not get worse. Group goals improved group performance in meta-analysis. The guardrails respond to the risk that a speed target pushes harm onto complex cases. It also tells reviewers that the whole team owns the result, including the hardest cases.

choices.label: Fifteen plans per reviewer per week.
choices.feedback: This is specific, countable and easy to track, which is why it is tempting. But plan review depends on handoffs and varies in difficulty. In interdependent work, individual goals focused on personal output hurt group performance in the few studies that tested them. Reviewers may also avoid hard cases.

choices.label: Ask staff to do their best to speed things up, and track the median.
choices.feedback: This avoids pressure and keeps attention on the shared outcome. But 'do your best' has no reference point, so almost any result counts as success. Specific, difficult goals beat do-your-best goals across decades of research. Tracking the median is a good start. Add a number and a date to make it a goal.

steps.situation: At the meeting, a Program Consultant says nobody actually knows why plans take 21 days. Some think it is missing documents; others think it is county handoffs.
steps.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Keep the June target, but make the first three weeks a learning goal: find the three most common delays and test one fix for each.
choices.feedback: This fits the evidence on complex, new tasks. When people do not yet know how to reach a target, a learning goal works better than pushing harder on the number. The June target stays as direction, and the team learns what actually works first. It also turns the Program Consultant's concern into the team's first task.

choices.label: Tell the team to push toward 14 days and figure it out as they go.
choices.feedback: This keeps momentum and shows confidence in staff. But on complex work, a hard performance target can make people anxious and unsystematic. They may try many things without learning which ones help. The team may try many changes at once and never learn which one helped.

choices.label: Postpone the goal until someone completes a full analysis of delays.
choices.feedback: Understanding the cause first is wise. But an open-ended analysis can drift. A time-limited learning goal gets the same understanding with a deadline and keeps the priority visible. Set a three-week limit and name who will look at which cases.

steps.situation: Two weeks in, the median has barely moved. A Human Services Supervisor reports that some reviewers are picking simpler plans first, and complex plans are aging.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Replace the measure with a shared team goal for the median, add a guardrail on how long complex plans wait, and explain why.
choices.feedback: This corrects the incentive. Individual output goals can push people toward easy cases, which is the kind of side effect goal critics warn about. A shared goal with a guardrail for complex plans protects the people with the most at stake. Explain the change openly, so reviewers understand the reason and not only the new rule.

choices.label: Keep the measure, but assign complex plans by rotation.
choices.feedback: Rotation reduces cherry-picking and is a reasonable fix. But the measure still rewards personal output in shared work, so other workarounds may appear. Consider moving the goal to the team level as well. Watch whether complex plans start moving faster after the change.

choices.label: Remind reviewers to take plans in order received.
choices.feedback: This names the right rule but leaves the incentive that caused the problem in place. Reminders rarely beat the pull of a target people are measured on. When a measure produces the wrong behavior, change the measure rather than asking people to resist it.

steps.situation: The team has found that missing provider documents cause the most delay. Two fixes are possible this quarter: a checklist for county case managers, or a redesigned request letter to providers. There is time for only one.
steps.question: How do you decide and launch it?

choices.label: Pick the fix the case evidence links most to delay, explain the choice using the priority, and write if-then first steps with names, dates and a review date.
choices.feedback: This uses the vision to choose between two good options and makes the reason visible. Naming when, where and who turns intention into action, as the flu-shot experiment showed for date-and-time plans. The review date keeps the plan alive. It also gives you a clear point to check whether the fix worked.

choices.label: Do a lighter version of both so nobody's idea is dropped.
choices.feedback: This feels inclusive. But splitting effort often means neither fix is done well, and you lose the chance to learn which one works. A clear choice tied to the priority is easier to explain and evaluate. Choose one, and tell the team when the other will be reconsidered.

choices.label: Choose the letter and ask the team to get started when they can.
choices.feedback: The choice may be right. But 'when they can' leaves the first step without a time, place or owner. Plans with specific when-and-where steps are more likely to be carried out. Add a first step with a name, a day and a place.

simulation.debrief: The strongest path set a specific, challenging goal at the level of the shared work. That matches evidence that group goals raise group performance and that individual output targets can hurt interdependent work. It paired the goal with guardrails, because goals can narrow focus and push harm onto the hardest cases. When the cause of delay was unknown, it used a learning goal first, which the research favors for new, complex tasks. It then chose between two good options by returning to the priority. It launched the choice with if-then steps that named people, dates and places, because naming when and where improves follow-through. The tempting alternatives each had something right, such as countable targets, a gentle tone or inclusiveness, but they lost specificity, protection or follow-through.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving the vision as the goal.
mistakes.why: Broad priorities feel inspiring and safe, and nobody objects to them. But 'do your best' and vague aims have no reference point, so they rarely change behavior.
mistakes.instead: Turn the priority into one specific, challenging goal with a date.

mistakes.mistake: Setting individual output targets for shared work.
mistakes.why: Individual numbers are easy to count and feel fair. In interdependent groups, goals focused on personal output hurt group performance in the few studies that tested them.
mistakes.instead: Set the goal at the team level, and frame individual work as contribution to it.

mistakes.mistake: Pushing a hard target on work nobody knows how to do yet.
mistakes.why: Targets feel like accountability. On new, complex tasks, they can make people anxious and unsystematic.
mistakes.instead: Start with a time-limited learning goal, then set the performance target.

mistakes.mistake: Setting a goal without guardrails.
mistakes.why: The goal gets attention and the side effects are not measured. Goals can narrow focus and encourage shortcuts.
mistakes.instead: Write what must not get worse before you set the target, and review both together.

mistakes.mistake: Ending the plan with 'get started when you can.'
mistakes.why: It trusts staff and avoids micromanaging. But intentions without a when and where are easy to postpone.
mistakes.instead: Write if-then first steps that name when, where and who.

jobAid.title: One-page plan from a priority
jobAid.use: Use this when a vision, priority or strategic goal reaches your team and you need a plan people can act on.
steps: Priority in one sentence: what should be different for the people served?
Team goal: what specific, challenging result, measured how, by when?
Goal type: does the team know how to reach it? If not, what learning goal comes first?
Guardrails: what must not get worse, such as accuracy, access, notices or complex cases?
First three if-then steps: when, where and who for each.
Choice: what good option are you saying no to this quarter, and why?
Review: when will you check progress and guardrails together?

media.reason: Moving from vision to plan is a short sequence of decisions. One narrator can carry a single example from a broad priority to a one-page plan without losing the thread.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: A division director announces a priority for the year. People should get waiver services started sooner after their plan is complete. Everyone agrees. And on Monday morning, almost nothing changes. That is the usual fate of a vision. It is not wrong. It just is not yet something anyone can do.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The first step is a goal people can see. Decades of research on goal setting point the same way. Specific, challenging goals lead to better performance than telling people to do their best. 'Do your best' sounds supportive, but it has no reference point, so almost any result can count. A better goal for a review team might be cutting the median time from complete plan to decision from 21 days to 14 by June.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Notice that the goal belongs to the team, not to each reviewer. Plan review is shared work. It moves from county to state, and from one reviewer to another. A meta-analysis of group goals found that team goals improved team performance. In the few studies that tested it, individual targets focused on personal output hurt work that depends on teamwork. A count of plans per reviewer looks fair. It can also teach people to pick the easy cases first.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now suppose no one knows why plans take 21 days. Here the research adds an exception. On new, complex work, a hard target can make people anxious and scattered. They try many things and learn little. A learning goal works better. Within three weeks, find the three most common delays and test one fix for each. The June target stays as direction. The first job is learning.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Every goal needs a limit. Researchers who study the side effects of goals warn that targets narrow attention. They can also invite shortcuts. In public work, the cost of a shortcut often lands on the people with the most complex needs. So write the guardrails first. Accuracy must hold. Appeal rates must not rise. Complex plans must not wait longer than the rest. Check those lines every time you check progress.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Then make the first step concrete. In a large workplace experiment, asking employees to write down the date and time they would get a flu shot raised vaccination rates. Writing only the date did not have a clear effect. The same idea works for a team plan. On Tuesday after the team meeting, two program consultants pull ten stalled cases and note where each one stopped.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Finally, use the vision to choose. You will have two good options and time for one. Ask which one is more likely to get services started sooner. Then explain your choice in those words. A vision earns its place when it helps a team say no to something good, for a reason everyone can see.

prompts: Which priority will you turn into a team goal, what will the goal be, and by what date will you share it with your team?
What guardrails will you set for that goal, and which staff will you ask to help name them?
What is the first if-then step, and who will do it, where and when?

title: Evaluating a program while it can still change
objective: Set up a pilot so that its early evidence can still change the design, and spot when a number has started to measure the counting instead of the work.
outcomes: Write a specific, measurable aim and a prediction before a pilot starts.
Choose a small set of measures that pair an activity count with an outcome for people served and a check on cost to others.
Plan short test cycles with data reviewed at least monthly, and name what result would change the design.
Name the ways a chosen target could be met without the work improving, and add a balancing check for each.
Explain to a director what the pilot does and does not show before it is expanded.

evidence.summary: Plan-do-study-act cycles are meant to test small changes, predict results, and learn from data over time. In practice, reviews of health care projects find the method is rarely used that way: fewer than one in five fully documented repeated cycles, and almost every project still reported success. Separate research on public targets shows that a number with high stakes can drive real improvement and also invite distortion. English ambulance services met an eight-minute target, while about a third altered some response times. Another high-stakes target improved emergency waits with no detectable distortion. The honest lesson is mixed. Measurement helps when aims are set in advance, data come often, and someone checks what the number might be hiding. Most of this evidence comes from health care and job training, so its use in DHS work is by careful analogy.

findings.claim: Fewer than 20% of published PDSA projects (14 of 73) fully documented a sequence of repeated test cycles, and only 15% (7 of 47) used data collected monthly or more often.
findings.detail: Systematic review of 73 health care improvement articles drawn from 409 identified; 47 had enough detail for full analysis. Published 2014.
findings.source: Taylor, McNicholas, Nicolay, Darzi, Bell and Reed, 2014

findings.claim: 98% of PDSA projects reported improvement, but only 27% (32 of 120) had a specific numeric aim and reached it, and only 4% followed all four key features of the method.
findings.detail: Systematic review of 120 quality improvement projects published in 2015 and 2016. Published 2019.
findings.source: Knudsen, Laursen, Johnsen, Bartels, Ehlers and Mainz, 2019

findings.claim: When an eight-minute ambulance target was tied to public star ratings, English services meeting it rose from 3 to 26 of 31, while manual corrections of response times appeared in about a third of services.
findings.detail: Comparison of UK ambulance services under different measurement systems, about 2000 to 2006, using administrative and audit data. Regulators estimated the largest corrections raised performance by at most 6%; one service changed times on nearly 600 urgent calls. Published 2009.

findings.claim: The share of calls classed as most urgent varied fivefold across ambulance services, showing that the definition behind a measure can move results as much as the work does.
findings.detail: Same study, data from 2001 to 2005, 31 English ambulance services.

findings.claim: A four-hour emergency department wait target in England produced large reductions in waits with no evidence of the expected neglect of unmeasured work or gaming.
findings.detail: Panel data on all 155 English hospital trusts, 2003 to 2006. Published 2009 in a public administration journal.

findings.claim: In a large U.S. government job-training program, staff strategically reported performance outcomes to raise their awards, and this hurt the program's true goal.
findings.detail: Observational study of explicit performance incentives in a federal job-training program. Published 2004. No effect size taken from the abstract.

findings.claim: Target systems rest on two assumptions: that the measured part stands for the whole, and that gaming does not matter. English health care evidence to 2004 showed both assumptions can fail.
findings.detail: Analysis of English public health care targets and audit arrangements. Published 2006.

counterintuitive.headline: Almost every improvement project says it worked, which is exactly why 'it worked' tells you little.
counterintuitive.text: A 2019 review by Knudsen and colleagues looked at 120 plan-do-study-act projects. Ninety-eight percent reported improvement. Yet only 27% had set a specific numeric aim in advance and reached it, and only 4% followed all four core features of the method. A report that a pilot improved things is common and cheap. What makes it believable is a prediction written down before the work began, data gathered often enough to see change, and a plain account of what did not move. Ask for those before you ask whether the result was good.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.text:
A pilot is worth running only if its results can still change something. That sounds obvious. In practice, many pilots are set up so that the only possible finding is success. The team launches, counts activity, and reports a number that looks good. By the time anyone asks whether people were better served, the program has already been expanded or locked into a budget. The window for learning has closed.

Two bodies of research help here. The first is about plan-do-study-act, a method for testing small changes in short cycles. Reviews of health care projects find that the method is rarely used as designed. Fewer than one in five projects fully documented repeated cycles, and almost all still reported improvement. The second is about targets. When a number carries high stakes, people work hard to move it. Sometimes the work improves. Sometimes only the number does.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text:
Before the pilot starts, write three things on one page. First, a specific aim with a number and a date. For example, most people who ask for an evening callback reach someone who can help them take their next step within two business days. Second, your prediction of what will happen and why. Third, the result that would make you change the design.

Then pair every activity count with an outcome for the people served. 'Calls completed' describes staff effort. 'Share of requesters who reached help and could act afterward' describes what the public got. Add one check on cost to others, such as daytime wait times. Review the numbers at least monthly with the people doing the work.

sections.title: What to watch for
sections.text: Ask one question about every target you set: how could someone meet this without the work getting better? If the answer is easy, add a second measure that would catch it. English ambulance services met an eight-minute target, and about a third also altered some response times. Most of the people involved were not dishonest by nature. They were under pressure, and the number was the thing being judged. Your job is to keep the number connected to the people it is meant to describe.

sections.title: What plan-do-study-act is supposed to look like
sections.text:
The plan-do-study-act cycle is simple on paper. You plan a small change and predict what will happen. You try it on a small scale. You study the data against your prediction. You act: adopt the change, adapt it, or drop it. Then you run the next cycle. The power comes from repetition and from comparing results to a prediction made in advance.

The evidence shows how often this breaks down. A 2014 systematic review by Taylor and colleagues examined 73 published health care projects that said they used the method. Fewer than 20% fully documented a sequence of repeated cycles. Of the 47 with enough detail to analyze, only 15% used data gathered monthly or more often. Many projects ran one large change and called it a cycle.

A 2019 review by Knudsen and colleagues looked at 120 more projects. Ninety-eight percent reported improvement. Only 27% had a specific numeric aim and met it. Only 4% followed all four key features of the method. Neither review tests whether the method works when done well. They show that most teams do not do it well, and that self-reported success is nearly universal regardless.

sections.title: Why a number drifts away from the work
sections.text:
When a measure becomes the basis for judging people, it starts to change. Researchers describe two main patterns. Effort substitution means people put energy into what is measured and less into what is not. Gaming means the reported number improves more than the real performance does.

The best-documented case comes from English ambulance services. Bevan and Hamblin studied a target of reaching 75% of life-threatening calls within eight minutes. Only England tied this target to public star ratings, and only England met it. Services meeting the target rose from 3 to 26 of 31 over four years. Real improvement happened. At the same time, regulators found manual corrections to response times in about a third of services. Some services showed a spike of responses logged at exactly eight minutes and a sharp drop just after. The share of calls classed as most urgent varied fivefold between services. That last point matters most for DHS work. The definition behind a measure can move results as much as the work itself.

Other evidence points the same way. Courty and Marschke found staff in a large federal job-training program timed and reported outcomes to raise their performance awards, which hurt the program's real goal.

sections.title: Targets do not always distort
sections.text: The research is not a case against measurement. Kelman and Friedman studied England's four-hour emergency department wait target across all 155 hospital trusts from 2003 to 2006. Waits fell sharply. The researchers looked for neglect of unmeasured care and for gaming and found no evidence of either. Distortion is a risk to manage, not a certainty. It grows when a measure is easy to move without changing the work, when stakes are high, and when no one checks.

sections.title: Applying this to a DHS pilot
sections.text:
Suppose your unit pilots evening callbacks for people who cannot reach a disability services line during the day. Build the evaluation before launch.

Write the aim as a number and a date. Write a prediction, such as most requests will come from people who work daytime shifts, and half will need a second contact. Name the decision the evidence will support, such as expanding to a second evening or redesigning the callback script.

Choose a small family of measures. Pair an activity count, such as callbacks completed, with an outcome, such as the share of requesters who reached someone and could take their next step. Add a balancing measure, such as daytime hold times, to see whether evening coverage pulled staff away. Add one quality check, such as a short review of a sample of calls by a lead worker.

Run short cycles. Two to four weeks is long enough to see a pattern and short enough to adjust. Review the data with the staff making the calls. They will see problems the numbers miss.

Finally, protect privacy. Use the smallest amount of personal data the question needs, and follow the data practices set by the person or area responsible for data governance.

sections.title: What the evidence can and cannot tell you
sections.text:
Be clear about the limits. The plan-do-study-act reviews come from health care. They describe how teams report their work, not whether the method improves outcomes when used fully. A project that skips repeated cycles may still have helped people, and a project that followed every step may still have failed. What the reviews do show is that published success is almost universal and therefore weak evidence by itself.

The target research is mostly from English public services and one U.S. job-training program. These are large, high-stakes systems with public rankings or financial awards. A DHS pilot is smaller and lower in stakes, which may reduce pressure to distort. Yet many state programs report measures to legislators, federal partners and the public, and staff often feel those numbers in their performance reviews. The mechanisms in the research can operate at any scale where a number becomes the way people are judged.

sections.title: How to tell real change from a moved number
sections.text:
Several warning signs appear in the ambulance study and are useful in any program.

Watch the edge of the target. If many cases cluster just inside a threshold, such as at exactly 24 hours or exactly eight minutes, look closer. Real work rarely piles up at a line drawn by a policy.

Watch the definitions. If the share of cases in a counted category shifts after a target is set, the category may be doing the work. In DHS settings this could be how a request is classed, when a clock starts, or what counts as a completed contact.

Watch what is not counted. If calls completed rise while repeat calls rise too, people may be getting quick contacts that do not solve the problem.

Watch who is left out. A measure built on people who reached the program says nothing about people who gave up. Ask how many requests went unanswered, and whether some groups dropped out more than others. Do not assume a pattern by group without data; check it.

sections.title: When stakes help and when they hurt
sections.text:
The contrast between the ambulance target and the emergency wait target is instructive. Both were high stakes. Both drove improvement. Only one showed clear distortion. Kelman and Friedman discuss conditions that make distortion more or less likely. One reading of their work and the ambulance case is this. Distortion is easier when a keystroke or a reclassification can move the number. It is harder when moving the number requires changing how the work is done.

This suggests a design rule. Prefer measures that are hard to move without real change. A count of contacts is easy to inflate. The share of people who could take their next step, checked by a short follow-up question, is harder. Pair the easy measure with the hard one, and treat a gap between them as a signal worth investigating.

sections.title: Who the average hides
sections.text:
An overall result can improve while some people are served worse. None of the studies in this course measured differences by group, so they cannot tell you who is most likely to be missed. That is a reason to look, not a reason to guess.

In a callback pilot, the people least likely to be counted are often those who never got through. They may have limited phone minutes, a shared phone, a changing work schedule, or a need for an interpreter or relay service. Ask how many requests went unanswered and why. If your data allow it, and if data governance rules permit, compare results across the groups the program is meant to reach. Look at language, region, or type of request.

If you find a gap, treat it as a design question for the next cycle. Ask the staff and, through the appropriate channel, the people affected what got in the way. Then test a change aimed at that barrier. A pilot that improves the average while widening a gap has not yet worked.

sections.title: Harder situations
sections.text:
A director wants a single number. Directors often need one number for a briefing. You can give one, but present it with its partner measure and one sentence on what it does not show. For example: 'Callbacks within one business day rose to 85%. The share of people who could take their next step stayed near 60%. Daytime holds did not change.'

The pilot is already promised. Sometimes leaders announce expansion before results arrive. You can still shape what expands. Propose that the expansion carry the same measures and a review point, and name the result that would trigger a redesign.

Staff fear the numbers. If people believe a measure will be used against them, distortion becomes more likely. Say clearly how the numbers will be used, review them together, and use them to fix the process before judging any person. Treat a surprising result as a question for the team.

The data system cannot capture the outcome. Some outcomes, such as whether a person could act on the information, are not in any system. A short follow-up question asked of a small sample can fill the gap. Keep it brief, ask only what you need, and follow data practices from the person or area responsible for data governance.

Results are mixed. Many pilots help some people and not others, or help at a cost elsewhere. Report this plainly. A mixed result that is honestly described is more useful to the next decision than a clean result that hides the trade-off.

sections.title: A practical rhythm
sections.text:
A workable pattern for most DHS pilots looks like this. Before launch, write the aim, the prediction, the decision rule and the measure family on one page. Share it with the staff doing the work and the person who will decide on expansion. Run the first cycle for two to four weeks. Meet for 30 minutes to compare results to the prediction, look at the edge of any target, and hear from staff about what the numbers missed. Decide whether to adopt, adapt or drop the change. Write down the decision and the reason. Repeat.

After three or four cycles, you will know far more than a single launch-and-report would show. You will also have the evidence a director needs to expand with confidence, or the evidence to stop before money and goodwill are spent.

simulation.setup: You are a Human Services Supervisor in the Disability Services Division. Your unit is about to pilot evening callbacks for people who cannot reach the disability services line during the day. The division director has set aside staff time for eight weeks and will decide whether to fund a permanent evening shift. A lead worker, two call-line staff and a data analyst are on the pilot team. What is at stake is whether people who work daytime jobs can get help, and whether the evening shift pulls staff from daytime callers.

steps.situation: The pilot starts Monday. The data analyst asks what to track. The director's assistant has already suggested one number for the weekly update: total callbacks completed.
steps.question: What do you set up before launch?

choices.label: Track total callbacks completed, as suggested, and plan to add more measures once you see how the first month goes.
choices.feedback: This is easy and fits the director's update. But a count of calls describes staff effort, not what callers got. Reviews of improvement projects find almost all report success when the measure is activity. Without an aim or prediction set now, the first month will show a rising count and little else. Adding measures later also makes it hard to compare against a starting point.

choices.label: Write an aim with a number and date, a prediction, and a decision rule. Pair callbacks completed with the share of requesters who could take their next step and with daytime hold times.
choices.feedback: This sets up a real test. The aim and prediction let you compare results to what you expected, the core of plan-do-study-act. The outcome measure shows what callers got. The balancing measure catches a cost to daytime callers. Taylor and colleagues found few projects did this, which is why so few could show what they learned.

choices.label: Ask the analyst to build a full dashboard with every available field so nothing is missed.
choices.feedback: The instinct to be thorough is good, but a dashboard of everything has no aim and no prediction. It invites the team to find whatever looks good later. It also collects more personal data than the question needs. A small family of measures tied to a stated decision is easier to review monthly and harder to misread.

steps.situation: After four weeks, callbacks completed are high. The share of requesters who could take their next step is about 55%, below your prediction of 70%. Daytime hold times have crept up slightly. Call-line staff say many evening callers need forms mailed, which they cannot send after hours.
steps.question: What do you do with this first cycle?

choices.label: Adapt the design: test sending forms by email or text with the caller's consent, and check whether hold times rise further. Review again in two weeks.
choices.feedback: This is the act step done well. The gap between prediction and result pointed to a specific barrier, and staff explained it. A small change tested for two weeks can show whether the outcome moves. Keeping an eye on hold times protects daytime callers. This is the iterative cycle most published projects skipped.

choices.label: Report the high callback count to the director and note the outcome measure is still being refined.
choices.feedback: This is tempting because the count looks good and the outcome is disappointing. But it hides the most useful finding. The director would be deciding on expansion with half the picture. When leaders see only the favorable number, the program can grow before the barrier is fixed.

choices.label: Keep the design unchanged for the full eight weeks so the data stay clean.
choices.feedback: Holding steady can make sense in a formal trial. But the purpose of this pilot is to learn while the design can still change. Waiting four more weeks means more callers hit the same barrier. Plan-do-study-act works by adjusting after each short cycle.

steps.situation: After four weeks, the weekly update shows callbacks completed rising each week. The director is pleased. A call-line worker mentions in passing that many evening callers seem to call back again the next day.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Add two measures now: repeat calls within three days and a short follow-up question on whether the caller could take their next step. Explain the change to the director.
choices.feedback: Late is better than never. Repeat calls are a sign that contacts are not solving the problem, one of the warning signs in target research. You lose a clean starting point, so say that in your update. The director gets a more honest picture before deciding.

choices.label: Treat the comment as one worker's impression. The count is clear and the director is satisfied.
choices.feedback: This is understandable. The count is real and the director is happy. But staff comments are often the first sign that a number has drifted from the work. Ignoring it means the pilot may expand a service that creates repeat contact. The cost lands on callers and on daytime staff.

choices.label: Ask the analyst to pull repeat call data quietly before telling anyone.
choices.feedback: Checking the facts first is reasonable. Keeping it quiet is not. The team doing the work is part of the evaluation, and the director will make a decision soon. Share that you are checking a concern and when you will report back.

steps.situation: The director plans to make the evening shift permanent and wants a target for staff performance reviews: 90% of callback requests answered within one business day.
steps.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Support a timeliness goal, but propose it be paired with the next-step outcome and repeat calls, reviewed as a team, and not used alone in individual reviews.
choices.feedback: This keeps the useful pressure of a target while lowering the risk of distortion. A one-day clock is easy to meet with a quick call that solves nothing, or by changing when the clock starts. Pairing it with a harder-to-move outcome and reviewing it as a team follows the lesson of the ambulance and job-training research.

choices.label: Accept the target as written. It is clear, and staff respond to clear goals.
choices.feedback: Clear targets can drive real improvement, as the emergency wait research shows. But this target is easy to move without better service, and tying it to individual reviews raises the stakes. Watch for calls clustered just under the deadline and changes in how requests are classed. Those were the signs in the ambulance study.

choices.label: Argue against any target. Numbers in performance reviews always backfire.
choices.feedback: This overstates the evidence. Kelman and Friedman found a high-stakes target improved waits with no detectable distortion. Refusing any measure leaves the director without a way to track the new shift. A better move is to shape the target so it is hard to meet without real improvement.

simulation.debrief: The strongest path set an aim, a prediction and a small family of measures before launch. That made the first cycle informative. When the outcome fell short, the gap pointed to a fixable barrier, and the design changed while it still could. This is what plan-do-study-act intends, and what reviews by Taylor and Knudsen found most projects did not do. The final step is about the shift from learning to managing. A target helps when it is hard to meet without real change and when someone watches its edges and definitions. The ambulance research shows both real improvement and altered records under the same target. Your role is to keep the number tied to what callers actually got, and to give the director an honest picture, including what did not work.

mistakes.mistake: Counting activity and calling it the result.
mistakes.why: Activity counts are easy to get from existing systems, they rise quickly, and they look good in an update. Reviews show nearly all projects report success, often based on measures like these.
mistakes.instead: Pair each activity count with an outcome for the people served, such as whether they could take their next step.

mistakes.mistake: Setting the aim after the data come in.
mistakes.why: It feels more practical to see what is possible first. But without an aim and prediction set in advance, any result can be described as success.
mistakes.instead: Write a numeric aim, a date and a prediction before launch, and name the result that would change the design.

mistakes.mistake: Running one long pilot instead of short cycles.
mistakes.why: Leaders want a clean test and a single report. Fewer than one in five published projects documented repeated cycles.
mistakes.instead: Run two- to four-week cycles, compare each to the prediction, and adjust.

mistakes.mistake: Using a single timeliness target in individual performance reviews.
mistakes.why: Clear targets do drive effort, and supervisors want accountability. But high stakes on an easy-to-move number invite reclassification and clustering at the deadline, as in the ambulance study.
mistakes.instead: Pair the target with a harder-to-move outcome and review it as a team before judging any person.

mistakes.mistake: Treating staff comments as anecdotes that the data overrule.
mistakes.why: Numbers feel objective and comments feel personal. Yet front-line staff often see distortion first.
mistakes.instead: Treat a staff observation as a hypothesis and add a measure to test it.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming that measurement always corrupts the work.
mistakes.why: Stories of gaming are vivid and memorable. But the emergency wait research found real improvement without detectable distortion.
mistakes.instead: Keep measures, and design them so they are hard to meet without changing the work.

jobAid.title: One-page pilot evaluation plan
jobAid.use: Before a pilot or program change starts, and at each review point during it.
steps: Aim: what will change for people served, by how much, by when?
Prediction: what do you expect to happen, and why?
Decision rule: what result would make you adopt, adapt or drop the change?
Measures: one activity count, one outcome for people served, one balancing measure for cost to others, one quality check.
Distortion check: how could each target be met without the work improving? What second measure would catch it?
Cycle: how long is each test, who reviews the data, and when do you meet?
People: which staff doing the work will review results with you?
Privacy: what is the least personal data the question needs, and who is the person or area responsible for data governance?

media.reason: A program manager who needs a clear number and an analyst who sees what the number hides each hold part of the truth. Hearing both lets the learner weigh the value of a target against its risks.

script.speaker: female
script.text: The director wants one number for the evening callback pilot. Callbacks completed went from 40 to 110 in a month. That is the story, isn't it?

script.speaker: male
script.text: It is part of the story. That number tells you staff made more calls. It does not tell you whether callers got what they needed.

script.speaker: female
script.text: If they called back, they got help. What else would they need?

script.speaker: male
script.text: About 45% of them called again within three days. That suggests many evening contacts did not solve the problem. Staff say they could not mail forms after hours.

script.speaker: female
script.text: So the count went up partly because people had to call twice. That changes things. But I still need something simple for the director.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Then give two numbers side by side. Callbacks completed, and the share of callers who could take their next step. When those two move together, you have real progress. When they split, you have a question.

script.speaker: female
script.text: The director also wants a target for staff reviews. Ninety percent answered within one business day.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Research on English ambulance services is worth knowing here. When an eight-minute target carried public ratings, services did improve. But about a third also corrected some response times, and some showed a spike right at eight minutes.

script.speaker: female
script.text: The staff on this team are not going to falsify data.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Most people in that study were not dishonest either. The pressure works through small choices, like when the clock starts or how a request is classed. And a different target, for emergency waits, improved care with no sign of distortion. The difference is often whether the number can move without the work changing.

script.speaker: female
script.text: So I keep the timeliness goal, pair it with the next-step measure, and review it as a team before anyone's individual review.

script.speaker: male
script.text: And look at the edges. If requests cluster just under one day, look closer. That is where a target tells you what it is really measuring.

prompts: What pilot or change in your area could still be adjusted, and what aim and prediction will you write for it?
Who doing the work will review the first cycle's results with you?
By what date will you hold the first review, and what result would make you change the design?
