title: Engaging the public while decisions are open
objective: Invite the public into a decision while it can still change, state plainly what is open and fixed, and show people how their input shaped the result.
outcomes: Identify which parts of a decision are still open before inviting public input.
Write an invitation that states the decision, its limits, who decides, and when people will hear back.
Bring costly or challenging public proposals to decision makers with options, rather than filtering them out early.
Report back to participants what changed, what did not, and why.
Reach people beyond established partners, and route county and Tribal matters through the person or area responsible.

evidence.summary: Research on public participation shows that consultation changes outcomes some of the time, not automatically. In a study of 571 proposals from local participatory processes in Spain, about a third were fully implemented, a third modified, and a third rejected. Proposals were far more likely to be adopted when both elected leaders and public servants supported them, and when the process was high quality. Costly or challenging proposals were dropped more often. Other studies link good participation to people seeing an agency as responsive, and fair treatment to accepting decisions people dislike. A review of 122 co-production studies found most examine conditions, not outcomes. The evidence is largely observational and from outside Minnesota human services, so treat it as strong guidance, not proof.

findings.claim: Of 571 proposals from local participatory processes, 36% were fully implemented, 32% partially implemented or modified, and 32% rejected.
findings.detail: Multilevel observational study of proposals from 39 participatory processes in three Spanish regions. Published 2018.

findings.claim: When both public servants and elected leaders supported a proposal, its chance of full implementation was 46%, compared with 17% without that support.
findings.detail: Same study. Rejection was 30 percentage points less likely with support from both.

findings.claim: Challenging proposals were almost twice as likely to be rejected as non-challenging ones, and fully implemented 26% of the time versus 42%.
findings.detail: Same study. Costly proposals were about 20 points more likely to be rejected than low-cost ones. The authors call this selective listening.

findings.claim: Proposals from processes that met all three quality criteria had a 45% chance of full implementation and were almost 20 points less likely to be rejected than those from processes meeting none.
findings.detail: Same study. Participatory budgeting proposals were fully implemented 51% of the time versus 30% for other process types.

findings.claim: A review of 122 studies on co-creation and co-production with citizens found that most examine influencing factors and hardly any examine outcomes.
findings.detail: Systematic review of articles and books from 1987 to 2013. The field is mostly qualitative case studies. Published 2015.

findings.claim: Participants who attended quality public meetings were significantly more likely to see the agency as responsive to public concerns.
findings.detail: Study of participants in U.S. Forest Service project meetings. Associational design; sample size not given in the abstract. Published 2003.

findings.claim: How officials treat people raises acceptance of a decision that goes against them, and perceived fairness matters more than officials' actual conduct.
findings.detail: Two scenario experiments holding an unfavorable decision constant. People who felt morally entitled to a different result were less likely to accept it regardless. Published 2010.

findings.claim: Brazilian cities that adopted participatory budgeting saw higher health spending and lower infant mortality, with stronger links the longer the program ran.
findings.detail: Observational panel of Brazil's largest cities over about 20 years. Adoption was not random. Published 2014.

findings.claim: Minnesota agencies must request public comment at least 60 days before formally proposing a rule, on a subject under active consideration.
findings.detail: Minnesota Statutes section 14.101, subdivision 1. Notice is published in the State Register and must say who is likely affected and how to comment.

counterintuitive.headline: The public's most challenging ideas are the ones most likely to be quietly dropped.
counterintuitive.text: Font and colleagues tracked 571 proposals from local participatory processes in Spain. Non-challenging proposals were fully adopted 42% of the time. Challenging ones were adopted 26% of the time and were almost twice as likely to be rejected. Costly ideas fared worse too. The authors call this selective listening: agencies take the easy suggestions and let the hard ones fade. Yet the hard ideas often carry the most information about what is not working. A leader who wants engagement to matter has to carry the difficult proposals forward on purpose, with costs and options attached.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.text:
Public engagement matters only if it can still change something. Many invitations ask people to give feedback after the main choices are made. Community members notice. They spend an evening preparing comments, then see a final decision that looks the same as the draft. Next time, fewer people come.

Research shows that consultation changes outcomes some of the time, not automatically. In one large study of 571 proposals from public processes in Spain, about a third were fully adopted, a third were changed, and a third were rejected. The proposals that succeeded most often had support from both elected leaders and public servants. That second group includes people in roles like yours.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text:
Before you invite anyone, write down three things. First, which parts of the decision are still open. Second, which parts are fixed and why. Third, who will make the final choice and by when.

Put all three in the invitation. Ask a question people can answer from their own experience. For example: 'When you tried to apply, what made it hard to finish?' Say how people can take part, including by phone, in writing or with an interpreter, and whom to contact for access needs. Say when they will hear what changed.

Then keep that promise. Send a short note to everyone who took part. Name what changed because of their input, what did not, and why.

sections.title: What to watch for
sections.text: Watch for selective listening. In the same study, challenging or costly proposals were dropped far more often. It is natural to adopt the easy fixes and let the hard ones fade. Instead, carry the difficult ideas to decision makers with a cost, a few options and a clear recommendation. A hard idea may still be declined, but it should be declined on purpose, with a reason people can hear.

sections.title: When consultation changes outcomes
sections.text:
The best large-scale evidence on whether public input gets used comes from Font and colleagues. They followed 571 proposals that came out of 39 local participatory processes in three Spanish regions. Overall, 36% were fully implemented, 32% were partially implemented or modified, and 32% were rejected.

Several factors made adoption more likely. The strongest was internal support. When both public servants and elected leaders backed a proposal, it had a 46% chance of full implementation. Without that support, the chance was 17%. Process quality also mattered. Some processes met all three of the authors' quality criteria. Their proposals had a 45% chance of full adoption and were almost 20 points less likely to be rejected. Proposals from participatory budgeting, where people decide on real money, were fully adopted 51% of the time, compared with 30% for other processes.

Other factors worked against adoption. Challenging proposals were almost twice as likely to be rejected as non-challenging ones. Costly proposals were about 20 points more likely to be rejected than cheap ones. Characteristics of the municipality itself made no significant difference. In other words, what happened inside the process and inside the agency mattered more than the place.

sections.title: Why this happens
sections.text:
Agencies face real limits. Budgets are set, laws constrain choices, and staff time is short. Under those limits, the easiest path is to adopt low-cost, low-conflict ideas. The authors call this selective listening. It can look like responsiveness while leaving the main problem untouched.

The public notices the difference. Halvorsen studied participants in U.S. Forest Service project meetings. People who attended quality meetings were significantly more likely to see the agency as responsive to public concerns. Esaiasson ran experiments in which a decision went against people. How officials treated them raised acceptance of that decision, and perceived fairness mattered more than what officials actually did. People can accept a no when they believe they were heard and the reasons were honest. People who felt they deserved a different result were less likely to accept it however they were treated. Fair process helps, but it does not erase every disagreement.

sections.title: What the research cannot tell you
sections.text: Voorberg and colleagues reviewed 122 studies on co-creation and co-production with citizens. Most studied the conditions that help or hinder participation. Hardly any measured outcomes. The field is mostly case studies. So the evidence for any one engagement method is thinner than practitioners often assume. Font's study is a notable exception, and it is observational, so it shows patterns rather than proven causes.

sections.title: Applying this to DHS work
sections.text:
Start with the decision, not the event. Ask what is truly open. In a grant program, eligibility rules may be set by law while the application process, the timeline and the outreach plan are open. In rulemaking, Minnesota Statutes section 14.101 requires agencies to request comments at least 60 days before formally proposing a rule, on a subject under active consideration. That early window is when input can matter most.

Write an invitation that answers the questions a busy partner would ask. What decision is this? What can still change? Who decides, and when? How can I take part if I cannot come in person? When will I hear back?

Invite beyond the usual partners. Established organizations bring valuable experience, but they may not speak for people who stopped trying to reach the program. Ask partners who else should be invited. Offer more than one way to take part, such as phone, written comment and a session at a time outside the workday. For county partners, work through the person or area responsible for county relationships. For Tribal Nations, all contact goes through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations.

After input comes in, sort it honestly. Group proposals by theme. For each, note whether it is in scope, its likely cost and who would need to approve it. Bring the challenging proposals forward with options rather than setting them aside. Then report back to everyone who took part.

sections.title: A short test before you send the invitation
sections.text: Read your draft invitation as a busy family member would. Can you tell in the first two sentences what decision is open? Can you tell how to take part without a computer? Can you tell when you will hear back? If any answer is no, revise before sending. A clear invitation is the first sign of a quality process.

sections.title: Your role in whether input is used
sections.text:
The finding about internal support deserves attention. In Font's study, a proposal backed by both public servants and elected leaders was almost three times as likely to be fully adopted. Public servants are not neutral pipes. They decide what goes in a briefing, how a cost is framed, and whether a proposal reaches the person who can approve it.

That gives you real influence, and a responsibility to use it fairly. Supporting a proposal does not mean promising it. It means describing it accurately, estimating what it would take, and making sure the decision maker sees it. If you think a proposal is unworkable, say why in writing, and say what part of the concern could still be addressed.

sections.title: Handling challenging proposals
sections.text:
Challenging proposals often ask for something the program was not designed to do. For example, people may ask that applications be accepted in person at county locations, not only online. That costs money and requires partners to agree.

The research suggests these are the proposals most likely to be dropped. Before you let that happen, do three things. First, separate the underlying need from the specific fix. The need may be help completing an application. The fix may be in-person drop-off, a phone option or a trained navigator. Second, estimate the cost and who would need to agree for each option. Third, bring the options to the decision maker with a recommendation and the participants' own words about why it matters.

If the answer is still no, it should be a decision someone made on purpose. Then explain it. The experiments by Esaiasson suggest people accept unfavorable outcomes more readily when they see the process as fair.

sections.title: When a decision is already made
sections.text:
Sometimes leaders want public input on something already settled. Be honest about this. Calling a briefing a consultation damages trust for the next real one. If the main choice is fixed, say so, and look for what is still open. Implementation details, timelines, communication methods and supports for people affected are often still flexible. Invite input on those, and say clearly that the main choice is not on the table.

If nothing is open, call it what it is: an information session. Offer a way for people to raise concerns, and say who will receive them.

sections.title: Reaching people who are not in the room
sections.text:
Established partners are often the easiest to reach and the most practiced at giving feedback. Their input is valuable. But a process that hears only from them can miss people who face the greatest barriers. These may include people who work hourly shifts, people who need interpreters or relay services, and people who gave up on the program.

Design for access from the start. Offer sessions at different times. Accept comments by phone and in writing. Provide materials in plain language and in the languages your program serves. Ask partners who is missing and how to reach them. Pay attention to whether some groups are underrepresented in the input you receive. The research here does not show which outreach methods work best for which groups, so watch what happens and adjust.

County and Tribal relationships have their own channels. Work through the person or area responsible for county relationships. For any matter that affects Tribal Nations, the person or area responsible for Tribal relations leads, and you follow their guidance on timing and format. Do not reach out on your own or speak for Tribal Nations.

sections.title: When participants disagree with each other
sections.text:
Public input rarely points one way. Some families may want a short, simple form. Others may want room to explain complex needs. A community organization may favor one approach while county partners favor another.

Do not average the views or pick the loudest. Describe the trade-off plainly to the decision maker. Say who favored each option and why, in their own words where you can. Then, in the report back, explain how the choice was made. Esaiasson's experiments suggest that people who see the process as fair are more willing to accept a result that did not go their way. That is especially important when two groups of participants wanted different things.

It also helps to ask participants directly about the trade-off. A question such as 'If the form must stay short, what one thing must it ask?' can surface common ground that a general request for feedback would miss.

sections.title: Limits and honest expectations
sections.text:
Be careful not to overpromise based on this evidence. The Spanish study is observational. Proposals with internal support may have been better proposals to begin with. Touchton and Wampler linked participatory budgeting in Brazilian cities to lower infant mortality over many years. But cities chose to adopt it, so other factors may explain part of the link. The co-production review found that outcomes are rarely measured at all.

What the evidence does support is a set of practical lessons. Engagement is more likely to change outcomes when the decision is still open, the process is well designed, and people inside government carry proposals forward. People are more likely to see an agency as responsive, and to accept outcomes they dislike, when the process is fair and the reasons are honest. None of that guarantees agreement. Some people will still disagree, and that is part of public decision making.

sections.title: Closing the loop
sections.text:
Report back to every participant. Keep it short. List the main themes you heard. For each, say what changed, what did not and why. Name the next step and when it will happen. If a proposal was declined because of cost or law, say so plainly. If it is being studied further, say who is studying it and when there will be news.

This step is often skipped because the project has moved on. Yet it is the part participants remember. It also helps the next team, because people are more willing to take part when the last invitation led somewhere they could see.

simulation.setup: You are a Policy Program Manager in the Disability Services Division. Your team is designing the application process for a new state grant that helps families of people with disabilities pay for short-term respite. The eligibility rules are set in law. The application method, timeline and outreach are still being decided. Leadership wants to hold public sessions. What is at stake is whether families who most need respite can actually apply, and whether community partners trust the next invitation.

steps.situation: Your team has a draft process: an online portal with a six-week application window. A deputy director suggests holding public sessions after the process is final, so there is something concrete to show.
steps.question: How do you plan the engagement?

choices.label: Hold sessions now on the draft. In the invitation, state what is fixed by law, what is open, who decides and when people will hear back. Offer phone, written and evening options.
choices.feedback: This invites people while the design can still change. Stating what is open and fixed helps people decide whether to spend their time. Offering several ways to take part widens who is heard. Font and colleagues found that process quality was linked to proposals being adopted. This is the setup that gives input the best chance to matter.

choices.label: Follow the deputy director's plan. Present the final process and take questions.
choices.feedback: Showing something concrete is appealing, and it avoids raising expectations. But calling this engagement when nothing can change damages trust for later invitations. If you choose this path, call it an information session. Any problem people raise will now be expensive to fix.

choices.label: Send a broad online survey asking families what they think about respite in general.
choices.feedback: A survey can reach many people, and general views are useful context. But the questions are not tied to the open decision, so the answers will be hard to act on. An online-only survey may also miss families with the least time or internet access, the same barrier the portal might create.

steps.situation: Input comes in. Several easy fixes are suggested: larger text, a clearer checklist and a longer window. A group of families and two community organizations ask that applications also be accepted by phone and on paper through local partners. That would cost staff time and require agreements with partners.
steps.question: What do you do with the challenging proposal?

choices.label: Adopt the easy fixes and note the phone and paper request as out of scope for this year.
choices.feedback: This is the selective listening pattern Font and colleagues documented. Easy fixes are real improvements, so this feels responsive. But challenging proposals often carry the most information. Here it points to families who cannot use a portal at all. Dropping it quietly means those families may never apply.

choices.label: Adopt the easy fixes. Bring the phone and paper request to the director with costs, two or three options and families' own words about the barrier.
choices.feedback: This carries the hard idea forward on purpose. In Font's study, proposals with support from public servants were far more likely to be adopted. You are not promising it. You are making sure the decision maker sees it clearly. Options such as phone only, or paper at a few sites, make a yes more possible.

choices.label: Tell participants their request will be built in, then work out the details.
choices.feedback: This shows commitment, but you do not have authority to promise it, and it may not be funded. If the promise fails, trust drops further than if you had been honest about the decision. Bring it forward with options, and tell participants who decides and when.

steps.situation: At the information session, several family members say they have no reliable internet and cannot use the portal. A community organization says it was not asked before the process was set and is reluctant to promote it.
steps.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Acknowledge the process was set before input. Name what is still open, such as outreach and help with applying, and bring the access problem to the director with options.
choices.feedback: This is honest and still useful. Esaiasson's experiments found that fair treatment raises acceptance of decisions people dislike. Naming what is still open gives people a real role. Bringing the access problem forward with options gives it a chance, even late. Expect some lasting frustration.

choices.label: Explain that the portal was chosen to be efficient and that most families have internet access.
choices.feedback: The reason may be true for many families, and you want to defend the team's work. But it dismisses the specific barrier raised. It is also an assumption you have not checked. People who see an agency as unresponsive are less likely to take part next time.

choices.label: Promise to reopen the whole process.
choices.feedback: This responds to the frustration, but you may not have authority to reopen it, and it may delay the grant for families who can apply now. A narrower commitment that you can keep, such as testing a phone option, builds more trust than a broad promise that may fail.

steps.situation: The director has decided. The longer window and checklist are in. A phone application option will be tested in the first year. Paper applications through partners were declined for now because of cost. The grant launches in six weeks.
steps.question: How do you close the loop with participants?

choices.label: Send everyone a short note: themes heard, what changed, what did not and why, and when the phone option will be reviewed.
choices.feedback: This step is easy to skip once a decision is made. Naming what was declined, with the reason, treats people as partners. Halvorsen found quality participation was linked to seeing the agency as responsive. A clear report also shows people what their time produced.

choices.label: Post a general thank-you on the program web page and announce the launch.
choices.feedback: This is quick and positive, and the launch is good news. But participants cannot see whether their input mattered. Families who asked for paper applications will learn the answer by noticing it is missing. A general thank-you often reads as a sign that nothing changed.

choices.label: Wait until after the first year's review to report back, so you can share results.
choices.feedback: Waiting for results is careful, and you will know more later. But a year of silence after a public process looks like nothing happened. Report back now on the decision, and promise a second update after the review with a date.

simulation.debrief: The strongest path invited people while the application process was still open, stated what law fixed, and offered several ways to take part. When a costly, challenging proposal came in, it was carried to the director with options instead of being quietly dropped. Font and colleagues found this is exactly the kind of proposal most often lost, and that support from public servants sharply raised the chance of adoption. The director said yes to part of it and no to part of it. That is a normal result. Closing the loop with a plain account of both is what lets people accept a partial no and come back next time. The research is mostly observational and from outside Minnesota, but its practical lessons fit DHS work well.

mistakes.mistake: Inviting input after the main decision is made.
mistakes.why: Leaders want something concrete to show and worry about raising expectations. But people who find nothing can change lose trust in the next invitation.
mistakes.instead: Invite input while choices are open, or call the event an information session.

mistakes.mistake: Adopting the easy suggestions and letting the hard ones fade.
mistakes.why: Budgets and authority are limited, and quick fixes feel responsive. Font and colleagues found challenging proposals were almost twice as likely to be rejected.
mistakes.instead: Carry challenging proposals forward with costs, options and a recommendation.

mistakes.mistake: Promising what you cannot deliver.
mistakes.why: Wanting to show commitment is natural, especially when participants are frustrated. A broken promise does more harm than an honest 'that is not my decision'.
mistakes.instead: Say who decides and when, and commit only to what you can keep.

mistakes.mistake: Hearing only from established partners.
mistakes.why: They are easy to reach, experienced, and well informed. But they may not represent people who have stopped trying to use the program.
mistakes.instead: Ask partners who is missing, and offer phone, written and off-hours options.

mistakes.mistake: Skipping the report back.
mistakes.why: The project moves on and the team is busy. Yet participants judge the process by whether they can see their input mattered.
mistakes.instead: Send a short note on what changed, what did not and why, with a next date.

mistakes.mistake: Contacting Tribal Nations or counties directly without the right channel.
mistakes.why: Staff want to move quickly and include everyone. Going around established relationships can cause harm and confusion.
mistakes.instead: Work through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations or county relationships.

jobAid.title: Open-decision engagement checklist
jobAid.use: Before you send any invitation for public or partner input, and again before you close the process.
steps: What decision is this, and which parts are still open?
What is fixed, and why? Can you say so in one sentence?
Who makes the final choice, and by what date?
What question can people answer from their own experience?
How can people take part besides a daytime meeting: phone, written, interpreter, relay, evening?
Who is missing? Which partners can help reach them? Do county or Tribal matters need the person or area responsible?
For each challenging proposal: what is the underlying need, what are two or three options, what does each cost and who must agree?
When and how will you tell every participant what changed, what did not and why?

media.reason: The lesson turns on one sequence: invite while open, carry hard ideas forward, close the loop. A single narrator can walk through it as a story without dividing the point.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Picture a community organization that serves families of people with disabilities. Its director receives another invitation from a state agency to give feedback. She has done this before. Her staff spent evenings preparing comments. Then the final decision looked just like the draft. This time, before she agrees, she wants to know one thing. Can anything still change?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That question is at the heart of public engagement. Research by Font and colleagues followed 571 proposals that came out of public processes in Spanish cities. About a third were fully adopted. About a third were changed. About a third were rejected. Consultation can change outcomes, but it does not do so automatically.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: What made the difference? The strongest factor was support inside government. When both public servants and elected leaders backed a proposal, it was fully adopted 46 percent of the time. Without that support, the figure was 17 percent. Public servants decide what goes in a briefing and how a cost is described. That is real influence.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The same study found a pattern worth remembering. Challenging proposals were almost twice as likely to be rejected. Costly ones fared worse too. The authors call this selective listening. Agencies take the easy ideas and let the hard ones fade. Yet the hard ideas often carry the most important news, such as who cannot use the program at all.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: So what does good practice look like? Start before the decision is made. Write down what is open, what is fixed and who decides. Put all three in the invitation. Ask a question people can answer from experience. Offer more than one way to take part, such as phone, written comment and an evening session. Ask partners who else should be invited.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: When input comes in, sort it honestly. For each challenging proposal, separate the need from the fix. Estimate what each option would cost and who must agree. Then bring it to the person who decides, with a recommendation. You are not promising a yes. You are making sure a no, if it comes, is a choice someone made on purpose.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Finally, close the loop. Experiments by Esaiasson found that people accept decisions they dislike more readily when they see the process as fair. Tell every participant what changed, what did not and why. Name the next step and its date. That short note is what the community director will remember the next time an invitation arrives.

prompts: What decision in your area is still open enough for public or partner input to change it?
Which partners, and which people beyond the usual partners, will you invite, and through which person or area responsible for county or Tribal relationships?
By what date will you report back to participants on what changed?

title: Person-centered decisions: who decides
objective: Keep the person who receives services at the center of decisions about their own life, by asking them first, offering real informed choice, and treating guardianship as a last resort rather than a default.
outcomes: Ask the person directly about goals and daily choices before asking family or providers.
Explain the elements of informed choice in Minnesota law and check whether a team practice meets them.
Describe supported decision making and less restrictive alternatives to guardianship accurately, including what the evidence does not yet show.
Spot a team habit that routes decisions away from the person, and propose a change to the person or area responsible.
Talk with a worried family member about risk without dismissing the concern or overriding the person.

evidence.summary: Person-centered planning appears to help, but modestly. A systematic review found low-quality evidence of moderate gains in community participation, activities and daily choice, with inconsistent results for jobs. A two-year study found access to planning and its benefits were unequal. Self-determination at the end of high school predicted employment and community access a year later. Supported decision making is promising, but reviews call the evidence limited, and a 2025 Minnesota DHS report says data on guardianship are thin while evidence points to overuse. Minnesota law already requires less restrictive alternatives before guardianship and defines informed choice in detail. The honest message is that law and values are clear, while the research is still catching up.

findings.claim: Person-centered planning had a moderate positive effect on community participation, activities and daily choice-making, with inconsistent effects on employment.
findings.detail: Systematic review of 16 studies (7 quantitative, 5 qualitative, 4 mixed methods), 1990 to 2014. Evidence quality rated low. Published 2016.
findings.source: Ratti, Hassiotis, Crabtree, Deb, Gallagher and Unwin, 2016

findings.claim: Both access to person-centered planning and its benefits showed powerful inequalities linked to the person's characteristics, context and the planning process.
findings.detail: Longitudinal study of 93 adults with intellectual disabilities in England, followed about two years. Published 2007.

findings.claim: The most common benefit people named from planning was more activities and opportunities (57%), followed by feeling better about themselves (48%).
findings.detail: Analysis of open-ended comments from 65 people with intellectual disabilities in England. Self-report, no comparison group. Published 2008.

findings.claim: Self-determination when leaving high school predicted employment and community access one year later among 779 students with disabilities.
findings.detail: Follow-up of students from group-randomized intervention studies, outcomes at one and two years. Community access beta 1.078 at year one; employment beta 0.504 at year one. An unexpected negative link to financial independence appeared at year two. Published 2015.
findings.source: Shogren, Wehmeyer, Palmer, Rifenbark and Little, 2015

findings.claim: Reviews find evidence on the implementation and impact of supported decision making is limited, and one warns it could enable undue influence by supporters.
findings.detail: Rapid evidence assessment (2015) and critical review focused on people aging with intellectual disabilities (2014).
findings.source: Davidson, Kelly and colleagues, 2015; Kohn and Blumenthal, 2014

findings.claim: About 35,000 people in Minnesota were estimated to be under guardianship as of May 2024, and DHS reports that evidence points to overuse while data are too thin to know the true number.
findings.detail: Minnesota DHS interim report to the Legislature, January 2025. Names drivers of overuse including the transition at age 18, hospital discharge, facility admission, lack of information about alternatives and supporters' wish to limit risk. Pilot studies of supported decision making are small but suggest positive effects on well-being.

findings.claim: Minnesota courts may appoint a guardian only if needs cannot be met by less restrictive means, including supported decision making, and must explain specifically why alternatives do not work.
findings.detail: Minnesota Statutes section 524.5-310. The court grants only the powers needed and encourages maximum self-reliance and independence whenever feasible.

findings.claim: Minnesota defines informed choice as a choice made after receiving accessible information and the tools and opportunities to understand all options, and sets employment first, independent living first and self-direction policies.
findings.detail: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.4905. Informed decision making has 12 elements, including accommodations, discussing preferences and goals, visits to alternative settings and ample time. For members of Minnesota Tribal Nations, informed choice includes the right to Tribal services.

counterintuitive.headline: A planning method built around the person can still leave some people behind.
counterintuitive.text: Person-centered planning is meant to put each person's own goals first. Yet when Robertson and colleagues followed 93 adults in England for about two years, they found powerful inequalities. Whether someone got a plan, and whether it helped, depended on the person's characteristics, their setting and how the planning was done. A good method does not guarantee a good result for everyone. Leaders need to check who is getting real choice and who is getting a form that someone else filled in.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.text:
Person-centered practice comes down to one question: who decides? For people who receive disability services, the answer in Minnesota law is clear. The person makes informed choices about their own services and life, with the support they want. Guardianship is meant to be a last resort.

In daily work, the answer is often less clear. Staff talk to a parent because the parent called. A provider fills in the person's goals because the meeting ran long. A team assumes guardianship at age 18 because that is what families are often told. None of these choices is made with bad intent. Each one moves the decision a little further from the person.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text:
Ask the person first. Before you ask family, providers or staff what someone wants, ask the person directly, in the way they communicate best. Ask about daily choices, not only big goals. What do you want to do with your day? Where do you want to live? Who do you want helping you decide?

Then check that the choice is informed. Minnesota law describes informed choice as a decision made after the person has accessible information and the tools and opportunities to understand all options. That can mean visiting a setting, trying a job, or having time to think.

sections.title: What the evidence says, briefly
sections.text: Person-centered planning appears to help with community participation and daily choice, though the evidence is low in quality and the gains are moderate. People who leave high school with stronger self-determination are more likely to have jobs and community access a year later. Supported decision making is promising, but research on it is still limited. A 2025 Minnesota DHS report found signs that guardianship is overused and that good data are scarce. Values and law point one way. Research is still catching up, and it is fair to say so.

sections.title: What person-centered planning does and does not do
sections.text:
Person-centered planning asks the person what matters to them and builds supports around those goals. A 2016 systematic review by Ratti and colleagues looked at 16 studies from 1990 to 2014. The evidence was low in quality. It suggested moderate positive effects on community participation, participation in activities and daily choice-making. Effects on employment were inconsistent. The authors were careful to say the evidence does not show planning produces radical change.

Other studies add detail. Wigham and colleagues asked 65 people in England what they gained from planning. The most common answer was more activities and opportunities, named by 57%. Nearly half, 48%, said they felt better about themselves. Robertson and colleagues followed 93 adults for about two years. They found powerful inequalities in who got a plan and who benefited. The person's characteristics, their setting and how the planning was done all mattered.

sections.title: Why self-determination matters
sections.text:
Self-determination means acting as the main decision maker in your own life. Shogren and colleagues followed 779 students with disabilities who had been part of earlier intervention studies. Students with higher self-determination when they left high school were more likely to have jobs and community access one year later. The link to community access held at two years.

The same study found a surprise. Higher self-determination predicted lower financial independence at two years. The authors call the relationship complex. One possible reading is that people making their own choices may also choose options that cost more at first. The study cannot say. What it does show is that making decisions is linked to outcomes people value, and that the picture is not simple.

sections.title: Supported decision making and guardianship
sections.text:
Supported decision making lets a person keep the right to decide while choosing trusted people to help them understand options and communicate choices. It is an alternative to guardianship, where a court gives another person the power to decide.

Minnesota law already sets the order. Under Minnesota Statutes section 524.5-310, a court may appoint a guardian only if the person's needs cannot be met by less restrictive means, including supported decision making. The court must explain why alternatives do not work, and grant only the powers that are needed.

The research base is still young. A 2015 review by Davidson and colleagues found evidence on impact to be limited. Kohn and Blumenthal warned in 2014 that supporters could exert undue influence if safeguards are weak. A January 2025 DHS report to the Legislature found that pilot studies are small, but suggest positive effects on decision makers' well-being. It estimated about 35,000 people in Minnesota were under guardianship as of May 2024 and said the true number is not known.

sections.title: What informed choice sounds like
sections.text:
Informed choice is a conversation, not a checkbox. Compare two openings. 'Your plan has you at the day program again this year. Any changes?' Or: 'Last year you said you wanted to earn money. Do you still want that? There are a few ways to try it, and you can visit or try one before deciding.'

The second version names the person's goal, offers more than one option and builds in a trial. It also leaves room for the person to say no. Informed choice includes the right to choose what staff would not choose. The law's 12 elements of informed decision making include discussing preferences and goals and giving ample time and timely opportunity to decide.

sections.title: Applying this in DHS work
sections.text:
Most DHS staff do not write individual plans. But many shape the practices that lead agencies, providers and families follow. Policy guidance, call-line scripts, training materials and form design all signal who decides.

Look at your team's materials with three questions. Does this speak to the person first, or to whoever is helping them? Does it explain options in a form the person can use, such as plain language, easy read or a conversation? Does it mention less restrictive alternatives before guardianship?

Minnesota Statutes section 256B.4905 sets detailed policies. People should be offered competitive work before only day services. They should be offered the chance to live in a setting they control before a provider-controlled one. They should have the chance to direct their own services. Each of these follows an informed decision-making process with 12 listed elements, including accommodations, visits to alternative settings and ample time to decide.

If a team habit routes decisions away from the person, raise it with the person or area responsible for that guidance or training. Bring a specific example and a proposed fix.

sections.title: Why decisions drift away from the person
sections.text:
The 2025 DHS report names several reasons guardianship is overused. Families are often told at age 18 that guardianship is the next step, without hearing about alternatives. Hospitals may seek guardianship to speed a discharge. Facilities may seek it to admit someone. Lack of information about alternatives makes guardianship the default. Friends and family may want to limit risk for someone they love.

The same forces act on everyday practice. A worker calls the parent because the parent answers the phone. A plan lists goals a provider suggested because there was no time to ask. A form has a line for the guardian's signature but no line for the person's own words. Each choice is reasonable in the moment. Together they teach everyone that someone else decides.

sections.title: Risk, safety and the right to choose
sections.text:
Worried families and staff often frame the question as safety against independence. That framing deserves care. Real risks exist, and people who love someone want to protect them. Guardianship, though, does not remove all risk, and it removes rights.

A more useful question is what support would let the person make this choice as safely as possible. That might be a trusted friend who reviews contracts, a phone check-in, assistive technology or a trial period. Minnesota law lists technology, supported decision making and community services among the less restrictive options a court must consider.

When you talk with a worried family member, acknowledge the concern first. Then ask what specifically they fear. Then ask the person what they want and what help they would accept. Often the specific fear can be addressed without taking the decision away.

sections.title: Limits of the evidence
sections.text:
Be honest about what the research shows. The review of person-centered planning rated the evidence low in quality. Most studies were small, and many lacked comparison groups. The self-determination study shows a predictive link, not proof that teaching self-determination causes better outcomes. Supported decision making has no large controlled trial behind it. Pilot projects have struggled to recruit and keep participants.

This does not weaken the case for choice. In Minnesota, informed choice and less restrictive alternatives are legal requirements, not experimental programs. The research helps you understand where practice tends to fall short, and what kinds of gains to expect. It does not tell you that one method works for everyone.

sections.title: When the person chooses something you would not
sections.text:
Respecting choice is easy when the person picks what staff would have picked. The test comes when they do not. A person may turn down a job offer, keep a friendship that worries family, or choose a setting with less support than staff recommend.

Start by checking that the choice is informed. Did the person have the information in a usable form? Did they have a chance to see or try the alternatives? Did they have time? If yes, the choice is theirs, even if you disagree.

You can still share your concern honestly and offer support. You can also agree to revisit the decision after a set time. What you should not do is keep raising the question until the person gives the answer you prefer. That turns support into pressure. Kohn and Blumenthal's warning about undue influence applies to staff as well as to family and friends.

sections.title: Differences across people
sections.text:
Robertson's finding of powerful inequalities is a warning. Some people got plans and benefited. Others did not. The study linked this to personal characteristics, context and the planning process, though the abstract does not say which groups were most affected. No study in this course shows effects for a specific racial or cultural group, so do not assume one.

What you can do is check. Look at who your team's practices reach. Consider people who communicate without speech, people with high support needs, and people whose families speak a language other than English. Do they get the same chance to state their own goals? If you do not know, that is the first thing to find out.

Culture shapes how people make decisions. In some families, major choices are made together, and the person may want that. Person-centered practice respects the person's own preference about who helps them decide. It does not impose an individual model on someone who wants a family one, and it does not let a family model replace the person's voice.

sections.title: Tribal Nations and informed choice
sections.text: Minnesota Statutes section 256B.4905 states that informed choice for members of Minnesota Tribal Nations includes the right to Tribal services. It also states that the section does not limit Tribal sovereignty. Any question about how this applies goes to the person or area responsible for Tribal relations. Do not interpret it on your own or speak for Tribal Nations.

sections.title: Harder situations
sections.text:
The person and the family disagree. A young adult wants to live in an apartment. Parents want them at home. Ask each what matters most and what they fear. Look for a plan the person accepts that addresses the specific fear, such as a trial period with check-ins. If there is a guardian, the guardian's role is set by the court order. Even then, Minnesota law directs the court to grant only the powers needed and to encourage maximum self-reliance where feasible.

The person's communication is hard to read. Take more time, not less. Ask people who know the person well how they communicate choice. Use pictures, objects, visits or trial experiences. Watch what the person does as well as what others say.

A supporter seems to be steering. Kohn and Blumenthal raised this risk. Signs include a supporter answering every question or the person's stated wishes changing only when the supporter is present. Speak with the person alone if they agree. Follow your area's procedures for any concern about exploitation or abuse.

Your team's guidance defaults to the guardian or family. Bring a specific example to the person or area responsible for the guidance. Propose wording that speaks to the person first and names less restrictive alternatives.

simulation.setup: You are a Human Services Supervisor in the Disability Services Division. Your team answers questions from families and lead agencies about disability waiver services and gives general information about options. Staff do not give legal advice and refer individual planning to the person's lead agency case manager. Today a parent calls about an adult child who just turned 18. What is at stake is whether the young adult is part of decisions about their own life, and whether your team's practice supports informed choice.

steps.situation: A call-line worker brings you the call. The parent says the school told them to get guardianship now. The young adult wants to work at a grocery store and move in with a friend. The parent is worried about money and safety and asks how to start guardianship.
steps.question: How do you guide the worker's response?

choices.label: Have the worker explain where to start guardianship paperwork, since that is what the parent asked for.
choices.feedback: This is responsive and the parent will feel helped. But it skips the alternatives that Minnesota law says a court must consider first, including supported decision making. The 2025 DHS report names this exact moment, the transition at 18, as a common path to unnecessary guardianship. The young adult has not been part of the conversation.

choices.label: Have the worker acknowledge the worry, describe less restrictive alternatives such as supported decision making, and suggest the family and young adult talk with the case manager together.
choices.feedback: This gives accurate information without legal advice. It names the options the law puts first and brings the young adult into the next step. The parent's concern is taken seriously, not dismissed. It also respects the team's role: general information here, individual planning with the lead agency.

choices.label: Have the worker tell the parent that guardianship is usually unnecessary and that the young adult should decide.
choices.feedback: The values are right, but the delivery may backfire. A worried parent who feels lectured may stop listening. The worker also does not know this young adult's situation. Acknowledge the concern, give accurate options, and point to the people who can plan with the family.

steps.situation: A week later, the case manager contacts your team through the usual channel for guidance. The family is considering supported decision making. The parent still worries the young adult will sign a lease or loan without understanding it.
steps.question: What guidance do you offer?

choices.label: Suggest the case manager ask the young adult what help they would accept for big money decisions, such as a trusted supporter reviewing contracts, and build that into the plan.
choices.feedback: This addresses the specific fear without removing the right to decide. Minnesota law lists supported decision making and other supports among less restrictive options. Asking the young adult what help they want keeps them at the center. It also fits the research finding that self-determination is linked to employment and community access.

choices.label: Suggest a limited guardianship over finances only, as a middle ground.
choices.feedback: Limited guardianship is less restrictive than full guardianship and may be appropriate for some people. But it still removes a right through a court. The law asks whether needs can be met by less restrictive means first. Suggest trying supports first and reviewing whether they work.

choices.label: Say the decision belongs to the family and case manager, and stay out of it.
choices.feedback: Respecting roles is right, and your team should not take over planning. But the case manager asked for guidance. Saying nothing leaves the parent's fear unaddressed, which often leads back to guardianship as the default. General guidance on supports is within your team's role.

steps.situation: Two weeks later, the same parent calls back. The court process has started. The young adult called the line too, upset, saying no one asked what they wanted.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Have a worker speak with the young adult directly, in the way they communicate best, share general information about their rights and alternatives, and refer them to the case manager and to legal help.
choices.feedback: This puts the person back at the center. Minnesota law requires the court to consider less restrictive alternatives and to explain why they do not work. The young adult has a right to know that and to be heard. Your team gives general information and refers. It does not take sides in the court process.

choices.label: Tell the young adult this is a family matter now that the court process has started.
choices.feedback: This avoids stepping into a court matter, which is a real concern. But it tells the person whose life is at stake that their voice no longer matters. General information about rights and where to get help is within your team's role and respects the person.

choices.label: Call the parent to suggest they pause the court process.
choices.feedback: This may help the young adult, but it puts your team in the middle of a family and court matter. A better route is to inform the young adult directly and refer both to the case manager and to legal help, where options can be explored properly.

steps.situation: Reviewing the call, you notice your team's script for calls about turning 18 begins: 'Ask the parent or guardian what support they need.' It does not mention alternatives to guardianship or speaking with the young adult.
steps.question: What do you do about the script?

choices.label: Draft new wording that asks to speak with the person, names less restrictive alternatives and informed choice, and bring it to the person or area responsible for the script.
choices.feedback: This fixes the habit at its source. The 2025 DHS report found that lack of information about alternatives drives guardianship overuse. A script that reaches every call can change many conversations. Bringing a specific draft to the person or area responsible makes the change easier to approve.

choices.label: Remind your own staff to speak with the young adult, without changing the script.
choices.feedback: A reminder helps your current staff and is quick. But habits built into a script outlast reminders. New staff will follow the written words. Robertson and colleagues found unequal access to person-centered planning, which is often how unchanged practices play out.

choices.label: Leave the script alone. Most callers are parents, so it fits who calls.
choices.feedback: The script does match who usually calls, and changing it takes effort. But it builds in the assumption that someone else decides. Minnesota law defines informed choice around the person. A script that never mentions the person or alternatives works against that.

simulation.debrief: The strongest path treated the parent's worry as real and still kept the young adult at the center. It shared accurate information about less restrictive alternatives, which Minnesota law requires courts to consider before guardianship. It turned a general fear about money into a specific support the young adult could accept. It also fixed the team script that had made the parent the default decision maker. The research supports this direction with honest limits. Person-centered planning shows moderate gains and unequal reach. Self-determination is linked to jobs and community access. Supported decision making is promising but not yet proven at scale. The 2025 DHS report found that missing information at age 18 is a common path to unnecessary guardianship, which is exactly where your team can help.

mistakes.mistake: Talking to whoever calls instead of the person.
mistakes.why: The parent or provider is on the phone and has questions. It feels efficient and polite to answer them.
mistakes.instead: Answer the caller, and ask to speak with the person in the way they communicate best.

mistakes.mistake: Treating guardianship at 18 as a routine step.
mistakes.why: Schools and others often present it that way, and families want to keep helping. The 2025 DHS report names this as a common path to overuse.
mistakes.instead: Share less restrictive alternatives, including supported decision making, before any talk of court.

mistakes.mistake: Calling a choice informed when the person only heard one option.
mistakes.why: Time is short and one option seems obvious. Minnesota law defines informed choice as understanding all options with accessible information and tools.
mistakes.instead: Offer the options in a form the person can use, including visits or trials, and allow time.

mistakes.mistake: Overstating the evidence for supported decision making.
mistakes.why: Advocates want to make a strong case. Reviews call the evidence limited and note a risk of undue influence.
mistakes.instead: Say it is required to be considered in Minnesota, promising in pilots, and still being studied.

mistakes.mistake: Dismissing a family's fear as overprotection.
mistakes.why: Staff who value choice can hear any worry as a threat to it. Families then dig in.
mistakes.instead: Ask what specifically they fear, then look for a support the person accepts.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming the planning method guarantees fairness.
mistakes.why: Person-centered planning is designed around each person. Robertson and colleagues still found powerful inequalities in access and benefit.
mistakes.instead: Check who your team's practices actually reach and who gets the chance to state their own goals.

jobAid.title: Who decides: a five-minute check
jobAid.use: When a call, plan, form or guidance document involves a decision about a person's services or life.
steps: Has the person been asked directly, in the way they communicate best?
Have they had accessible information on all options, with time, visits or trials if needed?
Are less restrictive alternatives, including supported decision making, named before guardianship?
What specific risk worries family or staff, and what support could the person accept for it?
Who does the person want helping them decide, and is anyone speaking over them?
Does this practice reach people who communicate without speech or whose families use another language?
Does any Tribal or county question go to the person or area responsible?
If a team habit routes decisions away from the person, who is the person or area responsible for changing it?

media.reason: A worried case manager and a supervisor who knows the law and the evidence each hold part of the answer. Hearing them work through one case shows how to respect both safety concerns and the person's right to decide.

script.speaker: female
script.text: I have a young man who just turned 18. He wants to move in with a friend and work at a grocery store. His parents want guardianship. Honestly, I worry about him signing a lease he does not understand.

script.speaker: male
script.text: That is a real worry. Before anyone talks about guardianship, what has he said he wants help with?

script.speaker: female
script.text: I have mostly talked with his mother. She calls, and he is usually at school.

script.speaker: male
script.text: That happens a lot. The parent is the one on the phone. But under Minnesota law, a court can appoint a guardian only if his needs cannot be met in a less restrictive way. Supported decision making is one of the alternatives named. So his own view is the starting point.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Does supported decision making actually work? I hear a lot of enthusiasm and not many numbers.

script.speaker: male
script.text: That is a fair challenge. Reviews call the evidence limited. Pilots are small. A 2025 DHS report says early results suggest better well-being, but it is still being studied. What is known is that young people with stronger self-determination are more likely to have jobs and community access a year after high school.

script.speaker: female
script.text: So the case for choice is strong even if the program evidence is thin.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Yes. And the law is clear. Now, your worry about the lease. What exactly could go wrong?

script.speaker: female
script.text: He might agree to rent he cannot afford, or a lease with terms he does not follow.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Then ask him who he trusts to look at contracts with him before he signs. An uncle, a friend, a benefits counselor. That addresses the specific risk and leaves the decision with him.

script.speaker: female
script.text: His mother may still want guardianship.

script.speaker: male
script.text: She may. Listen to what she fears most. Often a fear about money or safety has a specific answer. If she still goes to court, the court has to consider alternatives and explain why they would not work. What he wants, and which supports were tried, will matter.

prompts: Which call, form, script or guidance in your area speaks to someone other than the person first?
Who is the person or area responsible for it, and who on your team can help you draft better wording?
By what date will you bring a specific example and proposed fix to them?
