title: Why culture matters in leading DHS work
objective: Explain how culture shapes everyday DHS decisions, use intercultural models as a lens rather than a label, and build skill through guided practice rather than self-ratings.
outcomes: Name two routine decisions in your unit, such as a channel, a deadline or a meeting format, where culture shapes who can take part.
Describe what intercultural development models claim and where their evidence is thin.
Decline to use assessment results to sort, assign or label people, and explain why.
Set up a recurring, guided debrief after real interactions with people and partners.
Ask for specific outside feedback on your own intercultural skill instead of relying on how it felt.

evidence.summary: Culture shapes how people read a notice, how they disagree in a meeting and whether they trust an agency. Research gives leaders three practical lessons. First, people are poor judges of their own intercultural skill. In one nursing school, 98% of students rated themselves higher than an assessment did. Second, exposure alone does little. In a study of 1,297 students, those abroad gained only about two points on an intercultural measure. Those enrolled mainly with local students barely changed, while students with a cultural mentor gained more. Third, one-time training fades. Across 260 samples, effects on attitudes decayed, while knowledge held and longer, integrated efforts worked better. The limits are real. Most evidence comes from students, and no study links these models to job performance at DHS.

findings.claim: 98% of nursing students overestimated their intercultural competence compared with an assessment; 2% were accurate.
findings.detail: Prospective cohort, pre-test phase, 277 students and 37 faculty and staff at one Midwestern college of nursing, published 2014. Most students' assessed orientation fell in the middle of the model (183 of 277). One school; one instrument.

findings.claim: Students abroad gained only about 2.4 points on an intercultural measure, and students enrolled mainly alongside host-country students barely changed (96.12 to 96.83).
findings.detail: Multi-year pre-post study with a home comparison group: 1,297 students (1,159 abroad, 138 controls), published 2009. Controls did not change (94.02 to 93.95). Students who met with a cultural mentor gained more; mentoring subsamples were small.

findings.claim: Training effects on attitudes faded over time, while knowledge held; effects were larger when training was longer, built skills and was paired with other efforts.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 260 independent samples of diversity training, published 2016. Overall Hedges g = .38, with the largest effects on reactions and knowledge and smaller effects on behavior and attitudes.

findings.claim: Self-reports of intercultural ability often do not match actual ability. A review of 10 tests found three with the strongest evidence; the developmental inventory was not among them.
findings.detail: Cross-sectional study of 353 adults in four countries, 2020, discussing the authors' 2013 review of 10 cross-cultural competence tests. Two authors work for the company that sells one of the tests rated strongest.

findings.claim: People have only moderate insight into their own abilities, and insight is worst for complex, hard-to-measure skills.
findings.detail: Metasynthesis of about two dozen meta-analyses covering more than 330,000 people, 2014.

findings.claim: The developmental inventory's structure was supported in 4,763 people across 11 cultural samples.
findings.detail: Confirmatory factor analysis of a 50-item instrument, published 2011. Much other validation comes from the instrument's publisher; structure evidence does not show the scores predict job behavior.

findings.claim: In human service and other organizations, a climate of inclusion was consistently linked to positive outcomes (rho = .42), while diversity alone had mixed effects.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 30 studies, 496,740 workers, published 2016 in a human service management journal.

counterintuitive.headline: Living among another culture did not, by itself, build intercultural skill.
counterintuitive.text: It seems obvious that the most immersion produces the most growth. Vande Berg, Connor-Linton and Paige (2009) tracked 1,297 students. Students who took classes mainly alongside host-country students, the most immersive arrangement, moved from 96.12 to 96.83 on an intercultural measure. That change was not statistically significant. Students who met regularly with a cultural mentor gained more. The authors concluded that placing people in contact with difference is not enough. Someone has to help them make sense of it. For DHS leaders, years of serving diverse communities do not guarantee skill. Guided reflection on real interactions is what the evidence favors.

sections.title: Culture lives in routine decisions
sections.text: Think about the last time someone on your team said, “Let me know if you have concerns.” Who could reach that person? How long before silence counted as agreement? The invitation, the channel and the deadline are all decisions. Someone chose them, even if the team has used them for years. Culture shapes how people read those choices. One person hears “let me know” as a real request. Another hears it as a polite close and would never push back on a supervisor in writing. The same is true for the people DHS serves. A notice, a phone script or a meeting time can work well for one person and shut another out.

sections.title: You are probably not the best judge of your own skill
sections.text: In one nursing school, 98% of students rated their intercultural competence higher than an assessment did. A large review of self-assessment found people have only moderate insight into their own abilities. Insight is weakest for complex skills, and working across cultures is a complex skill. Feeling comfortable with difference is not the same as handling it well. The people who could tell you how an interaction landed often will not say so to a state employee unless asked directly.

sections.title: Exposure is not enough
sections.text: A study of 1,297 students found that time abroad produced only small gains on an intercultural measure. Students who took classes mainly alongside local students barely changed. Students who worked with a cultural mentor gained more. Years of serving diverse communities do not guarantee skill. Reflection with guidance is what builds it.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: Pick one recurring interaction, such as calls with a county partner or a monthly community meeting. After it, spend ten minutes with a trusted colleague. Ask what you assumed, what the other person might have experienced, and what you would try next time. Do this regularly. Treat any assessment you have taken as a starting point for that conversation, never as a label for you or anyone else.

sections.title: What the models describe
sections.text: Two related models appear often in public-sector training. Bennett's Developmental Model of Intercultural Sensitivity describes six stages in how people make sense of cultural difference. They range from not noticing it, to defending against it, to minimizing it, to accepting it and adapting to it. The Intercultural Development Continuum, linked to the Intercultural Development Inventory, describes five related orientations. Both models make a useful point. People do not simply know or not know about other cultures. They differ in how they interpret difference, and that interpretation shapes what they do. A supervisor who minimizes difference may say “I treat everyone the same” and mean it sincerely. The same supervisor may still miss that a uniform process lands very differently on different people.

sections.title: What the evidence shows about the models
sections.text: The inventory's structure has been tested. A 2011 study of 4,763 people across 11 cultural samples supported the orientations the model describes. That shows the questions group together as the model predicts. It does not show that scores predict how well someone does their job. A 2013 review examined 10 tests of cross-cultural competence. It found three with the strongest evidence for reliability and validity, and the developmental inventory was not among them. Those reviewers have a commercial link to one of the top-rated tests, so read their ranking with that in mind. The honest summary is this. The models are useful maps for thinking. The evidence that any single score tells you how someone will act at work is thin.

sections.title: The self-assessment problem
sections.text: In the nursing school study, students rated themselves around 122 on average, while the assessment placed them around 95. Ninety-eight percent overestimated. The review of self-assessment research found the same pattern more broadly. People have only moderate insight into their abilities, and insight is worse for complex skills. The 2020 review of intercultural measures notes there is ample evidence that self-reports of ability do not necessarily match actual ability. For a leader, this means a confident self-description is weak evidence. That includes your own. Specific feedback from people who watched you work is stronger evidence.

sections.title: Why exposure and one-time training fall short
sections.text: The study-abroad research tracked 1,297 students. On average, students abroad gained about 2.4 points, while students at home did not change. Students in the most immersive classroom arrangement barely moved. Students who met with a cultural mentor gained more. A meta-analysis of 260 diversity training samples found a related pattern. Training changed knowledge, and that knowledge held. Changes in attitudes faded over time. Training worked better when it built skills as well as awareness, ran over a longer period and was paired with other efforts. The common thread is that people need repeated, guided chances to make sense of what they experience.

sections.title: Applying it in DHS work
sections.text: Start with decisions you control. Look at your unit's channels, deadlines, meeting formats and scripts. For each one, ask who it works well for and who has to do extra work to use it. Then build practice into real work. After a hard call with a partner, a community meeting or a contentious case review, hold a short debrief with a peer. Use the same three questions each time. What did I assume? What might the other person have experienced? What will I try next time? Rotate who leads the debrief so it is not one person's job to explain culture to everyone else. When someone mentions an assessment result, steer the conversation to a specific interaction they want to improve. Never use results to sort, assign or describe people.

sections.title: A DHS example
sections.text: Consider a unit that answers questions from county eligibility workers about a change in health care renewal rules. One county worker raises the same concern three times in a month. Each time, the state staff member answers politely and accurately, and the call ends on a friendly note. In a debrief, a peer who listened points out something. The county worker never said the guidance was wrong. Instead, they kept describing families who were confused by it. The state staff member had heard each call as a request for clarification. The county worker may have been trying to say, as politely as they could, that the guidance was not working for the people they serve. Neither reading is certain, and that uncertainty is the point. But the debrief produced a useful next step. On the next call, the staff member asks directly: “If you could change one thing about this guidance, what would it be?” The answer is specific, and it reaches the person or area responsible for the guidance with the county's example attached. Nothing in that sequence required a score or a label. It required a second set of eyes and a better question.

sections.title: Limits of the research
sections.text: Most of the evidence in this lesson comes from students, not public employees. The study-abroad research and the nursing school study used the same developmental inventory. The finding that 98% overestimated depends on that instrument's own scoring of the gap. The training meta-analysis covers diversity training broadly, not intercultural development programs alone. No study found here measured whether a DHS employee's intercultural skill changes outcomes for the people they serve. The human services meta-analysis is relevant in a different way. Across 30 studies and nearly half a million workers, a climate of inclusion was consistently linked to positive outcomes, while diversity alone had mixed effects. That points to leadership practice as the lever, not individual scores. Keep both ideas in view: culture clearly matters, and the tools that claim to measure skill with culture are imperfect.

sections.title: Why labels do harm
sections.text: Developmental models describe ways of making meaning, and people move between them depending on setting and stress. A score is a snapshot from one questionnaire on one day. Using it to describe a person turns a snapshot into a fixed trait. Picture saying “she is in Minimization” or using scores to decide who handles community calls. That treats weak evidence as strong and invites the very stereotyping the models warn against. It also pushes people to answer future assessments strategically, which makes the results even less useful. If your unit has assessment results, they belong to the individual. They can open a private development conversation if that person chooses. They do not belong in assignments, performance reviews or team discussions about who is “ahead.”

sections.title: Overconfidence cuts both ways
sections.text: The self-assessment research cautions everyone, including people who see themselves as skilled at working across cultures. Long experience can produce confidence that outruns skill, especially when feedback is rare. That is often true in DHS, where you may never learn how a notice or a call landed. Comfort is also not the same as accuracy. A person may feel at ease with a community because they rarely face disagreement there. The practical answer is the same for everyone. Seek specific feedback from people who saw the interaction. Where you can, compare what you meant with what the other person understood.

sections.title: Guidance matters more than immersion
sections.text: The most surprising result in the study-abroad research came from immersion. Students enrolled mainly alongside host-country students moved less than one point. Students with mentors gained more. One likely explanation is that contact without help to interpret it can confirm existing assumptions as easily as challenge them. That is a reasonable reading, not a tested mechanism. For DHS, a new supervisor in a diverse county-facing unit will not grow automatically. They need a peer or mentor who helps them review real interactions. That person should ask good questions and point out patterns the supervisor cannot see alone.

sections.title: Designing practice that lasts
sections.text: The training meta-analysis found three features linked to stronger effects. Training built skills, not only awareness. It ran over a meaningful period. It was paired with other efforts. Translate that into unit practice. Short, recurring debriefs tied to real work beat a single workshop. Changes to actual processes, such as a second contact channel or a plain-language notice review, give people something to practice on. Leader behavior counts too: you go first, you name your own misreadings and you ask for feedback in front of the team. That shows the debrief is about learning, not judgment.

sections.title: Harder situations
sections.text: A team member may say culture does not matter because consistent treatment is fair. Agree with part of that. Consistent standards protect people. Then ask what consistent treatment requires in a specific case, such as a renewal notice going to someone who reads English as a second language. Consistency in the standard can still allow a different route to meet it. Another hard situation is a team member who feels labeled by a past assessment. Acknowledge it, confirm that results will not be used to judge or assign anyone, and move to a skill they want to build. Work with Tribal Nations runs on government-to-government relationships under state law. Bring those matters to the person or area responsible for Tribal relations rather than treating them as an intercultural exercise.

sections.title: When leaders want a number
sections.text: Managers are under real pressure to show progress, and an assessment result can look like the obvious measure. Resist that. The instrument's structure holds together statistically, but no study found here shows the score predicts how well a public employee works with the people they serve. A team average also hides more than it shows, and it invites comparisons between people. Better evidence of progress sits in the work itself. Did a notice get rewritten after staff noticed how it was misread? Did partners raise concerns earlier, through the channels they already use? Did a meeting format change so more people could take part? Those changes are visible and specific, and they do not require anyone to disclose a personal result. They also match what the training research found. Effects last when learning is tied to real changes in how an organization works.

sections.title: Your own development
sections.text: Everything in this lesson applies to you first. Choose one interaction you lead regularly. Ask a colleague whose judgment you trust to observe it and tell you one thing you did not see. Accept the feedback without explaining it away, even when it surprises you. In the nursing school study, the gap between how people saw themselves and how the assessment saw them was large for nearly everyone. That does not mean people were careless. It means self-perception is a weak instrument for a complex skill. Leaders who ask for feedback openly make it easier for their teams to do the same.

sections.title: What to claim and what not to claim
sections.text: You can say with confidence that people overestimate their own intercultural skill. You can say that exposure alone builds little and that one-time attitude change fades. You cannot say that a particular score predicts job performance. You cannot say that any racial, cultural or disability group responds in a particular way, based on these studies. They did not test that. Speak about specific interactions and specific decisions. That keeps the conversation useful and keeps people from being sorted by a number.

simulation.setup: You supervise a unit of eight staff in a DHS eligibility policy area. Your team often fields calls from county eligibility workers and community organizations that serve recent immigrants. Last year the division ran an intercultural training, and each person received a private assessment profile. Your manager wants partner calls handled well and is under pressure after two complaints from a community organization. What is at stake is better partner relationships, and whether your team trusts that development efforts are for growth, not for sorting people.

steps.situation: Your manager suggests asking staff to share their assessment results so the highest scorers can take over community partner calls.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Decline to use the results for assignments, explain the limits of the scores, and propose choosing based on recent work plus a regular debrief for everyone.
choices.feedback: Your manager is skeptical but agrees to try. The evidence supports you. The inventory's structure has been tested, but no study found shows scores predict job performance. A review of 10 tests did not rank it among the strongest. Basing assignments on observed work, with guided practice, matches what research shows builds skill.

choices.label: Suggest using results as one factor among several, alongside experience.
choices.feedback: This feels balanced and keeps your manager satisfied. But a weak signal blended with stronger ones still pushes people to share private results and still sorts colleagues by a questionnaire. Staff learn quickly that their profile affects their work. That tends to make future assessments strategic rather than honest.

choices.label: Agree, since the data already exists and the complaints need a fast fix.
choices.feedback: This is tempting because the scores look objective and the pressure is real. But it treats a snapshot from one questionnaire as a measure of job skill, which the evidence does not support. It also turns a private development tool into a staffing tool. That is a decision many staff will see as a breach of trust.

steps.situation: Your manager asks what you will do instead to build the team's skill with partner calls within the next three months.
steps.question: What do you choose?

choices.label: Set up short, recurring debriefs after real partner calls, with rotating peer leads and the same three questions each time.
choices.feedback: Within weeks, staff start naming patterns, such as callers who will not say no directly to a state employee. The study-abroad research found that guided reflection with a mentor produced more growth than exposure alone. The training meta-analysis found that longer, skills-focused efforts lasted better than one-time sessions.

choices.label: Bring in a facilitator for a one-day refresher workshop.
choices.feedback: The workshop is well received, and staff say they learned a lot. Across 260 training samples, knowledge gains held, but attitude gains faded over time, and behavior changed less. Without follow-up tied to real calls, the energy fades by the next complaint. A workshop can start practice, but it cannot replace it.

choices.label: Send the team a reading list on cultural communication and ask them to review it.
choices.feedback: Reading builds knowledge, and some staff find it useful. But it puts the work on individuals and gives no one a chance to test ideas against real interactions. The research is clear that exposure to information, like exposure to a culture, builds little skill without guided practice.

steps.situation: A staff member comes to you privately. They heard their assessment profile was considered, and they were left off partner calls. They feel labeled.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Acknowledge the concern, stop using profiles for assignments, and explain that assignments will rest on observed work and practice.
choices.feedback: The staff member is relieved, and word spreads that the change is real. You corrected course before the practice hardened. Treating a single questionnaire result as a trait is what the developmental models themselves warn against. Moving to observed work and guided practice is better supported by the evidence.

choices.label: Explain that the profile was only one factor and encourage them to retake the assessment next year.
choices.feedback: This is honest about the process, but it confirms that a private score shapes their work. Encouraging a retake signals that the goal is a better number, not better practice. People who expect scores to matter often answer strategically, which makes the results less useful for everyone.

choices.label: Reassure them that the results are objective and suggest they focus on development.
choices.feedback: This sounds supportive but is not accurate. Self-report instruments carry real limits, and no study found links these scores to job performance. Calling the result objective deepens the label and closes the conversation. The staff member is now less likely to raise concerns with you at all.

steps.situation: In a team meeting, a respected senior staff member says: “Culture doesn't really matter in this job. The rules are the same for everyone. That's what fair means.” Several people nod.
steps.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Agree that consistent standards matter, then walk through one real case where the same notice worked very differently for two people.
choices.feedback: The example lands. One caller read the notice as a final denial, while another read it as routine. The team starts listing other examples. You kept the valid point and made culture concrete. Research on attitude change suggests that specific, practical cases build more lasting understanding than abstract arguments.

choices.label: Summarize the research on how culture affects communication.
choices.feedback: Your summary is accurate, and a few people take notes. But the senior colleague hears a lecture, not a response, and the room does not connect it to their work. Knowledge from research holds, but it rarely changes a strongly held belief unless it connects to an experience people recognize.

choices.label: Let it pass to avoid a debate with a respected colleague.
choices.feedback: This keeps the meeting calm and avoids embarrassing a senior person. But silence from the supervisor reads as agreement, and staff who see the problem learn not to raise it. The belief that identical treatment is always fair goes unexamined, along with the processes built on it.

steps.situation: After a tense call with a county eligibility worker, you feel you handled it well. A peer listened in on the call.
steps.question: What do you do next?

choices.label: Ask the peer what they noticed, what the county worker might have experienced and one thing to try differently.
choices.feedback: The peer points out that you interrupted twice when the worker paused, and the worker went quiet afterward. You had not noticed. Self-assessment research shows only moderate insight into complex skills. Specific feedback from someone who watched you closes the gap your own sense of the call cannot.

choices.label: Take a few minutes to reflect on the call on your own.
choices.feedback: Reflection is useful, and you notice one moment you would change. But you are reviewing the call through the same lens you used during it. The nursing school study found 98% overestimated their skill. A peer who was there is your best check, and you did not use it.

choices.label: Move on. The call ended politely, so it went fine.
choices.feedback: Polite endings are common even when something went wrong, especially when a partner does not feel free to object to the state. This is exactly where self-assessment is weakest. A missed pattern now is likely to repeat on the next call.

simulation.debrief: Each choice tested whether you treated culture as a matter of practice or as a number. Using assessment results to assign work felt efficient, but the evidence does not support scores as measures of job skill. Even the strongest-rated tests rely on self-report, which often does not match ability. Exposure did not build skill on its own. In the study-abroad research, the most immersive students barely changed, while mentored students gained more. One-time training raised knowledge, but attitude changes faded. Recurring debriefs on real calls and concrete cases in team meetings follow what the research favors. So does asking a peer for feedback. If you let the senior colleague's comment pass, the path ended there, because the team lost a chance to examine its own habits.

mistakes.mistake: Using assessment results to assign work or describe colleagues.
mistakes.why: Scores look objective and save time. But the evidence supports the instrument's structure, not its ability to predict job behavior, and a score is one questionnaire on one day.
mistakes.instead: Base assignments on observed work. Treat results as private starting points for development that the person can choose to discuss.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming long experience with diverse communities equals skill.
mistakes.why: Experience feels like evidence, and many skilled people have it. But the most immersive students in the study-abroad research barely changed without guidance.
mistakes.instead: Pair experience with regular guided debriefs on real interactions.

mistakes.mistake: Relying on a single workshop to change how a team works.
mistakes.why: Workshops are visible, well received and easy to schedule. But across 260 samples, attitude changes faded while knowledge held, and behavior changed less.
mistakes.instead: Use recurring, skills-focused practice tied to real work, paired with changes to actual processes.

mistakes.mistake: Trusting your own sense that an interaction went well.
mistakes.why: Confidence feels like information. But people have only moderate insight into complex skills, and in one study 98% overestimated their intercultural skill.
mistakes.instead: Ask someone who observed the interaction for specific feedback.

mistakes.mistake: Arguing against “same rules for everyone” in the abstract.
mistakes.why: Leaders want to correct a misunderstanding quickly. But abstract arguments rarely shift strongly held beliefs.
mistakes.instead: Agree that consistent standards matter, then examine one real case where the same process landed differently.

jobAid.title: Ten-minute interaction debrief
jobAid.use: Use it after a hard call, a community or partner meeting, or a contentious case discussion, with one peer.
steps: Name the interaction and what you were trying to accomplish.
What did you assume about the other person's goals, constraints or way of communicating?
What might the other person have experienced, including what they could not easily say to a state employee?
Peer: what did you notice that the speaker may have missed? Be specific.
Which part of the process, such as channel, timing, wording or format, made this harder?
What one thing will you try next time?
Leave scores and labels out. Talk only about this interaction.

media.reason: This lesson corrects common assumptions about experience, self-assessment and training. A single calm narrator can lay out the evidence in order and model the reflective questions.

prompts: Which recurring interaction in your work will you debrief, and which colleague will you ask to do it with you?
Which routine decision in your unit, such as a channel, deadline, format or script, will you review for who it works for, and by when?

title: Who DHS serves, and who is on your team
objective: Use Minnesota data to describe who your work reaches, and respond well to a team member's need tied to a name, holiday or faith practice.
outcomes: Cite at least three current facts about Minnesota's population from official sources and explain what they mean for your unit's work.
Explain why Tribal matters go through government-to-government channels and the person or area responsible for Tribal relations.
Respond to a schedule request tied to a faith practice by starting with the work need, not the reason for the belief.
Plan coverage early and keep the reason for an absence between the people who need to know.
Answer a colleague who says knowing the people DHS serves does not matter to their job.

evidence.summary: Minnesota grew more diverse between 2010 and 2020 in cities of every size, including the smallest. About 13% of residents speak a language other than English at home. State law recognizes 11 Tribal governments, each with a government-to-government relationship with state agencies. More than one in four U.S. adults has a disability. On teams, a human services meta-analysis of nearly 500,000 workers found that diversity alone had mixed effects. A climate of inclusion, by contrast, was consistently linked to positive outcomes. Field experiments show religious identity can reduce employer responses, and the drop for Muslim applicants was larger than the average for religious identifiers overall. Limits: the bias studies looked at hiring outside Minnesota, and there is little rigorous research on belonging or religious accommodation inside public agencies.

findings.claim: The White share of Minnesota city residents fell from 80.5% to 73.2% between 2010 and 2020. In cities of fewer than 250 people, it fell from 94.1% to 89.1%.
findings.detail: Minnesota State Demographic Center population brief, Census 2010 and 2020, published April 2024. Black city residents grew 46.2%, Two or More Races 122.6%, Hispanic 38.2%, Asian 40.5%.

findings.claim: About 13.1% of Minnesotans age 5 and over speak a language other than English at home, and 9% were born outside the United States.
findings.detail: American Community Survey 2024 one-year estimates for Minnesota, population 5,793,151.

findings.claim: Minnesota law names 11 Tribal governments and requires agencies to consult each one, designate a Tribal liaison and train staff whose work has Tribal implications.
findings.detail: Minnesota Statutes section 10.65. Coordination with groups such as the Minnesota Indian Affairs Council does not replace consulting each Tribal government.

findings.claim: More than one in four U.S. adults has a disability; the most common types involve cognition (13.9%) and mobility (12.2%).
findings.detail: CDC Disability and Health Data System summary, page updated July 2024. National figures, not Minnesota-specific.
findings.source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2024

findings.claim: Diversity alone was linked to both good and bad outcomes, but a climate of inclusion was consistently linked to positive outcomes (rho = .42).
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 30 studies covering 496,740 workers, published 2016 in a human service management journal. 95% CI .29 to .54.

findings.claim: Résumés listing a religious affiliation drew fewer employer responses; Muslim applicants drew 32% fewer emails and 48% fewer calls in New England.
findings.detail: Randomized résumé audit studies, 6,400 applications in New England and 3,200 in the South, 2014. In the South, Muslim applicants drew 38% fewer emails and 54% fewer calls than controls. Any religious identifier: 19% fewer contacts in New England; 29% fewer emails and 33% fewer calls in the South.

findings.claim: Women applying in a hijab faced more formal and interpersonal discrimination, with smaller effects where employee diversity was high.
findings.detail: Field experiment, 112 trials at retail stores and restaurants in two Midwestern malls, 2013. Exact rates not visible in the summary opened.
findings.source: Ghumman & Ryan, 2013 (University of Hawaii news release)

findings.claim: An employer may deny a religious accommodation only when the burden is substantial in the overall context of its business.
findings.detail: EEOC Compliance Manual on religious discrimination, with notice applying Groff v. DeJoy (2023). Common accommodations include schedule changes, voluntary shift swaps and dress exceptions.

counterintuitive.headline: A more diverse team did not reliably mean better results. A more inclusive one did.
counterintuitive.text: Many leaders assume that hiring a more diverse team will improve results on its own. Mor Barak and colleagues (2016) pooled 30 studies covering nearly half a million workers, many in human services. Diversity by itself was linked to both beneficial and harmful outcomes. Perceptions that the organization was building a climate of inclusion were consistently linked to positive outcomes, with a correlation of .42. The authors' conclusion is direct. Human service organizations should move beyond counting who is on the team. They should build the practices that let everyone take part. Representation matters. How the team works together decides what it produces.

sections.title: Two questions every leader can answer
sections.text: Who does your work reach? Who is on your team, and what do they need to do their best work? Both questions matter in DHS, even in units that never speak with the public. Contract language reaches providers. Policy wording reaches county workers, and through them it reaches people and families. A scheduling decision reaches every person on your team. Leaders who can answer both questions with accurate facts make better choices than leaders working from impressions. Impressions of Minnesota are often a decade or more out of date.

sections.title: Minnesota is changing everywhere
sections.text: Between 2010 and 2020, the White share of Minnesota city residents fell from about 81% to 73%. Every other group grew. The change was not only in the Twin Cities. In cities of 5,000 to 9,999 people, the White share fell from about 90% to 85%. In cities of fewer than 250 people, it fell from 94% to 89%. About 13% of Minnesotans speak a language other than English at home. Minnesota law recognizes 11 Tribal governments, each with its own relationship with state agencies. More than one in four U.S. adults has a disability. The most common types involve cognition and mobility.

sections.title: Headcount is not the same as inclusion
sections.text: A meta-analysis of nearly half a million workers found that diversity alone had mixed effects. A climate of inclusion was consistently linked to better outcomes. What your team does together matters more than who is listed on the roster.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: When a team member raises a need tied to a name, a holiday or a faith practice, start with the work. Ask what adjustment they are looking for and how they would like to discuss it. Then plan the coverage. Do not ask them to explain or justify the belief. When a formal accommodation may be involved, use your human resources contact and current procedures. Keep the reason between the two of you and the people who need to know.

sections.title: What the Minnesota data show
sections.text: The Minnesota State Demographic Center compared Census 2010 and 2020 for every city in the state. About 4.7 million Minnesotans, or 83% of the state, live in a city. Between 2010 and 2020, the number of White city residents fell slightly, by about half a percent. Black residents grew by 46%, Hispanic residents by 38% and Asian residents by 40%. People identifying with two or more races more than doubled. The shift reached every size of city. American Community Survey estimates for 2024 add more detail. About 9% of Minnesotans were born outside the United States, and 13.1% of people age 5 and over speak a language other than English at home. Nationally, the CDC reports that more than one in four adults has a disability. Cognitive disabilities, at 13.9%, and mobility disabilities, at 12.2%, are the most common. Those figures are national, not Minnesota-specific, but they are a reasonable reminder of scale.

sections.title: Tribal Nations are governments
sections.text: Minnesota Statutes section 10.65 names 11 Tribal governments. It requires each state agency to recognize the government-to-government relationship, consult with each Tribal government at least once a year and designate a Tribal liaison. Staff whose work is likely to involve Tribal matters must take Tribal-state relations training. The statute also says that coordinating with a group such as the Minnesota Indian Affairs Council does not replace consulting each government. For a unit leader, the practical rule is simple. A Tribal government is not a stakeholder group or a community audience. When your work touches Tribal matters, bring it to the person or area responsible for Tribal relations.

sections.title: What your service data can and cannot tell you
sections.text: Statewide numbers describe residents. Your unit's data describe the people a system has on file. Those are different. A low count of finished applications in one county could reflect population size, eligibility, distance or barriers that stop people before an application begins. Before acting on a number, ask which step in the process produced it. Use population data to ask better questions, not to predict what any individual needs.

sections.title: Who is on your team
sections.text: A 2016 meta-analysis in a human services journal pooled 30 studies of 496,740 workers. Diversity on its own was linked to both helpful and harmful outcomes. A climate of inclusion was consistently linked to positive outcomes. That includes fair treatment, a voice in decisions and access to information. The authors urged human service organizations to move beyond representation and build practices that engender inclusion. For a supervisor, everyday choices are where inclusion shows up. Those choices include how holidays and schedules are handled, how names are used and who gets invited to informal conversations.

sections.title: Religion at work
sections.text: Religious bias is measurable. In randomized résumé studies, applications that listed a campus religious group drew fewer employer responses than identical ones without. The drop for Muslim applicants was larger than the average for all religious identifiers. In New England they got 32% fewer emails and 48% fewer calls. In the South they got 38% fewer emails and 54% fewer calls. A field experiment in two Midwestern malls found that women applying for jobs in a hijab faced more formal and interpersonal discrimination. The effects were smaller in workplaces where employees were more diverse. These studies were about hiring, not about life inside public agencies. They still show that religious identity can change how people are treated, and that the surrounding workplace makes a difference.

sections.title: The accommodation standard
sections.text: Federal law requires employers to accommodate religious practice unless doing so would cause undue hardship. Since the Supreme Court's 2023 decision in Groff v. DeJoy, that means a burden that is substantial in the overall context of the employer's business. A small inconvenience is not enough. Common accommodations include schedule changes, shift swaps with willing coworkers, dress and grooming exceptions and time or space for prayer. As a supervisor, start with the practical question. Use the established process and your human resources contact for anything that may be a formal accommodation. Do not decide alone whether a belief is important enough.

sections.title: Applying it in DHS work
sections.text: Put the two questions to work in the same week. For the people your unit serves, pick one document you send often, such as a provider notice, a county instruction or a renewal letter. Read it as someone who reads English as a second language would. Read it again as someone with a cognitive disability would. Check whether it offers more than one way to respond and an easy way to ask for an interpreter or another format. For your team, look at the next two months of the calendar. Find the deadlines, the team events and the holidays that might collide. Ask in your next one-on-ones whether anyone has dates you should plan around, and give people room to say no or to share only what they choose. Neither step requires collecting personal information. Both require asking good questions early, before a deadline makes every request feel like a problem.

sections.title: Limits of the data
sections.text: The city figures come from the census and cover only people living in incorporated cities, about 83% of the state. Townships and rural areas outside city limits are not in those tables. The language and foreign-born figures are survey estimates with margins of error. The disability figures are national. Your unit's service population may look very different from the state as a whole. For example, people who use disability services are, by definition, not a sample of the general public. Treat statewide data as context. Then look at the data for the program you actually run, through the person or area responsible for that data.

sections.title: Numbers describe groups, not people
sections.text: Knowing that a share of residents speaks a language other than English at home does not tell you what any particular caller needs. Some people who speak another language at home read English well. Some English speakers struggle with complex written notices, including people with cognitive disabilities. The practical answer is to design for range. Write in plain language, offer more than one channel and make it easy to ask for an interpreter or another format. Ask each person what works rather than guessing from a name, an accent or a neighborhood.

sections.title: Tribal relations in practice
sections.text: Several kinds of relationships can look similar from inside a unit. A community provider that serves Native families, an individual Tribal citizen who calls for help and a Tribal government are not the same. Each brings different knowledge and different standing. Formal consultation has its own scope and channels, set out in state law and in agency consultation policy. A public listening session or a stakeholder survey cannot stand in for it. Do not ask a Native colleague to speak for Tribal Nations or Native communities. Route the matter to the person or area responsible for Tribal relations, who carries that relationship for the agency.

sections.title: Faith practices on your team: harder situations
sections.text: Several situations need care. Two team members may ask for the same date off during a deadline week. Handle the conflict as a scheduling problem with the same rules you would use for any competing requests. Then look for swaps, adjusted hours or a staggered plan before saying no. A coworker may complain about special treatment. Keep the reason for the absence confidential. Explain that schedule adjustments are available to everyone for many reasons, and keep the conversation on coverage. A request may involve prayer during work hours or a change to dress. Start with what the person needs and work through current procedures with your human resources contact. Team events also matter. Celebrations built around food during a fasting period, or always held on the same day of the week, can quietly exclude people. Vary the timing and format, and make it clear that people can take part in team life in more than one way.

sections.title: Names and introductions
sections.text: Ask how a colleague wants their name said or shown in the setting you share, and give them a way to answer one-on-one. People may use different forms of their name at work, in community settings and in official systems. When you mispronounce a name, acknowledge it briefly, use the correct form and move on. Correcting someone in public repeatedly puts the cost of teaching on the person whose name was missed. No rigorous study of name pronunciation at work turned up in this research, so this guidance rests on ordinary respect rather than measured effects.

sections.title: Belonging without guesswork
sections.text: It is tempting to assume what a particular colleague needs to feel they belong, based on their background. The evidence does not support that. The inclusion meta-analysis measured climate across teams and organizations, not the needs of any one person or group. The practical tools are the same for everyone. Give clear information, a real voice in decisions, fair access to assignments and development, and a supervisor who asks rather than assumes. When you do not know what someone needs, ask in a one-on-one setting and accept the answer, including “nothing special.”

sections.title: What the research does not show
sections.text: The religious bias studies measured hiring callbacks, mostly outside Minnesota, in the private sector. They do not tell you how often religious bias occurs inside DHS. They do not tell you how any colleague experiences your team. The hijab study's finding that effects were smaller in more diverse workplaces comes from one field experiment with 112 trials. There is little rigorous research on religious accommodation and belonging inside public agencies. That gap is a reason to rely on clear procedures, confidentiality and direct conversation, not on assumptions in either direction.

sections.title: When the change is close to home
sections.text: The state data show that small cities changed too. A supervisor who grew up in a small Minnesota town may picture it as it was twenty years ago. The data say that picture may no longer fit. This matters for policy and contract work that assumes rural areas look one way and metro areas another. A rural county may now have more families who speak a language other than English at home. It may also have more residents born outside the United States than a planner expects. Before you design outreach, training or a notice for a region, check the current figures. Then ask the people closest to that region. County partners and community providers can tell you what the numbers cannot.

sections.title: When a colleague says it does not matter
sections.text: Some colleagues believe that treating everyone the same means they do not need to know who is served. Agree with what is right in that view. Standards should be consistent, and no one should get worse service because of who they are. Then make it concrete. A notice written at a high reading level is the same for everyone, and it still fails many readers. A single phone line open only during business hours is the same for everyone, and it still shuts out people working those hours. Knowing who your work reaches is how you keep a consistent standard from producing uneven results. That is the subject of the next lesson in this series.

sections.title: Bringing the two questions together
sections.text: The people DHS serves and the people on your team are linked. Picture a team where people can raise a concern about a name, a holiday or a notice without risk. That team is more likely to notice when a process shuts someone out. In the inclusion meta-analysis, outcomes followed climate, not headcount. Leaders build that climate through small, repeated choices: a schedule handled with care, a name said correctly and a question asked before an assumption is made.

simulation.setup: You supervise a contracts and administrative support team of nine in the Disability Services Division. A provider grant reporting deadline falls in four weeks. One team member emails asking to adjust their schedule for a multi-day religious observance. The final day overlaps the deadline week. Two other team members already have leave planned that week. What is at stake is the deadline, and whether people on your team trust that they can raise needs like this without being judged or exposed.

steps.situation: The request arrives by email. It is short and does not say what the team member needs exactly. Your manager has stressed that the deadline cannot slip.
steps.question: What do you do first?

choices.label: Meet one-on-one, ask what adjustment they are looking for and how they would like to handle it, then start a coverage plan.
choices.feedback: The team member needs adjusted hours for most days and one full day off. You now have four weeks to plan. Starting with the work need, not the belief, keeps the conversation practical. If it turns into a formal accommodation, the federal standard requires a substantial burden to deny it. Early planning makes that unlikely.

choices.label: Reply “Approved, no problem” and plan to sort out coverage closer to the date.
choices.feedback: The team member feels supported, which matters. But you approved without knowing what was needed, and no coverage plan exists. Goodwill without planning often turns into resentment later, when the gap appears and someone else absorbs it. That outcome can undo the trust the quick yes created.

choices.label: Ask whether the observance could be adjusted this year, given the deadline.
choices.feedback: This feels reasonable under deadline pressure. But it asks the person to justify or bend a religious practice before you have looked at coverage. Under the federal standard, a deadline alone rarely makes an accommodation a substantial burden. Field research shows religious identity can change how people are treated at work. This response tells the team member that risk is real here.

steps.situation: Two colleagues offer to swap shifts. A third says, loudly enough for others to hear, that some people always get special treatment.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Talk with the third colleague one-on-one about coverage, note that schedule adjustments are available to everyone for many reasons, and keep the reason confidential.
choices.feedback: The colleague grumbles but drops it, and later asks about adjusting their own hours for a family obligation. You kept the focus on fair rules and coverage without exposing anyone's reasons. A climate of fair treatment is what the inclusion meta-analysis found consistently linked to positive outcomes.

choices.label: Explain at the next team meeting that the absence is for a religious observance, so people understand.
choices.feedback: Your intent is to build understanding. But you disclosed a personal reason without asking. Now the team member's faith is a topic for group discussion. Some people will be supportive, and some will not. The disclosure should have been the team member's choice, not yours.

choices.label: Tell the third colleague to drop it and get back to work.
choices.feedback: This stops the comment in the moment, and that is tempting when you are busy. But it gives the colleague no explanation of how scheduling works, so the resentment stays. It may surface again, possibly aimed at the team member. A short private conversation about the rules would have taken the same five minutes.

steps.situation: Deadline week arrives. With three people out or on reduced hours, the reporting work has fallen on one analyst, who comes to you frustrated.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Acknowledge that coverage was not planned well, redistribute the work today and set a coverage process for future requests.
choices.feedback: The analyst is still tired but feels heard, and the work gets redistributed. Owning the planning gap keeps the frustration from landing on the team member who asked for time. Clear, fair scheduling rules protect everyone, and they make it easier for the next person to raise a need early.

choices.label: Take on the extra work yourself for the week.
choices.feedback: The deadline is met, and the analyst is relieved. But you fixed this week without fixing the process, so the same gap will open next time. Leaders absorbing work quietly can also signal that requests for time off are a burden someone has to pay for.

choices.label: Ask the team member with the observance to come in for the final day after all.
choices.feedback: This feels like the fastest fix, and the deadline pressure is real. But it puts the cost of a planning lapse on the person with the religious practice. Under the federal standard, a substantial burden is needed to deny an accommodation, and redistributing work is rarely that. The team member and everyone watching learn that raising a need was risky.

steps.situation: After the deadline, a team member proposes a celebration lunch during the same observance period, when the colleague will be fasting. They say everyone should come, since it is team building.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Suggest a celebration at a time and in a format more people can join, and make clear people can take part in team life in more than one way.
choices.feedback: The team picks a morning gathering the following week, and the colleague who was fasting joins. You did not single anyone out or explain anyone's practice. Varying timing and format is a low-cost way to build the inclusive climate the research links to better outcomes.

choices.label: Quietly move the lunch to another week without saying why.
choices.feedback: The immediate conflict goes away. But the team learns nothing about how to plan events that work for everyone, and the same issue will come up next time. Some people may also guess the reason and connect it to one colleague, which is the exposure you wanted to avoid.

choices.label: Keep the lunch as planned. It is a team commitment, and anyone can just skip the food.
choices.feedback: This is tempting because the plan is already made. But calling it a commitment while scheduling it when one person cannot fully take part tells that person the team was not planned with them in mind. Inclusion shows up in small, repeated choices like this one.

steps.situation: At a planning meeting, a colleague asks: “Why does this team need to know who DSD serves? It just processes contracts.”
steps.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Connect it to the work: contract and notice language reaches providers and people with disabilities, many of whom read in another language or have cognitive disabilities.
choices.feedback: The colleague pauses and asks whether the provider notice template has been reviewed for plain language. You used specific facts. About 13% of Minnesotans speak another language at home, and cognitive disability is the most common type nationally. Those facts make the link to the team's own work concrete. That is more persuasive than a general appeal.

choices.label: Offer to share a slide deck of Minnesota demographic data at the next meeting.
choices.feedback: The data are accurate and useful. But without a link to the team's own documents and decisions, the numbers may feel like someone else's concern. Statewide figures work best as a prompt for a specific question about your own work.

choices.label: Agree that the team's job is mainly processing and move on.
choices.feedback: This avoids a detour in a busy meeting. But it suggests that people who never see the public need not think about them. Contract and notice wording still reaches every provider and family downstream. A chance to improve a template is missed.

simulation.debrief: Each decision tested whether you started with the work and kept people's reasons in their own hands. Asking what adjustment was needed, and planning early, turned a religious observance into a scheduling task. Under the federal standard, that task rarely rises to a substantial burden. Handling the special-treatment comment one-on-one, and keeping the reason confidential, protected the fair climate that the human services meta-analysis linked to better outcomes. If coverage slipped, owning the gap kept the cost off the person who asked. The celebration and the contracts question showed the same idea from two directions. Inclusion inside the team and awareness of who DHS serves both come down to specific, repeated choices, guided by accurate facts rather than assumptions.

mistakes.mistake: Asking a team member to justify or adjust a religious practice before looking at coverage.
mistakes.why: Deadline pressure is real, and asking feels like a fair question. But it puts the belief on trial. Under the federal standard, denial requires a substantial burden, which a deadline alone rarely creates.
mistakes.instead: Ask what adjustment the person needs, plan coverage and use your human resources contact for formal accommodations.

mistakes.mistake: Explaining someone's absence to the team so people understand.
mistakes.why: It comes from wanting to build understanding. But it discloses a personal reason the person may not want shared.
mistakes.instead: Keep the reason confidential and talk with the team about coverage and fair scheduling rules.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming a more diverse team will produce better results on its own.
mistakes.why: Representation is visible and easy to report. But across 30 studies, diversity alone had mixed effects, while inclusion climate was consistently positive.
mistakes.instead: Put effort into fair treatment, voice in decisions and access to information for everyone.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a Tribal government like a stakeholder group or community audience.
mistakes.why: Outreach habits carry over, and a listening session feels inclusive. But state law sets a government-to-government relationship, and consultation has its own channels.
mistakes.instead: Route Tribal matters to the person or area responsible for Tribal relations.

mistakes.mistake: Guessing what a caller or colleague needs from a name, accent or neighborhood.
mistakes.why: Population data make patterns feel predictive. But group figures describe groups, not individuals.
mistakes.instead: Design for range with plain language and several channels, and ask each person what works.

jobAid.title: Responding to a schedule, name or faith-related request
jobAid.use: Use it when a team member raises a need tied to a holiday, faith practice or name, or when you plan team events.
steps: Ask what adjustment the person is looking for and how they would like to discuss it.
Do not ask them to explain or prove the importance of a belief.
Separate the work need (dates, coverage, handoffs) from the personal reason.
If it may be a formal accommodation, contact your human resources partner and follow current procedures.
Build a coverage plan early, looking at swaps, adjusted hours and staggered schedules.
Keep the reason between the person and those who need to know.
Check team events: do timing and format work for the people on your team?
For names, ask one-on-one how the person wants their name said and shown in this setting.
