title: When the same rule is not fair
objective: Find who falls out of an identical process, separate what the rule requires from habit, and test a fairer route to the same standard.
outcomes: Explain administrative burden and its three costs: learning, compliance and psychological costs.
Ask the person or area responsible for a procedure which parts are required and which are habit.
Map the gap between when a notice is sent and when a person can actually act on it.
Design a second route to the same standard and check whether it shifts burden to staff or creates a privacy risk.
Judge a change using counts the system already produces, such as procedural closures, rather than effort counts.

evidence.summary: Administrative burden is the learning, compliance and psychological cost people face when dealing with government. Strong research shows that small, neutral-looking procedures change who gets benefits. When Social Security field offices closed, disability recipients nearby fell 13%. The losses were largest among people with less education and lower earnings. In San Francisco's SNAP program, households assigned a later interview date were over 20% less likely to recertify. In an IRS field experiment with 35,050 people, simpler notices raised benefit claims. Nationally, 69% of people who lost Medicaid during the 2023-2024 renewals lost it for procedural reasons. The limits matter too. Most studies come from federal programs or other states. They do not establish effects by race, and fixing one barrier can move burden somewhere else.

findings.claim: After Social Security field offices closed, the number of disability recipients in surrounding areas fell 13%, with the largest losses among people with lower education and earnings.
findings.detail: Natural experiment using Social Security Administration records on field office closings, NBER working paper 2017, published 2019. Most of the drop came from congestion at neighboring offices, not travel distance.

findings.claim: SNAP households assigned a later recertification interview date were over 20% less likely to recertify, losing an average of $600 in benefits over the next year.
findings.detail: Interview dates assigned as if at random within the month, San Francisco CalFresh, published 2021. About one quarter of those who lost benefits stayed off SNAP for more than a year.

findings.claim: Simpler notices and showing the benefit's value increased tax credit claims, while messages about stigma or audit fear did not.
findings.detail: Randomized field experiment with 35,050 tax filers who had not claimed about $26 million in Earned Income Tax Credit, published 2015. A federal review reports complex materials lowered take-up by about 6 percentage points.

findings.claim: About 18,000 Arkansas adults lost Medicaid under a work requirement. More than 95% of those subject to it already met it or should have been exempt, and employment did not rise.
findings.detail: Telephone survey of low-income adults ages 19-64 in Arkansas and three comparison states, difference-in-differences design, late 2018, published 2019. One third had not heard of the requirement.
findings.source: Sommers et al., 2019 (Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health summary)

findings.claim: Of at least 25.2 million people disenrolled from Medicaid during the 2023-2024 renewals, 69% lost coverage for procedural or paperwork reasons.
findings.detail: KFF compilation of state-reported data, archived September 2024. Many disenrolled for procedural reasons may still have been eligible. No Minnesota figure on the page.

findings.claim: Administrative burdens fall hardest on people with fewer cognitive resources, and the same hardships that create need also reduce the capacity to navigate burdens.
findings.detail: Conceptual review, 2020, drawing on research about scarcity, health and aging. The authors call this a human capital catch-22 and note it has not been tested directly.

counterintuitive.headline: Making it harder to apply did not screen out the least deserving.
counterintuitive.text: A common assumption is that hassle filters out people with weaker claims, because people who truly need help will push through. Deshpande and Li (2019) tested this using Social Security field office closings. Applications fell, and the number of disability recipients in surrounding areas fell 13%. The losses were concentrated among people with moderately severe conditions, lower education and lower earnings. The authors concluded that added application costs made the program less well targeted, not more. For DHS leaders, a procedure that feels like a reasonable screen may be screening out the very people a program is meant to reach.

sections.title: The same rule can produce different results
sections.text: Picture a renewal process in which staff make three morning callbacks. After three missed calls, a case goes to review. The rule is the same for everyone. For a person who works overnight, all three calls arrive while they are asleep. For a person whose phone minutes run out at the end of the month, the calls go nowhere. The rule treats everyone identically. It does not give everyone the same chance to meet it. Nobody designed it to exclude anyone. It simply grew around the hours the team was staffed, and over time the habit came to feel like a rule.

sections.title: What the research shows
sections.text: Researchers call this administrative burden: the learning, compliance and psychological cost of dealing with government. Small details matter more than most people expect. When Social Security field offices closed, the number of people receiving disability benefits nearby fell 13%. The losses were largest among people with less education and lower earnings. In a SNAP program, households given a later interview date were over 20% less likely to keep their benefits, because they had less time to reschedule. During the 2023-2024 Medicaid renewals, 69% of people who lost coverage nationally lost it for procedural reasons, not because they were found ineligible.

sections.title: Why it falls unevenly
sections.text: Burden is heaviest for people with the least time, money, health and mental bandwidth to spare. Those are often the people a program exists to serve. Researchers describe this as a catch-22. Hardship creates the need for help while making it harder to get through the process.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: Before defending or changing a procedure, ask the person or area responsible for it one question. Which parts are required, and which are habit? A statute may require a documented attempt to reach someone. It rarely requires a morning phone call. Keep the required standard the same for everyone. Then look for a second route to meet it.

sections.title: Three kinds of cost
sections.text: Administrative burden has three parts. Learning costs are the effort of finding out a program exists, whether you qualify and what to do. Compliance costs are the forms, documents, appointments, phone calls and travel. Psychological costs are the stress, stigma and loss of control people feel along the way. A procedure can be neutral on paper and still carry very different costs for different people. A morning callback costs little for someone home during the day. It costs a lot for someone working nights, sharing a phone or caring for a family member with a disability.

sections.title: Evidence from real programs
sections.text: Some of the strongest evidence comes from natural experiments, where a procedure changed for some people and not others. When the Social Security Administration closed field offices, Deshpande and Li compared nearby areas with others. The number of disability recipients fell 13%. The drop was largest among people with moderately severe conditions, lower education and lower earnings. Most of the effect came from crowding at the offices that stayed open, not from travel distance. In San Francisco's SNAP program, interview dates were assigned in a way that worked like a lottery. Households given dates late in the month were over 20% less likely to recertify. They lost an average of $600 in benefits over the next year, and about a quarter stayed off for more than a year. The only difference was how much time they had to reschedule a missed interview.

sections.title: Notices matter
sections.text: Bhargava and Manoli ran a randomized field experiment with the IRS. They mailed 35,050 people who had not claimed the Earned Income Tax Credit despite an earlier notice. Simpler notices, and notices that showed how much the credit was worth, produced substantially more claims. Messages meant to reduce stigma or fear of an audit did not help. The lesson for DHS is practical. Clear wording and a visible reason to act did more than reassurance.

sections.title: When people who qualify lose out
sections.text: Arkansas added a Medicaid work requirement in 2018. About 18,000 adults lost coverage that year. Researchers surveyed low-income adults in Arkansas and three comparison states. More than 95% of the people subject to the policy already met the requirement or should have been exempt. One third had not heard of it. Employment did not rise. Nationally, during the 2023-2024 Medicaid renewals, at least 25.2 million people were disenrolled, and 69% lost coverage for procedural reasons. Many of them may still have been eligible. In both cases, the process, not eligibility, decided many outcomes.

sections.title: The mechanism
sections.text: Christensen and colleagues explain why burden falls unevenly. Navigating a process draws on planning, memory and attention. Scarcity, health problems and age-related decline all strain those resources. The same conditions also make someone more likely to need public help. That creates what the authors call a human capital catch-22. The authors note the link has not been tested directly, but it fits the pattern in the field studies. Losses were concentrated among people with fewer resources.

sections.title: Psychological costs are real costs
sections.text: The third kind of cost is easy to overlook because it does not show up on a form. People who have had bad experiences with government may avoid a call from an unknown number. Some may read a notice as a threat, or delay opening a letter they expect to be bad news. In the Arkansas study, one third of the people subject to the new requirement had not heard of it. Learning costs and psychological costs often travel together. A person who does not understand what is being asked, and who fears the answer, is less likely to act in time. The IRS experiment points to a practical response. Clear wording and a visible reason to act raised claims. Reassurance alone did not. For DHS teams, that means notices should state plainly what is needed, by when, how to get help and what the person stands to keep.

sections.title: Applying it in DHS work
sections.text: Start with the gap between two clocks. Your team's clock starts when a notice leaves the system. The person's clock starts when they receive it in a form they can use, understand what is needed and can get help. Write down when each event happens. Then ask the person or area responsible for the procedure what is fixed by statute or rule and what is local practice. A supervisor who cannot change a filing date may still be able to change when a reminder goes out. They may also be able to change how it is worded and which channels are offered. Keep the standard identical: the same documents, the same proof, the same deadline in law. Change the route people can take to meet it.

sections.title: Limits of the evidence
sections.text: The strongest studies here come from federal programs, a California county and other states. None is from Minnesota DHS. The field office and SNAP studies use natural experiments, which are strong for showing cause. The Arkansas study compares states over time, which is reasonably strong, but its exact figures come from a summary rather than the full paper. The national Medicaid figures are compiled from state reports, and states counted procedural closures in different ways. The cognitive-resources explanation is a well-supported idea, not a tested result. None of these findings shows effects by race or ethnicity, so this lesson does not claim them. What the evidence does show clearly is this. Procedures change outcomes, and losses concentrate among people with fewer resources.

sections.title: Fixing one barrier can create another
sections.text: A second route is not automatically fair. A text-message reminder may help people who miss calls. It may also land on a shared phone and reveal private health or benefit information to someone else. An afternoon callback window may help people who work nights. It may also move all the hardest calls to one staff member's shift. An online upload may help some people and leave out people without reliable internet or with a device that does not work with the form. Before adopting a change, ask three questions. Who does it help? Whose work does it shift? What could it expose? Bring privacy questions to the person or area responsible for data privacy before testing.

sections.title: When the rule really is fixed
sections.text: Some requirements are set in federal law or state statute. You cannot change them at the unit level, and you should not pretend otherwise. You can still work on the route. Look at when the clock starts and what information arrives with the notice. Check whether help is available before the deadline rather than after. The SNAP study shows how much timing alone can matter. Nothing about the interview requirement changed. Only the date it fell in the month changed, and outcomes moved by more than 20%. Where a rule seems to produce unfair results and you cannot change it, document the pattern carefully. Bring it to the person or area responsible for the policy, with examples and the counts the system already produces.

sections.title: The fairness objection
sections.text: Colleagues may worry that a second route is special treatment. Take that seriously. Consistent standards protect people from arbitrary decisions. The answer is to separate the standard from the route. The proof required, the eligibility rules and the legal deadline stay the same for everyone. What changes is how and when people can meet them. A choice of callback window, for example, is open to anyone who needs it. That is different from relaxing the standard for some people. Explaining the distinction plainly usually settles the concern.

sections.title: Measuring without guessing
sections.text: Effort counts can mislead. A team that makes more calls has worked harder, but it may not have helped anyone. Better measures track outcomes the system already produces. How many renewals finish on time? How many cases close for procedural reasons? How long does it take between a notice going out and the first usable contact? Compare those before and after a change, over a long enough period to see past normal monthly swings. Use only data the system already keeps for this purpose, and work through the person or area responsible for data. Do not collect new personal information to test a change. When numbers are incomplete, a few accounts from people affected can explain an unexpected pattern. Ask through the channels the program already uses, and acknowledge the gap.

sections.title: Harder situations
sections.text: A senior colleague may argue that the current rule has worked for years. The research suggests a useful reply. A process can look like it works because the people it fails do not show up in the counts. They stop answering, stop applying or never start. A program integrity concern may arise: will an easier route invite errors? The IRS experiment is a useful reminder here. Clearer information increased claims from people who qualified, and the standard for proof did not change. Some changes reach Tribal Nations or county partners. Route Tribal matters through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations. Work with counties through the established partner channels, since both may run parts of the same process.

sections.title: Disability and burden
sections.text: Disability services raise these questions sharply. Many people who use them manage several programs at once, each with its own renewals, forms and contacts. The cognitive-resources research suggests that health problems strain the planning and attention needed to keep up. In the field office study, people with moderately severe conditions were among those most likely to drop out when applying got harder. Some processes assume a person can track several deadlines, travel to an appointment or take a call at a fixed time. Those processes may fail the people a disability program exists to serve. Practical steps include accepting help from an authorized representative and offering formats that work with assistive technology. Coordinating deadlines where you have the authority to do so also helps. Ask people what works for them rather than assuming what a diagnosis implies.

sections.title: Building the habit on your team
sections.text: This kind of review should not wait for a crisis. Once or twice a year, pick one step in a process your team runs and walk through it as the person on the other end would. Read the notice. Call the line at different hours. Try the online form on a phone. Look at where the counts show people dropping out. Then hold a short discussion. Which parts are required? Which are habit? What second route would meet the same standard? Researchers call this kind of review a sludge audit. The term is informal, but the practice is simple, and it keeps the gap between the rule and the route visible.

sections.title: What a fair process looks like
sections.text: A fair process keeps one standard and offers more than one realistic way to meet it. It starts the clock when a person can actually act. It uses plain language and shows people why acting matters. It offers help before the deadline, not only after a missed one. And it judges itself by who gets through, not by how much effort staff put in. None of this lowers expectations. It makes sure the expectations are the only thing deciding the outcome.

simulation.setup: You supervise a renewal support team for a Minnesota health care program at DHS. When a renewal is missing a document, staff make three callback attempts between 8 and 11 a.m. After three missed calls, the case goes to a review that can lead to closure. The practice has been in place for years. At stake are people's health coverage and your team's limited time. Also at stake is whether the process tests eligibility or just who can answer the phone in the morning.

steps.situation: A person whose case is in review calls the line. They work overnight, and all three callbacks came while they slept, even though their file asks for afternoon contact. A staff member mentions hearing similar stories.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Honor the afternoon request for this case now, and ask the person or area responsible for the procedure which parts are required and which are habit.
choices.feedback: The case is resolved in one afternoon call. The procedure's owner agrees to look at the requirement. Separating the required standard from local habit is the first step the evidence supports. The SNAP study showed that timing alone, with the requirement unchanged, moved recertification by more than 20%.

choices.label: Add a fourth callback attempt for everyone.
choices.feedback: This feels generous and treats everyone the same. But it adds staff time without asking why calls are missed. If the problem is timing, a fourth morning call reaches the same sleeping person. Effort goes up while the pattern stays. Burden research points to the route, not the number of attempts.

choices.label: Keep the rule as it is. Exceptions would be unfair to everyone else.
choices.feedback: Consistency is a real value, and this is a tempting answer. But the rule already treats people differently in effect. It only works for people who are reachable in the morning. Nationally, 69% of Medicaid disenrollments in recent renewals were procedural. Identical procedures can decide outcomes that eligibility should decide.

steps.situation: The procedure's owner reports back. The requirement is a documented good-faith attempt to reach the person plus a written notice. The morning window is local practice.
steps.question: What do you test?

choices.label: Let people choose a contact window and channel at renewal, keep the same documentation standard, and check staff workload and privacy before starting.
choices.feedback: Staff spread afternoon and early evening calls across shifts. The privacy contact signs off on generic text reminders. The standard stays identical, and only the route changes. That is the distinction that answers the fairness objection. It also fits the evidence that compliance costs, not eligibility, drive many losses.

choices.label: Move all callbacks to the afternoon.
choices.feedback: This helps people who work nights, and it is simple. But it shifts the problem to people who are only free in the morning, such as people working day shifts. Swapping one fixed window for another treats everyone the same in a new way, and it still leaves some people out.

choices.label: Wait for a formal policy update before changing anything.
choices.feedback: Caution feels responsible, especially in a large agency. But the owner just confirmed the morning window is local practice, inside your authority. Every month of waiting means more people reach review because of timing alone. The SNAP study showed that losses from timing can persist for more than a year.

steps.situation: Two months later, the review queue is about the same size. The call system's own report shows most missed calls happen before noon. Staff are frustrated by the extra work.
steps.question: What do you do now?

choices.label: Go back to the person or area responsible for the procedure and ask which parts are required and which are habit.
choices.feedback: You learn the morning window is local practice. You lost two months, but the call report gave you evidence to bring. Using counts the system already produces, rather than effort counts, showed the pattern. Now the change can target the route instead of adding more of the same.

choices.label: Add one evening callback slot without changing anything else.
choices.feedback: This is a reasonable guess, and some people will be reached. But you are still adjusting effort without confirming what the requirement is. Without that, you may keep steps that are not needed and miss easier fixes, such as letting people choose a window or a channel.

choices.label: Conclude that people who miss three calls are not making their coverage a priority.
choices.feedback: This is a common and understandable reading when staff are working hard. But the evidence points the other way. In Arkansas, more than 95% of those subject to a requirement already met it, and many lost coverage anyway. Missed contact more often reflects timing and circumstances than indifference.

steps.situation: A staff member proposes text reminders before each callback. Another points out that some people share phones, and that one staff member would end up handling all the replies.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Keep message wording generic, review it with the person or area responsible for data privacy, and rotate reply duty across the team.
choices.feedback: The reminder says only that the program will call and gives a number. It reveals nothing about health or benefits. Replies are shared across staff. A second route is fair only if it does not expose people or quietly shift burden onto one worker. Asking those questions first is what makes the fix hold.

choices.label: Launch the texts now and handle problems as they come up.
choices.feedback: Speed has value, and texts may help many people. But a message that names the program on a shared phone can reveal private information. Sending all replies to one person creates a new bottleneck. Fixing one barrier can create another, and a short review would have caught both risks.

choices.label: Drop the idea. It raises too many concerns.
choices.feedback: The concerns are real, and stopping can feel safe. But both have workable answers: generic wording and shared reply duty. In the IRS experiment, clearer outreach increased claims from eligible people. Dropping the route leaves the original barrier in place for everyone it was failing.

steps.situation: After three months, your manager asks whether the changes worked.
steps.question: How do you answer?

choices.label: Compare on-time renewals, procedural closures and time from notice to first contact, before and after, using counts the system already produces.
choices.feedback: Procedural closures from this step are down, and time to first contact is shorter. You can show it without collecting anything new. Outcome measures tell you who got through. That is the real test of a fair process, and it is how the research judged every change it studied.

choices.label: Report that staff feel the process is working better.
choices.feedback: Staff views matter, and they often notice problems early. But feelings are a weak test of whether more people kept coverage. Your manager will need outcome evidence to keep or expand the change. The system already produces that evidence for this purpose.

choices.label: Report the number of callbacks and texts sent.
choices.feedback: These numbers are easy to pull and show real effort. But effort counts do not show whether anyone was helped. A team could double its calls and leave closures unchanged. Measuring activity instead of outcomes is how unfair processes keep looking successful.

simulation.debrief: Each decision asked whether the process was testing eligibility or testing who could get through. Separating the required standard from local habit opened the door to change. The SNAP study showed that timing alone, with the requirement unchanged, moved recertification by over 20%. Adding attempts, or holding to the rule for fairness, kept the same people falling out. That fits the national pattern, where most Medicaid disenrollments were procedural. A second route kept one standard and offered more than one way to meet it. It held up because you checked privacy and workload first. Measuring outcomes the system already produces, rather than effort, showed whether people actually got through.

mistakes.mistake: Defending a procedure because it treats everyone the same.
mistakes.why: Consistency protects people from arbitrary decisions, so it feels like the fair answer. But identical procedures can carry very different costs, and losses concentrate among people with fewer resources.
mistakes.instead: Keep the standard identical and offer more than one realistic route to meet it.

mistakes.mistake: Adding more of the same, such as more calls or more reminders.
mistakes.why: Extra effort feels generous and is easy to approve. But if the barrier is timing, channel or wording, more of the same reaches no one new.
mistakes.instead: Find out why people miss the step, then change the route.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming hassle screens out people with weak claims.
mistakes.why: It seems logical that people who truly need help will push through. But when field offices closed, losses were concentrated among people with lower education and earnings, and targeting got worse.
mistakes.instead: Treat procedural losses as a signal to examine the process.

mistakes.mistake: Treating local practice as if it were law.
mistakes.why: Long-standing practices feel official, and no one remembers who set them. But many timing and channel choices are habits, not requirements.
mistakes.instead: Ask the person or area responsible which parts are required and which are habit.

mistakes.mistake: Launching a new channel without checking privacy and workload.
mistakes.why: The fix seems obviously helpful, and speed matters. But a text on a shared phone can expose private information, and replies can pile onto one worker.
mistakes.instead: Use generic wording, review with the person or area responsible for data privacy and share the new work.

mistakes.mistake: Judging a change by effort counts.
mistakes.why: Calls made and letters sent are easy to count. But they do not show whether anyone kept coverage.
mistakes.instead: Compare on-time renewals, procedural closures and time to first contact, using counts the system already produces.

jobAid.title: Same rule, fair route: a procedure check
jobAid.use: Use it when a procedure seems to work for some people and not others, or before you defend or change one.
steps: What is the required standard, and who set it? Confirm with the person or area responsible.
Which parts, such as timing, channel or format, are local practice?
When does your clock start, and when can the person actually act? Write down both.
Who has to spend extra time, money, travel or attention to meet this step?
What second route would meet the same standard?
Whose work does the new route shift, and what could it expose? Check privacy first.
Which counts the system already produces will show whether more people got through?
If the rule is fixed, who needs to see the pattern, with examples, and by when?

media.reason: The rule owner and the person who sees who falls out hold different, legitimate views. Two voices show how they reach a fair fix together without either one being the problem.

script.text: I want to talk about the morning callback window for renewals. My staff keep hearing from people who work nights. All three calls come while they're asleep, and then their case goes to review.

script.text: I hear you. My worry is consistency. If one group gets special timing, others will ask, and pretty soon nobody knows what the rule is.

script.speaker: female
script.text: That's fair. Can I ask what the requirement actually is? Is the morning window in statute, or is it practice?

script.speaker: male
script.role: Policy specialist responsible for the renewal procedure
script.text: Let me be precise. The requirement is a documented good-faith attempt to reach the person, plus a written notice. The morning window started years ago because that's when the team was staffed.

script.speaker: female
script.text: So the standard is the attempt and the notice. The timing is a habit. There's research on exactly this. In a SNAP program, families given interview dates late in the month were over twenty percent less likely to keep benefits. The requirement didn't change. Only the timing did.

script.speaker: male
script.role: Policy specialist responsible for the renewal procedure
script.text: That's striking. I'd have assumed people who really need coverage will find a way to call back.

script.speaker: female

script.speaker: male
script.role: Policy specialist responsible for the renewal procedure
script.text: All right. Here's what I can support. Everyone gets the same standard: a documented attempt and a written notice. But at renewal, anyone can pick a contact window. That isn't special treatment. It's one standard with more than one route.

script.speaker: female

title: Curiosity before conclusions
objective: Catch a quick judgment about a person's motive, replace it with a plain description, and get the missing facts by asking before you decide.
outcomes: Rewrite a judgment word in a case note or report as a description of what was seen or heard.
Name at least two situational explanations, including one about your own process, before settling on a motive.
Ask the person directly, through the right language access and channel, instead of guessing what they think.
Build a short pause for correction into busy work, such as a team review or a call-line handoff.
Coach a staff member to separate what happened from what it meant without shaming them.

evidence.summary: People tend to explain others' behavior by character, even when the situation explains it. The correction for the situation is the step most easily dropped when people are busy, which describes most DHS workdays. A striking set of 25 experiments found that imagining another person's view did not make people more accurate, and sometimes made them less accurate. Asking the person directly did improve accuracy. How strongly people discount the situation also varies across cultures, so the habit itself is cultural. The Describe, Interpret, Evaluate method was created at the University of Minnesota in the 1970s. It is a sound structure, but no controlled study was found showing it changes workplace decisions. Most of the evidence is from laboratory studies.

findings.claim: Imagining another person's perspective did not improve accuracy across 25 experiments, while directly asking them did.
findings.detail: 25 experiments, 2018. In the final experiment (about 104 participants), people predicting a partner's opinions got 4.90 of 20 exactly right in the control group, 3.95 when told to imagine the partner's view, and 8.60 when they had asked the partner first.

findings.claim: People who were mentally busy failed to adjust for the situation when judging someone, while people who were not busy did adjust.
findings.detail: Two lab experiments, 1988; Experiment 1 had 47 students who watched a person act anxious in an anxiety-provoking situation. Correction for the situation was the step most easily disrupted.

findings.claim: People read stable traits into behavior the situation explains in four ways: missing the situation, expecting too much of it, over-reading the act, and correcting too little.
findings.detail: Review article, Psychological Bulletin, 1995.

findings.claim: The well-known idea that people blame the situation for their own acts but blame character for others' acts was near zero on average across 173 studies.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 173 studies, 1971 to 2004, published 2006. The difference appeared mainly for negative events and reversed for positive ones, a pattern consistent with self-serving explanation.

findings.claim: How much people weigh the situation varies across cultures; when the situation is not obvious, people in all groups studied over-read character.
findings.detail: Review, 2000, summarizing newspaper analyses and lab studies with American, Chinese and Korean participants, including Morris and Peng (1994).

findings.claim: Describe, Interpret, Evaluate was developed at the University of Minnesota in the mid-1970s, and its support is teaching experience rather than outcome studies.
findings.detail: Historical and conceptual article, 2010. Credits Janet Bennett and Milton Bennett; proposes Describe, Analyze, Evaluate because interpret and evaluate were often confused. Reports no outcome data.

findings.claim: Choosing between two equally eligible welfare recipients, people weighed judgments of effort heavily. People with public-sector work history did so about as much as others.
findings.detail: Conjoint experiment, 2023 working paper; 1,937 adults after data cleaning, 352 with public-sector work history, plus a student sample. Need and earned deservingness had substantial effects in all samples. Not yet peer reviewed.

counterintuitive.headline: Imagining their side made people less accurate, not more.
counterintuitive.text: Most people believe that putting yourself in someone else's shoes helps you understand them. In 25 experiments, Eyal, Steffel and Epley (2018) tested that belief and failed to find a consistent benefit. Imagining the other view sometimes lowered accuracy while raising confidence. What worked was perspective getting: asking the person and using the answer. In their final study, people who asked a partner first got more than twice as many predictions exactly right as people who only imagined. The lesson for DHS work is direct. Empathy matters, but it does not supply facts. Ask.

sections.title: The quick story your mind tells
sections.text: A family misses two calls. A provider sends a short, blunt email. A person nods during a planning meeting, then asks a question that shows they did not agree. Within seconds, your mind supplies a reason. The family is avoiding you. The provider is hostile. The person was not paying attention. These quick stories feel like observations. They are guesses about character. Decades of research show that people lean toward explaining behavior by character, even when the situation explains it well.

sections.title: Why busy days make it worse
sections.text: Judging a person runs in three steps. You notice the act, you infer a trait, and then you correct for the situation. The first two steps happen fast and almost automatically. The third takes effort. In a classic set of experiments, people who were mentally busy skipped the correction step. People who were not busy made it. A full call queue, a stack of renewals or a tense meeting is exactly that kind of busy.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: Before a judgment word goes into a note, an email or a decision, describe first. Write what you saw or heard in words a camera could confirm. "Two calls at 10 a.m. on weekdays, voicemail left in English, no callback" is a description. "Family is resistant" is a conclusion. Then name at least two other explanations, including one about your own process. Finally, ask the person. Use the right language access and a channel that works for them.

sections.title: Why asking beats imagining
sections.text: Imagining someone's view feels like understanding. In 25 experiments, it did not reliably make people more accurate, and sometimes made them less accurate. Asking the person directly did. Curiosity is not a mood. It is a set of questions you actually put to the person who knows the answer. Before your next judgment about someone's motive, find the one fact you are missing and go get it.

sections.title: What the research shows
sections.text: Psychologists call the lean toward character explanations the correspondence bias. A 1995 review named four routes into it. People may not see the situation at all. They may expect the situation to push behavior more than it does. They may over-read what the act means. Or they may correct for the situation, but not enough. Each route ends in the same place: a confident statement about who someone is, built on what one moment showed. In DHS and DSD work, that statement can travel. It goes into a case note, a referral or a staffing discussion, and other people read it as fact.

sections.title: The step that drops out
sections.text: In 1988, Gilbert, Pelham and Krull showed students a silent video of a woman acting anxious. Some were told she was discussing anxiety-provoking topics. Those who could focus used that fact and judged her as less anxious by nature. Those who were doing a second mental task at the same time did not use it. They saw an anxious person. The correction step needs attention, and attention is the first thing a heavy workload takes. This is why good people with good values still write unfair notes on hard days.

sections.title: Imagining is not the same as knowing
sections.text: Many trainings tell staff to put themselves in the other person's shoes. Eyal, Steffel and Epley tested that advice in 25 experiments. Imagining the other person's view reduced some self-centered errors, but what replaced them was not more accurate. Confidence sometimes rose anyway. In the final study, people who asked their partner first got 8.60 of 20 predictions exactly right. People who only imagined got 3.95. The control group got 4.90. Asking more than doubled accuracy. For DHS work, that means a direct question, asked well, is worth more than a careful guess.

sections.title: Describe, Interpret, Evaluate
sections.text: Describe, Interpret, Evaluate is a simple tool built for this problem. It was created by Janet Bennett and Milton Bennett at the University of Minnesota in the mid-1970s. Describe means stating only what was seen or heard. Interpret means listing more than one possible meaning. Evaluate means naming your reaction and what you will do, while holding it open to correction. Later authors suggested replacing interpret with analyze, because people often slipped their judgment into the interpret step. Either way, the order matters. Description comes first, and judgment comes last.

sections.title: Applying it to a case note
sections.text: Take the note "Person agreed to the new schedule." Describe: the person nodded while the schedule was read aloud. Interpret: the nod may have meant agreement, or "I hear you," or politeness toward someone with authority over services, or waiting for a support person. Evaluate: the decision is not yet confirmed. Then ask: "What did you understand about the new schedule, and which option do you want?" Update the note with the answer. The rewrite takes less than a minute and can prevent a service gap.

sections.title: Include your own process
sections.text: When you list explanations, include at least one about the system. Were calls placed at times the person works? Was the voicemail in a language the person reads? Did the letter reach a current address? Did the person know who was calling? These questions are not excuses. They are the situational facts that busy perceivers skip. They are also the facts you can change, which makes them the most useful to find.

sections.title: A worked example from a call line
sections.text: A caller to a disability services line speaks sharply and asks for a supervisor within the first minute. The quick story is that the caller is difficult. Describe instead: the caller said this was the third call about the same notice and asked for a supervisor. Interpret: the caller may have been transferred twice already, may have a deadline, or may have been told different things each time. Evaluate: the caller needs a clear answer and an owner for the issue. Ask: "What have you been told so far, and what do you need settled today?" The answer usually tells you what went wrong in the process.

sections.title: Effort judgments in public service
sections.text: Public servants often decide who gets extra time or follow-up. A 2023 conjoint experiment asked 1,937 adults to choose between two equally eligible welfare recipients. Judgments of effort, which the authors call earned deservingness, mattered a lot. People with public-sector work history weighed effort about as much as everyone else. Effort is rarely seen directly. It is inferred from moments like missed calls or late forms. That inference is exactly where the correction step belongs.

sections.title: Using it as a leader
sections.text: As a supervisor, you can make this a team habit rather than a personal virtue. Ask for the description first in case reviews. Treat a judgment word, such as resistant, noncompliant, demanding or unmotivated, as a cue to ask what was observed. Do it with curiosity, not correction. Thank staff who bring back a fact that changed the picture. When the team sees that asking leads to better decisions, the practice spreads without a lecture.

sections.title: What the classic idea got wrong
sections.text: Textbooks long taught that people explain their own behavior by the situation and others' behavior by character. Malle's 2006 meta-analysis of 173 studies found that the average difference was close to zero. The pattern showed up mainly for negative events and reversed for positive ones. That fits a simpler story: people explain their own bad moments generously and their good moments as earned. For leaders, the lesson is humbling. Your own explanations are not neutral either. When a project of yours runs late, you will see the situation clearly. Apply the same generosity to others on purpose.

sections.title: The habit is cultural, too
sections.text: How strongly people discount the situation varies across cultures. Morris and Peng found that American newspapers and students explained murders mostly through the killers' personal traits. Chinese newspapers and Chinese students in the United States put more weight on circumstances and social context. In a later study, Korean participants who first experienced the same constraint as a writer stopped assuming the essay showed the writer's views. American participants did not adjust. The review also notes an important limit. When the situation is not obvious, people in every group studied over-read character. No group is free of the bias. The point is that your sense of what counts as a good explanation was learned, and others may have learned differently.

sections.title: Limits of the evidence
sections.text: Most attribution research comes from short laboratory studies, often with college students. The mechanism is well established. How often it changes real decisions in human services is less clear. No controlled study was found showing that teaching Describe, Interpret, Evaluate changes workplace judgments or outcomes for the people served. The 2010 article that traced its history reported teaching experience, not outcome data. The 2023 public-sector experiment was a working paper using hypothetical choices. Treat this course's method as a sound structure built on solid lab findings, not a proven program.

sections.title: When asking is not safe or simple
sections.text: Perspective getting depends on the other person being able to answer honestly. Power changes that. A person who depends on a worker for services may say yes to end a hard conversation. A provider whose license is under review may say little. Language access matters too. Asking through a family member or a bilingual coworker who is not a qualified interpreter can shape the answer. Offer a qualified interpreter, a choice of channel and time, and a private way to correct the record later. Say plainly what will happen with the answer and what will not.

sections.title: When the description itself is slanted
sections.text: Descriptions can carry hidden judgments. "Raised voice" and "yelled" may describe the same moment, but they invite different conclusions. "Did not return calls" assumes calls reached the person. Test a description by asking whether the person described would agree it is accurate. If they would not, it may be an interpretation in disguise. This is the problem that led later authors to rename the middle step. Slow down at the description step most when the stakes are highest.

sections.title: When the first story is right
sections.text: Sometimes the quick judgment turns out to be correct. A provider really did ignore repeated requests. A staff member really did skip a required step. Curiosity does not mean avoiding conclusions. It means earning them. When you have described the facts, checked the situation and asked, you can act firmly and fairly. Your decision will also hold up better. A conclusion that survived real questions is easier to explain to the person, a reviewer or the person or area responsible for an appeal.

sections.title: Coaching a staff member who jumped
sections.text: When a staff member writes a judgment, avoid labeling them as biased. That creates defensiveness and teaches them to hide their reasoning. Ask instead, "What did you see or hear that led to that word?" Then ask, "What else could explain it, and who would know?" These questions model the method. They also treat the staff member the same way you want them to treat the public. Remember the busy-perceiver finding. The fix is often workload and process, not character.

sections.title: Building correction into busy systems
sections.text: Because correction drops out under load, the best supports are built into the work. A case review template can ask for the observation before the assessment. A call-line handoff can include a line for what was tried and through which language. A rule of thumb can say that no judgment word enters a note without one supporting observation. These steps take seconds. They do for the whole team what a calm, focused mind does for one person.

sections.title: Partners and Tribal matters
sections.text: The same method applies to county partners and providers. A slow response from a county may reflect staffing or a different process, not resistance. Ask the person or area responsible for that partnership what is known. For any matter involving a Tribal nation, go through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations. Do not guess at cultural reasons, and do not speak for Native people. The right channel is part of getting the right facts.

sections.title: Differential effects and what is not known
sections.text: Do these errors fall harder on some groups of people served? The studies reviewed here do not answer that for DHS settings, and this course does not claim a group effect the evidence does not show. What the research does show is that the bias grows when the situation is hard to see. Language barriers, unfamiliar customs, disability-related communication differences and unstable housing can all hide the situation from a busy worker. That means people facing those barriers have more facts missing from their files. The practical answer is the same for everyone: describe, check the situation and ask. Pay closest attention where the situation is least visible to you.

sections.title: Putting it together
sections.text: The research points to three moves. Describe before you judge, because the first story is usually about character. Check the situation, including your own process, because busy minds skip that step. Then ask the person, because asking outperforms imagining. None of this requires a special program. It requires a few extra seconds at the moment a judgment wants to become a fact. As a leader, your job is to make those seconds normal for the whole team. Start with the decisions that matter most to people served: closing outreach, denying an exception, or marking someone as not engaged. Those are the moments where an unchecked story costs the most and a single question helps the most.

simulation.setup: You are a Human Services Supervisor in a Disability Services Division unit that helps people move to new waiver services. Your team carries heavy caseloads this month. A Case Aide has written in a file that a family is "resistant" and "refused contact" after missed calls. The aide recommends closing outreach so the time can go to other people waiting. If outreach closes, the person's planned service start could slip by weeks. You review the file before the weekly team review.

steps.situation: The note reads: "Family resistant. Refused two contact attempts. Recommend closing outreach." The Case Aide is careful and well liked. They are also covering two other caseloads this week. The team review starts in fifteen minutes.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Ask the Case Aide to walk you through exactly what happened on each attempt: when, how, and in what language.
choices.feedback: This goes straight to description without accusing anyone. It also respects the aide's workload, because the facts may change the plan faster than a debate would. Research on busy perceivers shows the situational correction is the step most often skipped under load. Your question restores it. You will learn whether the family refused anything or simply never received the message.

choices.label: Approve closing outreach. The note is clear, the aide is reliable, and other people are waiting.
choices.feedback: This is tempting because the aide is trustworthy and the queue is real. But the note contains conclusions, not observations. Trusting the person is not the same as checking the facts. Busy reviewers tend to accept trait explanations without adjusting for the situation. If the calls never reached the family, closing outreach turns a process gap into a service delay for the person.

choices.label: Tell the Case Aide the word resistant is biased and ask them to rewrite the note before the review.
choices.feedback: Your concern is right, but the framing may backfire. Calling the note biased puts the aide on the defensive and teaches them to soften words rather than gather facts. A rewritten note with gentler language can still hide the same missing information. The research supports asking what was observed, which fixes the note and the decision at the same time.

steps.situation: The Case Aide explains: both calls were at 10 a.m. on weekdays. Voicemails were left in English. The file lists a primary language other than English and an adult sibling as the main contact. No interpreter was used. The aide says, "I assumed they'd call back if they cared."
steps.question: How do you get the missing perspective?

choices.label: Arrange outreach with a qualified interpreter, offer several times and channels, and ask the family what works for them.
choices.feedback: This is perspective getting. You are asking the people who know the answer, through language access that makes an honest answer possible. In 25 experiments, asking improved accuracy while imagining did not. Offering choices also reduces the pressure a family may feel when talking to someone with power over services. Whatever you learn goes into the note as a description.

choices.label: Ask the Case Aide to imagine why the family might not have answered and add that reasoning to the note.
choices.feedback: This feels empathetic and costs no extra time. But imagined reasons are still guesses, now written as if they were understanding. Research found that imagining another person's view can raise confidence without raising accuracy. The note would look more thoughtful while staying just as uncertain. Use the aide's ideas as questions to ask the family, not answers to file.

choices.label: Ask a bilingual coworker who shares the family's background to explain what is probably going on.
choices.feedback: This is well meant and common. It still replaces the family's own answer with someone else's guess. It also places an unpaid burden on a coworker and assumes shared background means shared views. A coworker who is not a qualified interpreter should not stand in for one. Get the family's perspective directly, with the right support.

steps.situation: Two weeks later, the county case manager calls you. The family's adult sibling told the county that no one ever reached them in their language. The service start date is now at risk. The Case Aide is upset and says the note was accurate: two calls were made.
steps.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Acknowledge the gap to the county, restart outreach with an interpreter, and then sit down with the aide to separate what happened from what the note concluded.
choices.feedback: You fix the service problem first, then the learning problem. With the aide, you can affirm the true part, that two calls were made, and show where the note moved from description to judgment. The fact that changed the picture came from asking. Treating the miss as a process lesson, not a character flaw, models the very correction the team needs.

choices.label: Tell the county the note was accurate, since two calls were documented, and ask the family to call the unit.
choices.feedback: This defends your team, which feels loyal. But it repeats the original error at a higher level. It treats the family's silence as a choice and puts the burden on them to fix a gap they did not create. The county partner now has reason to doubt the unit's notes. The facts available show the calls did not reach the family.

choices.label: Restart outreach with an interpreter and ask the Case Aide to send the family an apology.
choices.feedback: Restarting outreach with language access is right. Asking for an apology from the aide alone puts a team process gap on one person. It may also feel to the aide like public blame, which makes honest notes less likely next time. An acknowledgment from the unit, with a clear next step, serves the family better.

steps.situation: The family is reached and the service start is back on track. You want to prevent this pattern across the team without adding much time. Caseloads will stay high through the quarter.
steps.question: What change do you make?

choices.label: Add a short step to case reviews and notes: one observation before any judgment word, one other explanation, and how the person was asked.
choices.feedback: This builds the correction into the work, so it does not depend on anyone having a calm day. It takes seconds and follows the research: describe first, check the situation, then ask. Over time, staff will spot their own judgment words. Pair it with thanks when someone brings back a fact that changes a plan.

choices.label: Schedule a team session on bias in case notes, using this case as an example.
choices.feedback: Discussion can raise awareness, and some staff will find it useful. But awareness fades fastest under the workload that caused the problem. Using one aide's case as the example may also feel like public blame. A session works better alongside a built-in step that makes the right habit easy on busy days.

choices.label: Ban a list of words such as resistant, noncompliant and unmotivated from case notes.
choices.feedback: A word list is quick and visible, which makes it tempting. But it treats the symptom. Staff will find softer words that carry the same unchecked conclusion. The problem was missing facts, not vocabulary. Asking for the observation behind any judgment word keeps the useful signal and fixes the reasoning.

simulation.debrief: The path through this case followed the research closely. A careful, well-liked staff member wrote a character explanation on a busy week, which is what lab studies predict. The fix began with description: when, how and in what language the calls were made. That one question brought the situation back into view. The next step was perspective getting. Asking the family through a qualified interpreter supplied facts that no amount of imagining could. Across 25 experiments, asking outperformed imagining. Finally, because correction drops out under load, the lasting change was a small built-in step rather than a lecture. The evidence for Describe, Interpret, Evaluate as a program is thin. The evidence for its parts, describing first, checking the situation and asking directly, is much stronger.

mistakes.mistake: Treating empathy as a source of facts.
mistakes.why: Imagining another person's view feels like understanding, and most people expect it to work. Research found it often raises confidence without raising accuracy.
mistakes.instead: Use what you imagine as a list of questions. Then ask the person and use their answer.

mistakes.mistake: Writing conclusions as observations.
mistakes.why: Words like resistant or refused feel factual to the writer. Under a heavy workload, the correction for the situation is the step that drops out first.
mistakes.instead: Write what a camera could confirm: when, how, in what language, and what happened next.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving your own process out of the explanation.
mistakes.why: Your process is invisible to you because you live inside it. People also explain others' bad moments by character more readily than their own.
mistakes.instead: List at least one system explanation, such as timing, language, address or channel, before judging motive.

mistakes.mistake: Asking a coworker to explain someone who shares their background.
mistakes.why: It seems efficient and respectful of the coworker's knowledge. It still replaces the person's answer with a guess and places an unpaid burden on a colleague.
mistakes.instead: Ask the person directly with a qualified interpreter and a channel that works for them.

mistakes.mistake: Labeling the staff member who jumped to a conclusion.
mistakes.why: A supervisor who sees an unfair note wants to stop it quickly. Calling it bias makes staff defensive and teaches them to hide reasoning rather than check it.
mistakes.instead: Ask what was observed and what else could explain it. Treat the staff member the way you want them to treat the public.

jobAid.title: Describe, check, ask
jobAid.use: Use before a judgment about someone's motive goes into a note, email, referral or decision.
steps: Spot the judgment word: resistant, refused, demanding, unmotivated, agreed.
Describe what a camera could confirm: when, how, in what language, what happened next.
List two other explanations, including one about your own process.
Find the one fact you are missing and who can supply it.
Ask the person directly, with a qualified interpreter and a choice of time and channel.
Say what will happen with the answer, and offer a private way to correct it later.
Rewrite the note with the answer, then decide.
For Tribal matters, go through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations.

media.reason: This lesson teaches one internal habit, catching a quick story and replacing it with a question. A single calm voice can walk through the moment step by step without implying a right and wrong side.

prompts: Which note, report or recurring decision in your work most often carries a judgment word, and what observation should sit behind it?
With whom on your team could you try asking for the description first in your next case review or handoff?
By when will you add one built-in describe-first step to a template, checklist or meeting you lead?
