title: When difference feels like a threat
objective: Recognize when pressure and scarcity are turning a work disagreement into group-against-group talk, and steer the team back to the shared task without shaming anyone.
outcomes: Name the specific pressure behind a group-against-group comment, such as backlog, cuts or a changed process.
Turn a claim about another group's motives into a question about a specific step, file or decision.
Separate task disagreement from personal conflict and set working agreements that keep disagreement about the work.
Arrange structured contact on shared work, such as mixed pairs, so anxiety between groups goes down.
Choose shared measures that keep both staff pressure and the effect on people served in view.

evidence.summary: When people feel threatened, attitudes toward other groups tend to worsen. A meta-analysis of 95 samples found five kinds of threat linked to more negative views. In lab studies, simply framing resources as scarce changed how people perceived race and how they shared resources. Contact between groups generally reduces prejudice, mostly by lowering anxiety rather than by teaching facts. Randomized studies of contact show smaller effects, especially for racial and ethnic prejudice. In teams, conflict about people hurts, while conflict about the task can help when people feel safe to speak. In U.S. federal agencies, racial diversity related to stronger perceived performance only where diversity was well managed. Much of this evidence is correlational or from short lab studies.

findings.claim: Five of six kinds of perceived threat were linked to more negative attitudes toward other groups.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 95 samples, 2006. Threats included competition for resources, threats to values, anxiety about interacting, negative stereotypes and threats to group esteem. Correlational.

findings.claim: Framing resources as scarce changed how people perceived race, and faces drawn under scarcity were given fewer resources by other raters.
findings.detail: Four lab studies, PNAS, 2014. Scarcity lowered the point at which mixed-race faces were judged Black and led participants to picture Black faces as darker.

findings.claim: Under scarcity framing, people low in internal motivation to avoid prejudice gave less to Black recipients, most clearly in deliberate decisions.
findings.detail: Five studies, 2017. The effect appeared even when one person's gain was not another's loss. People high in internal motivation gave more to Black recipients.

findings.claim: Contact between groups generally reduces prejudice, and the effect extends to the whole other group.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 515 studies and 713 samples, 2006. Supportive conditions strengthened effects but were not required. Mostly correlational.

findings.claim: Contact reduces prejudice mainly by lowering anxiety and building empathy; learning facts about the other group was the weakest route.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 54 studies, 2008. For anxiety: 45 studies, 13,343 participants; contact to anxiety r = -.29, anxiety to prejudice r = +.37.

findings.claim: Randomized contact studies show real but smaller effects, and substantially weaker effects for racial and ethnic prejudice.
findings.detail: Review and meta-analysis, 2019; 27 randomized studies with outcomes at least a day later. Pooled effect 0.39 standard deviations; 0.25 for ethnic, racial, religious and immigrant groups.

findings.claim: Cultural diversity in teams brought more task conflict and less social cohesion, and also more creativity and satisfaction.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 108 studies and 10,632 teams, 2010. Effects depended on task complexity, team size, tenure and dispersion.

findings.claim: Relationship conflict consistently went with worse team outcomes, while task conflict was not strongly negative overall.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 116 studies and 8,880 groups, 2012. Task conflict was more positive when it was weakly tied to relationship conflict.

findings.claim: Task conflict improved team performance only where psychological safety was high.
findings.detail: 117 project teams, 2012.

findings.claim: In U.S. federal agencies, racial diversity alone related to lower perceived performance, but to higher perceived performance where diversity management and team processes were strong.
findings.detail: Cross-sectional study, 2010; 67 subagencies, about 150,000 employees in the 2004 Federal Human Capital Survey. Outcome was employee-perceived performance.

findings.claim: Norms encouraging open discussion of conflict were not always helpful, and task disagreement hurt routine work more than nonroutine work.
findings.detail: Multimethod study of 105 work groups and management teams, 1995.

counterintuitive.headline: Learning facts about another group was the weakest route to less prejudice.
counterintuitive.text: Many efforts to ease tension between groups start with information about the other group. Pettigrew and Tropp's 2008 meta-analysis tested three ways contact reduces prejudice. Gaining knowledge did help, but less than the other two routes. Lowering anxiety about the interaction and building empathy did more. Across 45 studies and 13,343 participants, more contact went with less anxiety, and less anxiety went with less prejudice. For a supervisor, this shifts the work. A fact sheet about another team helps less than regular, low-stakes, shared work that makes contact feel normal and safe.

sections.title: How pressure becomes group against group
sections.text: A backlog grows. Overtime is cut. Two teams with different procedures are merged. Soon you hear comments like "they keep dumping incomplete files on renewals" or "that group always wants special treatment." These comments rarely come from bad people. They come from people under pressure. Research links feeling threatened, whether by competition for resources, a change in values or simple anxiety, to more negative views of other groups. In lab studies, just framing resources as scarce changed how people perceived race.

sections.title: Why it matters at DHS
sections.text: When a disagreement about work turns into a story about another group's motives, two things suffer. The team loses the information inside the disagreement, such as which form field is really missing. And people served can absorb the cost, through slower files or colder service. Conflict about people consistently hurts teams. Conflict about the task can help, but mainly when people feel safe to speak.

sections.title: What it sounds like
sections.text: Group-against-group talk has a few common signs. A whole team or group is described by one motive. Words like always, never, they and those people appear. A real process problem, such as a missing field or a late handoff, is explained as a lack of caring. And the people being described go quiet. When you hear these signs, the team is moving from the work to the people.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: When you hear group-against-group talk, name the pressure and point to the task. Say what is true: "The backlog is real and everyone is stretched." Then turn the motive claim into a question about a step: "Which files, and which fields are missing?" This lowers defensiveness without shaming the speaker. It also moves the conversation to something you can check and fix together.

sections.title: What lowers the heat
sections.text: Contact between groups generally reduces prejudice. It works mainly by lowering anxiety, not by teaching facts about the other group. So the most useful thing a supervisor can do is create regular, structured, shared work across the line, like mixed pairs on hard files. Keep both measures in view: how stretched staff feel, and what happens to the people waiting.

sections.title: Threat comes in several forms
sections.text: A 2006 meta-analysis of 95 samples looked at six kinds of threat. They included competition for resources, threats to a group's values, anxiety about interacting, negative stereotypes, threats to a group's standing and threats to a group's distinctiveness. Five of the six were linked to more negative attitudes toward other groups. In a DHS unit, these show up in ordinary forms. A merged team fears losing its way of doing things. A unit facing cuts sees another unit as competition. A worker feels anxious about calls that need an interpreter and blames the callers for the stress.

sections.title: Scarcity changes perception
sections.text: Lab research shows how deep this can go. In four studies, Krosch and Amodio framed resources as scarce. Participants then judged mixed-race faces as Black at a lower threshold and pictured Black faces as darker. Other raters gave fewer resources to the faces drawn under scarcity. A later set of five studies found that, under scarcity framing, people low in internal motivation to avoid prejudice gave less to Black recipients. The effect was clearest in deliberate decisions. These are short lab studies. They show that scarcity can shift judgment without anyone intending it, which is why fair processes matter most when budgets are tight.

sections.title: Two kinds of conflict
sections.text: A 2012 meta-analysis of 116 studies and 8,880 groups separated conflict about people from conflict about the work. Relationship conflict consistently went with worse outcomes. Task conflict was not strongly negative overall. It was more positive when it stayed separate from personal friction. Another study of 117 project teams found task conflict improved performance only where psychological safety was high. The job of a supervisor is not to remove disagreement. It is to keep disagreement about the work and to make it safe.

sections.title: Culturally mixed teams have both costs and gains
sections.text: A meta-analysis of 108 studies and 10,632 teams found that cultural diversity brought more task conflict and less social cohesion. It also brought more creativity and satisfaction. Both are real. Pretending there is no friction leaves the costs unmanaged. Treating friction as proof that a mix cannot work throws away the gains. Effects depended on things leaders can influence, such as task complexity, team size and how long people had worked together.

sections.title: What management changes
sections.text: A study of U.S. federal agencies used data from 67 subagencies and about 150,000 employees. Racial diversity on its own related to lower perceived performance. Where diversity management and team processes were strong, racial diversity related to higher perceived performance. The outcome was employee perception, not measured results. Still, the pattern is useful. Diversity does not manage itself, and good team process can turn friction into strength.

sections.title: Contact that lowers anxiety
sections.text: Contact between groups generally reduces prejudice. A 2006 meta-analysis of 515 studies found the effect extends to the whole other group. A 2008 follow-up asked why. Lowering anxiety and building empathy did more than learning facts. In DHS terms, regular shared work across a team line helps more than a presentation about the other team. Mixed pairs on hard files, rotating huddle leads and joint problem reviews create the kind of contact that lowers anxiety.

sections.title: Applying it in the moment
sections.text: When a group-against-group comment comes up, use three steps. First, name the stake: "The backlog is real." Second, ask about a step: "Which files, and what was missing?" Third, invite the other side's facts: "What does intake see from their end?" Do not ask a colleague to explain or defend a group they belong to. Do not let the comment stand as fact either. If the claim turns out to be true, it now points to a fixable step. If it was a stereotype, the facts will show that without a public scolding.

sections.title: Two outcomes, both visible
sections.text: Pressure on staff and outcomes for people served can move in opposite directions. A team can speed up by pushing work onto people outside the unit, such as asking callers to return another day. Track both. Ask staff how stretched they are and ask what happened to the people waiting. When both stay visible, the team is less likely to solve its stress by shifting the cost to someone else.

sections.title: A note on safety
sections.text: Turning a conversation back to the task only works if people believe they can speak without penalty. Watch who talks after a tense moment. If one group goes quiet, follow up individually and ask what they saw. Thank anyone who brings a fact that changes the picture, especially when it cuts against their own team. That follow-through is what makes the next disagreement safer.

sections.title: How strong is the evidence?
sections.text: The threat findings come mainly from a meta-analysis of correlational studies. People who feel more threatened tend to hold more negative views, but the direction of cause is not always clear. The scarcity findings come from short, controlled lab experiments, which show cause but in artificial settings. The contact findings rest on hundreds of studies, most of them correlational. When Paluck and colleagues looked only at randomized studies with outcomes at least a day later, they found 27. The pooled effect was 0.39 standard deviations. For ethnic, racial, religious and immigrant groups, the estimate was 0.25, and the authors described effects on racial and ethnic prejudice as substantially weaker. Contact helps. It is not a quick fix.

sections.title: Open-conflict norms are not a cure-all
sections.text: It is tempting to tell a tense team, "Let's just put everything on the table." A 1995 study of 105 work groups found that norms encouraging open discussion of conflict were not always helpful. The same study found that task disagreement hurt groups doing routine work but not groups doing nonroutine work, and sometimes helped them. Eligibility processing has many routine steps. Arguing about every step can slow the work. The better target is disagreement about the steps that are unclear, new or causing errors. Settle routine steps with a shared standard and save open debate for the parts that need judgment.

sections.title: Working agreements that actually work
sections.text: Group agreements help when they are specific and used. Useful ones are short. Talk about the file, not the person. Bring an example when you raise a pattern. Anyone can ask for a pause. Concerns can also be raised after the meeting through a named route. The leader must show what happens when someone uses the agreement. If a worker raises a concern and hears nothing back, the agreement becomes words on a wall. Psychological safety, which made task conflict helpful in the project-team study, is built by this follow-through.

sections.title: When the claim is partly true
sections.text: Sometimes the other team really is sending incomplete files. The goal is not to defend any group. It is to move from motive to mechanism. "They don't care about accuracy" is a motive claim. "Thirty files this month lacked the income date because the two checklists differ" is a mechanism. Mechanisms can be fixed. Motive claims spread. When a claim is partly true, say so, and fix the part that is true. Doing that builds trust with both sides.

sections.title: When the comment targets the public
sections.text: Group-against-group talk sometimes aims at people served. A worker may say that callers who need an interpreter are "slowing everyone down" or "expecting special treatment." Language access is part of the service, not a favor. The person or area responsible for language access can confirm what the program requires. Acknowledge the queue pressure and arrange coverage if you can. Then address the motive claim privately with the worker, with curiosity about what is driving the frustration. Do not debate it in front of the caller. A prolonged public dispute can expose the person and leave both the queue and the caller unattended.

sections.title: Differential effects
sections.text: The scarcity studies found effects on how Black faces were perceived and on allocations to Black recipients. They also found that people high in internal motivation to avoid prejudice gave more, not less, under scarcity. So scarcity does not affect everyone the same way. Outside those studies, this course does not claim that any specific group in DHS settings is harmed more by threat-driven judgments. The evidence for that in public agencies was not found. What the research supports is a general caution: tight resources make fair, consistent processes more important.

sections.title: Your own reactions under pressure
sections.text: Leaders feel threat too. A budget cut, a reorganization or a critical audit can make you see another unit or partner as the problem. Watch for the same signs in yourself. Look for a motive story about a group, a sense of sides, or impatience with people who need more time. When you notice it, name the pressure to yourself, then ask what specific step is failing. Modeling this is more persuasive than any instruction to staff.

sections.title: Partners and Tribal relations
sections.text: Friction between DHS units and county partners or providers can follow the same pattern. A county that is slow to respond may be short-staffed or using a different system. Ask the person or area responsible for that partnership what is known before forming a view. For matters involving a Tribal nation, work through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations. Do not speak for Native people or describe their motives.

sections.title: Designing contact that helps
sections.text: Contact works best when it lowers anxiety. That means repeated, low-stakes, shared work with a common goal, not a single event. Mixed pairs on difficult files, joint reviews of a process both teams touch and rotating meeting roles all qualify. Make sure the contact is fair. If one team always does the cleanup or the other team always leads, the contact can reinforce status gaps. Equal roles in the shared work matter.

sections.title: Measures that unite or divide
sections.text: Measures can deepen group-against-group thinking. Posting each team's error rate side by side invites blame. A shared measure, such as the percentage of files done right from start to finish, ties both teams to one result. Add a measure of what people served experience, such as time to a decision or repeat calls about the same issue. Shared measures make it easier to treat the other team as part of the same system.

sections.title: When the tension is about identity
sections.text: Some friction is not about a checklist. It is about a sense that one group's way of working, speaking or showing respect is treated as the standard. Staff may feel their competence is judged by style rather than results. Here, task talk alone is not enough. Ask what each group values in good work and what each feels is overlooked. Then agree on a standard based on outcomes, such as accuracy and timeliness, not on whose style feels normal. This keeps attention on results while taking the concern seriously.

sections.title: Putting it together
sections.text: Threat and scarcity make difference feel dangerous, even to good people. The research suggests four leader moves. Name the real pressure. Turn motive claims into questions about specific steps. Keep conflict about the work and make it safe. Build repeated, fair contact through shared work and shared measures. None of these requires anyone to be shamed. They make it easier for the team to do the right thing on a hard day.

simulation.setup: You supervise a DHS eligibility processing unit formed three months ago by merging a renewals team with an intake team. The two teams used different checklists before the merge. A policy change has doubled the backlog and overtime has been cut. People waiting on decisions are calling more often. Your role is to keep the work moving, keep both groups working as one team and protect timely decisions for the people served.

steps.situation: At the morning huddle, a respected renewals worker says, "The intake people keep dumping incomplete files on renewals. They just don't care about accuracy." Several renewals staff nod. The intake staff go quiet. You have ten minutes before phones open.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Acknowledge the backlog, then ask which files and which fields are missing, and invite intake to share what they see from their end.
choices.feedback: You name the real pressure, which lowers defensiveness. Then you move from a motive claim to a mechanism you can check. Inviting intake's view brings the missing facts into the room without asking anyone to defend their group. Research shows conflict about the task can help when people feel safe. Conflict about people hurts. This keeps it on the task.

choices.label: Say firmly that group-against-group talk is not acceptable here, then move to the next agenda item.
choices.feedback: This protects the intake staff in the moment, which matters. But it leaves the claim unexamined and the real problem unsolved. The renewals worker may feel publicly shamed and keep the view, now in side conversations. A rule against the talk without attention to the pressure behind it often drives friction underground rather than ending it.

choices.label: Let it pass. People are stressed, and you will talk with the worker privately later.
choices.feedback: This feels kind and avoids a scene before phones open. But silence from the leader can read as agreement, especially to the group being described. The intake staff hear the claim go unchallenged. Under pressure, a motive story that goes unanswered tends to harden. A short, calm redirect now costs little and prevents a larger repair later.

steps.situation: A quick joint review shows about thirty files this month lacked an income date. Intake uses the old intake checklist, which never had that field. The renewals worker says, "See, they're missing things." The intake lead replies, "Your checklist changed and nobody told intake." Voices are rising.
steps.question: How do you handle the next few minutes?

choices.label: Name it as a checklist problem both teams can fix. Ask one person from each team to draft a single checklist together and test it for two weeks.
choices.feedback: You affirm what each side got right: the field was missing, and the change was not shared. That keeps the disagreement on the task. A joint draft creates the kind of shared, equal-status work that lowers anxiety between groups. A two-week test makes the decision reversible, which reduces the stakes of disagreeing. Both groups now own the fix.

choices.label: Decide on the checklist yourself, announce it and close the discussion to protect phone time.
choices.feedback: This is fast and ends the tension, which is tempting with phones about to open. You may even pick the right checklist. But you lose a chance for the two groups to work together, and one side may hear your choice as taking sides. Use authority to set a deadline, and let both teams shape the content.

choices.label: Ask each team to send you a list of the other team's errors so you have the full picture.
choices.feedback: Gathering data sounds fair and thorough. But asking each side to document the other's mistakes frames the work as a contest. It invites people to hunt for the other group's faults instead of fixing a shared process. Relationship conflict consistently harms teams. Ask for errors by process step instead, without naming which team made them.

steps.situation: A week later, an intake worker asks to transfer out. The two groups now sit apart at lunch. A file that bounced between teams was decided late, and the person waiting called three times. The renewals worker from the huddle tells you, "This is what I was talking about."
steps.question: What do you do now?

choices.label: Meet one on one with a few people from each group. Then hold a joint review of the bounced file with clear ground rules.
choices.feedback: Individual conversations lower anxiety and surface facts people will not share in a tense group. A joint review of one real file gives both groups a shared, concrete task. Ground rules such as talk about the file, not the person, keep conflict on the work. You can also tell the person waiting what will change.

choices.label: Hold a team lunch or social event to rebuild relationships.
choices.feedback: Relationships matter, and a social event signals care. But a single event rarely changes patterns under daily pressure, and it leaves the file problem untouched. Research suggests contact helps most when it is repeated, equal and tied to a shared goal. Use the goodwill from an event to launch shared work, not to replace it.

choices.label: Reorganize the work so the two groups rarely need to interact.
choices.feedback: Separating the groups reduces visible friction, which can feel like a fix. But it removes the contact that reduces anxiety and prejudice. It also hardens the line between groups, and files that need both still bounce. Over time the group-against-group story becomes built into the structure.

steps.situation: The backlog will stay high for at least two more months. Your manager wants weekly numbers. You want the friction to stay down and decisions for people waiting to speed up.
steps.question: What do you put in place?

choices.label: Set mixed pairs on hard files and one shared measure of files done right. Track time to decision, and hold a regular slot for process concerns with your follow-up.
choices.feedback: This combines what the evidence supports. Mixed pairs create repeated, equal contact that lowers anxiety. A shared measure ties both groups to one result. Tracking time to decision keeps people served in view. A regular slot with follow-up builds the safety that makes task conflict useful. In federal agencies, good team process went with diversity becoming a strength.

choices.label: Post each group's error rate weekly to motivate improvement.
choices.feedback: Numbers feel objective, and your manager wants them. But side-by-side rates turn two groups into competitors, which feeds the threat that caused the trouble. People will defend their team's number rather than fix shared steps. Report errors by process step and use a measure both groups own together.

choices.label: Bring in a session on stereotypes and working across difference.
choices.feedback: A session can give shared language and some people will value it. But learning facts was the weakest route to less prejudice in the 2008 meta-analysis, and one session fades under daily pressure. It works best alongside the structural steps: shared work, shared measures and a safe way to raise concerns.

simulation.debrief: This case followed a pattern the research predicts. A real pressure, a doubled backlog with less overtime, turned a process gap into a story about another group's motives. The strongest path named the pressure without blaming anyone and moved from motive to mechanism, a missing field on a checklist. It kept conflict about the work, which teams can use, and away from people, which consistently harms teams. It built repeated, equal contact through shared work, the route that lowers anxiety most. It also kept two outcomes visible: staff strain and timely decisions for people served. The evidence has limits. Threat findings are largely correlational, scarcity studies are short lab experiments and randomized contact effects are smaller than the broader literature suggests.

mistakes.mistake: Treating group-against-group talk as a character problem.
mistakes.why: The comment sounds unfair, so it is natural to see the speaker as the problem. Research links such talk to perceived threat, which good people feel under pressure.
mistakes.instead: Name the pressure first, then turn the motive claim into a question about a specific step.

mistakes.mistake: Banning conflict to keep the peace.
mistakes.why: Tension is uncomfortable and slows the day. Leaders often see all conflict as harmful.
mistakes.instead: Keep disagreement about the work and make it safe. Task conflict helped performance where psychological safety was high.

mistakes.mistake: Relying on information about the other group.
mistakes.why: Teaching facts feels like the respectful, educational response. Yet knowledge was the weakest route to less prejudice.
mistakes.instead: Create repeated, equal, shared work across the line, such as mixed pairs on hard files.

mistakes.mistake: Asking a staff member to explain or defend their group.
mistakes.why: It seems like a way to bring in an insider view. It puts the person on the spot and makes one person carry a whole group.
mistakes.instead: Ask each side for facts about the work and the process, not about their group.

mistakes.mistake: Using side-by-side team numbers to motivate.
mistakes.why: Comparison feels objective and motivating. It also turns groups into competitors and raises the threat that caused the friction.
mistakes.instead: Use a shared measure both groups own, plus a measure of what people served experience.

mistakes.mistake: Opening every routine step to debate.
mistakes.why: Openness feels healthy. A study of 105 groups found open-conflict norms were not always helpful, and task disagreement hurt routine work.
mistakes.instead: Settle routine steps with one shared standard and save debate for steps that are new, unclear or causing errors.

jobAid.title: From threat to task
jobAid.use: Use when a comment about another team, partner or group of people served starts to sound like group against group.
steps: Name the real pressure out loud: backlog, cuts, change or a hard call.
Turn the motive claim into a question: which files, which step, how often?
Invite the other side's facts about the work, not about their group.
Agree on one specific, reversible fix to test, with a date to check it.
Set or restate a ground rule: talk about the file, not the person.
Plan repeated shared work across the line, with equal roles.
Track one shared measure and one measure of what people served experience.
Follow up with anyone who raised a concern, and say what changed.

media.reason: This lesson explains a mechanism, how pressure turns difference into threat, and then gives a sequence of leader moves. A single calm voice can do that without casting any group as the problem.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Imagine a unit three months after two teams were merged. The backlog has doubled. Overtime has been cut. At the morning huddle, someone says, "The other team keeps dumping incomplete files on renewals. They just don't care." A few heads nod. The other team goes quiet.

A meta-analysis of 95 samples found that several kinds of threat were linked to more negative views of other groups. Those threats included competing for resources, worrying about losing a way of doing things and simple anxiety about working with people who differ. A doubled backlog and fewer hours touch all of them.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Scarcity goes deeper than mood. In lab studies, just framing resources as scarce changed how people perceived race and how they shared resources. Nobody in those studies set out to be unfair. That is the point. Pressure can shift judgment quietly, which is why fair, consistent processes matter most when budgets are tight.

script.speaker: narrator

"Which files? Which fields were missing?" Third, invite the other side's facts. "What does intake see from their end?" Often a mechanism appears, like two teams still using two different checklists.

script.text: Now the disagreement is about the work. That matters. Across more than a hundred studies, conflict about people consistently hurt teams. script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Finally, watch your measures. Side-by-side team error rates invite blame. One shared measure, plus a measure of what people waiting experience, keeps everyone on the same side of the problem. When pressure makes difference feel like a threat, bring the team back to the task, together.

prompts: Where in your area is pressure, such as backlog, cuts or a recent change, most likely to turn into group-against-group talk?
With whom could you set up one piece of repeated shared work across a team or partner line?
By when will you replace one side-by-side comparison with a shared measure and a measure of what people served experience?

title: Common ground, and every group's blind spots
objective: Use a shared goal to bring people together without hiding real differences, and give the same honest, specific feedback to everyone on your team.
outcomes: State a shared goal and then ask each person what it looks like in practice, so different concerns stay visible.
Identify which burdens or costs a shared agreement still leaves on one group or person.
Give critical feedback that names the gap, the standard and your confidence that the person can meet it.
Check that the same work standard is applied to every staff member, using a sample of everyone's work.
Describe a strength and a blind spot in your own team's way of working without idealizing or condemning any group.

evidence.summary: A shared identity can reduce bias between groups, but groups often want different kinds of shared identity. Majority group members tend to prefer one common identity. Minority group members tend to prefer a shared identity that also keeps their own. Talking only about what people share can create false expectations that unequal treatment will not happen. On feedback, several experiments found that evaluators gave softer criticism to Black writers or minority authors, especially when they worried about appearing prejudiced. Praise was equal; criticism was withheld. In public school field experiments, critical feedback paired with high standards and assurance increased revisions and trust. Most of this evidence is from lab or school settings, and workplace studies are thin.

findings.claim: Majority group members tend to prefer one shared identity, while minority group members tend to prefer a shared identity that keeps their own.
findings.detail: Review of the common ingroup identity model, 2009. The kind of shared identity affects attitudes, whether unfair gaps are noticed, and support for change.

findings.claim: Contact focused only on commonalities led lower-power group members to expect fairer treatment than they then received.
findings.detail: Two studies, 2009: a lab experiment with groups assigned high or low power, and a survey of Israeli Arab participants linking positive contact to seeing the majority as fairer and to less support for change.

findings.claim: White evaluators gave softer feedback on an essay's content when they believed the writer was Black, but not on its mechanics.
findings.detail: Two experiments with White undergraduates, 1998.

findings.claim: Evaluators worried about appearing prejudiced gave equal praise but less criticism and higher grades to minority authors.
findings.detail: Two experiments, 2012. The effect tracked external, not internal, motivation to respond without prejudice.

findings.claim: Critical feedback paired with a note about high standards and confidence raised revision rates among African American students from an estimated 17 percent to 71 percent.
findings.detail: Randomized field experiment with 44 seventh graders in a public school, published 2014; covariate adjusted (raw 64% vs. 27%). White students showed a smaller, nonsignificant gain (87% vs. 62% adjusted). Two further experiments found better drafts and, in a low-income public high school, higher grades.

findings.claim: A widely used intercultural model warns that stressing similarity often rests on the familiar parts of one's own culture and can hide deeper differences.
findings.detail: Grounded theory, 2017 encyclopedia entry by the model's author. Not an experiment. Proposes holding similarity and difference together.

counterintuitive.headline: Holding back criticism to be kind is unequal treatment.
counterintuitive.text: Many supervisors soften or skip criticism for a staff member whose background differs from theirs, hoping to avoid seeming unfair. Experiments suggest that pattern is common. Harber (1998) found White evaluators gave softer feedback on content to writers they believed were Black. Croft and Schmader (2012) found evaluators worried about appearing prejudiced gave equal praise but less criticism and higher grades to minority authors. The person loses the information others receive. Yeager and colleagues (2014) showed a better path: specific criticism plus a clear statement of high standards and confidence. Kindness is the standard, explained, not the gap, hidden.

sections.title: Common ground helps, up to a point
sections.text: When staff disagree, a shared goal can bring them together. Safety, dignity, timely decisions and good service are goals most DHS staff share. Research on shared identity finds that seeing others as part of the same group can reduce bias. But there is a catch. Groups often want different kinds of shared identity. Majority group members tend to prefer one common identity. Minority group members tend to prefer a shared identity that also keeps their own. A shared word can also hide different meanings.

sections.title: Every group has blind spots
sections.text: Every team, shift and group has ways of working that serve it well and ways that miss things. A fast verbal handoff works when facts are settled. A written handoff helps when the next shift needs a trail. Neither group is the problem, and neither is the rescuer. The leader's job is to see both strengths and both blind spots, including those of the group the leader belongs to.

sections.title: The kindness that is not kind
sections.text: Experiments have found that evaluators often give softer criticism to people from other groups, especially when they worry about seeming prejudiced. Praise stays equal. Criticism quietly disappears. The person then lacks information that others get. Over time, that can stall their growth and surprise them at review time.

sections.title: Why the pattern is easy to miss
sections.text: Withholding rarely feels like a decision. You fix a letter yourself because it is faster. You soften a comment because the person seems new. Each choice looks kind on its own. The pattern only shows when you compare what different people were told.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: Give everyone the same honest, specific feedback, framed the same way. Name the gap and why it matters. Say plainly that you hold the whole team to this standard and that you believe the person can meet it. Then offer help or an example. In public school field experiments, this kind of feedback increased revisions and trust. Before your next round of feedback, ask yourself whether you are telling everyone the same truth.

sections.title: What shared identity research shows
sections.text: The common ingroup identity model proposes that bias falls when people see members of another group as part of one larger group. A 2009 review by Dovidio, Gaertner and Saguy found support for that idea. It also found limits. Majority group members tend to prefer a single shared identity. Minority group members tend to prefer a dual identity, a shared identity that keeps subgroup identity alive. Which version a leader chooses affects whether people notice unfair gaps and whether they support change.

sections.title: When harmony hides a gap
sections.text: Saguy and colleagues found that contact focused only on commonalities could backfire in a specific way. In a lab experiment, groups were given high or low power. When they talked only about what they had in common, low-power members expected fairer treatment than the high-power group then delivered. A survey of Israeli Arab participants found a similar pattern in daily life. For a DHS leader, the lesson is not to avoid common ground. It is to keep real differences and unequal burdens on the table while you build it.

sections.title: Turning a shared word into a plan
sections.text: When staff say they both care about safety, ask each what safety would look like. One may mean that a provider arrives on time. Another may mean that a person chooses who enters their home. Both are real. Then ask who holds which decision. A supervisor may decide how staff schedule contacts. A person receiving support may direct choices about their own life. Finally, ask which burden remains. Who would need to take time off, give up privacy or ask again if the plan fails?

sections.title: Seeing strengths and blind spots in every group
sections.text: Supervisors see different samples of each group's work. Day staff may solve problems in meetings leaders attend. Evening staff may leave careful written trails of problems they prevented. Visible work is not the same as better work. Ask each group what it is trying to protect with its way of working. Then decide what evidence should guide assignments and reviews, such as errors caught, files reopened and outcomes for people served.

sections.title: The feedback withholding pattern
sections.text: In 1998, Harber asked White undergraduates to critique an essay. When they believed the writer was Black, they gave softer feedback on the content but not on spelling and grammar. In 2012, Croft and Schmader found that evaluators gave minority and White authors equal praise. But evaluators who worried about appearing prejudiced gave minority authors less criticism and higher grades. These are lab studies with students and essays. They describe a pattern many supervisors will recognize in themselves.

sections.title: Signs you may be withholding
sections.text: A few signs suggest feedback is not reaching someone equally. You fix a person's work rather than return it. Your comments to one person are mostly praise, while others get specific corrections. A concern appears for the first time in a formal review. Or you feel relief when a hard conversation can be skipped. None of these prove bias. Each is a cue to compare what you tell different people for the same gap.

sections.title: Why it happens
sections.text: Withholding criticism usually comes from good intentions. A supervisor wants to be fair, avoid causing hurt or avoid being seen as biased. The result is unequal treatment. One person gets the full picture and another gets a partial one. The person who gets less criticism may also sense the difference and trust the praise less.

sections.title: Wise feedback
sections.text: Yeager and colleagues tested a better approach in public schools. Teachers wrote critical comments on student essays. Some essays also carried a short note saying the teacher had high standards and believed the student could meet them. Among African American students, an estimated 71 percent revised after the note, compared with 17 percent after a control note. White students showed a smaller gain that was not significant. The samples were small, but the approach is simple to use at work.

sections.title: Applying it at DHS
sections.text: Use the same three parts with every staff member. First, the specific gap: "This correction letter does not cite the requirement or the deadline." Second, the standard and your confidence: "Every letter from this team needs both, and I know you can do this well." Third, support: an example letter or a short review together. Then check yourself. Pull a sample of everyone's work and ask whether you gave the same feedback for the same gap.

sections.title: Building common ground at the same time
sections.text: Feedback and common ground support each other. When the team agrees on a shared goal, such as clear letters that providers can act on, feedback becomes about that goal rather than about the person. Name the goal in team meetings. Show examples of strong work from different reviewers, so no single style becomes the model. Then hold everyone to the same outcome.

sections.title: Limits of the research
sections.text: The shared identity studies are mostly lab experiments and surveys, and the 2009 review summarizes a large but mixed body of work. The feedback studies used students grading essays. The wise feedback experiments took place in public schools with small samples, 44 students in the first study. No workplace or government study was found that directly tests these ideas in a public agency. Applying them to DHS supervision is a reasonable inference, not a proven result. Treat them as strong guidance about a pattern to watch for, not a precise prediction.

sections.title: Differential effects, stated carefully
sections.text: The feedback findings concern Black writers or minority authors evaluated by White participants, and the wise feedback effects were largest for African American students who distrusted school. Those are verified results in those settings. This course does not claim that the same size of effect applies to every group or workplace. What can be said is that softened criticism denies information, and that pairing criticism with high standards and confidence helped most where trust was lowest.

sections.title: When common ground covers a cost
sections.text: Agreement on a goal can speed up a conversation while leaving an unequal cost in place. A team may agree that every follow-up should be booked during the first call. That works well for most people. It may not work for a person whose shifts rotate or who wants to consult someone they trust. Before you close the discussion, ask who carries the cost if the agreed plan fails. Write that remaining issue down in concrete terms and decide who owns it.

sections.title: Single versus dual identity in practice
sections.text: When you merge teams or build a cross-unit group, you choose how to talk about identity. "One team, one way" can feel inclusive to people whose way becomes the standard. It can feel like erasure to people whose way is replaced. A dual identity approach says the team shares one goal and one standard of results, while different groups bring different strengths. Name those strengths specifically. Then hold everyone to the same outcomes.

sections.title: What each group's strength can hide
sections.text: A group's strength often contains its blind spot. A team that values speed may skip steps that protect people later. A team that values thorough documentation may delay action while waiting for a full record. A group that prizes harmony may avoid naming a problem. A group that prizes directness may miss when others have stopped speaking. Ask each group to name its own blind spot first. People accept a blind spot more readily when they name it themselves.

sections.title: Whose ways become the standard
sections.text: Bennett's intercultural model warns that stressing similarity often rests on the familiar parts of one's own culture. Organizations may praise equal treatment while quietly treating one group's habits as the default. A meeting style, a writing style or a way of showing initiative can become the measure of good work without anyone deciding it should. Test a standard by asking whether it measures results or style. Keep the results. Make the style a choice.

sections.title: Coaching a supervisor who softens
sections.text: If you lead other supervisors, watch for the withholding pattern in their teams. Ask them to compare feedback across staff for the same kind of error. Frame it as a fairness check, not an accusation. Offer the three-part structure: the gap, the standard with confidence, and support. Supervisors who soften usually care a great deal about fairness. Showing them that softening creates unfairness often changes their practice quickly.

sections.title: Feedback when you fear being seen as biased
sections.text: The fear of appearing prejudiced is real, and it can push supervisors to say less. The research suggests a better use of that concern. Make your standard explicit and the same for everyone. Base feedback on specific examples. Explain why the standard matters for people served. When feedback is specific and consistent, it is easier for the person to trust it and harder for anyone to mistake it for bias.

sections.title: Asking how someone wants feedback
sections.text: People differ in how they prefer to receive feedback. Some want it in writing first. Others want a conversation. Ask each staff member privately how they prefer to receive it. Do not infer the answer from identity. A preference changes the channel and timing. It does not change the content. Everyone still gets the full, honest message.

sections.title: Receiving feedback about your own blind spots
sections.text: Leaders have blind spots too, and staff often see them first. If you want honest feedback from your team, show that criticism of your methods is welcome. Ask, "What does my review process miss?" Offer a way to answer outside the group, especially because you evaluate the people answering. Then say what you changed. A leader who takes criticism well makes it easier to give criticism well.

sections.title: When the feedback is about a cultural difference
sections.text: Sometimes the gap involves a style rooted in someone's background, such as how directly they disagree in meetings. First, ask whether the style affects results. If it does not, it is not a performance issue. If it does, describe the effect concretely and offer options. For example, a reviewer who does not challenge a provider's claim in the moment can follow up in writing the same day. The standard is the outcome, not the style.

sections.title: Partners and Tribal relations
sections.text: Common ground with county partners, providers and community groups follows the same rules. Ask what a shared goal means to each party and which costs remain. For any matter involving a Tribal nation, work through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations. Do not assume shared goals on a Tribal nation's behalf or speak for Native people.

sections.title: When the person disagrees with your feedback
sections.text: Honest feedback sometimes meets disagreement. The person may say the standard was never explained, or that others are not held to it. Treat that as information. Check whether the standard was written down and shared. Check a sample of others' work. If the person is right, say so and fix the process. If the standard holds, restate it with the reason it matters for people served. Disagreement handled this way builds trust in the feedback rather than weakening it.

sections.title: Putting it together
sections.text: Common ground is a starting point, not a finish line. Name the shared goal, then ask what it means to each person and who carries the remaining cost. See each group's strengths and blind spots, including your own group's. Give everyone the same honest, specific feedback, with high standards and real confidence. Check yourself with a sample of everyone's work. Fairness means everyone gets the truth and the support to act on it.

simulation.setup: You are a Human Services Supervisor on a DHS licensing review team. A Licensing Reviewer joined six months ago from a community organization. Their background differs from yours and from most of the team's. They are well regarded by providers. Correction order letters must cite the specific requirement and the deadline, or a provider may not know what to fix. You are deciding how to coach the reviewer and how to settle a team disagreement about follow-up methods.

steps.situation: The reviewer's draft correction letter is clear and respectful, but it does not cite the requirement or the deadline. A peer supervisor suggests, "Just fix it yourself and send it. They're new, and you don't want them to feel singled out." The letter is due today.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Meet briefly with the reviewer. Name the missing pieces and why they matter. Say every team letter needs both, express confidence and share an example.
choices.feedback: This is wise feedback. It names the gap and its consequence, states one standard for everyone and expresses real confidence. In public school experiments, this framing raised revision rates sharply where trust was lowest. It also gives the reviewer information they need for every future letter. The meeting costs a few minutes and the letter still goes out today.

choices.label: Fix the letter yourself and send it, as your peer suggests.
choices.feedback: This is tempting. It is fast, the letter is correct and the reviewer is spared discomfort. But it is the withholding pattern the research describes. Praise stays and criticism disappears. The reviewer does not learn the standard and will repeat the gap. Others on the team get corrected while this reviewer does not, which is unequal treatment.

choices.label: Send the reviewer a warm note praising the letter and suggesting they might tighten the wording a bit.
choices.feedback: The warmth is real, and the reviewer will appreciate it. But the vague suggestion hides the actual gap. Experiments found evaluators kept praise equal while softening criticism, and this note does just that. The reviewer may tighten wording and still omit the citation and deadline. Specific feedback is the kind version.

steps.situation: The reviewer revises the letter well. A week later they say quietly, "I noticed some letters from senior reviewers go out without the deadline too. Nobody seems to mention it."
steps.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Thank them, check a sample of everyone's letters against the same standard, and give the same feedback to anyone with the gap.
choices.feedback: This takes the concern seriously and tests it with evidence. If senior reviewers have the same gap, consistent feedback protects providers and shows the standard is real for everyone. It also shows the reviewer that raising a concern leads to action, which builds the trust that made wise feedback work in the research.

choices.label: Explain that senior reviewers have more experience, so you trust their judgment on when to leave details out.
choices.feedback: Experience matters, and you may believe this. But the standard exists for providers, not for reviewers. A provider without a deadline is just as confused whether a senior or new reviewer wrote the letter. Applying the rule unevenly also tells the reviewer that standards depend on status, which undercuts the feedback you just gave.

choices.label: Thank them for noticing and let the topic go for now.
choices.feedback: Thanking them is good, and you avoid a hard conversation with senior staff. But without a check, the reviewer learns that raising a concern changes nothing. The standard you set last week begins to look like it applies only to newer staff. A quick sample review would settle the question fairly.

steps.situation: Two months later, the reviewer's letters still lack citations and deadlines. A provider has complained that it did not know what to fix. At a check-in, the reviewer is surprised and says, "No one ever told me this was a problem."
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Acknowledge that you held back, give the specific feedback now with examples, state the standard and your confidence, and set a short practice plan together.
choices.feedback: Owning your part repairs trust and models the honesty you want. Then you give the full, specific message with high standards and assurance. A short practice plan offers support, not just judgment. The reviewer now has what others had all along, and the provider problem can be fixed quickly.

choices.label: Note the concern in the upcoming performance review so it is documented.
choices.feedback: Documentation matters, and the gap is real. But this turns a coaching problem you helped create into a formal mark against the reviewer. It also repeats the surprise. Feedback that arrives first in a review feels unfair and is harder to act on. Give the feedback now, with support, before anything formal.

choices.label: Explain the standard and wait until the next review cycle to address it formally, to be fair to the reviewer.
choices.feedback: Waiting shows some fairness, since the reviewer was not told. But explaining the standard once without examples or a plan may not be enough to change practice. The provider complaint also needs a response now. Pair the explanation with examples, a clear standard, your confidence and a short practice plan.

steps.situation: At a team meeting, the group splits. Some reviewers prefer quick phone follow-up with providers. Others insist on full written follow-up every time. Each side says, "This is about safety." The reviewer you coached is in the written-follow-up group.
steps.question: How do you find common ground?

choices.label: Ask each side what safety looks like for people in licensed settings. Name the shared goal and each concern, then set one outcome standard using both strengths.
choices.feedback: This builds common ground without hiding differences. Asking what safety means turns a shared word into concrete concerns, such as speed of correction and a clear trail. Naming each side's strength fits a dual identity approach, one goal with different contributions. Setting the standard on outcomes, not style, keeps the decision fair to both groups.

choices.label: Remind everyone that the team shares one goal and adopt the method most reviewers already use.
choices.feedback: This sounds unifying and ends the debate. But it treats the majority's habit as the shared standard without testing it. The research suggests one common identity often appeals most to the group whose way becomes the default. The other group may feel erased, and real safety concerns from their method may be lost.

choices.label: Let each reviewer use the method they prefer.
choices.feedback: This avoids conflict and respects both styles. But providers may get inconsistent follow-up, and the team never learns which method protects people better in which cases. A shared standard for outcomes, with room for different methods to meet it, keeps the respect and adds accountability.

simulation.debrief: This case tested two related habits. The first was feedback. The tempting path, fixing the letter quietly or softening the message, matches what experiments found: praise stays equal while criticism disappears for people from other groups. The stronger path gave specific feedback with a clear standard and real confidence, the wise feedback approach tested in public schools. It then checked that the same standard applied to everyone, including senior staff. The second habit was common ground. Naming a shared goal helped, but only after asking what safety meant to each side and setting a standard on outcomes, not on the majority's style. The research is mostly from labs and schools, so its workplace use is an inference. The core lesson holds: fairness means everyone gets the truth and support to act on it.

mistakes.mistake: Quietly fixing someone's work instead of telling them.
mistakes.why: It is fast and spares discomfort, especially when you fear seeming unfair. Experiments found this kind of withholding is common across group lines.
mistakes.instead: Name the gap, state the standard and your confidence, and offer an example.

mistakes.mistake: Giving warm, vague feedback to some people and specific feedback to others.
mistakes.why: Supervisors want to encourage people who seem new or different. Praise stays equal while criticism softens, so the gap is hard to notice.
mistakes.instead: Use the same three-part feedback for everyone and check a sample of everyone's work.

mistakes.mistake: Declaring "one team, one way" to end a disagreement.
mistakes.why: It sounds inclusive. Research shows majority members tend to prefer a single identity, often because their way becomes the standard.
mistakes.instead: Name the shared goal and each group's strength, then set one standard for outcomes.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming a shared word means a shared plan.
mistakes.why: Agreement on words like safety or dignity feels like progress. It can hide different meanings and unequal costs.
mistakes.instead: Ask each person what the goal looks like in practice and who carries the cost if the plan fails.

mistakes.mistake: Inferring someone's feedback preference from their identity.
mistakes.why: It can seem considerate. It still replaces the person's answer with a guess.
mistakes.instead: Ask each person privately how they prefer to receive feedback. Keep the content the same.

jobAid.title: Same truth, same support
jobAid.use: Use before giving feedback or settling a disagreement where people bring different backgrounds or ways of working.
steps: Write the specific gap and why it matters for people served.
State the standard you hold everyone to, in one sentence.
Add a sincere line of confidence that the person can meet it.
Offer an example, a model or a short practice session.
Check a sample of everyone's work: would you give the same feedback for the same gap?
In a disagreement, ask what the shared goal looks like to each person.
Ask who carries the cost if the agreed plan fails.
Set the standard on outcomes, not on whose style feels normal.

media.reason: Withheld feedback looks different from each side. A supervisor and a reviewer talking it through show the good intention behind softening. They also show the cost of receiving less.

script.speaker: male
script.text: I want to start with an apology. Your last three letters were missing the requirement citation and the deadline. I fixed them myself and never told you.

script.speaker: female
script.text: I wondered why my letters came back changed. I thought maybe it was just style. Why didn't you say something?

script.speaker: male
script.text: Honestly, I didn't want you to feel singled out. You were new, and you came from a different kind of work than most of the team. I worried you'd hear it as unfair.

script.speaker: female
script.text: I understand the intention. But it meant I was the only one not getting the real information. Everyone else learned the standard. I didn't, and then a provider complained.

script.speaker: male
script.text: That's exactly the pattern researchers have found. In experiments, evaluators gave people from other groups the same praise, but less criticism. Criticism just quietly disappeared.

script.speaker: female
script.text: And from my side, the praise starts to feel less trustworthy. If you never hear what's wrong, how do you know the good comments are real?

script.speaker: male
script.text: So here is the full message. Every correction letter needs the specific requirement and the deadline. Without both, a provider may not know what to fix or by when. I hold every reviewer to that standard.

script.speaker: female
script.text: That's clear. Thank you.

script.speaker: male
script.text: And I mean this part too. Providers already trust your letters because they're clear and respectful. I'm confident you can add these two pieces easily. Here's an example letter, if it helps.

script.speaker: female
script.text: That combination helps. The standard, plus knowing you think I can meet it. Can I ask one more thing? Some senior reviewers' letters miss the deadline too.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Fair question. I'll pull a sample of everyone's letters this week and give the same feedback to anyone with the gap. The standard isn't fair if it only applies to newer staff.

script.speaker: female
script.text: That would mean a lot. And if you ever want feedback on how you give feedback, I'm glad to tell you what I notice.

script.speaker: male
script.text: I'd like that. It seems only right to take the same medicine I'm handing out.

prompts: Whose work have you been quietly fixing or softly correcting, and what specific feedback have you not yet given?
With whom could you test a shared goal by asking what it looks like in practice and who carries the remaining cost?
By when will you review a sample of everyone's work to check that you give the same feedback for the same gap?
