title: Your own culture, made visible
objective: Name the unwritten rules of your team, check whether people actually hold them, and make the ones that affect access, decisions and opportunity explicit.
outcomes: List at least five unwritten rules in your team, such as how decisions are signaled, how opportunities are offered and how disagreement is shown.
Trace one unwritten rule to the reward or penalty that keeps it in place.
Check whether a norm is actually shared, using a quick, anonymous team check, before assuming it is.
Turn an unwritten route to an opportunity into written criteria, set before candidates are known, and shared on every channel.
Explain a team habit to a newcomer plainly, so they do not have to decode it.

evidence.summary: Culture is hard to see from inside it. People perceive their own culture in fine detail and tend to treat it as the normal way things are. Research shows unwritten norms can quietly disadvantage people who did not grow up with them. In university studies, making a hidden norm visible, or teaching how background shapes experience, closed achievement gaps. Hiring experiments show that when criteria are unwritten, people redefine merit to fit the candidate they prefer, and that setting criteria first removed the bias. A field experiment found most people privately disagreed with a norm they believed others held. Direct studies of unwritten rules inside government agencies were not found, so applying this to DHS is an inference.

findings.claim: In a field experiment, 87 percent of participants privately supported a practice they wrongly believed most peers opposed, and correcting that belief changed behavior.
findings.detail: Field experiment with 500 married men in Riyadh, 2018 working paper, published 2020. Correcting beliefs raised sign-ups for a job-matching service from 23 percent by 9 points. In a national survey of about 1,500, 92 percent underestimated peers' support.

findings.claim: Universities' unwritten emphasis on independence disadvantaged first-generation students, and framing the setting around interdependence removed the performance gap.
findings.detail: Four studies, 2012: a survey of administrators, a longitudinal student survey and two experiments at a private and a public university.

findings.claim: A one-hour session showing how background shapes experience eliminated the gap in year-end grades between first-generation and continuing-generation students.
findings.detail: Randomized trial with 168 incoming college students, 2014. First-generation students sought campus resources more, which explained the gain.

findings.claim: When hiring criteria were unwritten, people redefined merit to fit the candidate they preferred; committing to criteria first eliminated the bias.
findings.detail: Three experiments on gender-stereotyped jobs, 2005.

findings.claim: Organizational culture types were positively related to employee attitudes and performance, but the popular framework behind them was only partly supported.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 84 studies and 94 samples, 2011, using the Competing Values Framework.

findings.claim: On average, Minnesota ranked 6th of 49 states for agreeableness and 44th for openness to new experience.
findings.detail: Analysis of five samples totaling over 1.5 million people, 2013; Minnesota sample of 38,597. Ranks computed from the appendix table. Volunteer online samples; averages, not individuals.

findings.claim: A widely used intercultural model holds that people see their own culture in much finer detail than others' and experience it as more central to reality.
findings.detail: Grounded theory, 2017 encyclopedia entry by the model's author. Not an experiment.

counterintuitive.headline: Most people may privately disagree with the unwritten rule everyone follows.
counterintuitive.text: Leaders often assume a team habit continues because people like it. A field experiment by Bursztyn, González and Yanagizawa-Drott (2018) found a different pattern. Among 500 participants, 87 percent privately supported a practice, yet most believed their peers opposed it. When researchers showed people what their peers actually thought, behavior changed, and the change lasted months. The setting was very different from DHS, but the mechanism is general. An unwritten rule can survive because everyone thinks everyone else holds it. Asking quietly and sharing the answer can free a team to change.

sections.title: The water you do not notice
sections.text: Every team has rules no one wrote down. How you show you disagree. Whether a meeting starts on time. What "that should work" really means. Who gets asked to lead a project. If you have worked somewhere a long time, these rules feel like common sense. That is what makes them hard to see. A widely used intercultural model holds that people see their own culture in fine detail and experience it as the normal way things are.

sections.title: Why it matters for access
sections.text: Unwritten rules are not bad in themselves. Many carry real wisdom. But they work best for the people who already know them. In university studies, hidden expectations about independence put first-generation students at a disadvantage. When the expectations were made visible, the gap closed. At DHS, the same thing can happen with stretch assignments, meeting norms or how a new colleague reads a polite reply.

sections.title: A surprising finding
sections.text: Unwritten rules sometimes survive because everyone thinks everyone else holds them. In one field experiment, most people privately disagreed with a norm they believed their peers supported. When they learned what peers really thought, behavior changed. Your team may be keeping a habit that few people actually want.

sections.title: Where to look first
sections.text: Start where unwritten rules carry the most weight. Look at how opportunities are offered, how decisions are signaled and how disagreement is shown. Look at what gets praised as initiative or professionalism. These are the places where a newcomer who has not learned the code can lose out without anyone intending it.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: Pick one unwritten rule that affects opportunity or decisions. Write down how it really works today. Ask a quick, anonymous question about whether people want to keep it. Then make the route explicit: what the opportunity is, who can ask, what evidence counts and when the decision is made. Share it on every channel, including shifts and staff who work remotely.

sections.title: Why your own culture is hard to see
sections.text: Bennett's widely used intercultural model makes a simple point. The categories people have for their own culture are far more detailed than the ones they have for others. You can likely tell apart many kinds of a local polite "no." You may have far fewer ways to read a "no" from someone who learned a different code. That gap is not a moral failing. It is how culture works. It does mean your sense of "normal" is a poor guide to how a habit lands for someone else.

sections.title: A Minnesota example
sections.text: A large study of personality across U.S. states found Minnesota's average was among the highest for agreeableness, ranking 6th of 49. Its average for openness to new experience ranked 44th. These are averages from volunteer online samples. They say nothing reliable about any one Minnesotan, and many Minnesotans differ from them. But they help explain why a team in Minnesota might value smooth agreement and established ways, sometimes without noticing it.

sections.title: How hidden norms create unequal access
sections.text: Stephens and colleagues studied a hidden norm in universities: an emphasis on independence. Administrators' own descriptions showed the emphasis. Students from working-class backgrounds, who often came with more interdependent norms, earned lower grades when the mismatch was strong. In experiments at a private and a public university, framing the setting around interdependence removed the performance gap. In a later randomized trial with 168 students, a one-hour panel about how background shapes the college experience eliminated the gap in year-end grades. The students who gained sought out resources more. Once the rules were visible, they used them.

sections.title: When criteria stay unwritten
sections.text: Uhlmann and Cohen ran three hiring experiments. When criteria were not set in advance, participants decided that whatever qualifications their preferred candidate had were the important ones. When participants committed to criteria first, the bias disappeared. In a DHS unit, the same thing can happen with acting assignments, project leads or training slots. Suppose the route is "mention it to the director after a meeting." Then the people who know that rule, attend and feel comfortable approaching a director get chosen. Others never knew they could ask.

sections.title: Norms that no one may want
sections.text: Bursztyn and colleagues studied a social norm in a field experiment with 500 participants. Most privately supported a practice but believed most peers opposed it. When they learned their peers' real views, more of them acted on their own. The setting was very different from a state agency, so treat this as evidence of a general mechanism. Teams can keep habits, like making decisions in hallway conversations after meetings, because each person assumes the others like it.

sections.title: Culture and performance
sections.text: Organizational culture matters for results. A meta-analysis of 84 studies found that several culture types were positively linked to employee attitudes and performance. It also found the popular framework for sorting cultures only partly held up. The practical lesson is to spend less effort labeling your team's culture. Spend more on the specific rules that shape who gets heard, chosen and informed.

sections.title: Applying it in DHS work
sections.text: Start with three questions. How does someone get a stretch assignment here? How do people know a decision has been made? How does someone safely disagree with a supervisor? Ask a longtime staff member and a newer one. Compare the answers. Where they differ, you have found an unwritten rule. Then decide whether the rule serves the work. If it affects access or decisions, write it down and share it widely. If it is harmless, explain it to newcomers plainly.

sections.title: Questions that surface hidden rules
sections.text: Some questions reliably bring unwritten rules into view. What did you wish someone had told you in your first month? What do people get praised for here that is never written down? When someone disagrees with a supervisor, how do they do it? What happens to a person who breaks that pattern? Ask these in one-on-one conversations, where people speak more freely. Listen for the same rule described in different words.

sections.title: Reading an informal phrase both ways
sections.text: Consider a supervisor who ends a meeting with "That should work." A longtime colleague may hear polite hesitation. A newcomer may note it as approval and move ahead. Neither is wrong. The phrase carries two meanings, and only insiders know which one applies. The fix is simple. State decisions plainly: "I approve this," or "I am not ready to decide; I will tell you by Friday." Offer a private route to question it. Plain and kind can go together.

sections.title: Limits of the evidence
sections.text: No study was found that measures unwritten rules inside a government agency and tests a fix. The evidence comes from universities, hiring experiments and a field experiment abroad. The university studies are strong but specific to college settings, and the difference-education trial had 168 students. The hiring experiments used gender-stereotyped jobs in a lab. The misperceived-norm experiment took place in a very different society. Together they support a clear mechanism: hidden rules favor insiders, and making rules visible helps others use them. How large the effect would be in a DHS unit is not known.

sections.title: Locating the reward or penalty
sections.text: An unwritten rule lasts because something rewards following it or penalizes breaking it. To study your team's culture, find a real example. Who was praised as showing initiative last quarter, and what did they do? Who was seen as "not a team player," and why? If initiative means approaching a director uninvited, people who learned that this is overstepping will be read as less motivated. The reward shows you the rule. Once you can see it, you can decide whether it measures what matters.

sections.title: Majority culture without stereotypes
sections.text: It is worth asking whether long-dominant expectations in Minnesota workplaces shape what your agency rewards as professionalism or cooperation. That is a question about institutions, not individuals. Any one white Minnesotan may hold quite different expectations, and many staff of every background follow these norms easily. Avoid statements about what any group of people is like. Instead, look at specific rules and their effects. Ask who learned the rule early and who had to learn it on the job.

sections.title: Not every rule should go
sections.text: Making culture visible is not the same as discarding it. Warmth, modesty, careful consensus and politeness can be real strengths. The goal is to keep what serves the work and the people served, and to change what blocks access. A useful test is whether the rule measures results or style. A rule about getting accurate decisions out on time measures results. A rule about how one should sound when disagreeing measures style. Keep results standards firm. Where a style truly does not affect results, let people choose their own.

sections.title: When longtime staff feel criticized
sections.text: Naming a team's unwritten rules can feel like an accusation to people who built the team. They may hear that their way is wrong. Say clearly that every team has unwritten rules and that most started for good reasons. Ask longtime staff to explain why a rule began. Their history often shows what the rule protects. Then ask whether it still does. People are more willing to change a rule when they helped explain it.

sections.title: Checking whether a norm is shared
sections.text: Before changing or defending a norm, find out whether people actually hold it. A quick, anonymous question at a team meeting can do this, such as "Should decisions about assignments be announced in writing?" Share the result with the team. The misperceived-norm research suggests the answer may surprise everyone. Do not collect names or personal details. The point is to show the team what it already thinks.

sections.title: Setting criteria before candidates
sections.text: For any opportunity, write the criteria before you know who will apply. State what the opportunity is, who is eligible, how to express interest, what evidence counts and when decisions will be made. Post it on every channel, including evening shifts and staff who work remotely. Then compare who expressed interest with who usually gets chosen. If new names appear, the old route was screening people out. The hiring experiments found that committing to criteria first removed the bias.

sections.title: Explaining a rule to a newcomer
sections.text: Some unwritten rules are harmless but confusing, such as how long a meeting runs past its end time or how people signal that they need help. Tell newcomers directly. A short, plain explanation saves weeks of guessing. It also signals that asking about the rules is welcome. The difference-education trial suggests that explaining how background shapes experience can help people use resources they would otherwise miss.

sections.title: Differential effects
sections.text: The university studies found hidden norms disadvantaged first-generation students, and making them visible closed the gap without harming others. That is a verified result in that setting. This course does not claim that any specific racial, disability or other group in DHS is harmed by particular team rules. That evidence was not found. What can be said is simpler. People who did not learn a rule early are the most likely to miss it. That includes newcomers and people from other regions or work backgrounds.

sections.title: Partners and Tribal relations
sections.text: Partners have their own unwritten rules. A county or provider may signal decisions, urgency or disagreement differently. Ask the person or area responsible for that partnership what is known. For matters involving a Tribal nation, work through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations. Do not interpret a Tribal nation's practices or speak for Native people.

sections.title: Your own habits as a leader
sections.text: Leaders set many unwritten rules without meaning to. When you praise quick replies, staff learn that speed matters more than care. When you decide in hallway conversations, staff learn that being in the hallway matters. Ask a trusted colleague and a newer staff member what they think your unwritten rules are. Listen without defending. Then pick one habit to make explicit or change.

sections.title: When the rule is in a form or letter
sections.text: Unwritten rules also live in documents. A notice may assume the reader knows which hours apply, what a term means or that silence counts as agreement. A planning form may assume one picture of independence or family roles. Read a document as a newcomer would. Ask what the reader must already know to act on it. Then say it plainly.

sections.title: Putting it together
sections.text: Your own culture is the water you swim in. You see it least because you know it best. The research suggests three leader moves. Find the rules by comparing how insiders and newcomers describe the same process. Check whether people actually hold them, because many may not. Make the rules that affect access and decisions explicit, with criteria set in advance and shared on every channel. Keep the strengths. Change the barriers. Start with one route to opportunity this quarter. A single visible change shows the team that naming a rule leads somewhere.

simulation.setup: You supervise a DSD policy unit. Short acting assignments and project leads go to people who mention their interest to the director after the monthly all-staff meeting. Longtime staff describe the process as open to anyone. A Policy Analyst joined from another state four months ago. They work remotely three days a week, have strong reviews and ask why they never hear about these openings. You want fair access and a team that works well together.

steps.situation: The analyst says, "I keep hearing someone got a project lead, but I never saw it posted." A longtime Senior Policy Specialist nearby says kindly, "Everyone knows you just mention it to the director after the meeting."
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Treat this as an unwritten rule. Ask several staff, longtime and newer, how assignments really happen, then plan written criteria and an open process.
choices.feedback: You have spotted a hidden route to opportunity, and you start by learning how it really works. Comparing insiders and newcomers shows where the rule lives. Hiring experiments found that unwritten criteria let people redefine merit to fit the candidate they prefer. Setting criteria in advance removed that bias. You are fixing the route, not just helping one person through it.

choices.label: Coach the analyst on how and when to approach the director.
choices.feedback: This helps the analyst right away, and it is a kind act. But it leaves the route intact. Others who work remotely, work evenings or learned that approaching a director uninvited is overstepping will still miss out. The university studies showed that making the rule visible to everyone, not just one person, closed the gap.

choices.label: Reassure the analyst that the process is open to anyone and encourage them to speak up more.
choices.feedback: This is what the longtime staff sincerely believe. But a process open in theory can still be closed in practice. It depends on attending one meeting and knowing an unwritten rule. Telling the analyst to speak up puts the burden on the person with the least information. It also suggests the problem is their confidence, not the route.

steps.situation: Your conversations turn up more unwritten rules. "That should work" often means hesitation. Real decisions often happen in hallway talk after meetings. The Senior Policy Specialist says, a bit hurt, "So now being polite is a problem?"
steps.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Say that every team has unwritten rules and most started for good reasons. Ask the specialist why the habits began, and invite each person to name one rule that helped them and one that might confuse a newcomer.
choices.feedback: You lower defensiveness by treating culture as normal rather than wrong. Asking why a rule began often reveals what it protects, such as harmony or respect for authority. Inviting everyone to name a helpful rule and a confusing one keeps the strengths visible. People are more open to change when they helped explain the rule.

choices.label: Explain that the team's indirect style is excluding people and needs to change.
choices.feedback: You may be right about the effect, but this framing condemns the team's culture. The specialist hears that their way of showing respect is the problem. Defensiveness rises, and people may comply outwardly while keeping the hallway habits. Focus on specific rules and their effects, and keep warmth and politeness as strengths.

choices.label: Reassure the specialist and drop the topic to keep the peace.
choices.feedback: Keeping the peace protects a valued colleague, and that matters. But dropping the topic leaves the hidden routes in place, and the analyst and others still miss out. You can reassure the specialist that politeness is a strength while continuing to make decisions and opportunities explicit.

steps.situation: The analyst approaches the director and gets a project lead. A month later, another opening goes to someone who mentioned it after the meeting. Two staff who work evenings and a newer coworker say they never knew it existed.
steps.question: What do you do now?

choices.label: Before the next opening, write criteria with the director, post them on every channel and set a date for decisions.
choices.feedback: You turn the hidden route into a visible one. Writing criteria before candidates are known follows the hiring research, where committing in advance removed bias. Posting on every channel reaches evening and remote staff. A set decision date lets everyone plan. You can then compare who expressed interest with who usually gets chosen.

choices.label: Rotate future assignments through the team in alphabetical order.
choices.feedback: Rotation is transparent and easy to explain, and it does open access. But it ignores fit and readiness, which some assignments need. It may also frustrate staff who want to develop in a specific area. Written criteria with an open interest process keep both fairness and fit.

choices.label: Keep the current approach, since it rewards initiative.
choices.feedback: Initiative is worth rewarding. But this route measures something else: knowing an unwritten rule, attending one meeting and feeling comfortable approaching a director. The evening staff and the newer coworker showed no lack of initiative. They lacked information. Define initiative by actions everyone can see and take.

steps.situation: You suspect the hallway decision habit continues mainly because people think others like it. You plan to raise it at the next team meeting.
steps.question: How do you check whether the norm is actually shared?

choices.label: Ask one quick anonymous question, such as whether decisions should be announced in writing, share the result with the team and then decide on a change together.
choices.feedback: This tests the norm before you defend or change it. The misperceived-norm research found most people privately disagreed with a norm they thought peers held. Sharing the result shows the team what it already thinks. Deciding together builds ownership. No names or personal details are collected.

choices.label: Ask in the open meeting whether anyone has concerns about how decisions are shared.
choices.feedback: This is direct and respectful. But in a team that values smooth agreement, few people may speak up against a habit in front of colleagues and the director. Silence would look like support. An anonymous question gives a truer picture, and the open discussion can follow.

choices.label: Leave the habit alone, since no one has complained.
choices.feedback: No complaints can feel like a sign that things are fine. But the research suggests people often stay quiet because they think everyone else supports the norm. Newcomers may not even know the habit exists. A quick check costs little and may reveal that the team is ready for a change.

simulation.debrief: This case began with a sincere belief: the process is open to anyone. It was open in theory but not in practice. The strongest path treated it as an unwritten rule and learned how it really worked by comparing longtime and newer staff. It respected the reasons behind the team's habits while making the rules that affect access explicit. Writing criteria before candidates were known follows hiring experiments where that step removed bias. Sharing the route on every channel reached evening and remote staff. Checking the norm with a quick anonymous question follows field research showing people often misread what their peers want. The evidence comes from universities, labs and a field experiment abroad, so its size in a DHS unit is unknown. The mechanism is clear: hidden rules favor insiders, and visible rules help everyone.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming a process is open because no one is formally excluded.
mistakes.why: Longtime staff know the route and see it working for them. People see their own culture in fine detail and treat it as normal.
mistakes.instead: Ask newer staff and insiders how the process really works, and compare the answers.

mistakes.mistake: Coaching individuals through a hidden rule instead of changing it.
mistakes.why: It solves the problem in front of you and feels supportive. The route still screens out everyone else.
mistakes.instead: Make the route explicit: criteria set in advance, shared on every channel, with a decision date.

mistakes.mistake: Condemning the team's culture.
mistakes.why: When a rule causes harm, it is tempting to blame the whole style. That makes people defensive and hides real strengths.
mistakes.instead: Name specific rules and their effects. Keep strengths like warmth and politeness.

mistakes.mistake: Treating silence as agreement.
mistakes.why: No complaints feels reassuring. People often stay quiet because they believe others support the norm.
mistakes.instead: Ask a quick anonymous question and share the result before deciding.

mistakes.mistake: Explaining culture by describing groups of people.
mistakes.why: Generalizations feel like useful shortcuts. State averages say nothing reliable about any one person.
mistakes.instead: Describe rules and their effects, not people. Ask who learned the rule early and who did not.

jobAid.title: Find it, check it, write it
jobAid.use: Use when a team habit, phrase or route to opportunity may work differently for insiders and newcomers.
steps: Ask a longtime and a newer colleague the same question: how does this really work here?
Where the answers differ, name the unwritten rule in one sentence.
Find the reward or penalty that keeps the rule in place.
Ask why the rule began and what it protects.
Check whether people want to keep it with one quick anonymous question.
If it affects access or decisions, write the criteria before candidates are known.
Share the route on every channel, including evening and remote staff, with a decision date.
Explain harmless rules to newcomers plainly.

media.reason: Unwritten rules look different from inside and outside. A longtime staff member and a newcomer talking honestly can show both views, which one narrator cannot.

With which longtime colleague and which newer colleague will you compare how that route really works?

title: Patterns of difference, not profiles
objective: Use cultural patterns as a source of better questions about the person in front of you, never as a prediction of what that person thinks or wants.
outcomes: Explain in plain terms why national and group averages say little about one person, using the within-country variation finding.
Replace a guess about a person's communication style with two or three direct questions about the decision at hand.
Turn a vague time word such as soon into a specific date and check whether it works for the person.
Separate a real language access need, met by a professional interpreter, from an assumption about culture.
Coach a team member who relies on a cultural tip sheet toward a question-based approach without dismissing their knowledge.

evidence.summary: Culture research describes groups well and individuals poorly. In a meta-analysis of 558 studies, about 80 percent of the variation in work values sat inside countries rather than between them. Occupation and income level often predicted values better than nationality. Several famous contrasts, such as Americans being less collectivistic than Japanese or Korean people, did not hold up in meta-analysis. Imagining another person's view does not make you more accurate about it; asking does. Language barriers are different: professional interpreters measurably improve the quality of services. The honest limit is that most of this evidence comes from surveys and lab studies, not DHS settings, and no study shows that teaching country profiles improves service to individuals.

findings.claim: About 80 percent of variation in work-related cultural values lies within countries, not between them.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 558 studies across 32 countries using Hofstede's four dimensions, 2016. Individualism: 16.6 percent between countries. Power distance: 20.8 percent between countries, while occupation accounted for 50.1 percent.

findings.claim: European Americans were not more individualistic than African Americans or Latinos, and not less collectivistic than Japanese or Korean participants.
findings.detail: Meta-analyses of cross-national and within-US studies, Psychological Bulletin, 2002. Effects on attribution and thinking style were large; effects on self-concept were moderate.

findings.claim: Across dozens of countries, people agree more than they disagree about which values matter most.
findings.detail: Three large datasets, 2011: 67 countries (N = 41,968), 19 European countries (N = 42,359) and 62 countries (N = 84,887). Autonomy, relatedness and competence values ranked high almost everywhere.

findings.claim: Individual cultural values predict work outcomes modestly, with an average effect of about rho = 0.18.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 598 studies and more than 200,000 people, 2010. Values predicted job performance and turnover less well than personality and demographics, and predicted commitment better. Effects were stronger in culturally tighter countries.

findings.claim: Imagining another person's perspective did not improve accuracy about their thoughts and feelings; asking them did.
findings.detail: 25 experiments, 2018. Perspective taking sometimes reduced accuracy. Getting the perspective through conversation improved it.

findings.claim: Country labels of high-context and low-context communication rest on thin empirical support.
findings.detail: Systematic review of research using Hall's concept, 2011. The authors question whether national classifications rest on rigorous findings.

findings.claim: Treating culture as a list of group traits invites stereotyping; asking what matters to this person is the better routine.
findings.detail: Expert analysis in PLoS Medicine, 2006, proposing a six-step explanatory models approach. Argument, not an outcome study.

findings.claim: Cultural competence training shows moderate evidence of better staff outcomes and access, but weaker evidence for outcomes of the people served.
findings.detail: Systematic review of 19 reviews, 2000 to 2012, each covering 5 to 38 studies. Many studies relied on self-report. Health and human services.

findings.claim: Professional interpreters were associated with better care than ad hoc interpreters such as family or untrained staff.
findings.detail: Systematic review of 28 studies, 2007. Benefits covered communication errors, understanding, use of services, outcomes and satisfaction. Health and human services.

counterintuitive.headline: Some of the best-known cultural contrasts disappear in the data.
counterintuitive.text: Many trainings teach that Americans are individualists and East Asians are collectivists. A meta-analysis by Oyserman, Coon and Kemmelmeier in 2002 found European Americans were not less collectivistic than Japanese or Korean participants. They were also not more individualistic than African Americans or Latinos. Some differences were real and large, such as in how people explain events. But the headline contrast that fills slide decks did not hold. The lesson is not that culture is unimportant. It is that a famous pattern can be wrong even about averages, and averages never describe the person on your phone line.

sections.title: Groups, not people
sections.text: Culture research is good at describing groups. It is poor at predicting any one person. A meta-analysis of 558 studies across 32 countries found that about 80 percent of the variation in work values sits inside countries, not between them. Occupation and income level often predicted values better than nationality did. So a person's country, language or background tells you very little about how this person communicates today. That does not make patterns useless. A pattern can widen the list of possibilities you keep in mind. Someone might prefer to decide with family, avoid saying no to an authority, or want a fast answer alone. The pattern becomes harmful when it shrinks that list to one guess.

sections.title: Why the guess feels right
sections.text: When a person speaks softly or says yes several times, your mind fills in a meaning. It feels like empathy. Research says it is often wrong. In 25 experiments, people told to imagine another person's view did not become more accurate about that person. Sometimes they became less accurate. The one approach that worked was asking. A tip sheet about a culture is a form of imagining. It hands you a ready-made guess and makes the guess feel informed.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: Ask about the specific decision instead of predicting it. Three questions cover most situations. Who would you like involved when you look at the options? How would you like to let me know what you decide? What date would work for you, and is that realistic? Replace words like soon or later with a real date. Then check it. If language is a barrier, offer a professional interpreter rather than relying on a relative or a bilingual coworker. That step has evidence behind it. A guess about culture does not.

sections.title: What to take into your next conversation
sections.text: Keep patterns as questions in your head, not conclusions on a form. When you notice yourself thinking people from there usually, stop and ask this person instead. Their answer is the only data that fits them.

sections.title: What the averages actually show
sections.text: Three large bodies of research point the same way. Taras, Steel and Kirkman pooled 558 studies of work values in 32 countries. About 80 percent of the variation was within countries. For individualism, only 16.6 percent of the variation was between countries. For power distance, the comfort people have with unequal authority, country explained 20.8 percent. Occupation explained 50.1 percent and socioeconomic status 32.2 percent. In plain terms, a licensing investigator and a call-line worker from the same country may differ more than two investigators from different countries. Fischer and Schwartz studied value priorities in three datasets covering up to 67 countries and more than 160,000 people. They found more agreement than disagreement across countries. Values linked to autonomy, close relationships and competence ranked high nearly everywhere. Oyserman and colleagues tested the classic individualism and collectivism contrast in meta-analysis. Some expected differences appeared, but European Americans were not less collectivistic than Japanese or Korean participants.

sections.title: How much culture predicts at work
sections.text: Culture still matters. A meta-analysis of 598 studies and more than 200,000 people found that individual cultural values do relate to work outcomes. The average effect was modest, about rho = 0.18. Values predicted commitment and helping behavior better than personality did. They predicted performance, absence and turnover less well than personality and demographics. Effects were stronger in culturally tight countries, where norms are strict and widely enforced. So culture is one influence among many. It is a reason to stay curious, not a shortcut to an answer.

sections.title: Why perspective taking misleads
sections.text: Most people believe that imagining themselves in another's position makes them understand that person. Eyal, Steffel and Epley tested this in 25 experiments. Perspective taking reduced some self-centered bias, but it did not supply accurate information. In some studies it lowered accuracy. Only getting the perspective directly, through conversation, improved accuracy. A cultural tip sheet works like perspective taking. It gives you a confident picture of what someone probably thinks. The confidence is the risk. It makes you less likely to ask.

sections.title: Language access is not a cultural profile
sections.text: One difference between people is concrete and checkable: the language in which they can understand complex information. A systematic review of 28 studies found that professional interpreters were linked to fewer communication errors, better understanding and better outcomes than ad hoc interpreters. Family members and bilingual coworkers are ad hoc interpreters. They may be warm and well meaning. They are still more likely to omit, soften or change content. Offering a professional interpreter answers a real need. Assuming how someone communicates because of the language they speak is a different act entirely.

sections.title: Turning patterns into questions
sections.text: Use what you know about patterns to widen your questions. If you know some people prefer to decide with family, ask: who would you like involved? Do not assume the answer. If you know directness can drop when one person holds authority, make disagreement easy: what part of this does not work for you? If you know time words vary in meaning, name the date. Instead of soon, say by Friday the 14th. Then ask whether that date works and what would make it hard. Each question gives the person room to correct you. Each guess takes that room away.

sections.title: A quick test for any cultural claim
sections.text: When someone shares a claim about how a group communicates, run three checks. First, where did it come from: a measured study, a training slide or one memorable case? Second, what does it predict about this person, and how would you know if it were wrong? Third, what question would let the person tell you directly? If you cannot answer the second check, the claim is a guess. If the third check has an easy answer, ask the question and set the claim aside. This test keeps useful knowledge in play without letting it decide for anyone.

sections.title: Applying it in DHS work
sections.text: On a call line, a caller who says yes several times may mean I understand, I agree, or I am being polite while I think. Read back the key step and ask what they will do next. In eligibility work, confirm deadlines in writing and in the person's preferred language. In licensing or investigations, a provider's quiet manner is not evidence of agreement or of hiding something. In your own team, a staff member from any background may avoid disagreeing with you in a group. Ask for concerns in more than one way, including in writing or one-on-one. In each case the move is the same: replace the inference with a question, and make it easy to answer honestly.

sections.title: Where patterns earn their place
sections.text: Patterns are not worthless. Oyserman and colleagues found large group differences in how people explain events and in thinking style. Taras and colleagues found cultural values predict commitment better than personality does. And for uncertainty avoidance, country still beat occupation as a predictor. Patterns are useful for planning at the level of a program. They can tell you that some people may want family involved, so you design meetings that make family involvement easy to arrange. They can tell you that some people may hesitate to question an official, so you build in private ways to raise concerns. Design for the range. Then ask each person where they fall in it.

sections.title: The weak spots in famous frameworks
sections.text: Some frameworks taught as fact rest on thin ground. Edward Hall's idea of high-context and low-context communication is a useful lens. But a systematic review by Kittler, Rygl and Mackinnon found that the national rankings attached to it have not been well established by rigorous research. Many published country lists trace back to earlier citations rather than measurement. Hofstede-style scores also have critics, and the 80 percent within-country finding uses those same measures. When a training slide ranks countries on a single scale, ask where the numbers came from. Often the honest answer is that nobody measured the people you serve.

sections.title: What training evidence can and cannot say
sections.text: If cultural knowledge were the key, training in it would show strong results for the people served. A review of 19 reviews by Truong, Paradies and Priest found moderate evidence that cultural competence training improves staff knowledge and access to services. Evidence for better outcomes for the people served was weaker, and many studies relied on self-report. Kleinman and Benson, writing from medicine and anthropology, argue that trait lists encourage stereotyping. Their alternative starts by asking whether ethnicity even matters to this person, then asking what is at stake for them. That is expert argument rather than a trial. It fits the experimental finding that asking beats imagining.

sections.title: Cultures inside your own agency
sections.text: Taras and colleagues found occupation explained more of the variation in comfort with authority than country did. That points inward. DHS includes many professional cultures: policy analysts, licensing investigators, eligibility staff, data teams, contract managers and call-line workers. Each has its own habits about speed, directness and who speaks first. A policy team may treat a draft as open for debate, while a compliance team may treat it as nearly final. When two units clash, the cause may be professional culture rather than personality or background. Name the working norms directly: how final is this draft, who decides, and how should disagreement come in?

sections.title: Harder situations
sections.text: A person may tell you, people in my community usually decide this with elders. Take that seriously as their own statement about themselves. Then ask what it means for this decision and who they want involved. A coworker who shares a person's background may offer to explain what a gesture means. Thank them, and remember they cannot know this person's intent. If they can help with language, route that through proper interpreter services. A person may ask you to speak only with a family member. Respect the preference, confirm it directly with the person, and check whether any consent or authorization is required through the person or area responsible. If a matter involves a Tribal Nation or Tribal member, route it through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations. Do not apply a general pattern to a sovereign relationship.

sections.title: Coaching staff who rely on profiles
sections.text: Staff who use cultural profiles usually do so out of care. They want to avoid offense and serve people well. Coaching works best when it starts there. Ask what the profile is meant to prevent. Then show how a question prevents the same problem more reliably. Pair the staff member's knowledge with a specific question, and let them try it on real calls or cases. Review a few interactions together, looking at what the person actually said rather than what the profile predicted. Over time, the staff member's expertise shifts from predicting people to asking them well. That shift keeps their experience valuable and makes it safer for everyone.

sections.title: What is not known about differential effects
sections.text: It is tempting to say that profiles harm some groups more than others. That may be true, but no verified study found here measured it in a DHS setting. The research shows that individuals vary widely within every group, and that guessing is less accurate than asking. It does not tell you which callers are most often misread. So avoid claims such as this approach especially helps one community. Say instead what the evidence supports: asking, checking understanding and offering professional interpreters improve accuracy and access for the people served, whatever their background.

sections.title: When the stakes rise
sections.text: Communication style shifts with stakes, setting, language and trust. A person who is direct about a schedule may become quiet when a benefit is at risk. A staff member who debates freely in a small team may say nothing in front of a director. So a preference you learned last month may not hold today. Ask again when the stakes or the people in the room change. Make the question routine so it never sounds like suspicion. For example: before you decide, is there anyone else you want in this conversation, and how would you like to give me your answer?

sections.title: Honest limits of the research
sections.text: Most of this evidence comes from surveys, lab experiments and health care settings. None of it was done inside Minnesota DHS. The within-country finding is strong across studies, but it measures values, not moment-to-moment communication. No study found here shows that teaching country profiles improves service to individuals, and none shows it harms them directly. The case for asking rests on the Eyal experiments, the language access evidence and basic informed choice duties. Use patterns lightly, check them often, and let the person's own answer outrank any average.

sections.title: Putting it together
sections.text: The hard part of this skill is not knowing patterns. It is holding them loosely while work moves fast. Build the questions into your scripts, agendas and case notes so asking becomes the default. Treat a confident guess as a signal to ask. Treat a person's own description of themselves as the best evidence available. And when you lead others, reward the staff member who checked, even when checking took an extra minute.

simulation.setup: You are a Human Services Supervisor for a DHS call line that helps people with Medical Assistance renewals. A respected Senior Eligibility Worker has drafted a one-page cultural tips sheet for new staff. It lists how callers from several countries tend to communicate. Last week a new worker took a call where the caller said yes to every step, then missed the renewal deadline. Coverage for a family is now at risk. Your team wants guidance, and your senior worker wants recognition for real knowledge.

steps.situation: The Senior Eligibility Worker sends you the tips sheet before the team meeting. It is careful and kind in tone. It says, for example, that callers from certain countries may say yes to be polite. The worker asks you to approve it for new staff today.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Approve it with a line at the top saying these are general patterns and every person is different.
choices.feedback: The disclaimer feels responsible, but research suggests it will not change how the sheet is used. A ready-made pattern works like perspective taking: it gives a confident guess and lowers the urge to ask. With about 80 percent of value variation inside countries, the sheet will be wrong about most individual callers, and the disclaimer will be forgotten by the third call.

choices.label: Thank the worker, then propose turning the sheet into a short set of questions and language access steps, built from the same knowledge, and test it on calls for two weeks.
choices.feedback: This keeps the worker's expertise and changes its job. Their knowledge of patterns becomes the reason for each question, such as who else should be involved and what date works. It matches the evidence that asking improves accuracy and that professional interpreters improve outcomes. Testing it on real calls also gives the team its own evidence.

choices.label: Decline the sheet and tell the worker that cultural differences should not be discussed because every caller is an individual.
choices.feedback: This avoids stereotyping on paper, but it dismisses real knowledge and closes the conversation. Patterns are useful for designing questions and services. A respected worker who feels shut down may keep sharing tips informally, without any check. You lose the chance to shape how the knowledge gets used.

steps.situation: A new worker escalates another call. The caller said yes several times. The worker says, the sheet told me people from that country say yes to be polite, so I assumed they did not agree and closed the call without setting a date. The caller later called back, upset that no one explained the next step.
steps.question: How do you coach the new worker?

choices.label: Tell the worker the sheet was right in general but they applied it badly this time.
choices.feedback: This protects the sheet and puts the failure on the worker. The real problem is the inference itself. Whether the yes meant agreement or politeness, the worker never asked. The research on perspective taking shows that even good guesses miss often. Defending the guide teaches new staff to trust it more, not less.

choices.label: Walk through the call together and practice a read-back: ask the caller what they will do next and by what date, then confirm the date in writing in their preferred language.
choices.feedback: This moves the worker from guessing to checking. A read-back works whatever the yes meant. It also exposes language needs early. If the caller struggles, offer a professional interpreter. The coaching teaches a habit that fits every caller, rather than a rule that fits an average.

choices.label: Ask the worker to call back with a bilingual coworker who shares the caller's background to explain what the caller really meant.
choices.feedback: The impulse to repair is right, and language help may be needed. But a coworker who shares a background cannot know this caller's intent. Untrained interpreters also make more errors than professionals. Use a professional interpreter for language, and ask the caller directly about the next step.

steps.situation: During the two-week test, a new worker uses the question set. Midway through a call, the caller asks for an interpreter. With the interpreter on the line, the caller says they will decide with their adult children and asks for more time. The renewal date is in nine days.
steps.question: What guidance do you give the worker?

choices.label: Tell the worker to explain the deadline firmly and ask the caller to decide on this call to protect coverage.
choices.feedback: Protecting coverage matters, but pressure turns a stated preference into an obstacle. The caller has told you how they decide. A forced answer may be a yes that means nothing. Keep the deadline clear and design around the family conversation instead.

choices.label: Help the worker name a specific callback date before the deadline, ask whether the children should join that call, and confirm both in writing in the caller's language.
choices.feedback: This respects how the caller wants to decide and keeps the timeline real. A named date replaces the vague later. Inviting the children on the call makes the family process part of the plan rather than an unknown. The interpreter stays in place for the follow-up.

choices.label: Suggest the worker mail the forms and wait for the family to call back.
choices.feedback: This leaves room for the family, but it shifts all the follow-up onto the caller with no agreed date. With nine days left, waiting quietly puts coverage at risk. The caller told you how they want to decide, which is useful information. Patience is good. Patience without a named date and a plan for the family conversation is not.

steps.situation: At the team meeting, the Senior Eligibility Worker says, I have twenty years of experience with these communities. Patterns are real, and new staff need them. Several staff nod. Others look uneasy.
steps.question: How do you respond in the meeting?

choices.label: Agree that patterns are real and say the team will use them as starting questions, then ask the senior worker to lead practice on turning each pattern into a question.
choices.feedback: This honors real experience and keeps it in service of asking. The research supports both halves: patterns exist at the group level, and individuals vary far more within groups than between them. Giving the senior worker the lead on question practice turns a possible conflict into shared work.

choices.label: Share the 80 percent finding and explain that the data show the patterns are mostly wrong.
choices.feedback: The finding is accurate, but the framing overstates it. The data show patterns describe averages, not that they are wrong. Using research to win an argument in public can make an experienced colleague defensive. You may be right on the facts and still lose the team.

choices.label: Say both views are valid and move to the next agenda item.
choices.feedback: This avoids tension but leaves new staff with no guidance. Some will use the old tips and some will not. The next missed deadline will repeat the same problem. A supervisor's job here is to set the practice, not to referee views.

simulation.debrief: The path through this scenario turns on one question: does cultural knowledge produce a guess or a question? The research is consistent. About 80 percent of the variation in work values lies within countries. Famous contrasts sometimes fail even for group averages. Imagining another's view does not make you accurate; asking does. Language access is the exception that proves the rule, because it is concrete and checkable, and professional interpreters improve outcomes. The strongest choices kept the senior worker's knowledge and gave it a new job. They built read-backs and named dates into calls. They designed around how each caller said they wanted to decide. The weaker choices either trusted the average or threw away useful knowledge.

mistakes.mistake: Adding a disclaimer to a cultural tip sheet and treating the problem as solved.
mistakes.why: A disclaimer feels responsible, and the sheet comes from real experience. But a ready-made pattern works like perspective taking. It gives a confident guess and reduces asking, which is the one approach shown to improve accuracy.
mistakes.instead: Rewrite the sheet as questions and language access steps. Let each pattern become the reason for a question.

mistakes.mistake: Reading yes, silence or a smile as agreement or as politeness.
mistakes.why: Social cues feel like data, and quick interpretation saves time on a busy line. Yet any one cue can mean understanding, agreement, deference or simple thinking time.
mistakes.instead: Use a read-back. Ask what the person will do next and by what date, then confirm it in writing in their preferred language.

mistakes.mistake: Asking a coworker who shares a person's background to explain what the person meant.
mistakes.why: It seems respectful to seek inside knowledge. But a shared background does not reveal one person's intent, and ad hoc interpreters make more errors than professionals.
mistakes.instead: Use professional interpreter services for language. Ask the person directly about meaning and decisions.

mistakes.mistake: Using vague time words such as soon, later or in a while.
mistakes.why: These words feel softer and less pushy. Their meaning varies widely between people and situations, so they create missed deadlines.
mistakes.instead: Name a specific date. Ask whether it works and what might make it hard.

mistakes.mistake: Refusing to discuss cultural patterns at all.
mistakes.why: Leaders worry that any talk of patterns becomes stereotyping. But patterns are real at the group level and useful for designing services and questions.
mistakes.instead: Discuss patterns openly as a range of possibilities. Then set the practice: every pattern leads to a question, never to a conclusion.

jobAid.title: From pattern to question
jobAid.use: Before or during any conversation where you notice yourself predicting how someone will communicate or decide.
steps: Notice the guess. Finish the sentence: I think this person probably wants or means...
Name the pattern behind it, such as family decisions, deference to authority or flexible time.
Turn it into a question: who would you like involved, what part does not work for you, what date works?
Check language access. If understanding is uncertain, offer a professional interpreter, not a relative or coworker.
Replace every vague time word with a named date, and ask if it is realistic.
Use a read-back: what will you do next, and by when?
Confirm the key step in writing in the person's preferred language.
Ask again when the stakes or the people in the room change.

media.reason: The lesson lives in the tension between real field experience with patterns and the research on individual variation. Two colleagues working it out teaches the reframe better than a narrator explaining it.

script.speaker: male
script.text: I put a lot into that tips sheet. I have taken calls from these communities for twenty years. The patterns are real. New staff walk in blind.

script.speaker: female
script.text: I believe the patterns are real. I also read a meta-analysis of 558 studies. About 80 percent of the variation in work values was inside countries, not between them.

script.speaker: male
script.text: So you are saying my experience is wrong?

script.speaker: female
script.text: No. I am saying it describes the range, not the person. Your sheet says some callers say yes to be polite. That is true for some. For the caller last week, nobody knows, because nobody asked.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Fair. The new worker assumed the yes meant no and closed the call. That was not what I meant the sheet to do.

script.speaker: female
script.text: That is the risk. There are experiments on this. People told to imagine another person's view got no more accurate. Sometimes less. The only thing that helped was asking.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Then what do new staff do with what I know?

script.speaker: female
script.text: Your knowledge becomes the reason for the question. If some people decide with family, the worker asks who should be involved. If yes can mean many things, the worker does a read-back: what will you do next, and by what date?

script.speaker: male
script.text: And language? Half the confusion I see is really language.

script.speaker: female
script.text: That is the part with the strongest evidence. A review of 28 studies found professional interpreters beat family members and untrained staff. So the sheet should say: offer a professional interpreter early.

script.speaker: male
script.text: I can rewrite it. Each pattern, then the question it leads to. Then a date, never the word soon.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Would you lead the practice session with the team? They will listen to you more than to a study.

prompts: What guess about how someone communicates do you make most often at work, and what question could replace it this week?
With whom on your team could you turn a piece of cultural knowledge into a set of questions, and when will you ask them?
Which deadline or follow-up in your work still uses a vague time word, and by what date will you change it to a named date?
