title: Disability as culture and identity
objective: Lead meetings and decisions so that people with disabilities direct them in their own terms, at a pace and in a language that works for them.
outcomes: Ask each person for their own identity terms and access needs instead of choosing terms or methods for them.
Redesign a meeting's pace, materials and turn-taking so people who communicate in ASL, with a device or more slowly can shape the decision.
Notice and correct the moment when a conversation shifts from the person to a family member, interpreter or support person.
Explain the disability paradox and why professional assumptions about quality of life are often wrong.
Apply Minnesota's informed choice duties, including accessible information and ample time to decide.

evidence.summary: Disability is a medical fact for some purposes, and for many people it is also a culture and an identity. Studies link a stronger disability identity to higher life satisfaction. Deaf adults hold several distinct identities, from culturally Deaf to bicultural. People with serious disabilities often rate their quality of life as good, while most physicians assume it is worse. No single term is accepted by everyone, so asking beats guessing. Person-centered planning shows moderate benefits for choice and community participation, but the research base is weak. Minnesota law presumes people with disabilities can make informed choices and requires accessible information and ample time. Most identity studies are cross-sectional, so they show links, not causes.

findings.claim: 54.3 percent of people with moderate to serious disabilities rated their quality of life as excellent or good.
findings.detail: Qualitative interview study of 153 people with disabilities, 1999. The authors named this the disability paradox.

findings.claim: 82.4 percent of US physicians said people with significant disability have a worse quality of life than nondisabled people.
findings.detail: National survey of 714 practicing physicians, 2021. Only 40.7 percent were very confident they could give equal quality of care. Health services.

findings.claim: A stronger disability identity was linked to higher life satisfaction.
findings.detail: Cross-sectional online survey of 226 adults with mobility disabilities, 2014. Disability identity and disability self-efficacy partly explained why people with lifelong disabilities reported higher satisfaction.

findings.claim: Deaf adults fell into three identity groups of roughly equal size: culturally hearing, culturally Deaf and bicultural.
findings.detail: Cluster analysis of 267 deaf adults with interviews of 56, 2000. Qualified support for higher self-esteem among culturally Deaf and bicultural adults.

findings.claim: American Sign Language is described as the backbone of American Deaf culture.
findings.detail: National Association of the Deaf resource page on ASL, which also supports a bilingual ASL and English approach.

findings.claim: No single disability term was accepted by everyone; autistic adults and professionals often preferred different terms.
findings.detail: Survey of 3,470 autistic people, family members and professionals in the UK, 2016.

findings.claim: Professionals should use identity-first language alongside person-first language to respect disability communities.
findings.detail: Review in American Psychologist, 2015, linking language styles to models of disability.

findings.claim: Person-centered planning showed a moderate positive effect on community participation and daily choice, based on low-quality evidence.
findings.detail: Systematic review of 16 studies of people with intellectual disabilities, 1990 to 2014. Employment results were inconsistent. Human services.

findings.claim: An earlier review also found positive but moderate effects of person-centered planning on a weak evidence base.
findings.detail: Review of effectiveness research in intellectual and developmental disabilities, 2010. Human services.

findings.claim: Minnesota law presumes that people with disabilities can make informed choices and requires accessible information and ample time to decide.
findings.detail: Minnesota Statutes 256B.4905, subdivisions 1a, 2a, 3a, 9 and 10. Lead agencies must provide complete, accurate and culturally appropriate information. Minnesota public sector.

counterintuitive.headline: The people living with a disability often rate their lives higher than professionals expect.
counterintuitive.text: In interviews with 153 people with disabilities, Albrecht and Devlieger found that 54.3 percent of those with moderate to serious disabilities rated their quality of life as excellent or good. Two decades later, Iezzoni and colleagues surveyed 714 US physicians. 82.4 percent said people with significant disability have a worse quality of life. The gap matters for public service. When staff assume a life is diminished, they may lower expectations, speak to a family member instead, or steer choices toward safety over what the person wants. The person's own account is the better guide.

sections.title: More than a diagnosis
sections.text: For eligibility, a disability can be a set of criteria. For many people, it is also an identity and a culture. Some Deaf people see themselves as members of a linguistic community, with American Sign Language at its center. Others identify as hard of hearing, or as both Deaf and hearing in culture. A study of 267 deaf adults found these groups in roughly equal shares. Many disabled people describe pride, shared history and community. Research links a stronger disability identity to higher life satisfaction.

sections.title: The assumption to watch
sections.text: Professionals often misjudge disabled people's lives. In one study, 54.3 percent of people with serious disabilities rated their quality of life as good or excellent. In a national survey, 82.4 percent of physicians assumed such lives were worse. When you assume a life is diminished, you may lower expectations. You may also turn to a family member, speed past a slow answer, or choose safety over the person's own goals.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: Let the person set the terms. Ask how they describe themselves and what access works for them. Do not pick terms or methods from a label. Then protect their control in the meeting itself. Address the person directly, not the interpreter or the family member. Send materials ahead in an accessible format. Build time into the agenda for typing, signing or thinking. When someone asks a supporter to help with one part, keep that help to that part. Minnesota law presumes people with disabilities can make informed choices. It requires accessible information and ample time. A meeting run at the pace of the fastest speaker does not meet that standard.

sections.title: A quick check
sections.text: At the end of any meeting, ask yourself whose voice decided the outcome. If it was not the person most affected, find out why, and change the next meeting. Small design choices, such as pace and who is addressed, decide whether a person's view shapes the result.

sections.title: Disability identity and well-being
sections.text: Bogart surveyed 226 adults with mobility disabilities. Disability identity and disability self-efficacy, the confidence to handle disability-related challenges, both predicted life satisfaction. People with lifelong disabilities reported higher satisfaction than people whose disability came later. Their stronger identity and self-efficacy partly explained the difference. Bogart concluded that professionals should support disability identity, including community and pride, rather than trying to make people seem as nondisabled as possible. The study was cross-sectional, so it shows a link rather than a cause. It still points the same way as the lived accounts of many disabled people.

sections.title: Deaf culture is not one thing
sections.text: Bat-Chava studied 267 deaf adults and found three identities of roughly equal size. Some were culturally hearing and oriented to spoken language. Some were culturally Deaf, rooted in the signing community. Some were bicultural. The National Association of the Deaf describes ASL as the backbone of American Deaf culture and supports bilingual ASL and English approaches. So booking an ASL interpreter is often right, but not always. Some deaf people use captioning, speech reading, tactile signing or other methods. Ask each person which access works, and confirm it before the meeting rather than at the door.

sections.title: Language without guessing
sections.text: Person-first language, such as person with a disability, is common in government writing. Many disability communities prefer identity-first language, such as disabled person, autistic person or Deaf person. A UK survey of 3,470 people found no term everyone accepted. Autistic adults and professionals often preferred different terms. Dunn and Andrews argue professionals should use both styles, guided by the people concerned. The practical rule is simple. Use the person's own terms for them. For a group, follow the stated preferences of that community, and note where there is no consensus.

sections.title: Why professionals misjudge
sections.text: The disability paradox describes a gap between outside views and lived experience. Albrecht and Devlieger found that more than half of people with moderate to serious disabilities rated their quality of life as good or excellent. Their quality of life depended on balance, relationships and their environment. Iezzoni and colleagues found that 82.4 percent of physicians assumed significant disability meant worse quality of life. Only 40.7 percent felt very confident they could provide equal care. DHS staff are not physicians, but the same assumptions can shape service decisions, plan reviews and policy work.

sections.title: What person-centered planning can deliver
sections.text: Person-centered planning puts the person's goals and preferences at the center of service decisions. Ratti and colleagues reviewed 16 studies of people with intellectual disabilities. Low-quality evidence suggested moderate gains in community participation, activities and everyday choice. Employment results were inconsistent. An earlier review by Claes and colleagues reached a similar verdict. The honest takeaway is that person-centered practice helps, but a form or a meeting title does not deliver it. The gains depend on whether the person actually directs what happens.

sections.title: Minnesota's informed choice duties
sections.text: Minnesota Statutes 256B.4905 sets a clear standard for disability waiver services. Informed choice is a choice adults with disabilities make after receiving information in an accessible format. The law presumes people can make informed choices. Lead agencies must give complete, accurate and culturally appropriate information. The informed decision-making process includes accommodations, the person's preferences and goals, and ample time to decide. People also have the right to direct their own services. If you lead policy, contracts or training, these duties shape what good practice looks like across counties, Tribal Nations and managed care organizations.

sections.title: Questions that replace guesses
sections.text: A few plain questions cover most situations. How would you like to communicate in this meeting? What format works best for materials? Is there anyone you want with you, and what would you like them to help with? How would you like to tell the group your view: speaking, signing, typing or in writing afterward? How much time do you need before a decision? What words do you use to describe yourself? Ask these of every participant, not only people you think have a disability. Asking everyone avoids singling anyone out, and it often surfaces needs nobody expected.

sections.title: Applying it in a DHS meeting
sections.text: Before the meeting, ask each participant about access needs and preferred terms. Send agendas and materials ahead in accessible formats. Plan pauses for interpretation, typing and processing. During the meeting, address the person, not the interpreter or supporter. If a family member begins to answer for the person, return the question to the person. Ask what the supporter should help with. Afterward, share a plain-language summary and invite correction. Each step costs a few minutes. Together they decide whether the person's view shapes the result.

sections.title: Culture and impairment at the same time
sections.text: A disability can be both an access need and an identity. These do not conflict. A Deaf member of an advisory group may need an ASL interpreter and also see deafness as a language and culture, not a loss. A wheelchair user may need an accessible room and also take pride in disability community. Leaders sometimes treat the access need as the whole story. Others celebrate identity and forget to book the interpreter. Both matter. Get the access right first, because without it the person cannot take part. Then respect identity in how you speak and write.

sections.title: Support without substitution
sections.text: Many people choose a family member, friend or support person to help them. That choice is part of self-direction. The risk comes when help with one task grows into control over the whole conversation. A person might ask a relative to explain transport times, then watch staff turn to the relative for every later question. Minnesota's informed choice law includes support from families and legal representatives for children, and it presumes adults can make informed choices. If legal decision authority matters, such as guardianship, verify its actual scope through the person or area responsible. Do not assume it from who is sitting at the table.

sections.title: Pace is a form of power
sections.text: A fast round of questions rewards speech, quick processing and the ability to interrupt. People who sign through an interpreter, type on a device or need time to process may lose their turn without anyone intending it. The decision then reflects the fastest speakers. Minnesota law requires ample time in the informed decision-making process. Treat that as a design rule for any meeting about a person's services or a policy affecting them. Share questions in advance. Use rounds where each person speaks in turn. Wait through silence. Ask, is there anything you want to add before the group moves on?

sections.title: What the evidence can and cannot support
sections.text: The identity research is mostly cross-sectional. It shows that a stronger disability identity goes with higher well-being, not that one causes the other. Bogart's study included only mobility disabilities. Bat-Chava's study described identity groups among deaf adults, with qualified support for self-esteem differences. Person-centered planning reviews rate the evidence as weak or low quality. No verified study found here measures how often staff speak to companions rather than to the person. So treat those practice points as sound judgment, not as statistics. Do not claim that any approach helps one disability group more than another unless a study shows it.

sections.title: Designing for a range of identities
sections.text: Bat-Chava's three Deaf identity groups are a useful model for any disability community. Within one group of members, some people center disability in their identity, some barely mention it, and some move between worlds. A design that works for only one of these will miss the others. Offer more than one way to take part, such as speaking, signing, typing, or sending comments afterward. Let people choose how visible their disability is in group documents. Treat the choice itself as information about what respect looks like to them.

sections.title: When people disagree about language
sections.text: Within one meeting, a self-advocate may prefer disabled person, a parent may prefer person with a disability, and an agency style guide may require person-first language. The UK autism survey found these divides are real and lasting. Use each person's own terms for them. In a group document, you can explain the choice: for example, this summary uses the terms participants asked for. Avoid terms most communities reject, such as suffering from, confined to a wheelchair or special needs when a plainer term exists. When unsure, ask a member of the community you are writing about, and accept the answer.

sections.title: Harder situations
sections.text: A person may communicate in ways staff find hard to follow. Slow down and check understanding in both directions. Use a qualified interpreter or the person's chosen communication support. A family member may insist the person cannot understand a policy question. Thank them, and still offer the person accessible materials and time. Then ask the person what they think. A staff member may suggest simplifying a policy discussion so far that the real choices disappear. Plain language is right. Removing the decision is not. An issue may involve a Tribal Nation or a Tribal member's services. Route it through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations rather than applying a general approach.

sections.title: When the law, the style guide and the person differ
sections.text: Agency style guides, statutes and personal preferences sometimes use different words. Statutes use defined terms for legal reasons, and those terms belong in legal documents. A style guide sets a default for general writing. A person's own words belong in anything that describes them. When these conflict, say which rule you are following and why. For example, a policy notice may need the statutory term, while a meeting summary can use members' own terms. Being clear about the reason shows respect even when you cannot match every preference.

sections.title: Checking your own assumptions
sections.text: The physician survey is a mirror for any professional. When you review a plan or a policy, notice moments where you expect less of someone because of a disability. Notice when safety arguments override the person's stated goals without a specific, documented risk. Notice when you feel relief that a family member is present to speak. These are common reactions. The disability paradox suggests they often rest on wrong assumptions about how people experience their own lives. Ask the person what a good life looks like to them, and let that answer set the goal.

sections.title: Leading a team toward this practice
sections.text: As a leader, model the behavior in your own meetings. Ask everyone about access needs at the start of each project, not only people you think have a disability. Build interpreter and captioning costs into budgets so access is never a favor. Review meeting summaries for whose words shaped the decision. When a staff member returns a question to a person after a relative answered, name it as good practice. Over time, these habits make person-centered work a team norm rather than a single person's skill.

simulation.setup: You are a Human Services Program Manager in the Disability Services Division. You lead a work group advising on changes to community living services. Members include a Deaf self-advocate who uses an ASL interpreter, a self-advocate who communicates with a speech device, a parent, two county case managers, a provider representative and your own staff. The group's advice will shape guidance sent to lead agencies statewide. The first meeting is in two weeks, and the agenda is packed.

steps.situation: Your Planner drafts the first agenda: six topics in ninety minutes, open discussion on each, with an ASL interpreter booked. Materials will be handed out at the start. The Planner says this is the standard format and it works well.
steps.question: What do you do with the agenda?

choices.label: Keep the format, since the interpreter is booked and that covers access.
choices.feedback: Booking the interpreter is necessary, but it treats access as one checkbox. Six open discussions in ninety minutes reward the fastest speakers. A speech device user and an ASL user will both lose time to the pace. Minnesota's informed choice standard calls for accessible information and ample time. This agenda offers neither for some members.

choices.label: Cut to three topics, send materials two weeks ahead in accessible formats, ask each member about access needs and preferred terms, and build in turn-by-turn rounds with pauses.
choices.feedback: This designs the meeting around how members actually communicate. Advance materials let people prepare at their own pace. Asking every member about access avoids guessing from a label. Rounds and pauses give signing and typing equal standing with speech. You trade coverage for real participation, which is the point of the group.

choices.label: Ask the parent to share the self-advocates' views in advance so the meeting can move faster.
choices.feedback: This feels efficient and may come from respect for the parent's knowledge. But it hands the self-advocates' voice to someone else before they have spoken. The parent can share their own perspective. The self-advocates can share theirs. Substituting one for the other turns support into replacement.

steps.situation: Midway through the meeting, discussion speeds up. The self-advocate using a speech device has been typing for two minutes. The parent says, I think what they mean is they want more evening staff. A county case manager starts to respond to the parent.
steps.question: What do you do in the moment?

choices.label: Let the discussion continue and plan to follow up with the self-advocate after the meeting.
choices.feedback: Following up is kind, but the decision is forming now. A later conversation cannot easily reopen options the group has already narrowed. The person learns that typing means being skipped. Ratti and colleagues found person-centered gains depend on real control, not on consultation after the fact.

choices.label: Pause the group, say you want to hear the self-advocate directly, wait for them to finish typing, and then ask the parent what they would like to add for themselves.
choices.feedback: This restores the turn without blaming anyone. Waiting through the typing makes clear that this voice counts at its own pace. Inviting the parent to speak for themselves keeps their perspective without replacing the self-advocate's. The group sees the practice modeled, which changes later turns too.

choices.label: Ask the parent whether that is right, since they know the self-advocate best.
choices.feedback: This is a common and caring move, but it confirms the parent as the source of the self-advocate's view. The person in the room is the best source. Asking the parent to confirm sends the conversation further away from them. Return the question to the self-advocate.

steps.situation: The meeting is going well. Then a provider representative says, honestly, most people we serve cannot follow rate methodology. Should we really spend time on this with the whole group? Several heads nod. The Deaf self-advocate signs a reply, and the interpreter begins to voice it.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Agree to move rate details to a smaller technical group and keep the full group on service experience.
choices.feedback: Technical subgroups can be useful. But making the move right after a claim about what people cannot follow sends a message about who belongs in decisions. It also cuts off a reply already underway. If you split topics, do it by stated interest and with plain-language options, not by assumed ability.

choices.label: Wait for the interpretation to finish, address the self-advocate's reply directly, and offer a plain-language summary of the rate question so every member can weigh in.
choices.feedback: This honors the reply in progress and answers the concern without excluding anyone. Plain language keeps the real choice in view. Minnesota's informed choice standard expects accessible information, not withheld information. The disability paradox research is a reminder that outside assumptions about capacity are often wrong.

choices.label: Tell the provider representative that comment is ableist and move on.
choices.feedback: The concern about the comment is fair, but naming a colleague this way in the moment shuts them down without changing the plan. The interpreted reply is still waiting. A better response shows, through design, that every member can engage with the issue. You can raise the comment privately later.

steps.situation: Your staff member drafts the meeting summary for lead agencies. It describes members as the deaf member and the nonverbal member, and uses person-first language throughout because the agency style guide requires it. The staff member asks if that is fine.
steps.question: What guidance do you give?

choices.label: Tell them to follow the style guide exactly, since consistency protects the agency.
choices.feedback: Consistency matters, but this summary describes real people who told you their terms. The style guide and community preferences can differ. Research on disability language shows no single term is accepted by all. Applying one rule over people's own words tells them their identity is a style question.

choices.label: Ask the staff member to check each member's preferred terms, use those, describe contributions by role rather than by disability, and send the draft to members for correction.
choices.feedback: This puts each member's own terms first and keeps the focus on what members said, not on their disabilities. Sending the draft for correction gives members control of how their views travel to lead agencies. It also models informed, accessible practice for the counties and providers who will read it.

choices.label: Remove any mention of disability from the summary to avoid offending anyone.
choices.feedback: Avoiding offense is a real concern. But erasing disability from a disability work group's summary hides who shaped the advice. Lead agencies reading it lose the context of whose experience informed each point. Some members may want their identity named, and others may not. Ask them rather than deciding for them.

simulation.debrief: Each decision in this scenario asked the same question: who directs this? The evidence gives several reasons to let the person decide. Disability identity is linked to well-being. Deaf identities vary, so access and terms must be asked, not assumed. People with serious disabilities often rate their lives more highly than professionals expect. Person-centered planning helps when the person truly directs it, though the research base is weak. Minnesota law presumes people can make informed choices and requires accessible information and ample time. The strongest choices redesigned pace and materials, returned turns to the person, and used each member's own terms. The weaker ones relied on a parent, an interpreter booking or a style rule to do the work of asking.

mistakes.mistake: Treating an interpreter booking as the whole of access.
mistakes.why: Booking access feels like the hard part, and it is often the only step people are trained on. But pace, materials and turn-taking still decide who gets heard.
mistakes.instead: Ask every member about access needs, send materials ahead, and plan time for interpretation, typing and processing.

mistakes.mistake: Turning to a family member or supporter for answers.
mistakes.why: It feels faster and respectful of the family's knowledge. It also reflects common professional assumptions about disabled people's capacity, which research shows are often wrong.
mistakes.instead: Address the person directly. Ask what the supporter should help with, and keep help to that part.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing identity terms for someone based on a style guide or a label.
mistakes.why: Rules feel safe and consistent. But no single term is accepted by everyone, and autistic adults and professionals often prefer different terms.
mistakes.instead: Ask the person's own terms and use them. For groups, follow stated community preferences and note where they differ.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming a disabled person's quality of life is low and setting goals around safety alone.
mistakes.why: Outside observers often imagine disability as loss. Yet more than half of people with serious disabilities in one study rated their quality of life as good or excellent.
mistakes.instead: Ask the person what a good life looks like to them, and let documented, specific risks, not assumptions, shape safety planning.

mistakes.mistake: Simplifying a policy discussion until the real choice disappears.
mistakes.why: Leaders want to be clear and kind. But removing the decision denies people the informed choice Minnesota law presumes they can make.
mistakes.instead: Use plain language, accessible formats and time. Keep the actual options on the table.

jobAid.title: Who directs this meeting?
jobAid.use: Before, during and after any meeting about a person's services or a policy affecting people with disabilities.
steps: Ask every participant about access needs and preferred terms before the meeting.
Send materials ahead in accessible formats, such as plain language, large print or video in ASL when requested.
Cut the agenda so there is time for interpretation, typing and thinking.
Address the person directly, never the interpreter or supporter.
If someone answers for the person, return the question to the person and invite the supporter to add their own view.
Use rounds and wait through silence before moving on.
Describe people by role and in their own terms in any summary.
Send the summary to participants for correction before it goes further.

media.reason: This lesson asks the learner to notice a quiet shift in a meeting and to examine their own assumptions. A single calm narrator can slow down the moment and speak directly to the learner's judgment.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Picture a work group meeting. A self-advocate is typing a reply on a speech device. It takes time. The discussion moves on. A parent offers a guess about what the self-advocate means. A case manager answers the parent. In under a minute, the person most affected has been talked past. Nobody intended it. Everyone was trying to be helpful.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: This lesson is about that minute. For eligibility, a disability can be a set of criteria. For many people, it is also an identity and a culture. Some Deaf people belong to a community built around American Sign Language. A study of 267 deaf adults found three identities in roughly equal shares: culturally Deaf, culturally hearing and bicultural. So there is no single Deaf experience, and no single right accommodation. You have to ask.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Identity matters for well-being too. In a survey of 226 adults with mobility disabilities, a stronger disability identity went with higher life satisfaction. That study shows a link, not a cause. It still points away from treating disability only as something to fix.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now consider your own assumptions. In interviews with 153 people with disabilities, more than half of those with serious disabilities rated their quality of life as good or excellent. In a national survey, 82 percent of physicians assumed such lives were worse. When professionals expect less, they turn to family members, rush past slow answers and choose safety over a person's goals.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Minnesota law sets a different expectation. For disability waiver services, it presumes people can make informed choices. It requires information in an accessible format and ample time to decide. A meeting run at the speed of the fastest talker does not meet that standard.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: So what do you do in that minute? Pause the group. Say you want to hear the self-advocate directly. Wait for the typing to finish. Then ask the parent what they want to add for themselves. You have not scolded anyone. You have shown the room whose voice decides.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before the next meeting, change the design. Ask every member about access and preferred terms. Send materials early. Cut the agenda. Use rounds, and wait through silence. Afterward, send the summary to members so they can correct it. Person-centered planning shows real but moderate benefits, on a weak research base. The benefits seem to depend on whether the person actually directs what happens. Your meeting design is where that starts.

prompts: Which meeting you lead in the next month moves at the pace of the fastest speaker, and what one design change will you make before it?
With whom could you check preferred terms and access needs before your next project starts, and when will you ask?
Where in your work do you expect less of someone because of a disability, and what question will you ask instead by the end of this week?

title: Values in tension, and the history behind trust
objective: Respond to distrust with accurate answers you can verify, and handle a clash between family values and a legal duty by separating observation from unfamiliarity.
outcomes: Answer a question about who can see a person's information with what you know, what you do not know, and a specific follow-up date.
Explain how documented government harms, including Minnesota's own institutional history, shape present-day trust without asking anyone to justify their distrust.
Separate an observed, specific concern from a practice that is simply unfamiliar to you.
Act on Minnesota's immediate reporting duty for suspected maltreatment of a vulnerable adult when there is reason to believe it, without delaying for consultation.
Protect a person's chance to speak privately while respecting their choice to involve family.

evidence.summary: Distrust of public agencies often has a documented history. After the Tuskegee study was disclosed, older Black men's medical mistrust rose and their use of care fell, with measurable effects on life expectancy. Minnesota apologized in 2010 for harms in its state institutions. The federal government has documented the aims of the Indian boarding school system. Fear can spread beyond the people a rule targets: in 2018, some families whose foreign-born members were all citizens avoided benefits. Fair process predicts trust in civil servants more strongly than outcomes do. Evidence is thin on how staff can tell an unfamiliar cultural practice from harm. The safest guide is to separate observation from interpretation and follow the law.

findings.claim: After the 1972 Tuskegee disclosure, older Black men showed more medical mistrust, fewer doctor visits and life expectancy at 45 lower by up to 1.5 years.
findings.detail: Natural experiment using a difference-in-difference-in-differences design. Published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2018 (133:407-455); the published abstract gives up to 1.5 years. Effects were stronger closer to Macon County. The drop accounts for about 35 percent of the 1980 Black-white male life expectancy gap.

findings.claim: Minnesota formally apologized in 2010 to people with disabilities wrongfully committed to state institutions, naming unpaid labor, unconsented procedures and burial in numbered graves.
findings.detail: Minnesota Session Laws 2010, Resolution 4. The state committed to helping Minnesotans with disabilities receive services in the least restrictive manner. Minnesota public sector.

findings.claim: A federal investigation counted 408 federal Indian boarding schools in 37 states or then territories, found marked or unmarked burial sites at about 53 schools, and described the system's goals as cultural assimilation and territorial dispossession.
findings.detail: US Department of the Interior, Federal Indian Boarding School Initiative Investigative Report, Volume I, released May 11, 2022, as stated in the Department's official press release. The Department expected the burial-site count to rise. Federal government record.

findings.claim: Fair process had a consistently large effect on trust in civil servants, in some models several times larger than outcomes.
findings.detail: Survey data from the US and 33 countries with structural equation and country-level path models, 2011. Public sector.

findings.claim: In 2018, 13.7 percent of adults in immigrant families avoided a public benefit over green card fears. In all-citizen families, 9.3 percent still did.
findings.detail: Nationally representative survey of adults 18 to 64, December 2018. 20.7 percent in low-income immigrant families. Public sector and human services.

findings.claim: An estimated 37.4 percent of US children experience a child protective services investigation by age 18, including 53.0 percent of African American children.
findings.detail: Synthetic cohort life tables from national child maltreatment data, 2003 to 2014, published 2017. Human services.

findings.claim: Apology repaired trust better after competence failures, while denial worked better after integrity accusations that later proved false.
findings.detail: Two lab experiments, 2004. Individual trust; applying it to institutions is an inference.

findings.claim: In Minnesota, a mandated reporter with reason to believe a vulnerable adult is being or has been maltreated must report immediately to the common entry point.
findings.detail: Minnesota Statutes 626.557, subdivisions 3 and 9. The common entry point is available 24 hours a day. Minnesota public sector.

counterintuitive.headline: Fear of a rule reaches people the rule never touches.
counterintuitive.text: In December 2018, the Urban Institute surveyed adults in immigrant families about a proposed public charge rule. Bernstein and colleagues found 13.7 percent said they or a family member had avoided a public benefit out of fear for green card status. Among families where every foreign-born member was already a naturalized citizen, 9.3 percent still reported avoiding benefits. Those families had nothing to lose under the rule. Distrust does not follow policy details. It follows experience, history and what people hear. That is why a clear, accurate answer about who sees information matters so much.

sections.title: Distrust often has a history
sections.text: When someone hesitates to give DHS their information, it can feel personal. Often it is history. Minnesota apologized in 2010 to people with disabilities wrongfully committed to state institutions. The apology names unpaid labor, procedures done without consent and burials in numbered graves. A 2022 federal report documents the goals of the federal Indian boarding school system, including cultural assimilation. After the Tuskegee study became public, older Black men's mistrust of medicine rose and their use of care fell. These are records of government power. A person does not need to explain any of them to you to have a reason for caution.

sections.title: Answer the actual question
sections.text: Distrust usually comes with a specific question. Who will see this? Is it required? Can it be used against my family? Answer it as accurately as you can. Say what you know, say what you do not know, and name when you will come back with a verified answer. Reassurance such as DHS is here to help does not answer the question. Research on trust in civil servants finds that fair process predicts trust more strongly than results do.

sections.title: When values and duties collide
sections.text: Sometimes a family's way of doing things is unfamiliar to you. Unfamiliar is not the same as harmful. Separate what you observed from what you assumed. Ask the person, privately if needed, what they want. If you have reason to believe a vulnerable adult is being maltreated, Minnesota law requires an immediate report to the common entry point. Do not delay that duty to consult. If the only thing you have is discomfort with a practice, that is a reason to learn more, not to report.

sections.title: The one move
sections.text: Respond to distrust and to tension with specifics. Name the concrete question, the concrete observation or the concrete duty. Then act on that, and nothing broader. When you are unsure, say so, and name who will give the verified answer. Honest limits build more trust than confident guesses.

sections.title: What history does to trust
sections.text: The clearest evidence comes from economists Alsan and Wanamaker. They studied the effect of the 1972 public disclosure of the Tuskegee syphilis study. The government had left Black men with syphilis untreated for decades. After disclosure, older Black men showed more medical mistrust and fewer outpatient and inpatient physician visits. Life expectancy at 45 for Black men fell by up to 1.5 years. Men living closer to Tuskegee showed larger effects. This is a single historical case, but it shows that an institution's past actions can change behavior across a whole population for years.

sections.title: Minnesota's own history
sections.text: Minnesota's 2010 legislative apology addresses people with mental illness and developmental or other disabilities who were wrongfully committed to state institutions. It lists deaths and burials in unmarked or numbered graves. It names unpaid labor, medical procedures without consent including involuntary sterilization of women, punitive shock treatment and isolation. It describes children growing up without family life and parents advised to give up their children. The state committed to helping people with disabilities receive services in the least restrictive manner. Families affected by this history still live in Minnesota. Some of them call DHS today.

sections.title: Federal history and Tribal Nations
sections.text: The US Department of the Interior's 2022 investigative report counted 408 federal Indian boarding schools in 37 states or then territories. In its first analysis, it found marked or unmarked burial sites at about 53 schools, and it expected that number to rise. It described the system's goals as cultural assimilation and territorial dispossession. This is the federal government documenting its own actions. You can learn it from the public record without asking any person to share their family's experience. Do not describe what this history means to any Native person or community; that is not yours to say. Matters involving Tribal Nations or Tribal members go through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations. Tribal Nations are sovereign governments, and that relationship has its own channels.

sections.title: Fear travels beyond the rule
sections.text: In 2018, a proposed federal public charge rule raised concern about using benefits. An Urban Institute survey found 13.7 percent of adults in immigrant families avoided a public benefit out of fear for green card status. In low-income immigrant families, it was 20.7 percent. Among families where every foreign-born member was a naturalized citizen, 9.3 percent still avoided benefits. People do not read rules closely before deciding whether to trust. They act on what they have lived and heard. A specific, correct answer about information use can matter more than any outreach slogan.

sections.title: Why process beats reassurance
sections.text: Van Ryzin analyzed survey data from the US and 33 other countries. Perceptions of fair process had a consistently large effect on trust in civil servants. In some models, the effect was several times larger than the effect of outcomes. In practice, how you answer a question may shape trust more than the benefit itself. Fair process here means accurate information, honest limits, equal treatment and following through. Telling someone the agency means well is not process. Telling them who can see their form, and showing them, is.

sections.title: What fair process sounds like
sections.text: Fair process can fit into a single answer. Here is one shape for it. Name the question you heard: you want to know who can see this form. Give what you know: staff in this program use it to contact you about services. Name the limit: I need to confirm whether anyone outside the program can access it. Give a date and a method: I will send you the answer in writing by Thursday. Offer a choice now: you can get tonight's information without signing in. Each part is checkable. That is what makes it fair process rather than reassurance.

sections.title: Values in tension
sections.text: Some situations involve a real clash between a family's values and a legal duty. A family may manage an adult relative's money collectively. A person may want a sibling present for every conversation. These can express culture and self-direction. They can also, sometimes, hide harm. Research does not offer a reliable test that sorts one from the other. So separate three things. What did you observe or hear? What is your interpretation? What duty applies? Minnesota Statutes 626.557 requires a mandated reporter with reason to believe a vulnerable adult is being maltreated to report immediately to the common entry point.

sections.title: Applying it in DHS work
sections.text: At an information session, answer data questions with specifics and name a follow-up date for anything you cannot verify on the spot. On a call line, if a caller asks who will see their information, tell them what you know and offer to send the answer in writing. In a case review, ask staff to list observations separately from interpretations. If a staff member reports a concern, ask what exactly they saw or heard. If it gives reason to believe maltreatment, the report happens now. If it is unfamiliarity, the next step is learning, including asking the person privately what they want.

sections.title: Do not make people prove their distrust
sections.text: A common mistake is inviting someone to explain why they distrust government. It can feel respectful, as if you are making space. But it asks a person to disclose painful history, often in front of others, before they get an answer. They owe you no explanation. History should make you more willing to answer carefully. It should not make you curious about their story. If someone chooses to share, listen. Then return to their question.

sections.title: How to repair after an agency mistake
sections.text: Sometimes distrust follows a recent error, such as a lost form or a wrong notice. Kim and colleagues found in lab experiments that apology repaired trust better after competence failures, especially when guilt was later confirmed. Denial worked better only when an integrity accusation later proved false. Applying this to institutions is an inference, but it suggests a clear rule. When the agency made a mistake, say so plainly, explain the fix and give a date. Defensive explanations of process rarely help when the error is real.

sections.title: Group findings and the person in front of you
sections.text: Some findings in this course describe groups. Alsan and Wanamaker studied older Black men. Kim, Wildeman and colleagues (2017) estimated that 53.0 percent of African American children experience a child protection investigation by 18, compared with 37.4 percent of all US children. The Urban Institute studied immigrant families. These findings explain why distrust can be widespread and reasonable. They do not tell you what any individual believes or has lived. Do not treat a person's background as a prediction of their trust. Answer every person's question with the same care and accuracy.

sections.title: Where the evidence is thin
sections.text: There is no rigorous research showing how staff can reliably tell an unfamiliar cultural practice from harm. Training materials sometimes offer checklists, but none found here has been tested for accuracy. That gap matters. Without a tested tool, people fall back on what feels familiar, and familiarity is not a measure of safety. The Kim child protection finding is a reminder that system contact is already common and unequal. So the guidance here relies on structure rather than intuition: separate observation from interpretation, ask the person directly, and follow the statute when its threshold is met.

sections.title: Holding a family's values and a person's voice together
sections.text: An adult may want family present for every conversation. That can be self-direction. A safety concern may still need private space. You can honor both. Ask the person, in a way only they can answer, whether there is anything they want to discuss alone. Use an accessible format, such as a private message, a separate call or a written option. Explain honestly what you can and cannot keep confidential, because some concerns trigger a duty to report. Do not promise secrecy you cannot keep. Then let the person decide what to share and who stays in the room for the rest.

sections.title: When the reporting threshold is unclear
sections.text: Minnesota's statute uses the phrase reason to believe. It does not require proof. It also does not treat discomfort as a reason. If you are unsure whether what you saw meets the threshold, ask the person or area responsible for guidance promptly. Do not let a consultation delay a report that is due, because the statute says immediately. Also remember that reporting is not your judgment of a family's culture. It routes a concern to people trained to assess it. Your job is accurate observation and timely action, not a verdict.

sections.title: Leading a team through these tensions
sections.text: Staff often carry two fears at once. They fear missing harm, and they fear judging a family unfairly. Leaders can reduce both by building routines. In case discussions, ask staff to name observations first, interpretations second and duties third. Review the reporting statute together so the threshold is shared knowledge. Make it normal to ask for guidance without blame. When a staff member reports a concern that turns out to reflect a cultural practice, thank them for raising it and talk through what they learned. When a staff member hesitates on a clear concern because of cultural respect, remind them the duty protects the person, and that respect includes safety.

sections.title: Answering about information honestly
sections.text: Questions about information use are where history and present policy meet. Learn the real answers for your program: what is collected, why, who can access it, whether it is required and how long it is kept. When you do not know, say so and find out through the person or area responsible for data privacy. Fix materials that leave the question unanswered, such as a sign-in sheet that does not say whether names are needed. Van Ryzin's finding that process drives trust suggests this work is not a side task. It is part of the service.

sections.title: Trust inside your own team
sections.text: The same dynamics apply among staff. Employees who have seen past reorganizations, discipline or broken promises may hesitate to share concerns with leadership. The research here is about trust in public institutions, not workplaces, so treat the link as reasonable inference. Still, the practice transfers. Answer specific questions specifically. Admit what you do not know. Follow through on the date you named. When you made a mistake, say so plainly. Staff will judge your trustworthiness less by your intentions than by whether your process is visible and consistent.

sections.title: Materials that answer before people ask
sections.text: Many questions about information come from forms and notices that leave the purpose unstated. Review the materials your area uses. Does each one say why information is collected, who can see it and whether it is required? Is the answer in plain language and in the languages people use? Is there a way to get basic information without giving personal details? Fixing materials is slow, quiet work. It reaches the people who never raise a hand, including those the Urban Institute findings suggest stay away entirely.

sections.title: Limits of this evidence
sections.text: The trust findings are mostly correlational. Alsan and Wanamaker's natural experiment is the strongest causal evidence, and it studies one historical event. Van Ryzin's study is cross-national survey research with stated limits. The trust repair findings come from lab experiments with individuals. None of these studies was done inside Minnesota DHS. And on the hardest question, how to tell an unfamiliar practice from harm, there is no tested tool. Use these findings as reasons for care and specificity, not as precise predictions.

simulation.setup: You are a Human Services Supervisor in the Disability Services Division. Your team is holding community information sessions about home and community-based services. Attendance has been low. At tonight's session, a Program Consultant on your team is presenting. The sign-in sheet asks for names, addresses and phone numbers, with no explanation. At stake is whether people feel safe enough to ask about services. Later, your team will also face a harder concern.

steps.situation: A parent raises a hand and asks, if I put my name on this sheet, who outside this room can see it? Does it go to anyone else in government? The Program Consultant glances at you. Several people stop writing.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Step in and reassure everyone that DHS is here to help and signing in is just routine.
choices.feedback: This is kind in intent, but it does not answer the question. People asked who can see their information. A general promise of goodwill asks them to trust what they cannot check. Van Ryzin's research suggests trust follows fair process, including accurate information, more than good intentions.

choices.label: Say what you know and do not know. Tell the group signing in is not needed tonight, and commit to a verified written answer by a set date.
choices.feedback: This answers the real question with honest limits and removes the barrier immediately. Committing to a verified answer by a named date shows a process people can test. The Urban Institute findings suggest distrust spreads widely, so a clear answer helps people who did not ask, too.

choices.label: Invite the parent to share what makes them worried so the group can understand.
choices.feedback: This feels respectful, but it asks a person to disclose their reasons in public before getting an answer. They owe no explanation. History is a reason to answer carefully, not a reason to ask for someone's story. Answer the question first.

steps.situation: A week later, a community partner calls. People left the session believing their names would be shared with immigration authorities. Fewer people are coming to the next session. The partner asks what DHS will do.
steps.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Explain to the partner that the rumor is false and ask them to correct it in the community.
choices.feedback: The rumor may well be false, but asking a partner to carry your correction puts your work on them. It also skips your role in the confusion. The original question was never answered. The partner's trust and the community's both depend on what the agency itself does next.

choices.label: Admit the session missed the question. Get the verified answer from the person or area responsible for data privacy, and send it with a revised sign-in process.
choices.feedback: Owning the gap fits the research on repair: when an error is real, plain acknowledgment works better than defense. A written, verified answer and a changed process show fair process in action. This is the kind of evidence people can check and share.

choices.label: Decide to stop using sign-in sheets and say nothing further to avoid drawing attention.
choices.feedback: Dropping the sheet may help, but silence leaves the rumor standing. People who stayed away will not know anything changed. The underlying question, who sees information, still has no answer. Change the process and also tell people what changed and why.

steps.situation: You send the verified answer on time. Attendance at the next session rises. Afterward, the Program Consultant tells you a family asked how DHS used their information in the past. The consultant is unsure how much to say about the state's history with institutions.
steps.question: What guidance do you give?

choices.label: Tell the consultant to avoid history and focus on current services only.
choices.feedback: Staying current is safe, but avoiding history can sound like denial. Minnesota formally apologized in 2010 for harms in state institutions. Acknowledging a public record is not a risk. It shows the agency knows what people may be carrying, while still focusing on present services.

choices.label: Encourage the consultant to acknowledge the documented history briefly, including Minnesota's 2010 apology, then answer the family's present question accurately.
choices.feedback: This names a public fact without asking the family to share anything. It connects history to the current answer about information use. Fair process includes honesty about the past. The consultant does not need to speak for anyone's experience, only for what the state has acknowledged.

choices.label: Suggest the consultant ask the family to share their experiences so the team can learn from them.
choices.feedback: Learning from families matters, but this request puts the burden on them. They asked a question; they did not offer their history. If the team wants community input, it can invite it through a separate, clearly described process with real choice about participation.

steps.situation: Weeks later, a staff member tells you about a home visit with an adult with a developmental disability who lives with extended family. An uncle manages all of her money, which the family says is their tradition. The staff member feels uneasy and wants to report financial exploitation. When you ask what they saw, they mention the arrangement, and also that the woman said she cannot buy her own medicine.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Tell the staff member that collective money management is cultural and not a concern.
choices.feedback: Respecting the family's tradition is the right instinct for the arrangement itself. But the staff member also heard a specific statement: the woman cannot buy her own medicine. That observation is separate from the culture of the household. Dismissing it could miss maltreatment the law requires you to report.

choices.label: Separate the two. The arrangement alone is not a reason to report. Her statement about medicine is, so make sure a report goes to the common entry point now.
choices.feedback: This keeps observation and interpretation apart. Unfamiliarity with collective money management is not grounds for a report. A specific statement about being unable to get medicine may be. Minnesota law requires an immediate report when there is reason to believe. Reporting routes the concern to trained assessors rather than judging the family.

choices.label: Ask the staff member to visit again next week and gather more information before deciding.
choices.feedback: Gathering facts sounds careful, and it is right when nothing specific has surfaced. But the statute says immediately once there is reason to believe. Waiting a week on a statement about medicine could leave a vulnerable adult at risk. Get guidance promptly if unsure, but do not delay a report that is due.

simulation.debrief: Each choice in this scenario turned on specifics. A parent's question about information use deserved a specific, verified answer, not reassurance and not a request for their story. Van Ryzin's research suggests fair process drives trust in civil servants more than outcomes do. The Urban Institute findings show that fear spreads beyond the people a rule targets, so clear answers reach further than you expect. Minnesota's own 2010 apology is part of the public record you can acknowledge. In the final step, the tension between a family's tradition and a legal duty eased once observation was separated from interpretation. Unfamiliarity was not a reason to report. A specific statement about being unable to get medicine was, and the statute says immediately.

mistakes.mistake: Answering a question about information use with general reassurance.
mistakes.why: Staff want people to feel welcome, and reassurance feels warm. But it asks people to trust what they cannot check, and research links trust to fair process rather than intentions.
mistakes.instead: Say what you know, what you do not, and when you will give a verified answer.

mistakes.mistake: Asking people to explain why they distrust government.
mistakes.why: It feels like listening. In practice it asks for painful disclosure, sometimes in public, before an answer is given.
mistakes.instead: Answer the question first. If someone chooses to share their history, listen without probing.

mistakes.mistake: Treating an unfamiliar family practice as evidence of harm.
mistakes.why: Discomfort feels like a warning signal, and staff fear missing harm. But no tested tool sorts cultural practice from harm, and familiarity is not a measure of safety.
mistakes.instead: List what you observed separately from what you interpreted. Act on specific observations, not on unfamiliarity.

mistakes.mistake: Dismissing a specific concern because the family's practice is cultural.
mistakes.why: Staff work hard to avoid judging families and may overcorrect. Respect for a household's tradition can hide a separate, specific sign of harm.
mistakes.instead: Respect the practice and still act on specific observations. If there is reason to believe maltreatment, report immediately.

mistakes.mistake: Delaying a required report to consult or gather more facts.
mistakes.why: Consultation feels careful and fair to the family. But Minnesota law requires an immediate report once there is reason to believe a vulnerable adult is being maltreated.
mistakes.instead: Seek guidance promptly if unsure, and never let it delay a report that is already due.

mistakes.mistake: Avoiding all mention of the state's history.
mistakes.why: Leaders worry history will reopen wounds or invite blame. Silence can sound like denial when the state has publicly acknowledged harm.
mistakes.instead: Acknowledge documented history briefly and accurately, then answer the present question.

jobAid.title: Specifics first: distrust and values in tension
jobAid.use: When someone questions how DHS uses information, or when a family's practice feels in tension with a duty.
steps: Name the actual question or concern in one sentence.
For a question: say what you know, what you do not, and the date you will give a verified answer.
Get the verified answer from the person or area responsible, and give it in writing.
For a concern: list what you observed or heard, separately from what you interpreted.
Ask the person privately what they want, and be honest about what you cannot keep confidential.
If there is reason to believe a vulnerable adult is being maltreated, report immediately to the common entry point.
If it is only unfamiliar, learn more instead of reporting.
Route anything involving a Tribal Nation through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations.

media.reason: Two colleagues with different instincts, one to reassure and one to answer precisely, show the difference between goodwill and fair process better than narration can.

script.speaker: female
script.text: I keep thinking about that session. The parent asked who could see their name. I said DHS is here to help. I meant it.

script.speaker: male
script.text: I know you did. But that was not what they asked. They asked who could see it. We did not know the answer, and they could tell.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Fair. I just did not want to scare anyone off by saying I was not sure.

script.speaker: male
script.text: There is research on this. Across the US and thirty-three other countries, fair process predicted trust in civil servants more than outcomes did. Sometimes several times more. Saying I do not know yet, here is when I will tell you, is fair process.

script.speaker: female
script.text: And people have reasons to ask. Minnesota apologized in 2010 for what happened in state institutions. Unpaid labor. Procedures without consent. Graves with only numbers.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Right. And fear spreads past the people a rule covers. In 2018, even some families where everyone born abroad was already a citizen avoided benefits. They had nothing to lose under that rule.

script.speaker: female
script.text: So the answer matters more than the welcome. What do we do next time?

script.speaker: male
script.text: Tell people signing in is not needed for information. Get the real answer on access from the area responsible for data privacy. Send it in writing by a date we name.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Different topic, same skill. A staff member wants to report a family because an uncle manages his niece's money. They say it is tradition.

script.speaker: male
script.text: What did the staff member actually see or hear?

script.speaker: female
script.text: The arrangement. And the niece said she cannot buy her own medicine.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Then those are two different things. The tradition alone is not a reason to report. Her statement about medicine might be reason to believe she is being harmed.

script.speaker: female
script.text: And if it is reason to believe, the statute says immediately. Not after a second visit. I will make sure the report goes in today, and talk with the staff member about what they noticed.

prompts: What question about information use do people in your area ask most, and by when will you confirm the exact answer with the person or area responsible?
Which form, sign-in sheet or script in your work asks for trust without explaining why, and who can help you revise it this month?
With whom on your team will you review the reporting statute and practice separating observation from interpretation, and when?
