title: Power in the room
objective: Open decisions to the people affected by them honestly, by stating what is fixed and what is open, inviting input before the decision, and reporting back how input changed the result.
outcomes: Map a decision before inviting input: what is still open, who decides, who bears the result and by when.
Write an invitation that states fixed limits, open choices, ways to contribute and a report-back date.
Run a meeting so lower-status participants speak early and specific evidence survives into the decision.
Correct an invitation that overstated what was open, without making promises beyond your authority.
Give a report-back that names what was considered, what changed, what did not and why.

evidence.summary: Power shapes who speaks. In 23 intensive care units, lower-status staff felt less safe to speak up, and inclusive leaders narrowed that gap. Most employees in one interview study had stayed silent on an important issue, often from fear of being seen negatively or a sense of futility. Managerial openness is the leader behavior most consistently tied to voice. People rate a process as fairer when they can give input, especially before a decision. Small amounts of participation do little unless leaders share real information. In public life, people who feel they have a say trust government far more. Limits: much of this is lab, survey or workplace research, and leader effects on voice are small.

findings.claim: Lower-status health staff reported less psychological safety, and leader inclusiveness narrowed the status gap.
findings.detail: Survey of 1,440 professionals in 23 neonatal intensive care units, 2006. Psychological safety predicted engagement in quality improvement. Health and human services.

findings.claim: 34 of 40 employees (85 percent) said they had felt unable to raise an important issue at work.
findings.detail: Interview study of 40 full-time employees, 2003. Common reasons were fear of being seen negatively (30 percent), damaging relationships (27.5 percent) and futility (25 percent). Small convenience sample.

findings.claim: Managerial openness was the leader behavior most consistently related to employee voice, working through psychological safety.
findings.detail: Two field studies, 3,149 restaurant crew and 223 shift managers over ten months, 2007. Effects were small, about 2 to 8 percent of variance.

findings.claim: Voice before a decision raised perceived fairness most; voice after a decision still raised it above no voice.
findings.detail: Lab experiment with 179 undergraduates, 1990. Relevant information also raised fairness. Perceived control explained only part of the effect.

findings.claim: Below a moderate threshold, participative leadership was unrelated to performance; leader information sharing made participation pay off.
findings.detail: Two field studies of administrative, call-center and factory employees, 2015.

findings.claim: 69 percent of people who feel they have a say trust their national government, compared with 22 percent of those who do not.
findings.detail: OECD Survey on Drivers of Trust in Public Institutions, 30 countries, 2023 fieldwork, published 2024. Correlational. Public sector.

findings.claim: Community engagement in public health programs improved health behavior (d = 0.33) and self-efficacy (d = 0.41) for disadvantaged groups.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 131 controlled trials in OECD countries, 2015. No single engagement model worked significantly better. Public sector and human services.

findings.claim: Procedural, informational, interpersonal and outcome fairness are distinct, and each adds to how people judge an authority.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 183 organizational justice studies, 2001.

findings.claim: A well-known lab finding that power reduces perspective taking did not replicate.
findings.detail: Original study 2006; the Many Labs 3 replication, 2016, found no evidence of the effect.
findings.source: Galinsky et al., 2006; Ebersole et al., 2016

counterintuitive.headline: Asking after the decision still feels fair, and that is the danger.
counterintuitive.text: Lind, Kanfer and Earley ran an experiment with 179 participants in 1990. Voice before a decision produced the highest fairness ratings. But voice after the decision, when it could not change anything, still beat no voice at all. Control explained only part of the effect. People value being heard for its own sake. For leaders, this cuts two ways. Listening always matters. And a listening session held after choices are fixed can feel fair while changing nothing. Honest leaders say what is still open, and ask before they decide.

sections.title: Power decides who speaks
sections.text: In any meeting, some people control the decision, some bear the result and some do neither. These positions shape who talks. A study of 23 intensive care units found that lower-status staff felt less safe to speak up than physicians. Leaders who invited and valued input narrowed that gap. In another study, 34 of 40 employees said they had felt unable to raise an important issue. Common reasons were fear of looking bad and a sense that speaking would change nothing. Silence in a meeting is often a reasonable reading of power, not a lack of ideas.

sections.title: Why open invitations backfire
sections.text: Leaders often invite input on decisions that are mostly made. People can sense it. Research shows people rate a process fairer when they can give input, and fairest when the input comes before the decision. Input after the decision still feels somewhat fair, even when it changes nothing. That makes after-the-fact listening tempting. It also makes it misleading if you present a closed decision as open.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: Before you invite anyone, map the decision. Write down what is still open, what is fixed, who decides, who bears the result and the decision date. Put that map in the invitation. Say plainly: the site is set by contract, but two extra hours and the format are open. Then share the information people need to contribute. Participation without real information does little. After the decision, report back. Say what you considered, what changed, what did not and why.

sections.title: Inside DHS too
sections.text: The same applies when leaders invite frontline staff into decisions. A call-line worker may hold precise evidence about when people call. Ask early, ask in more than one way, and let that evidence reach the person who decides. Then tell them what happened to it, even when the answer is that nothing changed this time. Closing the loop is what makes the next invitation believable.

sections.title: Status and psychological safety
sections.text: Nembhard and Edmondson surveyed 1,440 health professionals in 23 neonatal intensive care units. Physicians reported more psychological safety than nurses, and nurses more than respiratory therapists. Psychological safety means believing you can speak up without being punished or embarrassed. Where leaders were more inclusive, inviting and appreciating others' contributions, the status gap was smaller. Lower-status staff gained the most. Psychological safety also predicted engagement in quality improvement. The lesson for DHS is direct. People with less positional power often hold the most detailed knowledge of how work actually happens. Whether they share it depends heavily on the leader.

sections.title: Why people stay silent
sections.text: Milliken, Morrison and Hewlin interviewed 40 employees. 34 had felt unable to raise an important issue. They most often held back concerns about a colleague's or supervisor's performance, about processes or about pay. Reasons included fear of being seen as a complainer, fear of damaging relationships, a sense of futility and fear of retaliation. Many pointed to their own lack of tenure or rank, or to hierarchical cultures. The study was small, but the pattern is familiar. Silence often comes from reasonable reading of power, not from lack of ideas.

sections.title: What leaders can do about it
sections.text: Detert and Burris studied 3,149 restaurant crew members and 223 shift managers. Managerial openness, meaning a leader who listens, considers ideas and acts on some of them, was the leader behavior most consistently related to voice. It worked through psychological safety. The effects were real but small, explaining a few percent of the differences in voice. Leadership is one influence among many. Still, openness is something you control. You can ask directly, respond with interest, and show what happened to the last idea someone raised.

sections.title: Voice, timing and fairness
sections.text: Lind, Kanfer and Earley ran an experiment with 179 participants. Those who gave input before a goal was set rated the process as fairest. Those who gave input after it was set rated it less fair, but still fairer than those who had no voice. Relevant information also increased fairness. A large meta-analysis by Colquitt and colleagues found that fairness has distinct parts: the outcome, the process, the respect shown and the information given. Each one matters. A good result does not make up for a hidden process, and a warm meeting does not make up for missing information.

sections.title: Participation needs a threshold and information
sections.text: Lam, Huang and Chan studied administrative, call-center and factory employees. Low levels of participative leadership were unrelated to performance. Only above a moderate level did more participation help, and it helped more when leaders shared information. An occasional any thoughts? does little. Participation works when people know the constraints, the data and what is genuinely open.

sections.title: Consultation and public trust
sections.text: Outside the agency, the pattern holds at scale. The OECD's 2024 trust survey across 30 countries found that 69 percent of people who feel they have a say trust their national government, compared with 22 percent of those who do not. The data are correlational, so they do not prove that consultation causes trust. A meta-analysis of 131 controlled trials found that public health programs that engaged disadvantaged communities improved health behavior and self-efficacy. No single model of engagement worked best. What mattered was real engagement.

sections.title: Writing an honest invitation
sections.text: An honest invitation answers five questions in plain language. What decision is being made? What is already fixed, and why? What is still open? How can people contribute, including in writing or one-on-one? When will the decision be made, and when will people hear back? For example: the venue is set by contract through next year. The time of two added sessions and whether to add a phone option are open. Send comments by the 10th or join the meeting on the 3rd. The decision will be made on the 15th, and a summary of what changed will follow within two weeks. An invitation like this respects people's time and makes their input count.

sections.title: Questions that open the floor
sections.text: How you ask shapes who answers. What concerns do you have about this? invites concerns better than does anyone object? A round where each person speaks in turn gives quieter people a protected moment. Asking the person with the most frontline experience to speak first keeps senior views from setting the frame. Saying I would like to hear what I am missing signals that disagreement is welcome. These are small moves. The research suggests openness works through psychological safety, and safety is built one response at a time.

sections.title: Applying it in DHS work
sections.text: When you plan a change, map the decision first. In the invitation, name what is fixed and why, what is open and the decision date. Offer more than one way to contribute: in a meeting, in writing or one-on-one. In the meeting, hear from those with the least positional power first. Keep specific evidence intact. If a worker reports that evening callers wait longest, carry that exact point forward, not a vague summary like people want flexibility. After the decision, report back on what changed and why.

sections.title: The ethics of the voice effect
sections.text: The finding that voice raises fairness even after a decision is double-edged. It shows that being heard matters to people for its own sake. It also means a leader can create a feeling of fairness without sharing any control. That gap can be exploited, often without intent. A team may hold a listening session after the budget is set because it feels respectful. Participants may leave feeling heard, then later discover nothing could have changed. That discovery tends to cost more trust than the session built. The honest course is to say, before people spend their time, which parts are open.

sections.title: Correcting an overstated invitation
sections.text: Sometimes an invitation promised more than the decision allows. Perhaps it said the whole plan was open, but a contract fixes the location. Correct it as early as possible, ideally before the meeting. Name the error plainly. State what is fixed and who controls it. State what is still open and when it will be decided. Avoid promising changes beyond your authority, such as moving a contracted site. Instead, identify who owns the contract and whether a change is possible later. People who rearranged work or paid for travel deserve to know where their effort can still make a difference.

sections.title: Keeping specific evidence alive
sections.text: Input often dies in the summary. A participant explains that a weekday morning session is impossible for people who work hourly shifts and rely on one bus route. The notes say: some attendees prefer other times. The decision maker reads the notes and sees nothing actionable. Protect specifics. Capture the condition, the effect and the suggested change. Let contributors check the summary before it moves on. Remove personal details they do not want shared. Specifics are what let a decision maker act.

sections.title: Power among partners and staff
sections.text: Power is not only between DHS and the public. In a meeting with county directors, providers and frontline DHS staff, the frontline worker may have the least positional power and the most precise evidence. Nembhard and Edmondson found that lower-status staff gain the most from inclusive leadership. Practical steps help. Send questions in advance. Use rounds in which each person speaks in turn. Start with people who hold less rank. Ask for written input from anyone who prefers it. Matters that involve Tribal Nations go through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations, using government-to-government channels rather than a general stakeholder meeting.

sections.title: When you are the one with less power
sections.text: Many DHS leaders sit in the middle. You may invite input from your team while your own director has already fixed key choices. Ask your leaders the same questions you ask yourself: what is open, what is fixed and by when? If you learn late that a choice was already made, tell your team promptly and honestly. Do not present a closed decision as open to protect your own position. Your staff will notice the difference, and the same research on openness applies to how they read you.

sections.title: What the evidence does not show
sections.text: Some popular claims about power are weaker than they seem. A widely cited lab study found that feeling powerful made people worse at taking others' perspectives. A large multi-lab replication did not find the effect. So this course does not claim that power itself makes leaders less empathetic. The verified findings are about structure: status shapes safety to speak, openness relates to voice, and timing and information shape fairness. No verified study here shows that these practices help one racial, disability or other group more than another. Status and rank are the verified differences. Leader effects on voice are also small, so do not expect one meeting to change a culture.

sections.title: Harder situations
sections.text: Sometimes nothing is open. A law, a federal rule or a funding decision has fixed the outcome. Say so. Do not invite input you cannot use. You can still explain the decision, its reasons and who to contact about the rule itself. Sometimes input conflicts: two groups want opposite schedules. Share the criteria you will use and explain the trade-off in the report-back. Sometimes a participant raises a concern outside your authority. Name the person or area responsible and offer to pass the specific point on, then tell the participant what happened to it.

sections.title: Measuring influence, not attendance
sections.text: Teams often judge engagement by how many people came and whether they liked the session. Those numbers say little about power. Better questions are about influence. Which options changed because of input? Which contributors' points appear in the decision? Did people with less rank shape any part of it? Did participants say their input reached the decision as intended? Answering these does not require tracking anyone. It requires a plain account of what happened between the meeting and the decision, written for the people who took part.

sections.title: The report-back as proof
sections.text: A report-back is the evidence that participation was real. It should name the options considered, what changed because of input, what did not change and why, and who will review the effect later. Attendance numbers and satisfaction ratings do not show whether input mattered. Write the report-back in plain language and share it through the same channels people used to contribute. If input could not alter a fixed element, say so and point to any other route for change. Over time, a history of honest report-backs is what makes the next invitation credible.

sections.title: Leading with openness every day
sections.text: Openness is not a single meeting. It is a pattern people watch. Ask for concerns in more than one way. Respond with interest when someone disagrees, especially someone with less rank. Share information early, including constraints you would rather not admit. Close the loop on ideas, including the ones you did not use. Detert and Burris found openness is the leader behavior most consistently tied to voice. It is also the one most within your control.

sections.title: In the moment
sections.text: When a meeting turns tense because people feel misled, slow down. Name what you heard. Acknowledge any error in the invitation. Restate what is fixed, who controls it and what is still open. Offer a way to contribute that does not require speaking in the room. Give the decision date and the report-back date. Then keep both promises. Trust after a misstep is rebuilt by the next visible, kept commitment, not by the apology alone.

simulation.setup: You are a Human Services Manager in the Disability Services Division. Your unit is redesigning the schedule for regional information sessions about disability waiver services. A contract fixes the venue in one region. You control two additional session hours and the format. An invitation sent last week told community members and partners the entire plan was open. The meeting with community members, county partners and your frontline staff is in three days.

steps.situation: Reviewing the invitation, you realize it overstated what is open. The venue cannot change under the current contract. Your Program Specialist suggests keeping things positive: let people share everything, and sort it out later.
steps.question: What do you do before the meeting?

choices.label: Keep the invitation as it is and listen broadly, then explain constraints at the end.
choices.feedback: This avoids an awkward correction, but it spends people's time on a choice they cannot make. Research shows voice feels fair even when it cannot change anything, which makes this approach tempting. When attendees learn the venue was never open, the disappointment usually costs more trust than the meeting built.

choices.label: Send a correction now: the venue is fixed by contract, the two extra hours and format are open, how input will be used and the decision date.
choices.feedback: This is honest before people invest more time. It focuses input where it can make a difference. Sharing constraints and information is what makes participation pay off, according to Lam and colleagues. People who cannot use the open choices can decide how to spend their time.

choices.label: Cancel the meeting and decide the hours internally to avoid confusion.
choices.feedback: This prevents false expectations but removes the people affected from the part that is genuinely open. They bear the result of the schedule. The OECD trust data suggest that feeling you have a say goes with much higher trust. Correct the invitation instead of closing the door.

steps.situation: At the meeting, attendees focus on moving the venue. A community member says, I took time off because the invitation said we could choose the location. Now you are telling me it is set? A county partner nods.
steps.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Acknowledge the invitation overstated what was open, explain the contract and who owns it, then put the two hours and format on the table with a decision date.
choices.feedback: This repairs trust by naming the error plainly and redirecting energy to real choices. Explaining who owns the contract offers a legitimate route for the venue concern. A decision date shows input will be used before the choice is made, which research links to the strongest fairness.

choices.label: Promise to look into moving the venue, since people care so much about it.
choices.feedback: This feels responsive, but the venue is outside your authority under the contract. A promise you cannot keep sets up a larger loss of trust later. You can name the contract owner and say whether a change is possible in a future cycle, without committing to it.

choices.label: Thank everyone and note all venue comments in the meeting minutes.
choices.feedback: Capturing comments matters, but minutes alone do not tell people what can change or when. The person who took time off still does not know where their input can make a difference. Combine the notes with a clear statement of what is fixed and open.

steps.situation: The meeting goes smoothly, but county partners and providers do most of the talking. A call-line worker on your team says nothing. Afterward, the worker emails you: evening callers wait longest, and most mention work schedules. The email includes specific weeks and times.
steps.question: What do you do with the email?

choices.label: Thank the worker and add the point to the meeting summary as staff feedback.
choices.feedback: Thanking the worker is right, but folding the evidence into a general summary risks losing the specifics a decision maker needs. Nembhard and Edmondson found lower-status staff gain most when leaders actively invite and value their input. A line in a summary does not do that.

choices.label: Ask the worker to share the data directly with the decision group, and change the next meeting to rounds that start with those holding the least rank.
choices.feedback: This carries specific evidence intact to the people who decide, and it addresses why the worker stayed silent. Rounds that start with lower-rank participants reduce the status gap in speaking up. Openness to a junior voice, shown in action, is the leader behavior most tied to future voice.

choices.label: Encourage the worker to speak up at the next meeting so their voice is heard directly.
choices.feedback: The intent to build confidence is good. But the worker already chose a safer channel, and the decision may come before the next meeting. Many employees stay silent because of rank and fear of looking bad. Change the structure rather than asking the person to overcome it alone.

steps.situation: The decision is made. One extra hour moves to a weekday evening and the format adds a phone option. The venue stays the same. Your Program Specialist drafts the report-back.
steps.question: What should the report-back include?

choices.label: Attendance numbers and positive feedback from the meeting.
choices.feedback: These show that people came, not that their input mattered. Fairness research separates the outcome, the process and the information people receive. A report-back built on attendance tells participants nothing about what their effort changed. It can also make the next invitation less credible.

choices.label: The options considered, what changed because of input and why, what did not change and why, who owns the contract, and when the schedule will be reviewed.
choices.feedback: This gives an honest account of influence. It credits the specific evidence that moved the evening hour. It explains the fixed venue and the route for changing it later. A review date shows the decision stays open to evidence. This is what makes participation believable next time.

choices.label: A short list of the changes adopted.
choices.feedback: Listing changes is a good start and more useful than attendance. But it leaves out what did not change and why, so people whose input was not adopted get no explanation. Informational fairness matters on its own. Add what was considered, what stayed fixed and why.

simulation.debrief: Power showed up at every step. The invitation decided whether people spent their effort on real choices. The meeting's structure decided whether the call-line worker's evidence reached the decision. The report-back decided whether participation looked real afterward. The research explains why each matters. Lower-status people feel less safe to speak, and inclusive leaders narrow that gap. Openness is the leader behavior most tied to voice. Input before a decision feels fairest, while input after it can feel fair and change nothing. Participation works when leaders share real information. And people who feel they have a say trust government more. The strongest path stated limits early, protected specific evidence and gave an honest account of influence.

mistakes.mistake: Inviting input on a decision that is mostly made, without saying so.
mistakes.why: Listening feels respectful, and voice after a decision still raises perceived fairness. That makes after-the-fact sessions tempting, even when nothing can change.
mistakes.instead: Map the decision first. In the invitation, state what is fixed, what is open and the decision date.

mistakes.mistake: Asking for input without sharing the constraints and data.
mistakes.why: Leaders want open, unbiased input and worry details will narrow it. But participation does little below a threshold, and information sharing is what makes it work.
mistakes.instead: Share the budget, rules, data and trade-offs up front, in plain language.

mistakes.mistake: Running open discussion and assuming everyone feels free to speak.
mistakes.why: Leaders often feel approachable from their own position. Yet lower-status staff report less psychological safety, and most employees have stayed silent on something important.
mistakes.instead: Use rounds, start with those holding less rank, and offer written and one-on-one routes.

mistakes.mistake: Summarizing specific evidence into a general theme.
mistakes.why: Summaries feel efficient and protect privacy. They also strip out the detail a decision maker needs to act.
mistakes.instead: Keep the condition, effect and suggested change. Let contributors check the summary.

mistakes.mistake: Promising changes beyond your authority to restore goodwill.
mistakes.why: It feels responsive in a tense moment. When the promise fails, trust drops further.
mistakes.instead: Name who owns the fixed element and whether change is possible later, without committing to it.

mistakes.mistake: Reporting back with attendance and satisfaction only.
mistakes.why: These numbers are easy to gather and look positive. They do not show whether input changed anything.
mistakes.instead: Report what was considered, what changed, what did not and why, and when it will be reviewed.

jobAid.title: Decision map and invitation check
jobAid.use: Before you invite anyone, inside or outside DHS, to give input on a decision.
steps: What exactly is still open? List it in one or two lines.
What is fixed, why, and who controls it?
Who decides, who bears the result, and what is the decision date?
What information do people need to contribute well, and have you shared it?
Does the invitation offer more than one way to contribute, including written and one-on-one?
In the meeting, who speaks first, and does that favor people with less rank?
How will specific evidence reach the decision intact?
When and how will you report back on what changed, what did not and why?

media.reason: Power is easiest to see from two positions at once. A conversation between a manager and a frontline worker shows what silence looks like from each side.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Thanks for the email about evening callers. That data is exactly what the schedule needs. I am curious, though. Why not raise it in the meeting?

script.speaker: male
script.text: Honestly? The county directors and providers were going back and forth. I am the newest person on the team. It did not feel like my place.

script.speaker: female
script.text: That is fair, and it is common. In one study, 34 of 40 employees said they had held back on an important issue. Lack of rank was one of the top reasons.

script.speaker: male
script.text: There was also a feeling it would not matter. The invitation said everything was open, but then the venue turned out to be fixed. People noticed.

script.speaker: female
script.text: That one is on me. I should have corrected the invitation before the meeting. Saying what is fixed and what is open is the least I owe people who show up.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Would it have changed anything if I had spoken up?

script.speaker: female
script.text: Yes. The two extra hours are still open. Your data points to a weekday evening. That is a real choice, and the decision is not until next week.

script.speaker: male
script.text: So what do you want me to do?

script.speaker: female
script.text: Share the weeks and times directly with the decision group. And next meeting, I will run rounds and start with people who hold the least rank. That way it is not on you to fight for a turn.

script.speaker: male
script.text: That would help. Will people hear what happened with their input?

script.speaker: female
script.text: They will. The report-back will say what was considered, what changed, what did not and why. If your evening hour gets adopted, it will say your data is the reason.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Then I will speak up next time. Mostly because I will know it can still change something.

prompts: Which decision on your calendar looks open but is mostly made, and by when will you tell people what is fixed and what is open?
Whose specific evidence, often from someone with less rank, should reach your next decision, and how will you ask for it this week?
For a recent decision, what would an honest report-back say about what changed and what did not, and when will you send it?

title: Adapting without losing yourself, and leading as a bridge
objective: Share the work of adapting across your team and lead two groups that blame each other toward one shared, checkable action.
outcomes: Name who on your team routinely adapts, translates or smooths things over, and estimate what it costs them in time and energy.
Ask a colleague privately which parts of bridge work they want to keep and which should be shared, then change meeting design to match.
Trace one handoff between two groups from both sides before deciding where it fails.
Agree with two groups on one shared action, an owner on each side and a date to compare evidence.
Route any matter with Tribal implications through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations instead of a personal contact.

evidence.summary: Adapting to the dominant style at work pays off in how people are judged. In experiments, a Black coworker who code-switched was rated more professional by Black and White participants alike. Keeping up a facade is tied to emotional exhaustion and intent to leave, and faking displayed feelings is tied to poorer well-being across 95 studies. Inviting people to bring their own strengths to work cut turnover in a field experiment. For bridging, a meta-analysis of 10,848 teams links boundary work to better performance, especially coordinating and representing rather than guarding. Limits: the code-switching studies measure perceptions, most well-being evidence is correlational, and no study found tests these ideas inside a state human-services agency.

findings.claim: Both Black and White participants rated a Black coworker who code-switched in speech, name and hairstyle as more professional than one who did not.
findings.detail: Two between-subjects experiments (voicemail and written email versions), U.S. adult participants, law-firm vignette, 2021. Black participants rated the non-code-switching coworker as more professional than White participants did in Study 2. Sample sizes not reported in the source opened.
findings.source: McCluney, Durkee, Smith, Robotham and Lee, 2021 (summary by Cornell ILR School)

findings.claim: Employees who held minority status or worked in nonparticipative settings were more likely to create facades of conformity, and emotional exhaustion linked those facades to intent to leave.
findings.detail: Cross-sectional survey of 238 employees across multiple industries, 2009. Self-report; cannot establish cause.

findings.claim: Surface acting, showing feelings you do not have, had substantial links to impaired well-being and poorer job attitudes and a small negative link to performance.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 494 correlations from 95 independent studies, 2011. Deep acting showed weak links to impaired well-being and positive links to emotional performance and customer satisfaction.

findings.claim: New hires invited to share their personal strengths left less often: turnover in standard onboarding was 47.2% higher than in the personal-strengths group.
findings.detail: Field experiment with new call-center agents at Wipro BPO in India, three conditions, about seven months of follow-up, published 2013. Customer satisfaction was also higher. A lab study of 175 students linked the effect to authentic self-expression.
findings.source: Cable, Gino and Staats, 2013 (summary by Harvard Business School Working Knowledge)

findings.claim: Team boundary work had a positive relationship with team performance (rho = .39), stronger for spanning activities such as coordinating and representing (.43) than for guarding (.31).
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 85 samples, 10,848 teams and 295 effect sizes from 1981 to 2021, published 2023. Formal leaders' boundary work was more effective than members' (tentative). No public-sector subgroup reported.
findings.source: Leicht-Deobald, Backmann, de Vries, Weiss, Hohmann, Walter, van der Vegt and Hoegl, 2023

findings.claim: In public-service partnerships, the people who manage relationships across organizations depend on specific relational skills and behavior, not only on formal structures.
findings.detail: Literature review plus surveys and in-depth interviews with several types of boundary spanners in UK public services, 2002. Sample size not verified.

findings.claim: Minnesota law requires listed state agencies to designate a Tribal liaison, follow consultation policies developed with Tribal governments and consult each Minnesota Tribal government at least annually.
findings.detail: Minnesota Statutes section 10.65, enacted 2021 and amended since. Also requires Tribal-state relations training for employees whose work is likely to involve Tribal matters.

counterintuitive.headline: The pressure to code-switch is shared, even by people who pay its cost.
counterintuitive.text: It is tempting to assume only people outside a group reward conformity. In two experiments by McCluney and colleagues (2021), Black and White participants both rated a Black coworker who adjusted speech, name and hairstyle as more professional. Black participants were more accepting of the coworker who did not adjust, and neither group thought anyone should change their name. The lesson for a leader is that the norm lives in the whole workplace. Telling one person to be more authentic leaves them facing the same judgment. Changing what the team treats as professional is the leader's work.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.text: Every team has people who quietly adapt so work can move. They soften their speech, explain one group to another, or translate after meetings. Some of this is a skill and a gift. Some of it is a hidden second job. Research on code-switching shows that adapting to the dominant style earns a professional premium. Black and White participants alike rated a Black coworker who adjusted speech, name and hairstyle as more professional. So adapting is often rational. It also has a cost. Employees who keep up a facade at work report more emotional exhaustion, and that exhaustion is tied to intent to leave.

sections.title: Bridges carry weight
sections.text: Leaders also act as bridges between programs, counties, providers and communities. A large meta-analysis of teams links this kind of boundary work to better performance. It works best when it means coordinating, representing and searching for information, not guarding territory. But a bridge that depends on one tired person is not a structure. It is a favor that will end.

sections.title: Why it matters for DHS work
sections.text: DHS work runs on handoffs. Eligibility units hand off to counties. Disability services staff work with lead agencies, providers and families. Call-line staff explain rules written by someone else. Each handoff needs someone who can translate between groups. When that person is always the same employee, two things happen. Their own work gets less attention, and the whole team depends on one person's energy. Sharing the bridge protects both the person and the service.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: This week, notice who on your team does the extra adapting. Ask that person, privately, which parts they want to keep and which they would like the team to share. Then change one meeting or handoff so the work does not fall on them by default. When you bridge two groups yourself, start by tracing one real handoff from both sides. Agree on one shared action, one owner on each side and one date to compare what happened. If the matter touches a Tribal Nation, bring in the person or area responsible for Tribal relations. Do not use a personal contact as a substitute.

sections.title: What code-switching research actually shows
sections.text: Code-switching means adjusting your speech, appearance or behavior to fit the dominant norms of a setting. McCluney and colleagues ran two experiments in 2021. Participants read or heard advice from a fictional Black coworker at a law firm. In one version the coworker adjusted speech style, name and hairstyle. In the other version the coworker did not. Both Black and White participants rated the code-switching coworker as more professional. Black participants were more favorable toward the coworker who did not adjust. Both groups supported adjusting speech. Neither group supported changing a name. Views on natural hair differed. The authors argue that constant self-monitoring is a burden that may add to fatigue and burnout. That last point is their argument, not a measured result in these studies.

sections.title: Why the cost is real
sections.text: Two other lines of research help explain the cost. Hewlin surveyed 238 employees across many industries. People in settings where they had little say, and people with minority status, were more likely to create facades of conformity. Those facades were linked to emotional exhaustion, and exhaustion was linked to intent to leave. A meta-analysis of 95 studies by Hülsheger and Schewe looked at emotional labor. Surface acting, showing feelings you do not actually have, had substantial links to poorer well-being and job attitudes. Deep acting, genuinely trying to see the situation differently, showed much weaker links to harm. The difference matters. Adapting because you understand and agree is not the same as hiding who you are all day.

sections.title: The other side: inviting people in
sections.text: Cable, Gino and Staats tested the opposite approach in a field experiment with new call-center agents. One group spent an extra hour on their personal strengths and how they could bring them to the job. Turnover in the standard onboarding group was 47.2% higher than in that group. Customer satisfaction was also higher. The setting was a private call center in India, so treat the size of the effect with care. The direction is still useful for a DHS leader. People stay and serve better when the job invites more of who they are, not less.

sections.title: What a bridge does
sections.text: Boundary spanning is the work of connecting a team with people outside it. Leicht-Deobald and colleagues combined 85 samples covering 10,848 teams. Boundary work had a solid positive link to team performance. Spanning activities, such as coordinating, representing the team and searching for information, showed stronger links than guarding activities, such as buffering and blocking. Work aimed outside the organization showed slightly stronger links than work inside it. Formal leaders' boundary work appeared more effective than members' work, though the authors call that tentative. In public services, Williams studied people who manage partnerships across agencies. His work centers on their relational skills and behavior, not only on formal agreements.

sections.title: How this looks in DHS work
sections.text: Picture a disability services team that works with county lead agencies and community providers. One program consultant is known as good with the counties. Every hard call goes to that consultant. Each call is reasonable. Together they become a second job that no position description names. Start by making the work visible. List the bridging tasks from the last month: who explained, who translated, who calmed a meeting, who followed up. Then ask the person what they want. Some people value being the connector. Others would rather present their own analysis.

sections.title: Questions to ask before you assign bridge work
sections.text: Before you hand the next hard call to the usual person, pause on four questions. Is this task part of their role, or has it drifted there? Have they told you they want it? Who else could learn it with some coaching? What would they be doing with that time instead? These questions take a minute. They turn a habit into a choice. They also signal that you see the work, which is part of what the onboarding experiment suggests keeps people engaged.

sections.title: Three practical shifts
sections.text: First, build clarification into the meeting instead of after it. Send written options ahead, allow time for questions and name who will follow up. Second, rotate bridging roles so knowledge spreads and no one carries all of it. Third, when two groups blame each other, trace one fictional or de-identified case from both sides. Ask what each group could see, when it knew action was needed and who had authority to fix the gap. Then agree on the smallest joint action, an owner on each side and a review date. For anything with Tribal implications, Minnesota law sets a government-to-government relationship. DHS works with Tribal Nations through designated Tribal liaisons and consultation policies. Route those matters through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations.

sections.title: Adaptation is not the problem
sections.text: It would be easy to take the wrong lesson from code-switching research. The answer is not to tell people to stop adapting. Adapting is part of skilled communication, and the research shows it earns a real premium in how people are judged. In the McCluney experiments, both Black and White participants supported adjusting speech style. The trouble is when adaptation becomes one-way. If one group always adjusts and the other never does, the norm is not shared. It is imposed. A leader's job is to make adaptation reciprocal. The team adjusts its meeting habits, writing and timing. Individuals adjust where they choose. Everyone can see who is doing what.

sections.title: Surface and depth
sections.text: The emotional labor meta-analysis offers a useful distinction. Surface acting means displaying a feeling you do not have. Deep acting means trying to actually see the situation in a way that changes how you feel. Surface acting showed substantial links to poorer well-being. Deep acting did not, to the same degree, and it was linked to better emotional performance and customer outcomes. For a leader this suggests a test. Ask whether a person is adapting from understanding or hiding to stay safe. You cannot answer that for them. You can create conditions where hiding is less necessary. Hewlin found facades were more common where people had little say in decisions. Participation is something a supervisor controls.

sections.title: Limits of the evidence
sections.text: Be honest about what these studies can and cannot show. The code-switching experiments measured how people rated a fictional coworker. They did not follow real careers or measure the code-switcher's health. The sample sizes were not reported in the summary opened for this course. Hewlin's study was a single cross-sectional survey, so it shows association, not cause. The emotional labor meta-analysis drew mostly on correlational studies, and applying it to code-switching is an analogy. The onboarding experiment took place in private call centers in India. The boundary-spanning meta-analysis is large but reports no public-sector subgroup. No study found for this course tested any of this inside a state human-services agency. That is why the moves in this course are small, reversible and checkable.

sections.title: Who carries the bridge
sections.text: Evidence on the hidden workload of bilingual or bicultural government employees is thin. Small qualitative studies exist, but none strong enough to cite here as a finding. So do not assume you know who carries the weight on your team. Look. Ask. Some people want the connector role and see it as central to their work. Others feel stuck in it. Rotate who has which trait in your own assumptions. The person most fluent with counties may not be the person you expect. The person most tired may be the one who looks most at ease. The boundary-spanning meta-analysis also found that leaders' boundary work appeared more effective than members' work. That is a reason for supervisors to carry more of the hardest bridging themselves rather than handing it down.

sections.title: Edge case: when the person wants to be the bridge
sections.text: Some employees take real pride in being the connector. Their language, background or long relationships make them good at it, and they want that recognized. Do not take the role away in the name of fairness. Ask what support would make it sustainable. That might be protected time, a named role in their position description, a partner who shares the load, or credit when you report results. The aim is choice and visibility, not removal. Check again in a few months, because what someone wants can change.

sections.title: Edge case: adapting across disability and language
sections.text: Adaptation is not only about race or culture. A Deaf colleague may adjust constantly to hearing meeting norms. A colleague whose first language is not English may spend extra time checking every email. A team member with a nonvisible disability may mask symptoms to seem steady. The research cited here does not test these groups directly, so do not assume the same costs. Ask, and make the team's habits flexible: captions, written agendas, time to respond, and choices about format.

sections.title: Harder situation: when you are the one adapting
sections.text: Many supervisors are themselves the person who adapts most. You may adjust your style to be heard by senior leaders, and adjust again for your team. That is skilled work, and it costs energy. Notice where you are surface acting rather than choosing. Find at least one setting where you can work in your own style. Name your own limits to your manager the same way you would want a team member to name theirs. Leading a team where adaptation is shared is easier when you are not hiding your own costs.

sections.title: Harder situation: two groups, two true stories
sections.text: When a county lead agency and a DHS unit blame each other, both accounts are often partly true. A county may say service plans come back late. The DHS unit may say plans arrive without required documents. Do not pick a side or hold a meeting about attitudes. Trace one case from both sides. Write down what each group could see, when it knew action was needed and who had authority to correct a gap. Keep both accounts where they differ. Then ask each group what it can change without waiting for the other. Choose one shared action, an owner on each side and a date to compare evidence. Include a way for the people receiving services to say whether anything improved. A bridge fails when the person using the service has to carry messages between agencies.

sections.title: Harder situation: Tribal matters
sections.text: A Tribal Nation is a sovereign government, not a stakeholder group or a community partner. Minnesota Statutes section 10.65 requires listed agencies to designate a Tribal liaison and follow consultation policies developed with Tribal governments. Agencies must consult each Tribal government at least annually. They must also train employees whose work is likely to involve Tribal matters. A personal friendship with someone who works for a Tribal Nation does not create authority to speak with or for that Nation. When a matter may affect a Tribal Nation, bring it to the person or area responsible for Tribal relations. Describe what you have observed, ask how to proceed and follow their lead. This is the bridge working as designed, not a delay.

sections.title: Differential effects to watch
sections.text: The code-switching research found that Black and White participants differed on some behaviors. Views on natural hair split, while both groups opposed changing a name. That is a reminder that adaptation pressures are not one thing. Do not assume that a rule about appearance or speech lands the same for everyone. Do not claim effects for any group beyond what the evidence shows. When in doubt, ask the people affected what a norm costs them, and change the norm before asking them to change themselves.

simulation.setup: You are a Human Services Supervisor in a Disability Services Division unit that reviews county lead agency service plans. One program consultant on your team is widely seen as good with counties. For months, every difficult county call and every tense meeting follow-up has gone to that consultant. Meanwhile, two county lead agencies say DHS approvals are slow, and your unit says county plans arrive incomplete. A joint meeting is next week. At stake: a colleague's energy and career, a working relationship with county partners, and whether people waiting for services get approvals sooner.

steps.situation: Before the joint meeting, a manager asks you to have the program consultant prepare the county relationship notes and lead the follow-up again. The consultant has been staying late and has not presented their own analysis in a team meeting for two months.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Meet privately with the consultant, list the bridging work from the last month together, and ask which parts they want to keep and which should be shared.
choices.feedback: This makes hidden work visible without deciding for the person. Hewlin's survey linked facades to settings where people have little say, and to exhaustion. Asking first gives the consultant a say. You learn they value the county relationships but want to present their own analysis. You can now split the work on purpose. It also signals that the work counts as work.

choices.label: Thank the consultant publicly, tell them they are the team's best bridge, and ask them to lead the follow-up again.
choices.feedback: Recognition matters, and it feels supportive. But it confirms the default and adds weight. Nothing about the hidden workload changes. The research on facades and surface acting links sustained effort of this kind to exhaustion and intent to leave. You have not asked what the person wants. Praise without a change in load can deepen the facade the person already keeps.

choices.label: Take over all the county follow-up yourself so the consultant gets a break.
choices.feedback: This is generous and partly right. The boundary-spanning meta-analysis suggests leaders' boundary work can be especially effective. But you decided without asking, and you removed relationships the consultant may value. Spreading the knowledge is stronger than moving it to one new person. Ask before you act, then share the load across several people.

steps.situation: At the joint meeting, a county lead agency supervisor says approvals take weeks. Your lead reviewer says plans keep arriving without required documents. The room is tense. The consultant is ready to present a short analysis of where delays occur.
steps.question: How do you run the next part of the meeting?

choices.label: Ask the group to trace one de-identified plan from both sides: what each side could see, when, and who could fix each gap.
choices.feedback: Tracing one case turns blame into shared facts. Both stories turn out partly true: a required form is missing from the county checklist, and your unit's request for it sits in a shared mailbox for days. Coordinating and searching for information are the spanning activities most linked to team performance. Each group leaves with a fix it owns.

choices.label: Propose a separate session on communication styles and respect between the agencies.
choices.feedback: Respect matters, but this treats a process gap as an attitude problem. It also delays any fix. People waiting for services gain nothing from it. Guarding and buffering activities showed weaker links to performance than coordinating and representing. The county supervisor agrees politely and nothing changes before the next round of plans.

choices.label: Promise the county that your unit will speed up approvals and ask them to send complete plans.
choices.feedback: It calms the room, and both requests are reasonable. But you have committed to a fix without knowing where the delay sits. Each side leaves believing the other was the problem. A single traced case would have given you facts to act on. Expect the same complaint to return within weeks.

steps.situation: At the joint meeting, the consultant leads the follow-up again and is visibly careful and quiet. Afterward, they tell you they soften their own recommendations to avoid seeming difficult with the counties.
steps.question: What do you do now?

choices.label: Thank them for telling you, ask what would make it safe to state their recommendation plainly, and offer to present the hardest point yourself.
choices.feedback: You are now reducing the need for a facade rather than praising it. Presenting the hardest point yourself shares the cost. It also uses the finding that leaders' boundary work appeared more effective than members'. The consultant agrees to present their analysis at the next meeting. You also learn what the consultant actually recommends, which the team has been missing.

choices.label: Tell them softening is wise with counties and that they handled it well.
choices.feedback: This is meant kindly, and adapting can be skilled. But you are rewarding surface acting the consultant just told you costs them. The emotional labor meta-analysis links surface acting with poorer well-being. You have also lost their real recommendation. Next time, the consultant will soften even more.

choices.label: Send them to a training on assertive communication.
choices.feedback: Skill building can help, but it puts the fix on the individual. The code-switching experiments show the pressure comes from shared norms in the workplace. Changing the setting, such as who presents hard news and how meetings run, addresses the source. Training can come later, once the setting supports plain speaking.

steps.situation: After the meeting, a county supervisor tells you that a nearby Tribal Nation's human services staff have similar concerns about approval timing. The county supervisor suggests you call a person you know who works for that Nation, since you have a good relationship.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Thank the county supervisor, then bring what you heard to the person or area responsible for Tribal relations and ask how to proceed.
choices.feedback: Minnesota law sets a government-to-government relationship through designated Tribal liaisons and consultation policies. Your observation is useful. Routing it correctly respects sovereignty and lets the person or area responsible decide whether and how to engage. You follow their lead. The county supervisor sees how the route works and can use it next time.

choices.label: Call your contact informally to ask whether the concern is real, since it is only a quick check.
choices.feedback: It feels respectful and fast. But a personal relationship does not create authority to speak with or for a Tribal Nation. An informal call can put your contact in an awkward position and bypass the consultation process. Bring it to the person or area responsible for Tribal relations. Your contact may also feel obliged to answer for their government, which is not their role.

choices.label: Decide the issue belongs to the county and take no further action.
choices.feedback: You avoid overstepping, which is a real concern. But you are holding information that may matter to a government-to-government relationship. Passing it to the person or area responsible for Tribal relations costs little and lets the right people decide. Silence can look like indifference to partners who raised it in good faith.

steps.situation: Two weeks later, the county and your unit have agreed to fix the missing form and the shared mailbox delay. You need to set up how the work continues.
steps.question: What do you put in place?

choices.label: Name one owner on each side, set a date to compare approval times, rotate county follow-up across three team members, and check workload with the consultant at the review.
choices.feedback: This turns a bridge into a structure. The shared action has owners and evidence. The bridging role no longer depends on one person. Checking workload directly guards against the hidden cost returning. You can show whether people waiting for services were helped. The consultant gets time back for their own analysis.

choices.label: Ask the consultant to monitor progress with the counties, since they know them best.
choices.feedback: Efficient and well-meant. But it rebuilds the pattern you started to change. The research on facades and surface acting suggests the cost of carrying a role alone builds over time. Spread it. In a few months you may be back where you started, with a more tired colleague.

choices.label: Set a review date with both sides but leave follow-up roles informal.
choices.feedback: A review date is good. Without named owners and rotation, the work will drift back to whoever is most willing. Make roles explicit so the next stretch of bridging is shared. Informal roles tend to settle on the most willing person, who is often already overloaded.

simulation.debrief: The strongest path did three things. It made hidden adapting visible and asked the person what they wanted, which addresses the lack of voice Hewlin linked to facades and exhaustion. It turned blame between two groups into one traced case and one shared action, the kind of coordinating work most linked to team performance in the boundary-spanning meta-analysis. And it routed a Tribal matter through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations, as Minnesota law requires. The code-switching research explains why tempting choices, like praising someone for softening, can feel kind and still add weight. The evidence here is mostly from outside state government, so watch what actually happens and adjust.

mistakes.mistake: Praising the team's best bridge and giving them more bridging work.
mistakes.why: Recognition feels like support, and the person really is skilled. The workload stays invisible because each request is small.
mistakes.instead: List the bridging tasks, ask the person which to keep, and share or rotate the rest.

mistakes.mistake: Telling someone to just be themselves at work.
mistakes.why: It sounds affirming. But code-switching is rated as more professional by many groups, so the person still faces the same judgment.
mistakes.instead: Change the norms you control: who presents hard news, how meetings run, what counts as professional on your team.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a breakdown between two groups as an attitude problem.
mistakes.why: Tension in the room looks like a relationship issue, and talking about respect feels safe.
mistakes.instead: Trace one de-identified case from both sides, find the process gap and agree on one shared action.

mistakes.mistake: Using a personal contact to check on a Tribal matter.
mistakes.why: It feels fast and respectful, and the relationship is real.
mistakes.instead: Bring what you heard to the person or area responsible for Tribal relations and follow their lead.

mistakes.mistake: Fixing the hidden workload by moving it all to yourself.
mistakes.why: Leaders want to protect their people, and leader boundary work can be effective.
mistakes.instead: Carry the hardest bridging yourself, and spread the rest so knowledge and relationships do not sit with one person.

jobAid.title: Bridge check: sharing the work of adapting
jobAid.use: Use before a meeting between groups that blame each other, or when one person keeps getting the hard calls.
steps: List the bridging tasks from the last month: explaining, translating, calming, following up. Who did each?
Ask that person privately: which parts do you want to keep, and which should the team share?
Change one meeting habit: send written options ahead, build in question time, name who follows up.
When two groups disagree, trace one de-identified case from both sides: what could each see, when, and who could fix it?
Agree on one shared action, one owner on each side and one date to compare evidence.
Include a way for people receiving services to say whether anything improved.
If a Tribal Nation may be affected, bring it to the person or area responsible for Tribal relations.
At the review, ask directly whether the workload actually fell.

media.reason: The cost of adapting looks different from the person carrying it and the supervisor assigning it. Two voices show that gap in a way narration cannot.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Thanks for making time. I asked to meet because I keep sending you the hardest county calls, and I realized I never asked how that lands.

script.speaker: male
script.text: Honestly, I like the counties. I know the lead agency staff, and I can usually tell what they mean when a call gets heated.

script.speaker: female
script.text: That shows. I also noticed you have not presented your own analysis in two months. Is that connected?

script.speaker: male
script.text: Probably. After a county meeting I spend the afternoon explaining what each side meant. By the time I get to my own work, the team has moved on.

script.speaker: female
script.text: So the bridging is real work, and it is eating the work you were hired for. Which parts do you want to keep?

script.speaker: male
script.text: The relationships. I would hate to lose those. What I do not want is being the only person who can explain anything to anyone.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Fair. Here is an idea. Before the next joint meeting, I will send written options ahead and build in question time, so less clarifying happens afterward.

script.speaker: male
script.text: That would help. And could two other reviewers start joining my county calls? They would learn the contacts, and I would not be the single point of failure.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Yes. And I will deliver the hardest message at the meeting myself. That is my job, not yours. Can I ask one more thing? Do you ever soften your recommendations to keep the peace?

script.speaker: male
script.text: All the time. I worry that if I am blunt, I will be seen as difficult. It is tiring to watch every word.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Thank you for saying that. Research on facades at work links that kind of constant self-monitoring to exhaustion. I would rather hear your real recommendation. What would make that feel safe?

script.speaker: male
script.text: Knowing you will back the substance if a county pushes back. And letting me present the delay analysis myself, start to finish.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Done. I will check in with you after the meeting about whether your week actually got lighter. If it did not, the plan changes again.

prompts: What bridging work on your team is invisible right now, and who is carrying it?
With whom will you have a private conversation about which parts of that work to keep and which to share, and by when?
Which two groups that blame each other could you help trace one shared case, and what date will you set to compare evidence?
