title: Designing services that adapt
objective: Lead a review of a notice, form or service step that tests it with the people who use it, keeps required content, meets language access duties and reports back to contributors.
outcomes: Test a notice or form by asking readers to find, choose and act on a real option, instead of relying on a readability score.
Separate plain wording, language access and accessible format as three different design questions, each with its own person or area responsible.
Arrange qualified interpreters or translations instead of relying on bilingual staff or family members to interpret informally.
Keep legally required content while redesigning layout and order so readers can act on it.
Report back to the people who gave input: what changed, what could not change and why.

evidence.summary: Design choices in notices and service steps change who gets help. In an IRS field experiment with 35,050 people, a simpler notice raised benefit take-up from 14% to 23%, and showing the possible benefit raised it to 31%. Messages meant to reduce stigma did nothing. In language access, professional interpreters are linked to better care than ad hoc ones, and trained interpreters made far fewer consequential errors. The National CLAS Standards and DHS policy set the duty to provide language assistance. Limits: cultural competency training shows weak evidence for client outcomes, and co-design is widely used but has rarely been tested for outcomes. Testing with real users is still the best check available.

findings.claim: A simpler notice or shorter worksheet raised benefit take-up from 14% to 23%, and showing the potential benefit raised it further to 31%. Messages to reduce stigma did not change take-up.
findings.detail: Randomized field experiment with the IRS, 35,050 California tax filers eligible for but not claiming the Earned Income Tax Credit, published 2015. Simplification helped some groups more, including low earners and, among single filers, women, and the authors note language barriers may have reduced take-up among Hispanic households.

findings.claim: Professional interpreters were associated with better communication, use of services, clinical outcomes and satisfaction than ad hoc interpreters, bringing care close to that of people without language barriers.
findings.detail: Systematic review of 28 studies (21 separated professional from ad hoc interpreters), 1966 to 2005, published 2007. One randomized trial; the rest observational, often without controls for confounding.

findings.claim: Errors with potential clinical consequences made up 12% of errors by professional interpreters, 20% with no interpreter and 22% with ad hoc interpreters. Interpreters with 100 or more hours of training had a 2% rate.
findings.detail: Cross-sectional analysis of 57 audiotaped pediatric emergency visits in two Massachusetts hospitals, 1,884 interpreter errors, published 2012. Training hours, not years of experience, were linked to fewer errors.

findings.claim: The National CLAS Standards set 15 standards, including free language assistance for people with limited English proficiency or other communication needs.
findings.detail: Federal framework from the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Minority Health. Three themes: governance, leadership and workforce; communication and language assistance; engagement, continuous improvement and accountability.
findings.source: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Minority Health

findings.claim: DHS policy says county, Tribal and state servicing agencies must provide appropriate language assistance, and no one should be denied access to DHS programs because they do not speak English fluently.
findings.detail: Minnesota Health Care Programs Eligibility Policy Manual, section 1.3.1.3. Lists 11 languages for translation information on forms and notices and cites Title VI regulations, Minnesota Statutes chapter 363A and section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act.

findings.claim: Most reviews of cultural competency interventions found moderate evidence of improvement in provider outcomes and in access to services, but weaker evidence for client outcomes.
findings.detail: Systematic review of 19 reviews published 2000 to 2012, each covering 5 to 38 studies, published 2014. Many studies relied on self-report; objective evidence was rare.

findings.claim: The effectiveness of co-design has rarely been tested empirically. Reported benefits include more relevant materials; reported harms include higher cost and participants feeling their involvement was tokenistic.
findings.detail: Rapid overview of 23 reviews, published 2020. No included study compared co-design with traditional methods on end-user health outcomes or cost.

counterintuitive.headline: An untrained interpreter did no better than no interpreter.
counterintuitive.text: It seems obvious that any interpreter is better than none. In the study by Flores and colleagues (2012), errors with potential clinical consequences made up 22% of errors by ad hoc interpreters, such as family members or untrained staff. The rate was 20% when no interpreter was used. Professional interpreters came in at 12%, and those with at least 100 hours of training at 2%. Training hours mattered more than years of experience. For a DHS leader, the lesson is direct. A helpful bilingual coworker or a family member is not a language access plan.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.text: A notice, form or phone step is a service. Its design decides who gets through. In a large IRS field experiment, a simpler notice raised the share of eligible people who claimed a benefit from 14% to 23%. Adding the possible benefit amount raised it to 31%. Messages meant to make people feel less stigma did nothing. The words and layout mattered more than reassurance.

sections.title: Language is part of the design
sections.text: Plain English is not language access. People with limited English proficiency need qualified language help. DHS policy says no one should be denied access to its programs because they do not speak English fluently. The National CLAS Standards call for free language assistance too. Who interprets matters. In one study, untrained interpreters made consequential errors as often as having no interpreter at all. Trained professional interpreters made far fewer.

sections.title: Three questions, three owners
sections.text: When a notice or service step fails, it can fail in three different ways. The wording may be unclear. The language may be missing or poorly translated. The format may not work for someone using a screen reader, large print or another accessible format. Each is a separate design question, and each usually has its own person or area responsible. Fixing one does not fix the others. Ask all three every time you change something people must act on.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: Pick one notice, form or service step your area owns. Ask a few people who use it to show you what they would do next. Include people who missed the step before, people who use the languages DHS translates into and people who use accessible formats. Watch where they get stuck. Keep any content the person or area responsible says is required, and change the order and layout around it. Then tell the people who helped what you changed and why. Be honest that co-design has rarely been tested for outcomes. Watching real readers do the real task is still the best check you have.

sections.title: The evidence on notice design
sections.text: Bhargava and Manoli ran a field experiment with the IRS. They mailed notices to 35,050 California tax filers who appeared eligible for the Earned Income Tax Credit but had not claimed it. Different groups got different versions. A simpler notice, or a shorter worksheet with unneeded screening questions removed, raised take-up from 14% to 23%. Showing the range of potential benefit in the headline raised it again, to 31%. Messages designed to reduce stigma, or to tell people claiming was easy and low risk, had no effect. The authors concluded that low awareness and complexity, not stigma, drove most of the gap. They also noted that language barriers may have reduced take-up among Hispanic households.

sections.title: Why this matters in DHS work
sections.text: DHS and its county and Tribal partners send notices about eligibility, renewals, service reassessments and appeals. Each one asks a person to understand an option and act on it in time. The experiment suggests that small design changes can move large numbers of people. It also suggests a trap. Teams often add reassuring language when they worry about a step. The experiment tested messages of that kind, and they did not change behavior. Clarity about what to do, and what the person stands to gain, did.

sections.title: Language access is not a translation of the English draft
sections.text: The National CLAS Standards set 15 standards for culturally and linguistically appropriate services. They include free language assistance for people with limited English proficiency or other communication needs. DHS policy, in the Minnesota Health Care Programs eligibility manual, says county, Tribal and state servicing agencies must provide appropriate language assistance. It lists 11 languages for translation information on forms and notices. It cites Title VI regulations, the Minnesota Human Rights Act and section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act. Your area does not invent these rules. The person or area responsible for language access does. Your job is to bring them in early.

sections.title: Who interprets makes a difference
sections.text: Karliner and colleagues reviewed 28 studies. Professional interpreters were linked to better communication, use of services, outcomes and satisfaction than ad hoc interpreters. With professional interpreters, care for people with limited English came close to care for people without language barriers. Flores and colleagues analyzed 57 audiotaped emergency visits. Consequential errors made up 12% of errors by professional interpreters, 20% with no interpreter and 22% with ad hoc interpreters. Interpreters with at least 100 hours of training had a 2% rate. Most of this evidence comes from health care, not benefits or disability services. The pattern is still the best guide available for any high-stakes conversation.

sections.title: What co-design can and cannot promise
sections.text: Co-design means involving the people who use a service in designing it. Slattery and colleagues reviewed 23 reviews of co-design in health research. They found it has rarely been tested empirically. Reported benefits include materials that are more relevant and acceptable, and gains in participants' confidence. Reported harms include higher cost, disagreements over trade-offs and participants who felt their involvement was tokenistic. That last finding is a warning. Asking for input and then ignoring it can do damage.

sections.title: A practical cycle
sections.text: Start with the decision the reader faces, not the text. Ask readers to show you what the notice requires, what options they see and what they would do next. Include people who missed the step before. Treat wording, language and accessible format as three separate questions. Plain words do not fix a missing translation, and a translation does not fix a screen reader that reads sections out of order. Ask the person or area responsible which content is required. Keep it, and redesign around it. Compare two versions on the real task. Then report back to contributors with what changed and what could not change, and why.

sections.title: Applying this to a DHS notice
sections.text: Suppose your area sends a notice about a service reassessment. Start by writing the one action the reader must take and the deadline. Ask the person or area responsible for compliance which sentences are required. Ask the person or area responsible for language access which translated versions exist and how interpreters are reached. Ask the person or area responsible for accessibility how the notice reads in accessible formats. Then sit with a few readers. Ask them what the notice requires, what options they see and what they would do next. Note where they stop. Change one thing at a time so you know what helped.

sections.title: What to measure
sections.text: Measure the task, not opinions about the notice. Can readers find the option? Do they know the deadline? Do they know how to act? After release, use aggregate process data that already exists, such as missed appointments or reschedule requests, through the person or area responsible for data. Do not collect personal details from testers. Ask county and Tribal partners what callers tell them. Their front-line view is part of the evidence.

sections.title: Why readability scores are not enough
sections.text: Many teams check a notice with a readability score and stop there. A score measures sentence and word length. It does not tell you whether a reader can find the option to request a different appointment, or whether they know the deadline. The IRS experiment tested behavior, not reading level. Its simpler notice changed layout, font and the amount of information, not only words. When you test a DHS notice, measure the task. Can the reader find the option, choose it and know how to act on it before the deadline?

sections.title: Differential effects
sections.text: Design changes do not land the same for everyone. Bhargava and Manoli found that simplification helped some groups more than others, including low earners and, among single filers, women. They also suggested that language barriers may have reduced take-up among Hispanic households. That is a reminder that an English simplification can widen a gap if translated versions lag behind. It is also a reminder not to claim effects for any group without evidence. When you test, include the people most likely to have missed the step before. Ask what got in their way rather than assuming.

sections.title: Limits of the language access evidence
sections.text: Most interpreter research comes from health care. Karliner's review found mostly observational studies, many without controls for confounding, and almost all in the United States. The Flores study was small: 57 audiotaped visits in two pediatric emergency departments. Its error counts are detailed, but it did not measure later outcomes for families. Neither study looked at eligibility interviews or disability service planning. Use the evidence for its clear direction. Trained interpreters reduce consequential errors. Do not stretch it to precise predictions about DHS settings.

sections.title: Edge case: when simplification removes something people need
sections.text: Simpler is not always better. A shorter notice can drop an explanation that some readers relied on. Examples include how to appeal or who to call for help in another language. In the IRS experiment, one simplified version shortened the worksheet by removing screening questions every recipient already met. It did not remove options. When you shorten a DHS notice, check that every option and right is still present and findable. If a reader who needs the appeal right cannot find it, the notice is shorter but not better.

sections.title: Limits of cultural competency and co-design evidence
sections.text: Truong and colleagues reviewed 19 reviews of cultural competency interventions in health care. Most found moderate evidence of improvement in provider outcomes and in access to services. Evidence for client outcomes was weaker. Many studies relied on self-report, and objective evidence was rare. Co-design is in a similar place. It has strong ethical reasons behind it and plausible benefits, but little outcome testing. So treat both as tools for finding problems, not as guarantees. The proof is whether people can complete the real task, in their language and format, in time.

sections.title: Harder situation: required language that confuses readers
sections.text: Sometimes the hardest sentence in a notice is the one you cannot cut. A compliance reviewer may say a timing statement or appeal right must stay word for word. Do not remove required content to improve a test score. Ask the person or area responsible what exactly must remain, and whether its position, heading or surrounding explanation can change. Often you can keep the required sentence and add a clear heading, a short plain summary before it, or a next-step box after it. Test that version. If readers still cannot act, bring the evidence back to the person or area responsible.

sections.title: Harder situation: the helpful bilingual coworker
sections.text: In many units, a bilingual staff member quietly explains notices to callers or families. It looks like good service, and the person may take pride in it. The Flores study suggests why it is risky. Ad hoc interpreters made consequential errors at a rate no better than having no interpreter. It is also a hidden workload, the same pattern covered in the course on leading as a bridge. Thank the person. Then work with the person or area responsible for language access to provide qualified interpreters and translated materials. Ask the bilingual staff member what role they want, such as helping test a translated version.

sections.title: Harder situation: disability and accessible formats
sections.text: Accessible formats are their own design question. A notice can be in plain English and still fail. A screen reader may read its sections out of order. A deadline may arrive before an accommodation is in place. For people receiving disability services, ask the person how they want to receive and understand information and direct their next decision. Do not assume a single format fits everyone. Bring in the person or area responsible for accessibility and test with people who use the format.

sections.title: Closing the loop
sections.text: The co-design review found that some participants felt their involvement was tokenistic and frustrating. The fastest way to create that feeling is to ask for input and go silent. Before you start, tell contributors what can change, who approves the final version and when they will hear back. Afterward, share what you changed and why some suggestions could not be used. Pay attention to the effort you asked of them. Testing should not add burden to the people a service is meant to help.

sections.title: When evidence is thin, say so
sections.text: Leaders often feel pressure to promise results. Be specific about what the evidence supports. Simplification and salient benefits raised take-up in one large, well-run experiment. Trained interpreters reduce consequential errors in health care. Cultural competency training has weaker evidence for client outcomes. Co-design has rarely been tested. Telling leadership this plainly builds trust. It also explains why your plan includes testing and review instead of a single launch.

sections.title: Tribal and county partners
sections.text: County and Tribal servicing agencies share language assistance duties under DHS policy. A redesign may affect how a Tribal Nation's human services staff deliver or explain a notice. If so, bring it to the person or area responsible for Tribal relations before testing. If counties will send the notice, include county staff in testing the handoff. Their view of what callers ask is part of the design evidence.

sections.title: A leader's role in the cycle
sections.text: You do not have to be a designer to lead this work. Your job is to protect time for testing, bring the right people in early and insist on evidence from real readers. Ask your team what they learned from each round, not only whether the notice is done. When a deadline presses, choose a smaller test rather than no test. A single afternoon with five readers is better than none.

simulation.setup: You lead a small policy team in a DHS division that sends notices about service reassessments to people receiving home and community-based services. Many people miss the option to request a different reassessment date, and county case managers report rescheduling problems. Your team has a shorter draft notice that passes a readability check. Leadership wants it sent in two weeks. A compliance reviewer must approve it. At stake: whether people keep their services on schedule, whether county partners trust the change, and whether the people who helped you feel heard.

steps.situation: The draft passes the readability check. A senior manager says it is ready and asks you to send it for approval today.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Ask for one week to test it with a small group of readers on the real task, including people who missed the step before, people who use translated versions and people who use accessible formats.
choices.feedback: A readability score measures sentence length, not whether people can act. The IRS experiment changed behavior through layout and clarity, and tested real behavior. A short test now is cheaper than a wave of missed reassessments. The manager agrees to one week. Ask that testers not share personal details; you only need to watch the task.

choices.label: Send it for approval. It is clearly better than the old one, and the readability score proves it.
choices.feedback: It probably is better, and speed matters. But you do not know whether readers can find the reschedule option. You also have not checked translated versions or formats. Problems will surface after release, when they are harder to fix. Fixing them then costs a second mailing and more calls.

choices.label: Ask experienced staff to proofread it before sending.
choices.feedback: Staff can catch errors and confirm content. But they already know where every option is. A first-time reader does not. This step improves accuracy without testing whether the notice works for the people who receive it. Ask staff to proofread, and also watch first-time readers try the task.

steps.situation: In testing, readers can repeat the first sentence. Several still miss the option to request a different date. The compliance reviewer says a timing statement must stay exactly as written.
steps.question: What change do you test next?

choices.label: Keep the timing statement word for word, add a clear heading and a short next-step box for the reschedule option, and retest that version, including translated and accessible versions.
choices.feedback: You respect the requirement and redesign around it. This mirrors the simplification that moved take-up in the IRS experiment: clearer structure and a visible action. Retesting all versions keeps an English-only fix from widening a gap. Readers now find the option. You also have evidence to show the compliance reviewer that the requirement and clarity can coexist.

choices.label: Remove the timing statement to see whether comprehension improves.
choices.feedback: It might improve the test, which is why it is tempting. But it changes a required element without approval. Ask the person or area responsible what must remain, then design around it. Removing it may also create a legal problem that delays the whole notice.

choices.label: Add a paragraph explaining why the reassessment matters, to reassure readers.
choices.feedback: Reassurance feels kind. In the IRS experiment, messages aimed at stigma and reassurance did not change behavior. Clarity about the action did. A longer notice may also bury the option further. Readers in testing still miss the option, now on a longer page.

steps.situation: The notice goes out. Calls to the line rise. A county case manager tells you bilingual front-desk staff are explaining the notice to families informally, and some families are still missing the reschedule option.
steps.question: What do you do now?

choices.label: Work with the person or area responsible for language access to check the translated versions and interpreter routes, and test a revised version with readers before the next mailing.
choices.feedback: This treats language access as part of the design. The Flores study found ad hoc interpreters made consequential errors as often as no interpreter. Qualified routes and a tested revision address the source. Thank the front-desk staff and ask what they have heard. The next mailing goes out with tested versions and a clear interpreter route.

choices.label: Ask the county to have its bilingual staff keep helping, since it is working for many families.
choices.feedback: It is working for some, and the staff are generous. But informal interpreting adds hidden workload and carries real error risk. Professional interpreters were linked to better outcomes in a review of 28 studies. Families who reach someone without that help still miss the option. Errors may go unnoticed.

choices.label: Add a phone number for questions to the English version.
choices.feedback: A phone number helps some readers. It does not fix whether translated versions work, and it moves the burden to a call. Test the notice itself, in each version. Callers who need another language may still not reach help in time.

steps.situation: A community partner and two people who helped test the notice ask what happened with their suggestions. Some suggestions were used. One, removing the timing statement, could not be.
steps.question: How do you respond?

choices.label: Send a short report back: what changed, what could not change and why, and how to raise problems with the new version.
choices.feedback: This closes the loop. The co-design review found participants sometimes felt their involvement was tokenistic. Showing what you did with their input, including the no, builds trust and makes the next test possible. Contributors also learn how to raise problems, so the notice keeps improving after release.

choices.label: Send a warm thank-you note and the final notice.
choices.feedback: Gratitude matters. But without explaining what changed, contributors cannot tell whether their input counted. That is the experience the co-design review described as tokenistic. Add a short summary of what changed and why one suggestion could not be used. A short, plain explanation is enough.

choices.label: Say nothing for now, since the work is done and the notice is out.
choices.feedback: It saves time, and the team has moved on. But silence after asking for input is the quickest way to lose trust. Next time, fewer people will help. The people who gave their time, often people who rely on these services, are left wondering whether it mattered.

simulation.debrief: The strongest path tested the notice against the real task rather than a readability score. It kept required content and redesigned around it, the kind of simplification that raised benefit take-up from 14% to 23% in the IRS experiment. It treated language access as a design question with qualified interpreters and translations, because untrained interpreters made consequential errors as often as no interpreter. And it reported back, which guards against the tokenism the co-design review warns about. Much of this evidence comes from health care and tax benefits, not disability services. That is why the cycle relies on testing with the people your notice actually reaches.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a passing readability score as proof a notice works.
mistakes.why: Scores are fast, objective-looking and easy to report.
mistakes.instead: Ask readers to find, choose and act on the real option, and watch where they get stuck.

mistakes.mistake: Adding reassuring paragraphs to a confusing notice.
mistakes.why: It feels caring, and teams worry about how a notice will land.
mistakes.instead: Make the action and its benefit clear. In the IRS experiment, stigma and reassurance messages did not change behavior; clarity did.

mistakes.mistake: Relying on bilingual staff or family members to interpret.
mistakes.why: They are available, willing and often skilled. It looks like good service.
mistakes.instead: Work with the person or area responsible for language access to provide qualified interpreters and tested translations.

mistakes.mistake: Cutting required content to make a notice simpler.
mistakes.why: The required sentence is often the hardest to read, and cutting it improves test results.
mistakes.instead: Ask what must remain, keep it, and redesign headings, order and next steps around it.

mistakes.mistake: Asking for community input and not reporting back.
mistakes.why: Teams are busy, and the work feels finished once the notice is out.
mistakes.instead: Tell contributors what changed, what could not change and why.

mistakes.mistake: Testing only the English version.
mistakes.why: It is the version the team writes, and translations come later.
mistakes.instead: Test translated and accessible versions on the same task before release.

jobAid.title: Notice and service-step test
jobAid.use: Use before changing any notice, form, script or service step that asks people to act.
steps: Write the one decision or action the reader must take, and the deadline.
Ask the person or area responsible which content is required word for word.
Find a few readers, including people who missed the step before, people who use translated versions and people who use accessible formats.
Ask each reader: what does this require, what options do you see, and what would you do next?
Fix order, headings and next-step boxes around required content. Test again.
Confirm qualified interpreter and translation routes with the person or area responsible for language access.
Check that testing did not add burden for readers or county and Tribal partners.
Report back to contributors: what changed, what could not change and why.

media.reason: The lesson follows one notice from draft to release. A single narrator can walk the learner through each test and its evidence in order.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Picture a notice. It tells a person receiving home and community-based services that a reassessment is coming. It gives a date. Somewhere in the third paragraph, it says the person can ask for a different date. Many people never find that sentence. Some miss the visit. Some lose time with their services while it gets sorted out.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: It is easy to think the fix is better writing. Shorter sentences. Friendlier words. A good readability score. Those help. But a readability score measures sentence length. It does not tell you whether a reader can find an option and act on it in time.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Consider what happened when the IRS tested its own notices. Researchers mailed different versions to more than thirty-five thousand people who seemed eligible for a tax credit but had not claimed it. A simpler notice raised the share who claimed from fourteen percent to twenty-three percent. Adding the possible benefit amount raised it to thirty-one percent. Messages meant to make people feel less stigma did nothing at all. Clarity about the action mattered. Reassurance did not.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now add language. Plain English is not language access. DHS policy says county, Tribal and state servicing agencies must provide appropriate language assistance. No one should be denied access to a DHS program because they do not speak English fluently. The National CLAS Standards call for free language assistance as well.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Who interprets matters too. In one study of audiotaped emergency visits, untrained interpreters, such as family members or staff who happened to speak the language, made consequential errors as often as having no interpreter at all. Trained professional interpreters made far fewer. Those with at least one hundred hours of training made the fewest. A helpful bilingual coworker is generous. That coworker is not a language access plan.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: So how do you design a notice that adapts? Start with the decision the reader faces. Ask a few readers to show you what they would do next. Include people who missed the step before. Include people who read the translated versions, and people who use accessible formats like screen readers. Watch where they stop.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Some content will be required. Do not cut it to make a test look better. Ask the person or area responsible what must stay. Then redesign around it. A clear heading. A short summary. A box that says, here is what to do next.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Be honest about one limit. Co-design, involving people in designing the services they use, has rarely been tested for outcomes. One review found it can make materials more relevant. It also found that some participants felt their input was ignored. So the last step matters most. Tell the people who helped what you changed, what you could not change, and why. That is how a service learns to adapt, one tested notice at a time.

prompts: Which notice, form or service step in your area most often leads people to miss an option, and what is the one action it asks for?
With whom will you check required content and language access routes, such as the person or area responsible for compliance or language access, and by when?
Who will you invite to test it, and on what date will you report back to them about what changed?

title: Capstone: leading intercultural change
objective: Lead one small, honest improvement cycle on a real barrier in your area, using direct inquiry, inclusive voice, a named owner and evidence you share back.
outcomes: Choose one barrier in your area and state what you can observe about it, separately from what you suspect causes it.
Gather the views of the people affected by asking them directly, in a format that lets lower-status voices speak first.
Name an owner with authority, and write a small test with a prediction, a time frame, frequent data and a workload check.
Report results honestly, including mixed results, and decide to keep, change or stop the change.
Explain to a newer leader the difference between training people and building responsibility for change.

evidence.summary: The series moved from seeing culture to changing systems, and its evidence points one way. People overrate their own intercultural skill, so practice and feedback matter more than self-ratings. Neutral procedures can push people out: a later interview date cut SNAP recertification by over 20%. Asking beats imagining, and leaders who invite input narrow status gaps in who speaks. For change itself, assigning clear responsibility had a better long-run record than training in 708 employers. A randomized training changed attitudes but not behavior. Limits: much of this evidence comes from private firms, health care and labs, and the strongest change study is observational.

findings.claim: 98% of nursing students overestimated their intercultural competence compared with an assessment; 2% were accurate.
findings.detail: Prospective cohort, pre-test phase, 277 students and 37 faculty and staff at one Midwestern college of nursing, published 2014. Most students' assessed orientation fell in the middle of the model (183 of 277). One school; one instrument.

findings.claim: In human service and other organizations, a climate of inclusion was consistently linked to positive outcomes (rho = .42), while diversity alone had mixed effects.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 30 studies, 496,740 workers, published 2016 in a human service management journal.

findings.claim: SNAP households assigned a later recertification interview date were over 20% less likely to recertify, losing an average of $600 in benefits over the next year.
findings.detail: Interview dates assigned as if at random within the month, San Francisco CalFresh, published 2021. About one quarter of those who lost benefits stayed off SNAP for more than a year.

findings.claim: Imagining another person's perspective did not improve accuracy across 25 experiments, while directly asking them did.
findings.detail: 25 experiments, 2018. In the final experiment (about 104 participants), people predicting a partner's opinions got 4.90 of 20 exactly right in the control group, 3.95 when told to imagine the partner's view, and 8.60 when they had asked the partner first.

findings.claim: Contact reduces prejudice mainly by lowering anxiety and building empathy; learning facts about the other group was the weakest route.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 54 studies, 2008. For anxiety: 45 studies, 13,343 participants; contact to anxiety r = -.29, anxiety to prejudice r = +.37.

findings.claim: Randomized contact studies show real but smaller effects, and substantially weaker effects for racial and ethnic prejudice.
findings.detail: Review and meta-analysis, 2019; 27 randomized studies with outcomes at least a day later. Pooled effect 0.39 standard deviations; 0.25 for ethnic, racial, religious and immigrant groups.

findings.claim: Evaluators worried about appearing prejudiced gave equal praise but less criticism and higher grades to minority authors.
findings.detail: Two experiments, 2012. The effect tracked external, not internal, motivation to respond without prejudice.

findings.claim: When hiring criteria were unwritten, people redefined merit to fit the candidate they preferred; committing to criteria first eliminated the bias.
findings.detail: Three experiments on gender-stereotyped jobs, 2005.

findings.claim: About 80 percent of variation in work-related cultural values lies within countries, not between them.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 558 studies across 32 countries using Hofstede's four dimensions, 2016. Individualism: 16.6 percent between countries. Power distance: 20.8 percent between countries, while occupation accounted for 50.1 percent.

findings.claim: Person-centered planning showed a moderate positive effect on community participation and daily choice, based on low-quality evidence.
findings.detail: Systematic review of 16 studies of people with intellectual disabilities, 1990 to 2014. Employment results were inconsistent. Human services.

findings.claim: Fair process had a consistently large effect on trust in civil servants, in some models several times larger than outcomes.
findings.detail: Survey data from the US and 33 countries with structural equation and country-level path models, 2011. Public sector.

findings.claim: Lower-status health staff reported less psychological safety, and leader inclusiveness narrowed the status gap.
findings.detail: Survey of 1,440 professionals in 23 neonatal intensive care units, 2006. Psychological safety predicted engagement in quality improvement. Health and human services.

findings.claim: Employees who held minority status or worked in nonparticipative settings were more likely to create facades of conformity, and emotional exhaustion linked those facades to intent to leave.
findings.detail: Cross-sectional survey of 238 employees across multiple industries, 2009. Self-report; cannot establish cause.

findings.claim: A simpler notice or shorter worksheet raised benefit take-up from 14% to 23%, and showing the potential benefit raised it further to 31%. Messages to reduce stigma did not change take-up.
findings.detail: Randomized field experiment with the IRS, 35,050 California tax filers eligible for but not claiming the Earned Income Tax Credit, published 2015. Simplification helped some groups more, and the authors note language barriers may have reduced take-up among Hispanic households.

findings.claim: Contact between groups generally reduces prejudice, and the effect extends to the whole other group.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 515 studies and 713 samples, 2006. Supportive conditions strengthened effects but were not required. Mostly correlational.

findings.claim: Assigning responsibility for change, through task forces, committees or dedicated staff, was followed by the broadest gains in management diversity. Training was among the least effective practices.
findings.detail: Longitudinal analysis of federal EEO data for 708 private-sector establishments, 1971 to 2002, published 2006. Diversity committees were followed by about 14% more white women, almost 30% more Black women and 10% more Black men in management. Observational; private sector.
findings.source: Kalev, Dobbin and Kelly, 2006 (summary by the Reducing Racial and Ethnic Inequality research review, Princeton)

findings.claim: A one-off online training changed attitudes but not workplace behavior among groups less supportive at the start. Behavior changed only among groups already strongly supportive.
findings.detail: Preregistered field experiment with an active placebo control, 3,016 employees of a global organization, decisions tracked up to 20 weeks, published 2019.
findings.source: Chang, Milkman, Gromet, Rebele, Massey, Duckworth and Grant, 2019

findings.claim: Training effects on attitudes faded over time, while knowledge held; effects were larger when training was longer, built skills and was paired with other efforts.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 260 independent samples of diversity training, published 2016. Overall Hedges g = .38, with the largest effects on reactions and knowledge and smaller effects on behavior and attitudes.

findings.claim: Fewer than 20% of published Plan-Do-Study-Act projects (14 of 73) fully documented a sequence of iterative cycles, and only 15% reported data monthly or more often.
findings.detail: Systematic review of 73 healthcare improvement articles, published 2014.
findings.source: Taylor, McNicholas, Nicolay, Darzi, Bell and Reed, 2014

findings.claim: Specific if-then plans, stating when, where and how you will act, had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals (d = .65).
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of 94 independent tests, published 2006. Effects in a workplace change effort may be smaller.

counterintuitive.headline: A course can change minds without changing what people do.
counterintuitive.text: This is a capstone to a series of courses, so it should be honest about courses. In a randomized field experiment by Chang and colleagues (2019), a one-off online training changed attitudes among the employees who started out least supportive. It did not change their workplace behavior. A meta-analysis of 260 samples by Bezrukova and colleagues (2016) found attitude effects fade over time while knowledge holds. What has a better record is responsibility: a named owner, a test and follow-up. The series gives you knowledge. Change comes from what you build with it.

sections.title: The path you have walked
sections.text: The series followed a path. It began with why culture matters and why self-ratings mislead. It moved to who DHS serves and how a neutral rule can push people out. Then it turned inward: curiosity before conclusions, threat, common ground, honest feedback and your own unwritten rules. Next came the people in front of you: patterns, not profiles; disability as identity; the history behind trust; and power in the room. Finally it turned outward to adapting, bridging and designing services. The capstone asks one question: what will you change, and how will you know it worked?

sections.title: Why knowing is not enough
sections.text: The evidence is blunt. In a field experiment with 3,016 employees, a one-off training changed attitudes but not behavior among the people who started out least supportive. Across 260 samples, attitude effects from training faded over time. In a study of 708 employers over three decades, assigning clear responsibility for change was followed by the broadest gains in who reached management. Training was among the least effective practices. Knowledge matters. Structure is what turns it into change.

sections.title: What good change looks like
sections.text: Good change in DHS work is usually small and specific. A notice gets clearer. An opening is announced on every shift. A meeting gives quieter staff a way to speak first. A handoff between a county and a DHS unit stops dropping cases. None of these require a new policy. Each requires someone to own it, test it and report what happened. That is leadership any supervisor, manager or director can practice.

sections.title: Keep it fair to the people involved
sections.text: Measure processes, not people. Do not label anyone by an intercultural stage or assessment score. Do not claim effects for any group unless the evidence shows them. Watch who carries extra work when a change goes in.

sections.title: The one move to make
sections.text: Choose one barrier in your area. Write down what you can actually observe, separately from what you suspect causes it. Ask the people affected directly, because imagining their view is often wrong. Let lower-status voices speak first. Name an owner who has authority. Then run one small test, with a prediction, a short time frame and data you check often. Share what happened, even if it is mixed. Keep, change or stop the change, and run the next cycle.

sections.title: Responsibility beats awareness
sections.text: Kalev, Dobbin and Kelly tracked 708 private-sector employers from 1971 to 2002. They compared seven kinds of programs. Practices that assigned responsibility, such as task forces, committees and dedicated staff, were followed by the broadest gains in management diversity. For example, diversity committees were followed by almost 30% more Black women in management. Training and evaluations of managers were among the least effective practices. Training worked better where responsibility structures already existed. The study is observational and private sector, so treat the numbers as direction, not a forecast for DHS.

sections.title: What training can and cannot do
sections.text: Chang and colleagues ran a randomized field experiment with 3,016 employees. They compared an online training to a placebo training on another topic. Among groups less supportive at the start, the training changed attitudes but not behavior. Behavior changed only among groups that were already strongly supportive. Bezrukova and colleagues combined 260 samples. Effects on reactions and attitudes faded over time. Knowledge held or grew. Effects were larger when training was sustained and paired with other efforts. So this series gives you knowledge that lasts. Your job is to pair it with action.

sections.title: Start with inquiry, not assumption
sections.text: The course on curiosity before conclusions and the course on patterns of difference both made the same point. Eyal, Steffel and Epley ran 25 experiments. Imagining another person's view did not reliably make people more accurate about it, and sometimes made them more confident. Asking the person did. Before you design a change, ask the people affected what is happening. That includes staff, people receiving services and partners. Route anything affecting a Tribal Nation through the person or area responsible for Tribal relations.

sections.title: Make it safe to speak
sections.text: The course on power in the room showed that status shapes voice. Nembhard and Edmondson studied teams in 23 neonatal intensive care units. Higher-status professionals felt safer speaking up. Leaders who invited and valued input narrowed that gap. That safety predicted engagement in improvement work. In practice, ask for written input before a meeting, go around the room, and speak last yourself. Thank people for bad news.

sections.title: Test small, and test properly
sections.text: A Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle is a short test. You plan a change and predict what will happen. You try it on a small scale. You study the data against your prediction. You act: keep, change or stop. Taylor and colleagues reviewed 73 published projects that used this method. Fewer than 20% documented a real sequence of cycles. Only 15% looked at data monthly or more often. A single pilot with one end-of-year number is not a cycle. Plan for at least two cycles and check data weekly if you can.

sections.title: Turn intention into a plan
sections.text: Gollwitzer and Sheeran combined 94 tests of if-then plans. Plans that name when, where and how you will act had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals. Effects in a workplace change may be smaller, but the method is cheap. Write: when this happens, I will do that. For example: when the weekly call report arrives on Monday, I will review transfers with the evening lead before noon.

sections.title: Building responsibility in a DHS unit
sections.text: You may not be able to create a task force or a new position. You can still build responsibility at your level. Name one person who owns the change and give them time for it. Add the issue to a standing meeting so it is reviewed on a schedule. Agree on the data that will show progress and who brings it. Decide in advance who you will tell about results, including staff, partners and your own manager. These steps are small. Together they do what the long-run employer study points to: they make someone answerable for follow-through.

sections.title: Choosing the first barrier
sections.text: Pick a barrier that matters to people, sits at least partly within your authority and can be seen in existing process data. Good candidates include how openings or information reach every shift and how a notice or script is worded. Others are how a handoff works or how a meeting gathers input. Avoid starting with the largest or most political issue. A first cycle that works builds trust for the next one.

sections.title: What each stage of the series adds to a change cycle
sections.text: Each stage of the series supplies one piece of a change cycle. From the orientation, remember that people overrate their own skill. In one nursing school, 98% of students rated their intercultural competence higher than an assessment did. So judge progress by what changes in the work, not by how capable you feel. From who DHS serves, remember that an inclusive climate, not diversity alone, was consistently linked to good outcomes across 30 studies. From when the same rule is not fair, look for neutral steps with unequal effects. A later interview date cut SNAP recertification by more than 20%. From curiosity, threat and common ground, ask before you conclude, lower anxiety in the room and give honest feedback to everyone. Evaluators worried about seeming biased gave minority authors less criticism, which is unequal treatment. From your own culture, write criteria down before you decide. Unwritten criteria let people redefine merit after the fact. From patterns, disability and trust, treat each person as more than a group average. Let people direct their own plans, and use fair process, which drives trust in civil servants. From power in the room, invite input before the decision. From the last two courses, share the work of adapting and test services with the people who use them.

sections.title: Limits of the change evidence
sections.text: The study of 708 employers is the strongest long-run evidence on what changes who advances. But it is observational. Companies that created task forces may have differed in other ways. It covered private employers, not state agencies. The training experiment by Chang and colleagues was randomized and large, but it tested one short online course about gender. The meta-analysis of 260 samples mixes many kinds of training and settings. The PDSA review covered healthcare projects. None of this tells you exactly what will happen in a DHS unit. It does tell you what to bet on: ownership, tests and follow-up, not awareness alone.

sections.title: Limits the series has already shown you
sections.text: Several courses found the evidence thinner than its reputation. Randomized contact studies showed real but smaller effects than correlational ones, and weaker effects for racial and ethnic prejudice. Contact worked mainly by lowering anxiety and building empathy, and learning facts about another group was the weakest route. About 80% of variation in work values lies within countries, so group patterns predict individuals poorly. Person-centered planning showed moderate benefits on a low-quality evidence base. Interpreter research comes mostly from health care. Carry the same honesty into your own change work. Claim what your data show, and no more.

sections.title: Why training still has a place
sections.text: None of this means training is useless. The meta-analysis of 260 samples found knowledge held or grew over time, and effects were larger when training was sustained and paired with other efforts. In the employer study, training worked better where responsibility structures existed. So training is a foundation, not a strategy. Use what you learned in this series to see problems more clearly and ask better questions. Then build the structure that acts on it.

sections.title: Contact and common work
sections.text: Pettigrew and Tropp combined 515 studies of contact between groups. Contact typically reduced prejudice. The effect was larger under conditions such as equal status and shared goals, though those conditions were not essential. Randomized studies found smaller effects, so do not expect contact alone to do the work. It still matters for how you design change. A cross-shift or cross-unit improvement team that works as equals on a shared problem is itself a form of contact. It can build trust while it fixes a process. A team where one group presents and the other listens does less.

sections.title: Harder situation: you cannot change the rule
sections.text: Many leaders see a barrier and feel stuck because the rule belongs to someone else. Start with what is within your authority: meeting design, how information reaches staff, who is asked for input, how your area explains a rule. Gather evidence on the effect. Then bring it to the person or area responsible for the larger rule. Describe what you observed, what you tested and what you suggest. A tested small change is more persuasive than a complaint. It also helps people now, while the larger change is considered.

sections.title: Harder situation: resistance from people who feel blamed
sections.text: Change aimed at fairness can make some staff feel accused. A senior lead may hear a question about who sees openings as a charge of bias. Frame the work around the process and the people it serves, not around anyone's character. Invite the person who feels blamed into the test as an owner or reviewer. Contact between groups working as equals on a shared goal was linked to less prejudice in the meta-analysis of 515 studies. Shared ownership of a process can do some of the same work.

sections.title: Harder situation: mixed results
sections.text: Small tests often give mixed answers. A change may help one shift and not another, or reduce delays while adding workload for bilingual staff. The temptation is to announce success or quietly stop. Both waste the learning. Report the result as it is. Ask the people affected why it worked in one place and not another. Adjust and run the next cycle. The PDSA review found most projects skipped this step. Doing it is what makes a test an improvement method rather than a pilot.

sections.title: Harder situation: measuring without counting people
sections.text: You need data, but you should not track individuals or ask people to share personal information. Measure the process, not the person. Count delays, transfers, missed notices or how many openings were announced on each shift. Use de-identified or aggregate data that already exists through the person or area responsible for data. Never label anyone by an intercultural stage or assessment score. Never claim an effect for a racial, disability or other group unless the evidence shows it. The orientation course showed why: self-ratings say little about what a person actually does.

sections.title: Differential effects and hidden costs
sections.text: A change that helps most people can still shift costs to some. The course on leading as a bridge showed that facades at work are linked to emotional exhaustion and intent to leave. A new process that relies on bilingual staff to make it work may succeed on paper and wear people out. The course on designing services that adapt showed that simplification can help some groups more than others. Build a workload check and a check on who benefits into every cycle.

sections.title: Harder situation: partners outside DHS
sections.text: Many barriers cross into counties, providers or Tribal Nations. You can invite county partners into a test of a handoff, with their agreement and through the people who manage that relationship. For anything that may affect a Tribal Nation, start with the person or area responsible for Tribal relations. Follow their guidance on whether and how to proceed. Do not run a test that changes another government's work without that route.

sections.title: Edge case: when the data you need does not exist
sections.text: Sometimes the process data you need is not collected. You may not know how many people on each shift saw an opening, or how often interpreter calls drop. Do not start tracking individuals to fill the gap. Count the process for the length of the test, such as how many notices went out on each shift or how many transfers occurred. Ask the person or area responsible for data what already exists and what can be counted without identifying anyone. A rough, honest count over two cycles is more useful than a precise number you cannot get.

sections.title: Edge case: when your own manager wants a faster answer
sections.text: Senior leaders often want a quick, visible response. Offer one that is still honest: a short period of asking, then a named owner and a first test with a date for results. That gives leadership something concrete without skipping the steps that make change work. If you are pushed toward a training-only response, say plainly what the evidence shows and propose training as one part of a larger plan.

sections.title: Teaching and mentoring
sections.text: Explaining an idea to someone else is a strong test of whether you understand it. Choose one idea from this series and explain it in two minutes to an imagined team. Then imagine a newer leader says: I can see the barrier, but I cannot change the rule. Write your response. Ask for one observation. Name one action within their authority. Name the person or area responsible for the larger change. That response is the capstone in miniature.

sections.title: What lasts
sections.text: Attitude effects from training fade. Knowledge holds. Structures persist after the people who built them move on. So the most lasting thing you can leave is a routine. Name a standing owner and set a regular review of the right data. Use a meeting format that lets everyone speak. Build a habit of reporting back. That is what turns a series of courses into a different way of working.

simulation.setup: You manage a Disability Services Division call line that helps people and families with questions about home and community-based services. A data analyst shows you an aggregate pattern: calls that need an interpreter are transferred more often before they are resolved, especially in the evening. Staff on both shifts are capable and committed. No one has explained the pattern yet. You have authority over call-line procedures but not over the interpreter vendor contract. At stake: whether callers who use another language get timely help, and whether your staff trust that the change is fair.

steps.situation: Your director asks what you plan to do about the transfer pattern and wants an answer this week.
steps.question: What is your first move?

choices.label: Tell the director you will spend one week asking staff on both shifts, the language access lead and a community partner what happens on these calls before choosing a change.
choices.feedback: You treat this as a neutral process with unequal effects, and you separate what you observe from what you suspect. Eyal and colleagues found that asking people directly is more accurate than imagining their view. A week of inquiry is short, and it lowers the risk of fixing the wrong thing. The director agrees. It also shows staff that their account of the work counts before anything changes.

choices.label: Require all call-line staff to complete a training on serving callers across languages and cultures within two weeks.
choices.feedback: It shows quick action and the content may be good. But you do not yet know the cause. In a randomized experiment, a one-off training changed attitudes but not behavior among those least supportive. In a study of 708 employers, training was among the least effective practices. Staff may also read a sudden mandate as blame, which makes honest input harder later.

choices.label: Write a new transfer procedure yourself, based on your experience of how calls go.
choices.feedback: You know the work, and acting within your authority is right. But your view is one perspective. Without asking evening staff and callers' partners, you may design around the wrong cause. Ask a few people on each shift first, then decide.

steps.situation: You hold a joint meeting with both shifts. A senior day-shift lead explains the problem confidently. Evening staff say little. Afterward, one evening staff member mentions that the interpreter line often drops when a call is transferred.
steps.question: How do you gather input from here?

choices.label: Ask everyone to send written observations before a second meeting, open with evening staff in a round, and speak last yourself.
choices.feedback: This narrows the status gap in who speaks. Nembhard and Edmondson found leader inclusiveness made lower-status members safer to speak, and that safety predicted engagement in improvement. In the second meeting, several staff describe dropped interpreter connections during transfers. You also model the habit you want team leads to copy.

choices.label: Go with the senior lead's explanation, since it was clear and detailed.
choices.feedback: The explanation may be partly right. But you heard mainly from one high-status voice. The evening comment points to a different cause. Moving now risks a fix that misses the dropped connections. Evening staff learn that speaking up in that room changes little.

choices.label: Follow up only with the evening staff member who spoke to you.
choices.feedback: That honors what they told you. But one private comment is not a pattern. Inviting written input from everyone would show whether others see the same thing, without putting one person on the spot. Others may share the same view but wait to be asked.

steps.situation: Six weeks later, the training or new procedure is in place. Staff rated it well. The transfer pattern has not changed.
steps.question: What do you do now?

choices.label: Name an owner for the issue, ask staff on both shifts and the language access lead what happens on these calls, and plan a small test.
choices.feedback: You have shifted from awareness to responsibility and inquiry. That is the pattern with the strongest record in the study of 708 employers. Staff soon describe dropped interpreter connections during transfers, which no one had asked about. The six weeks were not wasted; staff now share a vocabulary for the problem.

choices.label: Run a longer, more detailed version of the training.
choices.feedback: It is a natural response when training rates well. But the meta-analysis of 260 samples found attitude effects fade, and the problem may not be attitudes at all. You still do not know the cause. Staff may start to see the effort as performance rather than change.

choices.label: Wait three more months to see whether the effect appears.
choices.feedback: Patience can be wise. But without knowing the cause, waiting mostly delays help for callers. A short round of asking would tell you more than three months of the same data. Ask now, and keep the data running while you do.

steps.situation: Staff believe interpreter connections drop during transfers. You can change your call-line procedure. The vendor contract belongs to another area.
steps.question: How do you design the test?

choices.label: Test a warm transfer, with the interpreter kept on the line, for two weeks on the evening shift. Predict the change, check transfer data weekly, check workload with bilingual staff, and share the plan with the person or area responsible for the vendor contract.
choices.feedback: This is a real cycle: small scale, a prediction, frequent data and a workload check. The PDSA review found most projects skip iterative cycles and frequent data. Telling the contract owner early sets up the larger change if the test points to the vendor. Your prediction gives you something honest to compare against.

choices.label: Roll the warm transfer out across all shifts and units at once, since staff are confident it will work.
choices.feedback: Confidence is encouraging. But a full rollout gives you no comparison and no chance to adjust. If it adds hidden workload or fails on one shift, you will find out late. A failed full rollout can also make staff wary of the next idea, even a good one.

choices.label: Test the warm transfer, but measure only whether staff like the new procedure.
choices.feedback: Staff experience matters. But the problem is caller transfers. Without transfer data, you cannot tell whether callers were helped. Add the transfer measure and a workload check. Measuring both tells you whether the change works for callers and is sustainable for the people doing it.

steps.situation: After two weeks, evening transfers on interpreter calls fall. Bilingual staff report extra work explaining the new step to coworkers. A senior leader wants to announce the change as a success across the division.
steps.question: What do you do?

choices.label: Share the result honestly with staff, the language access lead and your director, including the extra workload. Adjust the step, run a second cycle, and name a standing owner for ongoing review.
choices.feedback: You report the mixed result, protect against hidden costs and keep learning. A standing owner turns a test into a routine, which is what the study of 708 employers suggests lasts. Staff see their input changed the plan. The senior leader also gets a more credible story to tell.

choices.label: Announce the success. The numbers improved and leaders need good news.
choices.feedback: Good news matters, and the numbers did improve. But the extra workload on bilingual staff is a real cost. Ignoring it repeats the pattern of hidden adapting from the bridge course and may undo the gains. Staff who raised the workload issue learn it did not count.

choices.label: Stop the test, since the results were mixed.
choices.feedback: Caution is reasonable. But you would throw away a change that helped callers. Adjusting the step and running another cycle is how a mixed result becomes an improvement. Callers who were helped lose that help while you wait for a perfect result.

simulation.debrief: The strongest path drew on the whole series. It treated the transfer pattern as a neutral process with unequal effects, as in the course on when the same rule is not fair. It asked before acting, since imagining others' views is often wrong. It invited voice across status lines, which leader inclusiveness makes safer. It named an owner and ran a real test cycle with frequent data, a step most published projects skip. And it reported hidden workload on bilingual staff, the cost the bridge course warned about. Training-first paths felt like action but missed the cause, matching evidence that one-off training changes attitudes more than behavior.

mistakes.mistake: Responding to a barrier by requiring a training.
mistakes.why: Training is visible, fast to arrange and feels responsible. It rates well afterward.
mistakes.instead: Ask what is happening, name an owner and test a change. Use training to support the change, not replace it.

mistakes.mistake: Designing the fix from your own experience.
mistakes.why: Leaders know the work well and want to move quickly. The curiosity course showed that imagining someone's view is often less accurate than asking.
mistakes.instead: Ask the people affected directly. Imagining their view is often less accurate than asking.

mistakes.mistake: Hearing mostly from the most senior or confident voices.
mistakes.why: Clear, confident explanations sound right, and meetings reward them.
mistakes.instead: Collect written input first, invite quieter groups to speak first, and speak last yourself.

mistakes.mistake: Announcing success and skipping the workload check.
mistakes.why: Leaders need good news, and the main number improved.
mistakes.instead: Report the full result, including who carried extra work, and adjust.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving the change without an owner.
mistakes.why: Once a test works, it feels finished.
mistakes.instead: Name a standing owner and a regular review so the change outlasts the people who built it.

mistakes.mistake: Judging readiness for change by how skilled people say they are.
mistakes.why: Confidence is easy to see and feels like progress. Most people overrate their own intercultural skill, as the orientation course showed.
mistakes.instead: Judge progress by observable changes in the work: who is reached, who speaks and who gets through a process.

jobAid.title: One honest improvement cycle
jobAid.use: Use when you see a barrier in your area and want to lead a change you can show worked.
steps: Write what you can observe about the barrier, and separately what you suspect causes it.
Ask the people affected directly: staff on every shift, people receiving services through the right channels, and partners.
Gather input in writing first; let quieter or lower-status voices speak first; speak last.
Name the owner who has authority, and the person or area responsible for anything outside your authority.
Write a small test: what you will change, for whom, for how long, and what you predict.
Check process data, not people, weekly or more often. Include a workload check.
Write one if-then plan: when this happens, I will do that.
Report back honestly, then keep, change or stop, and run the next cycle.

media.reason: The capstone is about turning knowledge into change. A newer leader and an experienced one show how that thinking is passed on, including the honest limits.

script.speaker: male
script.text: I finished the series, from the orientation through designing services. I see barriers everywhere now. Honestly, it is a little discouraging. Most of the rules are not mine to change.

script.speaker: female
script.text: That is a common feeling. Start with one barrier. What can you actually observe, not what you think is causing it?

script.speaker: male
script.text: Openings for acting lead roles in my unit get announced in the morning huddle. Evening staff rarely apply.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Good. That is an observation. Do you know why they rarely apply?

script.speaker: male
script.text: I assumed they were not interested. But the curiosity course made me doubt that.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Right. Research on perspective taking found that imagining someone's view does not make you more accurate. Asking does. So ask them, and make it easy to answer in writing.

script.speaker: male
script.text: My first instinct was to ask for a training for the day-shift leads about fairness.

script.speaker: female
script.text: I understand. But a field experiment found a one-off training changed attitudes without changing behavior for the people it most needed to reach. Studies of employers found that naming someone responsible did more. Who owns how openings are announced?

script.speaker: male
script.text: Me, actually. The selection rules belong to human resources, but how my unit announces openings is mine.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Then you have a test. For the next two openings, announce on both shifts and in writing. Predict what will happen. Track how many people on each shift saw the notice in time.

script.speaker: male
script.text: And if it is mixed? Say more evening staff apply but they still are not selected?

script.speaker: female
script.text: Then you report exactly that. You ask why, and you bring the evidence to the person or area responsible for selection. Most published improvement projects stop after one try. Do not.

script.speaker: male
script.text: So the series gave me the knowledge. The change comes from a named owner, a small test and honest follow-up.

script.speaker: female
script.text: Exactly. And when a newer leader tells you they cannot change the rule, you will know what to ask them.

prompts: What one barrier in your area will you test, and what can you observe about it today, separate from what you suspect?
With whom will you check your understanding first, including anyone whose voice rarely reaches decisions, and by when?
What is your first small test, who owns it, and on what date will you review the data and report back?
